stem: A 6-month-old, previously well male is brought to a metropolitan emergency department in late winter with 3 days of coryza and cough, now feeding about 60% of his usual volumes. He is alert and consolable in his mother's arms. On examination he has nasal flaring, tracheal tug, and mild subcostal recession. Bilateral fine inspiratory crackles and end-expiratory wheeze are audible throughout both lung fields. He has not received any prior treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158/min, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 56/min, SpO2 88% on room air, temperature 37.8°C
data_table.Examination: Alert, consolable; nasal flaring, tracheal tug, mild subcostal recession; bilateral crackles and wheeze; perfusion warm
data_table.Investigations: CXR not performed; viral PCR pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial respiratory support?

options.text: Heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min as the initial form of respiratory support.
options.rationale: HFNC is not first-line in Australian practice for bronchiolitis: low-flow should be tried first and HFNC reserved for low-flow failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min titrated to maintain SpO2 at or above 90 percent.
options.rationale: Low-flow nasal prong oxygen is first-line for hypoxic bronchiolitis with SpO2 below 90%, with HFNC reserved for failure after 2 hours of low-flow. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Continuous positive airway pressure via a tight-fitting mask set initially at 7 cmH2O of pressure.
options.rationale: CPAP is escalation after HFNC failure or for impending respiratory failure, not first-line support in a consolable infant. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg via face mask repeated every 20 minutes for three doses.
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended for bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months and do not change the disease course. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nebulised hypertonic 3 percent saline given with nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000.
options.rationale: Routine nebulised hypertonic saline and adrenaline are not recommended for typical bronchiolitis outside research protocols in Australia. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months is supportive: minimal handling, careful feeding, and oxygen only when SpO2 falls below 90% on room air. The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG specifies low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min as the initial mode, with HFNC reserved for failure of low-flow after 2 hours. The 90% threshold is deliberately lower than the 92 to 94% used in some international guidelines, reflecting Australian evidence that higher targets prolong admission without benefit.
key_points: RCH SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is 90%, not 92 to 94%.
Low-flow nasal prongs at 1 to 2 L/min are first-line; HFNC is second-line.
Salbutamol, adrenaline, hypertonic saline, and steroids are not recommended in typical bronchiolitis under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: If SpO2 sits at 89 to 90% on room air in an otherwise stable, feeding infant, observe closely without oxygen first; oxygen only when SpO2 drops below 90% and stays there.

stem: A 2-year-old girl, weighed in clinic last week at 14 kg, has been brought into the emergency department 12 minutes after biting into a cashew biscuit at a family gathering. She is now floppy in her father's arms. Spreading urticaria covers her face and trunk and her lips are swollen. Brassy inspiratory stridor and audible wheeze are heard at the bedside. She has no prior cardiorespiratory disease and no documented allergy history. Intravenous access has been attempted once unsuccessfully.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 175/min, blood pressure 75/45 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Floppy but rousable; widespread urticaria, lip swelling, stridor, wheeze; capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.8 mmol/L; tryptase to send after stabilisation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate adrenaline dose and route to give first?

options.text: Adrenaline 300 micrograms intramuscularly into the deltoid muscle of the right upper arm.
options.rationale: 300 mcg is the ASCIA dose for children over 20 kg, and deltoid is not the recommended IM site for paediatric anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Adrenaline 140 micrograms calculated as 10 mcg/kg intramuscularly into the lateral thigh.
options.rationale: ASCIA uses banded weight-based dosing for IM adrenaline rather than mg/kg arithmetic to avoid calculation errors in a crisis. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Adrenaline 150 micrograms intramuscularly into the anterolateral mid-thigh muscle.
options.rationale: ASCIA bands by weight: 10 to 20 kg receives 150 mcg IM into the anterolateral thigh as first dose. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Adrenaline 14 micrograms (1 mcg/kg) intravenously after gaining rapid intraosseous access.
options.rationale: IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis with cardiac monitoring and experienced staff; IM is the first dose. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 via nebuliser to manage the stridor while obtaining IV access.
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline can help upper airway oedema as an adjunct but does not replace IM adrenaline as first-line treatment. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

explanation.summary: ASCIA bands IM adrenaline dosing by approximate weight to remove arithmetic errors during an acute event. A child of 10 to 20 kg gets 150 mcg IM (the EpiPen Jr equivalent dose), 20 kg and above gets 300 mcg, and 50 kg and above gets 500 mcg. The IM site is the anterolateral mid-thigh, which delivers reliable absorption even in shock. IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory cases under monitoring.
key_points: 10 to 20 kg = 150 mcg IM adrenaline.
Anterolateral mid-thigh is the only recommended IM site in paediatric anaphylaxis.
Repeat IM adrenaline every 5 minutes until clinical response or commencement of adrenaline infusion.
explanation.pearls: If you cannot recall the band, an EpiPen Jr 150 mcg auto-injector is the right device for any child clearly in the 10 to 20 kg range; deploy it and call for help.

stem: A 4-day-old term male (born at 40+2 weeks, birth weight 3.4 kg) is brought to the general practice for review because his mother thinks he is more yellow than yesterday. He is exclusively breastfed, latching well, with about 6 heavy wet nappies per day and yellow seedy stool. He is alert and not floppy. Jaundice is visible to his chest but not below the umbilicus. Maternal blood group is O Rh-positive; baby cord blood direct antiglobulin test was negative. He has no risk factors for severe hyperbilirubinaemia. Total serum bilirubin at 96 hours is 305 micromol/L with a direct fraction of 8 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138/min, respiratory rate 42/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9°C, weight 3.32 kg (2.4 percent below birth weight)
data_table.Examination: Alert; jaundice extends to chest but not below umbilicus; no hepatosplenomegaly; tone normal
data_table.Investigations: TSB 305 micromol/L; direct 8 micromol/L; phototherapy threshold for this risk profile at 96 hours is 350 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy in hospital and recheck the bilirubin level after 6 hours.
options.rationale: The TSB is 45 micromol/L below threshold and phototherapy is not yet indicated for this risk band. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours and switch to formula to reduce enterohepatic recirculation.
options.rationale: Routinely stopping breastfeeding is not recommended and there is no evidence the jaundice is breastfeeding failure jaundice here. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin while preparing the team for a double-volume exchange transfusion.
options.rationale: IVIG and exchange transfusion are for proven immune haemolysis or TSB nearing exchange threshold, neither of which apply here. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Continue established breastfeeding, reassure the mother, and repeat the bilirubin in 24 hours.
options.rationale: TSB sits below the phototherapy threshold for a term well infant with no risk factors, so safety-netting with a repeat measurement is appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Send urgent G6PD assay and commence empirical IV ampicillin and gentamicin pending blood cultures.
options.rationale: There are no features of sepsis or haemolysis to justify empirical antibiotics and additional testing at this point. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: A term well infant on day 4 with TSB below the phototherapy threshold on the nomogram, a negative direct antiglobulin test, and adequate weight pattern needs ongoing breastfeeding support and a follow-up bilirubin rather than escalation. Stopping breastfeeding, starting phototherapy, or instituting sepsis treatment are reflexes to avoid when the numbers fit a benign trajectory. Document the threshold used so any repeat is interpreted on the same risk-banded curve.
key_points: Use the risk-banded nomogram to decide phototherapy, not an absolute TSB number.
Term well infants with negative DAT and no risk factors tolerate higher TSB before phototherapy.
Do not stop breastfeeding routinely; address jaundice without disrupting feeding wherever possible.
explanation.pearls: If TSB is within 50 micromol/L of the phototherapy threshold, repeat in 6 to 12 hours rather than 24, because the trajectory matters as much as the absolute number.

stem: A 3-year-old boy weighing 14 kg presents to a regional emergency department with 14 hours of fever and an evolving non-blanching purpuric rash on his trunk and lower limbs. He is rousable but increasingly irritable. He looks mottled with cool peripheries. Two attempts at peripheral intravenous access by experienced staff have failed; an intraosseous kit is open and on the trolley. The on-call paediatric retrieval team has been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 175/min, blood pressure 78/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 42/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 39.8°C
data_table.Examination: Rousable but irritable, capillary refill 5 seconds, mottled skin, spreading purpura on trunk; no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.22, lactate 5.6 mmol/L; bedside glucose 3.4 mmol/L; blood culture bottles primed

lead_in: What is the correct order of the next four interventions over the next 15 minutes?

options.text: Intraosseous access, 20 mL/kg saline bolus, blood cultures, then IV ceftriaxone afterwards.
options.rationale: Giving fluid before cultures and antibiotics delays time-critical antimicrobial therapy in meningococcal shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Intraosseous access, IV ceftriaxone, 20 mL/kg saline bolus, then adrenaline infusion 0.1 mcg/kg/min.
options.rationale: Inotropes should follow at least 40 to 60 mL/kg of fluid resuscitation, not the first 20 mL/kg. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Blood cultures peripherally, then IV ceftriaxone, then 20 mL/kg saline, intraosseous as backup.
options.rationale: Persisting with peripheral access in shocked children wastes minutes; intraosseous access is the next step after two failed attempts. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Saline bolus 20 mL/kg via IO, blood cultures, IV ceftriaxone, then commence noradrenaline infusion.
options.rationale: Cultures should be taken before any antibiotic dose where possible, and noradrenaline is not the first vasoactive in paediatric septic shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Intraosseous access, blood cultures drawn, IV ceftriaxone given, then 20 mL/kg saline bolus.
options.rationale: RCH sepsis pathway: secure IO/IV access, take cultures, give the first IV antibiotic within the hour, then a 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus over 5 to 10 minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

explanation.summary: In suspected meningococcal sepsis, every minute to first IV antibiotic matters. The RCH and ANZICS Paediatric Sepsis Pathway codifies the order as access then cultures then antibiotic then fluid, with the first antibiotic targeted within 60 minutes of recognition. Cultures must precede the antibiotic dose where they can be drawn at the time of access, because a single IO sample preserves diagnostic yield. Fluid resuscitation follows in 20 mL/kg aliquots reassessed for signs of overload before each repeat.
key_points: Sequence: access then cultures then antibiotic then fluid.
Intraosseous access after two failed peripheral attempts.
Fluid in 20 mL/kg aliquots up to 60 mL/kg, then escalate to inotropes.
explanation.pearls: If the IO sample volume is limited, prioritise blood culture bottles before VBG and other point-of-care tests, then push the antibiotic through the same IO.

stem:
A 9-year-old girl weighing 28 kg is in the paediatric high-dependency unit at hour 6 of a new-presentation diabetic ketoacidosis pathway. She received a 10 mL/kg saline bolus on arrival and is now on maintenance 0.9% saline with potassium and an insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hr. Initial pH was 6.92 with glucose 38 mmol/L and ketones 5.8 mmol/L; current glucose is 19 mmol/L. Over the last 30 minutes her mother says she became hard to rouse and complained of a headache.

On re-examination she opens her eyes to voice, says inappropriate words, and localises to pain. Her left pupil is 5 mm and sluggish; the right is 3 mm and reactive. The bedside nurse has just rechecked her observations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70/min (down from 120/min an hour ago), blood pressure 138/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5); left pupil 5 mm sluggish, right pupil 3 mm reactive; chest clear; perfusion adequate
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.12; glucose 19 mmol/L; sodium 138, potassium 3.6, ketones 4.2 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: 0.9% saline 75 mL/hr with KCl 40 mmol/L; insulin infusion 0.05 units/kg/hr

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Give 3 percent hypertonic saline 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes and reduce maintenance fluid rate by one third.
options.rationale: Acute cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA is treated empirically with hypertonic saline or mannitol plus a fluid rate reduction, without waiting for imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

options.text: Intubate and hyperventilate to PaCO2 25 mmHg until a CT brain has confirmed cerebral oedema.
options.rationale: Aggressive hyperventilation below PaCO2 30 mmHg worsens cerebral perfusion and outcomes in DKA-related cerebral oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

options.text: Give mannitol 1 g/kg intravenously over 10 minutes and continue current fluid and insulin rates.
options.rationale: Mannitol is an acceptable alternative osmotherapy, but the maintenance fluid rate must also be reduced by about one third when treating cerebral oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

options.text: Stop the insulin infusion, give 2 mL/kg of 10 percent dextrose intravenously, and recheck the glucose level.
options.rationale: Glucose is 19 mmol/L, not hypoglycaemic, and the deterioration is neurological rather than glycaemic. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus while arranging an urgent CT brain to exclude haemorrhage.
options.rationale: Additional fluid boluses worsen cerebral oedema, and imaging must not delay osmotherapy when classical signs are present. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema typically presents 4 to 12 hours into DKA treatment with headache, declining conscious state, bradycardia with hypertension (Cushing response), and pupil changes. Australian and ISPAD practice favours 3% hypertonic saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes as the preferred hyperosmolar therapy, paired with a reduction in maintenance fluid rate by about one third. Treatment is empirical at the bedside; CT confirms the diagnosis but must not delay therapy. Hyperventilation below PaCO2 30 mmHg is associated with worse outcomes.
key_points: Bradycardia with hypertension and altered consciousness in DKA equals cerebral oedema until proven otherwise.
3 percent saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes is preferred AU osmotherapy.
Reduce maintenance fluid rate by approximately one third when treating cerebral oedema.
explanation.pearls: Treat the moment the constellation appears: every additional fluid bolus or hour of normal-rate maintenance worsens midline shift before imaging confirms it.

stem:
A 5-week-old first-born male presents with a 6-day history of vomiting that started as small post-feed possets and has become forceful after every feed over the last 48 hours. His mother describes the vomit as just looking like milk. He has been feeding hungrily between vomits. Today she noted his nappies are noticeably less wet. On a test feed in ED, a 1.5 cm firm mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant of his abdomen.

Blood results are now back from the ED point-of-care analyser and he is awaiting a paediatric surgical opinion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 165/min, blood pressure 78/45 mmHg, respiratory rate 38/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Sunken anterior fontanelle, dry mucous membranes; abdomen soft with palpable RUQ mass during test feed; visible gastric peristalsis
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 134 mmol/L; potassium 3.0 mmol/L; chloride 90 mmol/L; bicarbonate 32 mmol/L; pH 7.51; glucose 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Proceed directly to pyloromyotomy after a single 20 mL/kg saline bolus is delivered in the emergency department.
options.rationale: Operating on an alkalotic, hypokalaemic infant risks postoperative apnoea and is the anti-pattern to recognise. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Trial a three day course of oral erythromycin ethylsuccinate 12.5 mg/kg given four times daily.
options.rationale: Erythromycin is used in some non-Australian centres for early prokinetic effect but is not the AU first-line and risks pyloric stenosis itself in young infants. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Commence 0.9 percent saline with added potassium and refer the infant for definitive surgical repair.
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis is medical first then surgical: correct the hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis before pyloromyotomy. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Recommend thickened feeds with ranitidine 1 mg/kg given three times daily and outpatient review next week.
options.rationale: Thickened feeds and acid suppression treat gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, which does not produce a palpable pyloric mass and biochemical alkalosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Arrange an upper gastrointestinal contrast study before any fluid resuscitation to confirm the diagnosis.
options.rationale: When a pyloric mass is palpable on test feed and biochemistry fits, imaging is for confirmation but must not delay fluid and electrolyte correction. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

explanation.summary: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically gives projectile non-bilious vomiting between weeks 3 and 8, a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from gastric losses, and a palpable olive in the right upper quadrant. Surgery is curative but must be deferred until chloride is at least 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate is below 28 mmol/L, and potassium has been replaced, because alkalosis predisposes to postoperative central apnoea. Initial management is 0.9% saline with potassium at 1.5 to 2 times maintenance for rehydration.
key_points: Treat the alkalosis before the operation: Cl above 100, HCO3 below 28, K corrected.
0.9 percent saline with KCl is the resuscitation fluid of choice.
Persistent alkalosis predisposes to postoperative apnoea.
explanation.pearls: If chloride is below 90 mmol/L on arrival, expect 24 to 48 hours of fluid correction before anaesthesia is safe; book theatre but resist pressure to operate early.

stem:
An 8-day-old, previously well term breastfed male becomes acutely unwell at home with three vomits in the last 4 hours that his mother describes as bright green. He has not had a wet nappy in the last 6 hours and has not opened his bowels today. On arrival to the emergency department he is mottled, sleepy but rousable, and grunting intermittently. His abdomen is soft but slightly distended with reduced bowel sounds and no palpable mass.

Intravenous access has been secured and bloods are being processed; the surgical registrar has been paged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 180/min, blood pressure 65/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 50/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.4°C
data_table.Examination: Mottled, sleepy but rousable; capillary refill 4 seconds; abdomen soft, slightly distended; no palpable mass or hernia
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.27, lactate 3.8 mmol/L; bedside glucose 3.6 mmol/L; bloods pending

lead_in: After initial resuscitation, what is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Erect abdominal radiograph plus a left lateral decubitus film to look for free intra-abdominal air.
options.rationale: A normal AXR does not exclude malrotation with midgut volvulus and free air implies perforation, which is a late finding. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal bilious vomiting)

options.text: Ultrasound of the abdomen looking for the target sign of an ileocolic intussusception.
options.rationale: Intussusception classically presents between 3 and 12 months of age and is rare in the first 2 weeks of life. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Stool culture with rotavirus PCR together with rehydration and observation in the short stay unit.
options.rationale: Gastroenteritis does not typically cause bilious vomiting in a previously well neonate, and observation risks bowel infarction. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal bilious vomiting)

options.text: Upper gastrointestinal contrast study after a 10 mL/kg saline bolus and ongoing maintenance fluid.
options.rationale: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with volvulus until disproved, and upper GI contrast is the diagnostic test of choice. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal bilious vomiting)

options.text: Per rectal contrast enema to look for meconium ileus or another distal bowel obstruction.
options.rationale: Contrast enema evaluates distal obstruction but does not show malrotation, the most time-critical diagnosis here. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal bilious vomiting)

explanation.summary: Bile-stained vomiting in any neonate carries malrotation with midgut volvulus on the differential until imaging excludes it, because untreated volvulus leads to bowel ischaemia within hours. Upper gastrointestinal contrast study is the first-line investigation, looking for an abnormal duodenojejunal flexure position to the right of the midline or a corkscrew appearance. Resuscitation, nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, and urgent paediatric surgical involvement precede or run alongside imaging.
key_points: Bilious vomit equals malrotation until proven otherwise.
Upper GI contrast is the diagnostic test of choice.
Resuscitate and call surgery before imaging delays definitive care.
explanation.pearls: If the upper GI cannot be obtained within an hour at your site, transfer arrangements to a paediatric surgical centre must start immediately rather than waiting for imaging.

stem:
A 4-year-old previously well boy is on day 6 of a fluctuating fever that peaks at 39.8°C and is poorly responsive to paracetamol. His parents describe his eyes as red without any discharge for three days, a strawberry tongue from day 4, a polymorphous truncal rash since day 4, and recently noted redness and swelling of his hands. He has a single 1.8 cm tender anterior cervical lymph node on the right. There are no oral vesicles. He has had no contact with anyone known to have COVID-19; nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 PCR returned negative this morning.

A blood panel and echocardiogram have just been completed by the cardiology fellow.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 140/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.2°C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, polymorphous truncal rash, swollen erythematous hands, single 1.8 cm right cervical node; no oral vesicles
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.5 x10^9/L; CRP 165 mg/L; ESR 78 mm/hr; platelets 480 x10^9/L; Hb 95 g/L (110-140); ALT 90 U/L; albumin 28 g/L (35-50); sodium 131 mmol/L; urine 30 leukocytes per HPF, no organisms; echocardiogram shows LMCA z-score +2.1, RCA z-score +2.4, small pericardial effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg IV daily for three days, withholding IVIG until day 10 of fever.
options.rationale: Steroid monotherapy is not first-line in Australian practice and IVIG should not be delayed when criteria are met. (Source: AHA Kawasaki disease statement)

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg plus IV vancomycin 15 mg/kg pending blood culture results overnight.
options.rationale: Empirical sepsis treatment alone misses the IVIG window and does not address coronary inflammation. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Anakinra 2 mg/kg/day given subcutaneously as monotherapy because the criteria are only partial.
options.rationale: Anakinra is reserved for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease, not initial therapy. (Source: AHA Kawasaki disease statement)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily plus aspirin 5 mg/kg daily as antiplatelet cover.
options.rationale: Low-dose aspirin with prednisolone alone fails to address acute coronary inflammation and is insufficient initial therapy. (Source: AHA Kawasaki disease statement)

options.text: IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg infused over 12 hours plus oral aspirin 30 mg/kg/day in four divided doses.
options.rationale: Incomplete Kawasaki criteria are met with persistent fever, three principal features, supportive labs, and coronary z-scores at or above 2.0, mandating IVIG plus high-dose aspirin. (Source: AHA Kawasaki disease statement)

explanation.summary: This child meets incomplete Kawasaki criteria: fever for at least 5 days with three of five principal clinical features and supplementary laboratory findings (anaemia for age, albumin below 30 g/L, ALT elevation, platelets above 450, WCC above 15, sterile pyuria, sodium below 135) plus coronary z-scores at or above 2.0 to 2.5. A negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR with classic Kawasaki phenotype argues against multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children. Treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg with high-dose aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg/day divided four-hourly until afebrile 48 hours, then 3 to 5 mg/kg daily for at least 6 weeks.
key_points: Coronary z-score at or above 2.0 with three principal features supports incomplete KD.
IVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin remains first-line in Australian practice.
IVIG resistance defined by persistent fever 36 hours post-infusion triggers a second IVIG dose or anakinra.
explanation.pearls: Hyponatraemia and a sterile pyuria are easily missed supplementary criteria that tilt a fever-of-unknown-origin towards incomplete Kawasaki when the principal features are partial.

stem: A four-month-old has been on humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 0.40 for four hours for RSV bronchiolitis. Mother says he breastfed only briefly before tiring. On examination there is marked substernal recession, head bob, and audible grunting. Capillary blood gas: pH 7.28, pCO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation with no focal consolidation. The paediatric retrieval team has been contacted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178, BP 78/45 mmHg, RR 68, SpO2 89%, temperature 37.9°C
data_table.Examination: Substernal recession, head bob, grunting, lethargic but rousable
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.28, pCO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L; chest X-ray hyperinflated, no focal consolidation
data_table.Medications: Humidified HFNC 2 L/kg/min, FiO2 0.40 for 4 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Initiate CPAP at 6 cm H2O via retrieval team prior to PICU transfer
options.rationale: Rising pCO2 with persistent severe work of breathing on the maximal RCH HFNC ceiling defines HFNC failure. CPAP is the next non-invasive escalation, started during retrieval and continued in PICU. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Endotracheal intubation and conventional ventilation immediately
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for apnoea, exhaustion, or CPAP failure. With lactate 1.4 mmol/L and no shock, a CPAP trial precedes intubation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Increase HFNC flow to 3 L/kg/min and reassess after one hour
options.rationale: RCH ceiling for HFNC in bronchiolitis is 2 L/kg/min. Further flow does not improve outcomes and delays appropriate escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with hypertonic saline 3% nebuliser
options.rationale: Salbutamol and hypertonic saline are not recommended for routine bronchiolitis under 12 months in Australia and do not reverse respiratory failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg empirically for bacterial co-infection
options.rationale: Bacterial co-infection is uncommon in bronchiolitis. With a clear viral cause and no focal X-ray finding, empirical antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: This infant meets HFNC-failure criteria: persistent severe work of breathing with rising pCO2 (58 mmHg) and SpO2 below the RCH target of 90% on maximal flow. The correct response is non-invasive escalation to CPAP, ideally during PICU retrieval. Intubation is held back for apnoea, GCS drop, or CPAP failure. Increasing HFNC above 2 L/kg/min has no evidence base and delays appropriate escalation.
key_points: RCH bronchiolitis HFNC ceiling is 2 L/kg/min
HFNC failure criteria: persistent severe WOB, rising pCO2, SpO2 below 90% target
CPAP precedes intubation when no apnoea or shock
explanation.pearls: If pCO2 rises above 55 mmHg on maximal HFNC, escalate non-invasively within 30 minutes; intubate for apnoea or GCS drop, not for the gas number alone.

stem: A five-week-old boy presents with two weeks of forceful non-bilious vomiting after every feed. Mother describes the vomiting as 'shooting across the cot'. He looks sunken-eyed and his nappies have been very dry. Ultrasound shows pyloric muscle thickness 4.5 mm and channel length 18 mm. Surgical team plans pyloromyotomy. Venous gas: pH 7.52, pCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 36 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 2.9 mmol/L, chloride 88 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 82/48 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Sunken anterior fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, weight 3.8 kg (was 4.4 kg)
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.52, pCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 36 mmol/L, Na 132, K 2.9, Cl 88 mmol/L; ultrasound pylorus 4.5 mm thick, channel 18 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Resuscitate with 0.45% saline plus 5% dextrose plus 20 mmol/L KCl
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid worsens the hyponatraemia and is contraindicated for paediatric resuscitation in Australia. (Source: ANZICS paediatric fluid statement 2020)

options.text: Correct alkalosis and electrolytes with 0.9% saline plus 20 mmol/L KCl before theatre
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis with hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis requires correction (Cl above 100 mmol/L, HCO3 below 28 mmol/L, K above 3.5 mmol/L) before anaesthesia. Isotonic saline with added potassium is the RCH standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Proceed directly to pyloromyotomy after one 20 mL/kg saline bolus
options.rationale: Anaesthetic apnoea is prolonged by uncorrected metabolic alkalosis. Surgery is delayed until biochemistry is corrected. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Start IV omeprazole and nasogastric feeding to bypass the pylorus
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis is mechanical; acid suppression and NG feeding do not address obstruction. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Give 4% albumin 20 mL/kg bolus then transfer urgently for theatre
options.rationale: Colloid is not first-line; isotonic crystalloid with potassium addresses the specific alkalosis. (Source: ANZICS paediatric fluid statement 2020)

explanation.summary: Infantile pyloric stenosis produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from prolonged vomiting of gastric HCl. Anaesthesia before correction risks prolonged apnoea and arrhythmia. RCH targets chloride above 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate below 28 mmol/L, potassium above 3.5 mmol/L, and adequate urine output before theatre. Isotonic saline with added potassium achieves all three; hypotonic fluid worsens the hyponatraemia.
key_points: Resuscitation targets: Cl above 100, HCO3 below 28, K above 3.5 mmol/L
0.9% saline plus 20 mmol/L KCl is RCH standard
Hypotonic maintenance fluid is contraindicated in paediatric resuscitation
explanation.pearls: Surgery for pyloric stenosis is never an emergency; biochemistry first, scalpel second.

stem: An eight-year-old known asthmatic presents with worsening dyspnoea over six hours. He has had three back-to-back salbutamol nebulisers with ipratropium and oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg in ED. Forty minutes after the third nebuliser he still has marked subcostal recession, a silent left lower zone, and is speaking in single words. Pulse rate 140, blood pressure 102/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 36, SpO2 91% on 6 L/min via Hudson mask, temperature 36.9°C. Peak flow cannot be obtained. Venous gas: pH 7.32, pCO2 46 mmHg, HCO3 23 mmol/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140, BP 102/68 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 91% on 6 L Hudson, temperature 36.9°C
data_table.Examination: Speaks single words, marked recession, silent LLZ
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.32, pCO2 46 mmHg, HCO3 23 mmol/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Salbutamol 5 mg nebs x3 with ipratropium 250 mcg x3; prednisolone 2 mg/kg PO

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continuous salbutamol nebulisation at 0.5 mg/kg/hour for 60 minutes
options.rationale: He has had maximal intermittent nebulisation without response and tachycardia plus lactate above 3 mmol/L indicate beta-agonist toxicity. Further salbutamol without IV magnesium is unlikely to help. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: IV aminophylline 5 mg/kg loading over 20 minutes then infusion
options.rationale: Aminophylline is third-line after IV magnesium has failed and carries arrhythmia and seizure risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Failure to respond to maximal first-line bronchodilator and steroid in severe asthma is the trigger for IV magnesium. RCH dose is 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg as he has had only oral steroid
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone is equivalent to IV hydrocortisone for asthma; switching does not bridge ongoing bronchospasm. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Intubate and ventilate with ketamine induction in resus bay
options.rationale: Intubation in severe asthma is high-risk and reserved for arrest, exhaustion, or persistent hypoxia despite second-line therapy. IV magnesium precedes it. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

explanation.summary: Failure to respond to three back-to-back salbutamol-ipratropium nebulisers plus systemic steroid in a child with severe asthma triggers IV magnesium sulfate. RCH dose is 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring. Aminophylline is third-line. Intubation is reserved for exhaustion, arrest, or persistent hypoxia despite second-line therapy.
key_points: IV magnesium 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes is RCH second-line in severe asthma
Steroid route does not matter for asthma; PO equals IV
Lactate above 3 mmol/L in salbutamol-treated asthma usually reflects beta-agonist effect, not sepsis
explanation.pearls: If the child is still working hard 30 to 60 minutes after the third bronchodilator burst, give IV magnesium - do not keep nebulising in hope.

stem: A nine-week-old presents to ED with father who reports the baby 'rolled off the change table' onto carpet 90 minutes ago. The baby has not yet rolled developmentally and was 'a bit floppy' afterwards but is now feeding. Examination shows a torn upper lip frenulum, a 2 cm boggy left parietal swelling, and three small round bruises on the left cheek and right upper arm. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral pre-retinal haemorrhages. CT brain shows a thin left subdural haematoma and an associated parietal skull fracture. The father is distressed and asks to leave with the baby to return tomorrow.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158, BP 78/46 mmHg, RR 42, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Torn upper lip frenulum, left parietal boggy swelling 2 cm, three small round bruises (cheek and right upper arm), AF soft and flat
data_table.Investigations: CT brain: thin left subdural haematoma plus parietal skull fracture; bilateral pre-retinal haemorrhages on fundoscopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Discharge home with parents after social work phone follow-up tomorrow
options.rationale: The injury pattern is medically inconsistent with the history and meets mandatory reporting thresholds for serious physical abuse. Discharging is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Arrange outpatient MRI brain and request a coagulation screen as priority
options.rationale: Coagulation screen is appropriate but secondary; the immediate priority is protective admission and statutory notification, not outpatient imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Allow father to leave with the baby pending paediatric review next week
options.rationale: Allowing return with the carer leaves the infant at risk. Admission and statutory notification are mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Admit, notify child protection services, and complete a skeletal survey
options.rationale: Bruising in a pre-mobile infant, torn frenulum, subdural with fracture, and retinal haemorrhages are sentinel injuries. Mandatory reporting, admission for safety, and skeletal survey within 24 hours are the RCH protocol. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Order a metabolic bone disease workup to exclude osteogenesis imperfecta
options.rationale: Differentials are pursued in parallel with protection, not instead of it. Statutory notification cannot wait for metabolic results. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Bruising in a pre-mobile infant, torn frenulum, subdural haematoma with skull fracture from a low-fall history, and bilateral retinal haemorrhages each independently meet sentinel-injury criteria. Mandatory reporting to child protection services, protective admission, and a skeletal survey within 24 hours are all required. Differential workup (coagulation, metabolic bone disease) proceeds in parallel, not instead. The carer is not given the choice to leave.
key_points: Any bruise in a pre-mobile infant warrants child protection consideration
Sentinel injuries: torn frenulum, retinal haemorrhages, posterior rib or metaphyseal fractures
Skeletal survey within 24 hours per RCH protocol
explanation.pearls: If a story does not match physiology (90-minute-old fall but baby cannot yet roll), believe the injuries, not the history.

sources.label: Victorian Children Youth and Families Act 2005

stem: A previously well 19-month-old has a single 90-second generalised tonic-clonic seizure during a febrile URTI. By the time you assess her she is alert, interactive, and feeding normally. She has no focal neurological signs and her anterior fontanelle is closed. Her older brother had two febrile seizures at two years of age. There is no family history of epilepsy. The mother asks whether her daughter needs admission, anti-seizure medication, or imaging.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 99%, temperature 39.1°C
data_table.Examination: Alert, no neck stiffness, no rash, ENT mildly inflamed tympanic membranes bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition and counselling?

options.text: Admit overnight and start prophylactic oral diazepam for the next febrile illness
options.rationale: Prophylactic benzodiazepines for febrile seizures are not recommended; recurrence does not predict epilepsy. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

options.text: Arrange outpatient EEG and brain MRI before allowing return home
options.rationale: EEG and imaging are not indicated for a simple febrile seizure with normal neurology. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

options.text: Admit for 24 hours of paracetamol every 4 hours to prevent further fever spikes
options.rationale: Regular antipyretics do not reduce recurrence and admission is not required for a simple febrile seizure. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture before any decision is taken on disposition
options.rationale: LP is not routine in a well child over 12 months without meningism, prolonged post-ictal state, or sepsis features. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

options.text: Discharge with parental advice on first aid and risk of one-in-three recurrence
options.rationale: Simple febrile seizure with a normal post-ictal child and no red flags is managed by discharge with first-aid education and accurate recurrence quotation (around 30%). (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

explanation.summary: A simple febrile seizure is generalised, lasts under 15 minutes, does not recur within 24 hours, and occurs in a 6-month to 5-year-old with no focal deficit. Imaging, EEG, and admission are not indicated when the child is well post-ictally and no sepsis or meningitis features are present. Parents are counselled on first aid, the roughly one-in-three recurrence risk, and the small absolute increase in lifetime epilepsy risk (about 1% above baseline 1%). Antipyretics treat discomfort but do not prevent recurrence.
key_points: Simple febrile seizure: generalised, under 15 minutes, single in 24 hours, age 6 months to 5 years
Recurrence about 30%; lifetime epilepsy risk only about 2% absolute
No imaging, EEG, prophylaxis, or routine LP if child well over 12 months
explanation.pearls: Antipyretics make a hot child feel better; they do not prevent febrile seizures.

stem: A 14-year-old presents with three weeks of fatigue, scleral icterus, and new tremor that the school noticed in handwriting class. She has not been on any new medications and there is no travel or paracetamol exposure. Her mother died of liver failure at 38. On examination she has hepatomegaly, dysarthria, and dark coloured urine. Bloods: haemoglobin 84 g/L (115-155), reticulocytes 6%, bilirubin 78 micromol/L (5-20), ALT 220 U/L (5-40), AST 290 U/L, ALP only 32 U/L (115-300), INR 1.6, ceruloplasmin 0.07 g/L (0.20-0.60), direct antiglobulin test negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 112/64 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Scleral icterus, hepatomegaly 3 cm, dysarthria, intention tremor on finger-nose; Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit lamp
data_table.Investigations: Hb 84 g/L, retics 6%, bilirubin 78 micromol/L, ALT 220 U/L, AST 290 U/L, ALP 32 U/L, INR 1.6, ceruloplasmin 0.07 g/L, DAT negative, 24-hour urinary copper pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Perform 24-hour urinary copper and arrange urgent percutaneous liver biopsy
options.rationale: Low ceruloplasmin, KF rings, Coombs-negative haemolysis, neuropsychiatric signs, and ALP:bilirubin ratio below 4 meet Wilson disease criteria. 24-hour urinary copper plus liver biopsy for hepatic copper quantification confirm diagnosis and guide chelation. (Source: AASLD Wilson disease guidance 2022)

options.text: Send peripheral blood film and direct antiglobulin testing for cold agglutinins
options.rationale: A negative DAT plus very low ALP and dysarthria with KF rings makes immune haemolysis far less likely than Wilson disease. (Source: AASLD Wilson disease guidance 2022)

options.text: Repeat full blood count and reticulocyte count in 72 hours to confirm trend
options.rationale: Watching the trend delays definitive diagnosis and risks fulminant hepatic failure. The clinical picture already strongly suggests Wilson disease. (Source: AASLD Wilson disease guidance 2022)

options.text: Order MRI brain with susceptibility imaging for basal ganglia copper deposits
options.rationale: MRI may show basal ganglia changes but does not establish the diagnosis or guide chelation; biochemical and biopsy confirmation come first. (Source: AASLD Wilson disease guidance 2022)

options.text: Send paracetamol level, alpha-1 antitrypsin, and autoimmune hepatitis panel
options.rationale: These differentials are part of acute liver failure workup but do not explain the Coombs-negative haemolysis and KF rings; Wilson confirmation cannot wait. (Source: AASLD Wilson disease guidance 2022)

explanation.summary: An adolescent with Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia, low alkaline phosphatase relative to a high bilirubin (ALP:bilirubin ratio under 4 strongly supports Wilson), neuropsychiatric tremor, KF rings, and very low ceruloplasmin should be worked up for fulminant Wilsonian crisis. Twenty-four-hour urinary copper above 1.6 micromol/24 hours and hepatic copper above 250 micrograms/g dry weight on biopsy confirm the diagnosis and direct urgent chelation (or transplant referral if INR continues to rise).
key_points: ALP:bilirubin ratio under 4 in acute liver failure suggests Wilson
Coombs-negative haemolysis plus liver failure should prompt copper workup
Ceruloplasmin below 0.10 g/L plus KF rings has high specificity in adolescents
explanation.pearls: In an adolescent with liver failure and a tremor, always order ceruloplasmin and slit-lamp examination before settling on autoimmune hepatitis.

stem: A six-year-old boy presents with two days of refusal to weight bear on his right leg following a viral URTI last week. He has had a low-grade fever overnight. He holds the right hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated, and resists log-roll on the right. Pulse rate 116, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99%, temperature 38.7°C. Bloods: WCC 14.5 x10^9/L, CRP 64 mg/L, ESR 48 mm/hr. Ultrasound shows a moderate right hip joint effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99%, temperature 38.7°C
data_table.Examination: Right hip held in flexion, abduction, external rotation; refuses weight bearing; log-roll resisted
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.5 x10^9/L, neutrophils 11.0, CRP 64 mg/L, ESR 48 mm/hr; ultrasound right hip moderate effusion; blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with rest and ibuprofen and review in 48 hours for transient synovitis
options.rationale: All four Kocher predictors are met (fever above 38.5°C, refusal to weight bear, ESR above 40 mm/hr, WCC above 12 x10^9/L), making septic arthritis far more likely than transient synovitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

options.text: Refer for theatre aspiration and washout with IV flucloxacillin after cultures
options.rationale: With all four Kocher predictors met the probability of septic arthritis is around 99%. Urgent joint aspiration plus washout and empirical IV flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg q6h (covering S. aureus and S. pyogenes) is the RCH pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis)

options.text: Arrange MRI hip with contrast before any decision on aspiration is taken
options.rationale: MRI can clarify osteomyelitis but should not delay theatre when Kocher criteria are met. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis)

options.text: Admit for serial examination and repeat inflammatory markers in 24 hours
options.rationale: Delaying joint aspiration risks irreversible cartilage damage in confirmed septic arthritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis)

options.text: Start oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg q6h and arrange outpatient orthopaedic review
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics and outpatient review are inappropriate for likely septic arthritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis)

explanation.summary: Kocher criteria for paediatric septic hip identify four predictors: fever above 38.5°C, non-weight-bearing, ESR above 40 mm/hr, and WCC above 12 x10^9/L. Meeting all four gives roughly 99% probability of septic arthritis. The RCH pathway is urgent theatre for aspiration plus washout and empirical IV flucloxacillin after blood cultures, with cover broadened for at-risk groups (e.g. neonates, immunocompromised, Kingella suspicion). MRI clarifies osteomyelitis but should not delay washout.
key_points: All four Kocher predictors: septic arthritis probability about 99%
Empirical IV flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg q6h covers S. aureus and S. pyogenes
Theatre and aspiration precede MRI when Kocher is positive
explanation.pearls: A child who refuses to weight bear with raised CRP and a hip effusion goes to theatre, not radiology, until septic arthritis is excluded by aspirate.

stem:
A 7-year-old (weight 26 kg) presents with two days of polyuria, weight loss, and vomiting today. Mother reports rapid deep breathing for six hours. He responds to voice and is orientated but mildly drowsy. He has not received any insulin previously. Capillary glucose is 28 mmol/L (3.5-7.8 fasting), venous pH 7.10, HCO3 8 mmol/L (22-32), ketones 5.6 mmol/L. Sodium is 134 mmol/L (135-145) and potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0). He is alert but lethargic with capillary refill 3 seconds and dry mucous membranes. He weighs 26 kg.

The registrar is preparing the first hour of management.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 98/60 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, Kussmaul breathing, capillary refill 3 seconds, dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 28 mmol/L, venous pH 7.10, HCO3 8 mmol/L, ketones 5.6 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-hour fluid plan?

options.text: 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus, then maintenance plus deficit over 48 hours
options.rationale: RCH and ISPAD recommend a cautious 10 mL/kg crystalloid bolus only if shocked, then deficit replacement over 48 hours to reduce cerebral oedema risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

options.text: 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 15 minutes, repeated to 60 mL/kg if needed
options.rationale: Aggressive bolus volumes used in paediatric sepsis are not recommended in DKA; they increase cerebral oedema risk in a child who is not in frank shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

options.text: Commence IV insulin 0.1 unit/kg/hour immediately before any fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Insulin is started one hour after fluids in paediatric DKA to avoid rapid osmotic shifts and cerebral oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

options.text: 8.4% sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 30 minutes to correct acidosis
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA; it worsens intracellular acidosis and increases cerebral oedema risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride 5 mL/kg/hour with no initial bolus and no potassium
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid as initial resuscitation in paediatric DKA risks rapid osmotic shifts and is not the AU initial fluid; isotonic crystalloid is standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA fluid resuscitation differs from sepsis. Initial bolus is restricted to 10 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid, given only if there are objective signs of shock. The estimated deficit (5-7% in moderate DKA) is replaced over 48 hours alongside maintenance to minimise cerebral oedema, which carries a mortality of 20-25% and is the leading cause of paediatric DKA death.
key_points: Initial bolus 10 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid only if shocked
Replace deficit over 48 hours, not 24
Bicarbonate is contraindicated; insulin starts at 1 hour
explanation.pearls: If GCS drops or headache develops, give mannitol 0.5 g/kg or 3% saline 5 mL/kg IV within 5 minutes - do not wait for CT.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: DKA

stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought in because he started coughing and choking suddenly two days ago while eating peanuts. The episode settled within a minute and he resumed playing. Since then his parents have noticed intermittent cough and some breathlessness on running. He has no fever. On auscultation there is reduced air entry over the left lower zone and a localised expiratory wheeze on the left only. Chest X-ray with expiratory phase shows left-sided hyperinflation that does not deflate.

He is comfortable at rest with no stridor.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110, BP 96/62 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 97%, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Reduced left lower zone air entry, localised left expiratory wheeze, no stridor
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray: left-sided hyperinflation persisting on expiratory film, mediastinal shift to the right on expiration

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent rigid bronchoscopy in theatre with paediatric ENT and anaesthetics
options.rationale: Persistent unilateral hyperinflation after a witnessed choking episode is presumed retained airway foreign body; rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthetic is the AU and international standard for retrieval. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

options.text: Trial of inhaled salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer and reassess in one hour
options.rationale: Asymmetric wheeze with a clear aspiration history is foreign body until proven otherwise; bronchodilators delay definitive retrieval. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for five days and review in clinic
options.rationale: Steroids do not dislodge an airway foreign body and risk masking obstructive sequelae or post-obstructive pneumonia. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

options.text: Five back blows then five chest thrusts performed in the emergency department
options.rationale: Back blows and chest thrusts are reserved for an effective cough being lost or complete obstruction; they are contraindicated in a stable partial obstruction. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4: Airway)

options.text: Discharge with safety netting and review in 48 hours by general practice
options.rationale: Retained foreign body causes obstructive pneumonia and bronchiectasis if not removed; delayed retrieval is associated with worse outcomes. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

explanation.summary: A witnessed choking episode in a toddler followed by persistent unilateral findings (localised wheeze, reduced air entry, expiratory hyperinflation on chest X-ray) is foreign body aspiration until proven otherwise. The retained object acts as a ball-valve, trapping air distally on expiration. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthetic is the definitive procedure. A normal X-ray does not exclude foreign body and should not delay bronchoscopy when the history is suggestive.
key_points: Witnessed choking plus unilateral signs equals presumed foreign body
Ball-valve effect causes expiratory hyperinflation, not collapse
Rigid bronchoscopy is the definitive intervention
explanation.pearls: Peanut is the most common AU paediatric airway foreign body and releases an oil that causes lipoid pneumonitis if retained beyond 48 hours.

stem:
A 3-year-old girl was admitted three days ago with confirmed Kawasaki disease (fever for six days, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, right cervical lymphadenopathy 1.8 cm, and peripheral oedema). She received IVIG 2 g/kg over 12 hours plus aspirin 30 mg/kg/day on day 2 of admission. Her fever defervesced within 24 hours of IVIG. Today, 48 hours after the IVIG infusion completed, she has a temperature of 39.1°C, irritability, and recurrence of conjunctivitis. CRP has risen from 35 to 168 mg/L (0-5). The echocardiogram shows normal coronary arteries.

The paediatric cardiology team has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 96/56 mmHg, RR 30, SpO2 98%, temperature 39.1°C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, irritable
data_table.Investigations: CRP 168 mg/L (rose from 35), ESR 78 mm/h, WCC 18.4 x10^9/L, platelets 612 x10^9/L; echocardiogram coronary arteries normal
data_table.Medications: IVIG 2 g/kg completed 48 h ago; aspirin 30 mg/kg/day

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Second IVIG 2 g/kg infusion over 12 hours plus continued aspirin
options.rationale: IVIG resistance is defined as persistent or recurrent fever >=36 h after the first IVIG dose; the AU and AAP standard is a second IVIG 2 g/kg dose. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Disease Statement 2017)

options.text: Switch aspirin to clopidogrel and observe without further immunotherapy
options.rationale: Antiplatelet change does not address the underlying vasculitis; IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease requires further immunomodulation. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Disease Statement 2017)

options.text: Initiate infliximab 5 mg/kg as first-line second therapy
options.rationale: Infliximab is an option for second IVIG resistance; AU and AHA pathways use a second IVIG dose before TNF-alpha inhibition. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Disease Statement 2017)

options.text: Empiric IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg for occult bacterial co-infection
options.rationale: Recurrence of fever with a rising CRP after IVIG response is the defining pattern of IVIG resistance, not occult bacterial infection. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Disease Statement 2017)

options.text: Cease aspirin and start oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day monotherapy
options.rationale: Steroid monotherapy without further IVIG is not the AU pathway for IVIG resistance; corticosteroids are adjunctive, often with the second IVIG. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Disease Statement 2017)

explanation.summary: IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease is defined as persistent or recurrent fever 36 hours or more after the first IVIG dose, occurring in approximately 10-20% of children. The standard second-line treatment in Australian paediatric centres is a second 2 g/kg IVIG infusion. High-risk patients (coronary changes, age under 12 months, persistent inflammatory markers) may receive adjunctive methylprednisolone or infliximab. Aspirin is continued throughout.
key_points: IVIG resistance: fever recurrence at 36 h+ post-first dose
Second IVIG 2 g/kg is the AU first second-line
Infliximab and pulse steroids are third-line
explanation.pearls: Kobayashi score predicts IVIG resistance; a score of 5 or more identifies high-risk patients who benefit from steroid plus IVIG up-front.

stem:
A 14-month-old boy presents with eight hours of intermittent episodes where he suddenly starts crying, draws his legs up, and then settles. He has vomited twice but is not bilious. His mother saw dark red jelly-like material in his nappy this morning. On examination he is pale, mottled, with capillary refill 4 seconds and a palpable long thin lump in his right upper tummy. Ultrasound confirms an ileocolic target sign. Venous lactate is 4.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.0) and pH 7.31.

IV access has been obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 78/42 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.4°C
data_table.Examination: Pale, mottled, capillary refill 4 seconds, palpable right upper quadrant mass, dark red jelly stool
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: ileocolic target sign; lactate 4.2 mmol/L; pH 7.31

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus and urgent surgical reduction in theatre
options.rationale: Shock and acidosis are contraindications to air enema; resuscitation precedes surgical reduction by paediatric surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Proceed directly to air enema reduction under fluoroscopy
options.rationale: Air enema is contraindicated in shock or peritonitis; perforation rates rise sharply and surgical access is delayed. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Trial of oral rehydration with frequent small volumes and observe four hours
options.rationale: Shocked patient with peripheral mottling and rising lactate needs IV resuscitation, not oral rehydration. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Insert nasogastric tube and admit for serial abdominal examinations
options.rationale: Observation alone misses ongoing bowel ischaemia in a shocked child with confirmed intussusception; surgical reduction is needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Glycerol suppository to assist spontaneous reduction with bowel evacuation
options.rationale: Glycerol does not reduce intussusception and delays definitive management. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Stable intussusception with no peritonitis, no shock, and a typical ileocolic ultrasound is reduced by air enema (success ~85% within 24 hours of symptom onset). Shock, peritonitis, free air on imaging, or persistent failure of air enema are indications for surgical reduction. This child is shocked with rising lactate; resuscitation and theatre are needed without delay. Recurrence after air enema occurs in approximately 10%.
key_points: Air enema reduction is first-line in stable intussusception
Shock and peritonitis are contraindications to enema reduction
Surgical reduction follows resuscitation in unstable patients
explanation.pearls: A pathological lead point (Meckel diverticulum, lymphoma, polyp) is found in <5% under 2 years but increases with age above 2; consider in atypical or recurrent cases.

subtopic_detail: ALL presentation with tumour lysis prevention
stem:
A 5-year-old presents with three weeks of fatigue, bruising, and bilateral knee pain. His mother noted pallor. On examination he has petechiae, hepatomegaly 3 cm and splenomegaly 4 cm below the costal margin. The full blood count shows haemoglobin 64 g/L (115-155), white cells 96 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0) with 84% blasts on film, and platelets 24 x10^9/L (150-450). Urate is 0.62 mmol/L (0.20-0.42), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), phosphate 2.1 mmol/L (1.2-1.8), and creatinine 56 micromol/L (30-50). Lactate dehydrogenase is 4800 U/L.

The paediatric haematology team is en route.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 99%, temperature 37.5°C
data_table.Examination: Pallor, petechiae, hepatomegaly 3 cm, splenomegaly 4 cm
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 64 g/L, white cells 96 x10^9/L (84% blasts), platelets 24 x10^9/L, urate 0.62 mmol/L, potassium 5.4 mmol/L, phosphate 2.1 mmol/L, creatinine 56 micromol/L, LDH 4800 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line tumour lysis prevention?

options.text: IV hyperhydration 3 L/m^2/day without potassium and rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg
options.rationale: High-risk tumour lysis (WCC >100, blasts, urate >0.48 mmol/L) requires hyperhydration with potassium-free fluid plus rasburicase, not allopurinol. (Source: COG Tumour Lysis Syndrome guideline)

options.text: Allopurinol 10 mg/kg/day orally with normal maintenance fluids
options.rationale: Allopurinol prevents new urate formation but does not lower existing urate; high-risk patients need rasburicase plus hyperhydration. (Source: COG Tumour Lysis Syndrome guideline)

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate infusion targeting urine pH 7.5 plus allopurinol
options.rationale: Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended; it promotes calcium phosphate precipitation as phosphate rises. (Source: COG Tumour Lysis Syndrome guideline)

options.text: Furosemide 1 mg/kg IV every 6 hours to force diuresis with normal saline
options.rationale: Loop diuretics are reserved for fluid overload; routine forced diuresis is not part of tumour lysis prevention. (Source: COG Tumour Lysis Syndrome guideline)

options.text: Withhold all fluids and chemotherapy until urate normalises spontaneously
options.rationale: Spontaneous tumour lysis is already occurring with rising urate and LDH; delay of fluids and rasburicase worsens AKI risk. (Source: COG Tumour Lysis Syndrome guideline)

explanation.summary: This child has high-risk tumour lysis features at presentation: WCC over 100 x10^9/L with blasts, hyperuricaemia, hyperphosphataemia, and elevated LDH. AU and COG management uses hyperhydration with potassium-free isotonic fluid at 3 L/m^2/day plus rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV. Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended because it promotes calcium phosphate precipitation. Allopurinol is reserved for low or intermediate risk patients without established hyperuricaemia.
key_points: High-risk TLS: rasburicase + hyperhydration
Avoid potassium in initial fluids
Bicarbonate alkalinisation is no longer recommended
explanation.pearls: Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency; screen patients of African, Mediterranean, or Southeast Asian descent before administration.

subtopic_detail: Urea cycle disorder vs Reye in encephalopathy
stem:
A previously well 3-year-old presents with three days of vomiting after a viral illness, now confused and agitated with intermittent posturing. He has received paracetamol 15 mg/kg every six hours but no aspirin or other medications. Glucose is 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-7.8). Liver function shows ALT 220 U/L (0-40), AST 240 U/L (0-40), bilirubin 12 micromol/L (3-21), INR 1.2 (0.9-1.2). Ammonia is 380 micromol/L (less than 50). Venous gas shows pH 7.51, pCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L. Lactate is 1.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.0). Urine ketones are negative.

Metabolic and intensive care teams have been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 99%, temperature 37.0°C
data_table.Examination: Confused, intermittent decorticate posturing, no rash, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Ammonia 380 micromol/L, ALT 220 U/L, AST 240 U/L, bilirubin 12 micromol/L, INR 1.2, glucose 4.6 mmol/L, venous pH 7.51, pCO2 28 mmHg, lactate 1.8 mmol/L, urine ketones negative
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg six-hourly for three days

lead_in: Which is the most likely underlying disorder?

options.text: Late-onset ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency
options.rationale: Respiratory alkalosis with marked hyperammonaemia and absent ketosis in a previously well boy after catabolic stress is classic for a urea cycle disorder, most often OTC. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia)

options.text: Reye syndrome related to viral illness and aspirin exposure
options.rationale: Reye syndrome features metabolic acidosis with hypoglycaemia and exposure to salicylates; this child has alkalosis, normal glucose, and no aspirin. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Reye syndrome)

options.text: Paracetamol-induced acute fulminant liver failure
options.rationale: Therapeutic paracetamol dosing rarely causes liver failure; INR is normal and bilirubin is normal, arguing against acute liver failure. (Source: AMH: Paracetamol)

options.text: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency
options.rationale: MCAD causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting illness; this child is normoglycaemic and has only mild ammonia rise relative to MCAD episodes. (Source: HumGenome MCAD overview)

options.text: Acute viral hepatitis A with hepatic encephalopathy
options.rationale: Acute viral hepatitis with encephalopathy would show jaundice and an INR above 1.5; INR is normal here. (Source: GESA: Acute viral hepatitis)

explanation.summary: The triad of respiratory alkalosis (ammonia stimulates the brainstem), marked hyperammonaemia, and absent ketosis in a previously well child following catabolic stress is highly suggestive of a urea cycle disorder. OTC deficiency is X-linked and most commonly presents in heterozygote females or partial-deficiency males triggered by illness, surgery, or protein load. Immediate management is to stop protein intake, give IV 10% dextrose at 1.5x maintenance, and start sodium benzoate plus sodium phenylbutyrate while haemofiltration is arranged for ammonia above 400.
key_points: Respiratory alkalosis + hyperammonaemia + no ketosis suggests urea cycle disorder
Trigger is usually a catabolic illness with protein breakdown
Haemofiltration is indicated for ammonia >400 micromol/L
explanation.pearls: An ammonia >200 micromol/L in any encephalopathic child mandates a metabolic workup including plasma amino acids, urine orotic acid, and acylcarnitine profile - the genetic diagnosis follows.

stem:
A 7-month-old presents in early winter on day 3 of coryza followed by cough, wheeze and poor feeding. He has had no apnoeas. His mother says he is taking about half his usual feeds and is drowsier than usual but still rousable. He is on no regular medications and has no significant past history.

Nasopharyngeal aspirate is positive for RSV. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation without focal consolidation. He has just been transferred to the paediatric ward.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 160, BP 88/54 mmHg, RR 62, SpO2 89% in room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild intercostal recession, scattered fine inspiratory crackles, no grunting, alert when handled
data_table.Investigations: RSV positive, chest X-ray hyperinflation only, capillary blood gas pH 7.38 pCO2 42 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial respiratory support?

options.text: Trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with reassessment in 20 minutes
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended in viral bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months because there is no consistent benefit and they cause tachycardia and tremor; the issue here is oxygenation and feeding, not bronchospasm. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min as first-line support
options.rationale: HFNC is not the first-line oxygen step in the RCH pathway; it is reserved for infants who fail to respond to a trial of low-flow nasal-prong oxygen, because PARIS trial data did not show benefit when HFNC is used upfront. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Continuous positive airway pressure via paediatric mask at 6 cmH2O
options.rationale: CPAP is escalation beyond HFNC and is used after low-flow then HFNC have failed or where there is impending respiratory failure; this infant has compensated mild work of breathing and is not yet at that point. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Low-flow oxygen via nasal prongs at 1-2 L/min titrated to SpO2 ≥90%
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis pathway uses low-flow nasal-prong oxygen as the first escalation step, titrated to a target SpO2 of 90% or above; reserve HFNC for failure of low-flow after at least 60-120 minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nebulised hypertonic saline 3% every 6 hours for airway clearance
options.rationale: Routine nebulised hypertonic saline is not recommended in Australian bronchiolitis pathways; recent meta-analyses show no clinically important reduction in length of stay or improvement in severity. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in infants under 12 months with viral lower-airway inflammation, peaking in winter. AU paediatric pathways are explicitly supportive: feeding support and oxygen for hypoxaemia, with HFNC and CPAP escalation reserved for failure of low-flow oxygen. Routine bronchodilators, corticosteroids, hypertonic saline, antibiotics and chest physiotherapy are not recommended in typical disease. Apnoea risk is highest in infants under 8 weeks and ex-prems; those infants need a lower threshold for admission and monitoring.
key_points: RCH target SpO2 is 90% or above (not 92-94%) on minimal supplemental oxygen.
Low-flow nasal-prong oxygen is the first oxygen escalation; HFNC follows after failure of low-flow.
Bronchodilators, corticosteroids and hypertonic saline are not indicated in routine bronchiolitis.
Feeding via NGT or IV is indicated when oral intake falls below approximately 50% of normal.
explanation.pearls: RCH bronchiolitis SpO2 target is 90% on the lowest effective oxygen; PARIS trial showed no benefit from upfront HFNC over low-flow.

stem:
A previously well 4-year-old girl is at a birthday party. About 10 minutes after eating a slice of cake she develops urticaria over her trunk and limbs and starts to cough. Her father, who is a paramedic, places her on the floor and notes her colour and breathing are worsening. He has called an ambulance and is on the phone to you.

Her weight at her last GP visit was 18 kg. She has no known regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 150, BP not measured (no cuff), RR 40 with audible wheeze, SpO2 not measured, temperature not measured
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria, perioral swelling, wheeze on auscultation, no stridor, alert and crying
data_table.Investigations: Bedside only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first dose of intramuscular adrenaline?

options.text: Adrenaline 1:10 000 0.18 mg IV (180 mcg) over 5 minutes by ambulance
options.rationale: ASCIA reserves IV adrenaline for refractory anaphylaxis in a monitored setting with infusion capability; IM remains first-line and at the scene an IV bolus risks ventricular arrhythmia. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

options.text: Adrenaline 1:1000 0.30 mg IM (300 mcg) to the mid-anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: 0.30 mg (300 mcg, EpiPen adult) is the ASCIA band for children 20 kg or above; using it in this 18 kg child overshoots the banded dose and increases tachyarrhythmia risk without added clinical benefit. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

options.text: Adrenaline 1:1000 0.15 mg IM (150 mcg) to the mid-anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: ASCIA banded weight tables for IM adrenaline in anaphylaxis assign 0.15 mg (150 mcg) of 1:1000 to children weighing 10 to 20 kg; this child is 18 kg and falls in this band. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

options.text: Adrenaline 1:1000 0.18 mg IM (180 mcg) by calculated mg/kg arithmetic
options.rationale: ASCIA prefers a banded weight table in acute community anaphylaxis to avoid arithmetic errors under stress; the banded dose for 10-20 kg is 0.15 mg, not a per-kg calculation. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

options.text: Adrenaline 1:1000 0.15 mg IM (150 mcg) into the deltoid muscle
options.rationale: The dose is correct but the route is wrong; ASCIA specifies the mid-anterolateral thigh because deltoid injection in children has slower and more variable absorption due to less muscle bulk. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

explanation.summary: Australian community anaphylaxis is managed by ASCIA banded IM adrenaline doses tied to weight: under 7.5 kg use mg/kg, 7.5-20 kg use 0.15 mg, and 20 kg or more use 0.30 mg. The injection site is the mid-anterolateral thigh because of higher peak plasma concentration than deltoid. After IM adrenaline, lay the patient flat with legs raised, give oxygen, and prepare to repeat the dose every 5 minutes. Antihistamines and corticosteroids do not treat acute airway or circulatory compromise and are at best second-line adjuncts.
key_points: Banded ASCIA doses: 7.5-20 kg = 0.15 mg IM, 20 kg+ = 0.30 mg IM, infants <7.5 kg = 10 mcg/kg.
Inject mid-anterolateral thigh, not deltoid.
Repeat IM dose every 5 minutes if symptoms persist; escalate to IV infusion if refractory.
Antihistamines and steroids do not treat acute anaphylaxis cardiorespiratory compromise.
explanation.pearls: ASCIA EpiPen Jr 150 mcg is for 10-20 kg; EpiPen 300 mcg is for 20 kg or above.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

stem:
A 5-week-old boy is brought in by his mother who says he has been more sleepy than usual and is feeding poorly today. She last fed him 6 hours ago and he took only a few sucks. His older sister had a cold last week. He was born at term by normal vaginal delivery without complications, and has been gaining weight along the 50th centile.

On arrival to the emergency department he is irritable when handled but settles in mother's arms. There is no rash. He has had no recent overseas travel.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 180, BP 78/46 mmHg, RR 56, SpO2 97% in air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Anterior fontanelle soft and flat, mildly irritable but consolable, capillary refill 3 seconds, no rash, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 4.2 mmol/L, urinalysis pending, FBC and blood cultures not yet drawn

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urine, FBC and blood cultures only, then admit for observation off antibiotics
options.rationale: RCH does not permit omitting LP at this age because CSF pleocytosis can occur with normal peripheral inflammatory markers; observation off antibiotics is unsafe in an infant under 3 months with documented fever. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Full septic workup including lumbar puncture, then empirical IV cefotaxime
options.rationale: RCH and CDNA recommend a full septic workup including LP for any infant under 3 months with fever 38 °C or higher, regardless of focus or appearance, followed by IV antibiotics covering early late-onset organisms (cefotaxime, with amoxicillin under 28 days). (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Trial of oral fluids and discharge to GP review in 24 hours if improved
options.rationale: Discharging a febrile infant under 3 months without investigations is contrary to all AU paediatric guidance; the pre-test probability of serious bacterial infection in this age group is 10-15 percent. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg and reassess in 12 hours at the GP
options.rationale: IM ceftriaxone outpatient does not permit serial reassessment, CSF sampling, or escalation; the AU pathway requires inpatient IV antibiotics and full workup for this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Computed tomography of the head before any lumbar puncture
