options.rationale: Pre-LP imaging is reserved for focal neurology, papilloedema, GCS reduction or immunocompromise; an alert and consolable infant with a soft fontanelle does not need a CT and the delay would push first-dose antibiotics outside the 1-hour target. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

explanation.summary: The under-3-month febrile infant remains a high-risk group in Australian paediatric pathways. The dominant organisms are E. coli, group B streptococcus, Listeria (especially under 1 month) and HSV; meningitis incidence is high enough that LP is part of routine assessment even when the infant looks reasonably well between febrile episodes. The standard approach is full septic workup, then empirical IV cefotaxime (with added IV amoxicillin for under 28 days for Listeria cover), with re-evaluation when results return.
key_points: Any temperature ≥38.0 °C under 3 months triggers full septic workup including LP.
Empirical IV cefotaxime; add amoxicillin if under 28 days for Listeria cover.
Pre-LP CT only for focal neurology, papilloedema, decreased conscious state or immunocompromise.
Time-to-first antibiotic dose should be within 1 hour of recognition.
explanation.pearls: Under 28 days, add IV amoxicillin to cefotaxime to cover Listeria, which third-generation cephalosporins miss.

sources.label: CDNA Series of National Guidelines: Invasive meningococcal disease

stem:
A 2-year-old presents at midnight with a 1-day history of coryza and a barking cough that has progressively worsened. His mother says his voice is hoarse and that he sounds 'noisy when he breathes in', even when he is sitting still on her lap. He is not drooling. He is fully immunised.

On arrival he is sitting upright on his mother, alert and quietly tearful. You can hear intermittent inspiratory stridor at rest. There is mild chest-wall in-drawing but no tracheal tug, and no cyanosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 97% in air, temperature 37.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Sitting comfortably, inspiratory stridor at rest, mild intercostal recession only, no tracheal tug, no cyanosis, voice hoarse
data_table.Investigations: Bedside only, no imaging performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Observation without medication for 30 minutes, then reassess severity
options.rationale: Once stridor is present at rest with any work of breathing, AU paediatric guidance gives a single dose of dexamethasone immediately; the benefit at 30 minutes is unlikely to occur without treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup laryngotracheobronchitis)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.60 mg/kg as a single dose, then reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup (marked distress, exhaustion, cyanosis or impaired consciousness); using it for moderate croup over-treats and increases hyperglycaemia and behavioural side effects without added benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup laryngotracheobronchitis)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL alone, without any corticosteroid
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is added for severe croup but is short-acting and rebounds; AU practice always pairs it with corticosteroid, never replaces steroid with adrenaline. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup laryngotracheobronchitis)

options.text: Inhaled budesonide 2 mg via nebuliser, without any oral corticosteroid
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is reserved for children who cannot tolerate oral dexamethasone (vomiting or refusing); oral dexamethasone is the AU first-line because it works equally and is simpler. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup laryngotracheobronchitis)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose, then reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: RCH grades this presentation as moderate croup (stridor at rest, mild work of breathing, no severe distress), and the recommended dose is oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg; the higher 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup laryngotracheobronchitis)

explanation.summary: Croup is parainfluenza-driven viral laryngotracheobronchitis with peak incidence in 6 months to 6 years. RCH grades severity by stridor and work of breathing: mild (no stridor at rest, mild barking cough), moderate (stridor at rest with mild-moderate retractions, no marked distress), and severe (marked distress, exhaustion, cyanosis, decreased conscious state). Mild and moderate croup are treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg; severe gets 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 and a minimum 3-hour observation after the last adrenaline dose.
key_points: Mild/moderate croup: oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose.
Severe croup: oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PLUS nebulised adrenaline 5 mL 1:1000 (flat dose).
Observation 3 hours minimum after last nebulised adrenaline for rebound.
Nebulised budesonide is the backup for children who cannot tolerate oral dose.
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild-to-moderate, 0.6 mg/kg only when severe; nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1:1000.

stem:
A 2-year-old girl presents with a 2-day history of watery diarrhoea and intermittent vomiting. Her mother estimates she has had around 10 loose stools and 5 vomits in 24 hours, and she has not tolerated oral rehydration solution at home because she vomits within minutes of each cup. Her urine output is reduced - she has had only one wet nappy this morning. She weighs 13 kg.

She has no other significant past history and has had no overseas travel.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 150, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 30, SpO2 99% in air, temperature 37.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, capillary refill 2 seconds, abdomen soft non-tender, alert and irritable but consolable
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 4.6 mmol/L, ketones 1.2 mmol/L, no electrolytes drawn yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Single oral ondansetron 4 mg, then oral cup-by-cup rehydration for 4 hours
options.rationale: The ondansetron dose is incorrect for a 13 kg child (RCH gives 2 mg for 8-15 kg, 4 mg for 15-30 kg), and oral cup rehydration has already failed - NGT is the next escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Intravenous 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus then ongoing IV maintenance fluids
options.rationale: IV is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, NGT failure, or biochemical derangement; this child has mild-moderate dehydration without haemodynamic compromise so NGT is the AU first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Continue oral rehydration solution at home and review with GP in 12 hours
options.rationale: Oral rehydration has already failed at home because of vomiting; persisting with the same approach risks ongoing fluid loss and is not the AU pathway when oral fails. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Single oral ondansetron 2 mg, then nasogastric ORS at 25 mL/kg/h for 4 hours
options.rationale: RCH recommends a single oral ondansetron dose to control vomiting (2 mg for 8-15 kg), then nasogastric rehydration as the next step when oral rehydration fails in clinically mild-moderate dehydration. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Loperamide single oral dose with oral rehydration solution given by syringe
options.rationale: Antimotility agents like loperamide are contraindicated in paediatric viral gastroenteritis because they prolong illness and increase risk of toxic ileus; AU paediatric pathways do not use them. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: Australian paediatric gastroenteritis pathways escalate rehydration in a strict order: oral first, then NGT for mild-moderate dehydration that fails oral, then IV for severe dehydration, shock, NGT failure or biochemical derangement. A single dose of ondansetron (2 mg for 8-15 kg, 4 mg for 15-30 kg) is used to break the vomiting cycle and improve tolerance of NGT or oral fluids. Most viral gastroenteritis is self-limiting; investigation is reserved for atypical course, blood in stool, or systemic features.
key_points: Escalation order: oral → NGT → IV.
Ondansetron 2 mg for 8-15 kg, 4 mg for 15-30 kg, single dose.
NGT rehydration at approximately 25 mL/kg/h for 4 hours in mild-moderate dehydration.
Antimotility agents and antibiotics are not routine in paediatric viral gastroenteritis.
explanation.pearls: RCH rule: NGT before IV in mild-moderate paediatric dehydration; IV reserved for shock, severe dehydration, or NGT failure.

stem:
A 4-year-old boy with no past medical history is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with a 12-hour history of fever and lethargy. His parents say he 'just wants to lie on the couch' and has not opened his eyes for them for the last hour. There is no rash. He weighs approximately 17 kg.

On arrival he is mottled to the knees, peripherally cool, and only briefly opens his eyes to painful stimuli. You have a paediatric registrar and a senior nurse with you, and have just called the consultant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 180, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 44, SpO2 96% in air, temperature 39.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Mottled lower limbs, capillary refill 5 seconds, no rash, chest clear, abdomen soft, GCS 12
data_table.Investigations: Capillary lactate 4.8 mmol/L, capillary glucose 4.4 mmol/L, no other results yet

lead_in: After confirming IV access and drawing blood cultures, what is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Start IV peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.1 mcg/kg/min before any fluid bolus
options.rationale: Vasoactive support is escalation AFTER an initial 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus and reassessment in the AU paediatric sepsis pathway, not before; starting inotropes upfront risks underfilling and tissue hypoperfusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis recognition and resuscitation)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis recognition and resuscitation

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg, then 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus over 5-10 minutes
options.rationale: The RCH paediatric sepsis pathway calls for the first IV antibiotic dose within 60 minutes of recognition, immediately followed by a 20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus over 5-10 minutes, before considering vasoactive support. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis recognition and resuscitation)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis recognition and resuscitation

options.text: Administer IV dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as the first medication for septic shock
options.rationale: Steroids are not first-line in undifferentiated paediatric septic shock; they are reserved for refractory shock despite fluids and inotropes or specific indications such as meningitis with antibiotics. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis recognition and resuscitation)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis recognition and resuscitation

options.text: Give 40 mL/kg colloid (4% albumin) over 30 minutes before any antibiotic
options.rationale: AU paediatric pathways use isotonic crystalloid (0.9% saline or Hartmann's), not routine colloid; antibiotic delay beyond the first hour increases mortality. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis recognition and resuscitation)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis recognition and resuscitation

options.text: Place a central venous line before any fluid or antibiotic administration
options.rationale: Time-critical antibiotic and fluid delivery should not wait for central access; peripheral or intraosseous access is acceptable for the initial bolus and first antibiotic. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis recognition and resuscitation)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis recognition and resuscitation

explanation.summary: Paediatric sepsis pathways in Australia centre on the hour-1 bundle: recognition, IV or IO access, blood cultures, first antibiotic within 60 minutes, and 20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus over 5-10 minutes repeated up to 60 mL/kg with reassessment. Lactate is used as a perfusion marker. Adrenaline (preferred over noradrenaline for cold shock) is added if shock persists after 40-60 mL/kg of fluid. Steroids are reserved for refractory shock or for specific co-management (meningitis dexamethasone). Source control happens in parallel.
key_points: Hour-1 sepsis bundle: access → cultures → antibiotics → fluid bolus.
First fluid bolus is 20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid over 5-10 minutes.
Repeat fluid boluses up to 60 mL/kg before starting peripheral adrenaline infusion.
Antibiotic delay beyond 60 minutes increases paediatric sepsis mortality.
explanation.pearls: RCH paediatric sepsis: first IV antibiotic and first 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus both within 60 minutes of recognition.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis recognition and resuscitation

stem:
An 18-month-old girl had her first episode of urinary tract infection 5 days ago. Her urine culture grew Escherichia coli sensitive to cefalexin. She defervesced within 24 hours of starting oral cefalexin and finished her course yesterday. She is otherwise well, fully immunised, and was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy with antenatal scans documenting normal renal tracts.

She is meeting all developmental milestones. The family asks the practice nurse about follow-up imaging and you are asked to advise.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 100% in air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Well-grown along the 50th centile, abdomen soft non-tender, no palpable mass, genitalia normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine culture E. coli sensitive to cefalexin, FBC and UEC within normal limits, no abnormal antenatal renal scans

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for renal-tract imaging?

options.text: No routine imaging now; re-image only if a further UTI or atypical features develop
options.rationale: RCH does not recommend routine renal ultrasound after a single typical UTI even under 24 months when there has been normal antenatal monitoring and good response within 48 hours; imaging is reserved for atypical UTI or recurrence. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks for all children under 2 with a first UTI
options.rationale: This is the NICE-style cascade, not the RCH cascade; AU paediatric guidance no longer recommends routine ultrasound after typical UTI in children with normal antenatal scans. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: DMSA scan at 6 months to detect cortical scarring after the first febrile UTI
options.rationale: DMSA is part of NICE-style follow-up but is not in the RCH cascade for typical UTI; it adds radiation without changing management in well children with normal antenatal scans. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Micturating cystourethrogram now to exclude vesicoureteric reflux scarring
options.rationale: MCUG is reserved for atypical UTI or abnormal ultrasound; it is invasive and is not in the routine RCH cascade after a single typical UTI in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Indirect cystography with technetium tracer to look at reflux without catheterisation
options.rationale: Indirect cystography is a niche second-line investigation in older toilet-trained children with documented reflux; it has no role after a single typical UTI in a well 18-month-old. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: RCH guidance for paediatric UTI imaging is deliberately conservative compared with NICE. After a single typical UTI in a well child with normal antenatal renal monitoring and good response within 48 hours of empirical antibiotics, no routine imaging is recommended. Renal ultrasound during the acute illness is reserved for atypical UTI (poor response after 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics, non-E. coli, sepsis, palpable abdominal mass, raised creatinine), recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring. DMSA and MCUG are not part of the AU pathway.
key_points: RCH: no routine imaging after a single typical UTI in a well child with normal antenatal scans.
Atypical UTI triggers ultrasound during illness.
Recurrent UTI or no antenatal monitoring under 6 months also triggers ultrasound.
DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs; they are not in the AU routine cascade.
explanation.pearls: RCH UTI cascade: ultrasound only for atypical or recurrent UTI; DMSA and MCUG are not routine in AU.

subtopic_detail: DKA fluid plan with cerebral oedema risk
stem:
A 9-year-old girl with no past history presents with 2 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and 24 hours of vomiting and headache. Her parents say she has been increasingly drowsy on the drive in and has not been able to give clear answers to their questions. She weighs 30 kg.

Venous blood gas shows pH 7.05, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L. Capillary glucose is 32 mmol/L and capillary ketones are 6.2 mmol/L. Sodium (corrected for glucose) is 140 mmol/L. Her GCS is 12 (E3 V4 M5). Pupils are equal and reactive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140, BP 110/70 mmHg, RR 36 Kussmaul, SpO2 99% in air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, drowsy but rousable, fundoscopy not yet performed, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.05, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L (22-32), glucose 32 mmol/L, ketones 6.2 mmol/L, corrected sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid and insulin plan?

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 1 hour to correct acidosis before any fluid bolus
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is contraindicated in routine paediatric DKA management because it worsens intracellular acidosis, predisposes to hypokalaemia, and is associated with cerebral oedema in children. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline 2020)

options.text: 20 mL/kg saline bolus repeated to 60 mL/kg, then immediate insulin at 0.1 units/kg/h
options.rationale: Aggressive fluid resuscitation and immediate higher-dose insulin in a child with reduced GCS substantially raises cerebral oedema risk; AU paediatric DKA pathways have moved to slower deficit-correction over 48 hours and delayed insulin. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline 2020)

options.text: 10 mL/kg saline once, deficit plus maintenance over 48 hours, insulin 0.05 units/kg/h after 1 hour
options.rationale: AU paediatric DKA pathways use a single 10 mL/kg cautious bolus only if shocked, then deficit (capped at 8 percent) plus maintenance evenly over 48 hours, with insulin started AFTER an hour at 0.05 units/kg/h in children at higher cerebral oedema risk (age <5, severe acidosis, decreased GCS, longer history). (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline 2020)

options.text: Subcutaneous insulin glargine 0.3 units/kg plus oral rehydration with sugar-free fluids
options.rationale: Subcutaneous insulin and oral fluids are not appropriate for severe DKA with reduced conscious state; absorption is unpredictable in dehydration and ketosis will not clear without an IV insulin infusion. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline 2020)

options.text: Immediate intubation, hyperventilation to pCO2 30 mmHg, plus 3% saline 5 mL/kg bolus
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline and hyperventilation are reserved for confirmed cerebral oedema with neurological deterioration AFTER fluid resuscitation has started; pre-emptive use without those features is not the AU pathway. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline 2020)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management balances correction of acidosis against the risk of cerebral oedema, which carries 20-25 percent mortality. AU pathways (APEG, ISPAD-aligned) cap the assumed deficit at 8 percent, replace deficit plus maintenance evenly over 48 hours (or longer in high-risk children), reserve 10 mL/kg boluses for documented shock only, delay insulin start until 1 hour after fluids begin, and start insulin at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h. Bicarbonate is not used. Cerebral oedema treatment is hypertonic saline or mannitol AFTER neurological deterioration.
key_points: Cap deficit at 8 percent and replace over 48 hours.
10 mL/kg bolus only if shocked; avoid 20 mL/kg boluses in undifferentiated DKA.
Start insulin after 1 hour of fluids, at 0.05 units/kg/h in high-risk children.
Bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA.
explanation.pearls: Paediatric DKA: 0.05 units/kg/h insulin after a 1-hour fluid window in children at higher cerebral oedema risk (age <5, severe acidosis, reduced GCS).

subtopic_detail: Pertussis with apnoea in young infant
stem:
A 4-week-old girl is brought in by her mother on day 7 of what was initially a coryzal illness. Today she has had three coughing fits, each ending with brief cyanosis and a 10 to 15 second pause in breathing that resolved with stimulation. Between fits she has fed about half her usual volume and appears alert. Her mother had several weeks of a paroxysmal night cough that has since settled; she received Boostrix at 26 weeks gestation. The infant has had no fever and no vomiting between coughing fits.

She is now in the resuscitation cubicle on continuous monitoring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 162, BP 78/52 mmHg, RR 56, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Pink and alert between fits, mild bilateral fine crackles, no recessions or grunting, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 28 x10^9/L (5-19), lymphocytes 70%, neutrophils 18%; CRP 6 mg/L (<5); chest X-ray non-specific peribronchial markings; NPA PCR pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and reassess respiratory effort in 20 minutes
options.rationale: Pertussis is not a bronchospastic illness; salbutamol does not abort paroxysms and risks tachycardia and tremor. RCH explicitly advises against bronchodilators in infants under 12 months with viral lower respiratory illness. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit and start oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily on cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Paroxysmal cough with cyanotic apnoeas, lymphocytosis above 20, and a household contact with prolonged cough is clinical pertussis until NPA PCR returns. Infants under 6 months with documented apnoea need admission for cardiorespiratory monitoring because apnoea drives the case-fatality. Azithromycin 10 mg/kg orally daily for 5 days reduces transmission and is the AU first-line macrolide under 1 month and beyond. (Source: RCH CPG: Pertussis)

options.text: Admit for low-flow oxygen 1 L/min via nasal prongs without antibiotics
options.rationale: She is saturating 96% in room air so does not need oxygen, and withholding azithromycin misses both the case-management and public-health intervention - household contacts need post-exposure prophylaxis. (Source: RCH CPG: Pertussis)

options.text: Commence cefotaxime 50 mg/kg intravenously and perform a lumbar puncture
options.rationale: Empirical cefotaxime plus LP is the right step for an unwell febrile infant under 3 months with sepsis features, but this infant is afebrile, alert between fits, with CRP 6 and a lymphocyte-predominant white cell count - the picture points to Bordetella pertussis rather than bacteraemic sepsis. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Arrange discharge home with red-flag advice and review in 24 hours
options.rationale: Discharging an under-6-month-old with documented apnoeic episodes ignores the apnoea-driven mortality of infant pertussis; she may have a further unwitnessed apnoea at home. Even with reassuring inter-fit observations she meets RCH admission criteria. (Source: RCH CPG: Pertussis)

explanation.summary: Infants under 6 months with paroxysmal cough and apnoea require admission for cardiorespiratory monitoring and empirical azithromycin pending NPA PCR. Maternal Boostrix at 26 weeks gestation reduces but does not eliminate neonatal pertussis risk in the first 6 weeks of life. Lymphocytosis above 20 with a low CRP supports the diagnosis. Notification to public health is mandatory within 24 hours.
key_points: Apnoea drives mortality in infant pertussis - cardiorespiratory monitoring is mandatory under 6 months
Azithromycin 10 mg/kg orally once daily for 5 days is AU first-line, including in neonates
Household contact with prolonged paroxysmal cough is a high-yield epidemiological clue even when maternal vaccination is up to date
explanation.pearls: Erythromycin has been replaced by azithromycin in AU paediatric pertussis because of the pyloric-stenosis risk in neonates. NPA PCR is the diagnostic test of choice; serology is unreliable in infants. Notify public health within 24 hours and arrange post-exposure prophylaxis for at-risk contacts.

stem:
An 8-month-old boy on day 4 of RSV bronchiolitis was started on low-flow nasal-prong oxygen at 2 L/min two hours ago after his SpO2 dropped to 88% in room air. Despite this he has worsening intercostal and subcostal recessions and is now too tired to feed.

He was born at 38 weeks with no chronic lung disease or congenital cardiac disease. He has had no apnoeas. A repeat capillary blood gas has just returned.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 72, SpO2 91% on 2 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 37.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Marked recessions and tracheal tug, head bobbing, scattered crackles and wheeze, alert but exhausted
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.31, pCO2 56 mmHg, HCO3 25 mmol/L, base excess -1; chest X-ray hyperinflation without consolidation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next respiratory support step?

options.text: Add nebulised hypertonic saline 3% three times daily
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not recommended in the RCH pathway because randomised data show no consistent reduction in length of stay or admission rates, and it may worsen bronchospasm. It does not address impending respiratory failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Proceed to elective intubation and conventional mechanical ventilation
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for failure of non-invasive escalation (HFNC then CPAP), apnoeas requiring repeated stimulation, or refractory hypoxaemia. He should first be offered HFNC because most infants respond. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Escalate to heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis pathway reserves HFNC for infants who fail a trial of low-flow oxygen, defined by ongoing distress or rising pCO2 after 1 to 2 hours. He has now had a fair trial of low-flow with rising work of breathing, hypoxia despite 2 L/min, and a pCO2 of 56 with feeding failure - this meets the escalation criterion. HFNC at 2 L/kg/min is the next step before CPAP or intubation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and ipratropium 250 micrograms
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended in infants under 12 months with bronchiolitis because randomised data show no benefit and adverse effects of tachycardia and tremor. The pathophysiology is mucus plugging and airway oedema, not bronchospasm. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Continue low-flow oxygen at 2 L/min and reassess in a further 2 hours
options.rationale: Continuing low-flow misses the failure-of-low-flow criterion (rising pCO2, feeding inability, recessions despite 2 L/min) and risks decompensation. RCH explicitly defines this as the trigger to escalate. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: RCH bronchiolitis pathway makes low-flow nasal-prong oxygen the first step (target SpO2 above 90%) and reserves HFNC for failure of low-flow after about 1 to 2 hours. Rising pCO2, ongoing distress, and feeding inability define failure. HFNC is set at 2 L/kg/min for the first 10 kg.
key_points: Low-flow first, HFNC second, CPAP third in the RCH bronchiolitis pathway
Failure-of-low-flow criteria: rising pCO2, persistent recessions, feeding inability, SpO2 below 90% despite oxygen
Bronchodilators, steroids, hypertonic saline and chest physiotherapy are NOT routine in infant bronchiolitis
explanation.pearls: Target SpO2 in RCH is 90% or above, not 92 to 94% (the higher target leads to longer admissions without outcome benefit). HFNC weight-based flow is capped at 2 L/kg/min up to 10 kg, then 50 L/min absolute thereafter.

subtopic_detail: Moderate croup steroid dose and disposition
stem:
A 2-year-old presents at 2300 with a 1-day barking cough and stridor that is now audible at rest. His mother says he sounded "like a dog" all evening and is now "breathing harder". He is alert, engages with his parents, and tolerates examination.

He has been previously well and is fully immunised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 142, BP 96/62 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 38.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Audible inspiratory stridor at rest, moderate intercostal recession, no cyanosis, soft barking cough, no drool, no tripod posture
data_table.Investigations: Nil performed

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management plan in ED?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 plus dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, observe 3 hours
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup or in moderate croup that does not respond to steroid. RCH protocol is the flat 5 mL of 1:1000 (not weight-based) but only after the patient meets severe criteria - agitation, cyanosis, marked retractions, or exhaustion. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Intramuscular dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg with admission to short-stay unit
options.rationale: Oral dexamethasone has equivalent efficacy to intramuscular in croup and is preferred because intramuscular causes pain in a distressed child. The dose is also too high for moderate croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally with admission and 4-hourly review
options.rationale: RCH reserves the 0.6 mg/kg dose for severe croup with significant respiratory distress, marked recession, agitation, or hypoxia. Moderate croup gets the lower dose, and giving the higher dose does not improve outcomes but does increase nausea. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Humidified air via face mask and reassess respiratory effort in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Humidified mist has been removed from croup guidelines because randomised data show no benefit. Withholding steroid delays the treatment that improves natural history. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally, observe 30 minutes, then plan disposition
options.rationale: RCH defines moderate croup as stridor at rest with some recessions but the child is alert, well-perfused, and not exhausted. First-line is dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally; he does not yet meet severe criteria so nebulised adrenaline is not indicated. Most moderate croup can be discharged after a single dose of dexamethasone with 30 to 60 minutes observation for response. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: RCH grades croup as mild, moderate or severe. Moderate has stridor at rest with some recession in an alert, well-perfused child; first-line is dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally with brief observation. The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup. Nebulised adrenaline is also for severe croup, with a flat 5 mL of 1:1000.
key_points: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally for mild and moderate croup
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally only for severe croup
Observe at least 3 hours after the LAST dose of nebulised adrenaline because of rebound risk
explanation.pearls: Cooler outside air or humidified mist does NOT improve croup. Nebulised adrenaline rebounds at about 2 hours so the 3-hour post-last-dose observation rule exists to catch deterioration. Bacterial tracheitis is the look-alike if the child is toxic or has drool.

subtopic_detail: Severe paediatric asthma escalation past back-to-back salbutamol
stem:
A 12-year-old girl with known asthma is brought to ED at 0200 by her parents. She has had a viral coryza for 3 days and a worsening cough; she used her salbutamol inhaler eight times over the past 6 hours with limited relief. Her usual preventer is fluticasone 100 micrograms twice daily but she has been non-adherent. She has previously had one ICU admission for asthma at age 9.

She has been given continuous nebulised salbutamol 10 mg, nebulised ipratropium 250 micrograms three times, and a single dose of oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg in the last hour. She remains in significant distress and is now sitting forward in tripod posture and answering only in single words. The senior decision-maker has reviewed her in person.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 152, BP 132/76 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 91% on 8 L/min via Hudson mask, temperature 37.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Tripod posture, marked intercostal and subcostal recession, widespread polyphonic wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase, mild drowsiness on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.30, pCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, lactate 3.2; peak flow not obtainable
data_table.Medications: Continuous nebulised salbutamol, nebulised ipratropium, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg given 1 hour ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate rapid sequence intubation with ketamine and rocuronium
options.rationale: Intubation in severe asthma carries very high risk of cardiac arrest from breath-stacking and hypotension and is reserved for exhaustion, persistent hypoxia, severe acidosis, or coma despite maximal medical therapy. She is hypercapnic for asthma but still mentating; medical escalation should be attempted first. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma)

options.text: Loading dose intravenous aminophylline 5 mg/kg over 60 minutes
options.rationale: Aminophylline is reserved for asthma not responding to IV magnesium and salbutamol infusion. Going to aminophylline ahead of magnesium skips the better-evidenced step and increases the risk of tachyarrhythmia and seizures. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma)

options.text: Nebulised hypertonic saline 7% and chest physiotherapy
options.rationale: Neither hypertonic saline nor chest physiotherapy has a role in acute paediatric asthma; physiotherapy may precipitate bronchospasm. They are not in the RCH pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes
options.rationale: Severe asthma not responding to first-hour bronchodilators plus steroid (the RCH definition of life-threatening exacerbation if pCO2 is normal or rising) - the next step in the RCH pathway is intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes, then reassess. A normal-to-rising pCO2 in someone tiring is a warning sign but does not yet mandate intubation. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg into the lateral thigh
options.rationale: IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or as a temporising measure if IV access is unobtainable; she has access and her presentation is bronchospastic without urticaria, angioedema or hypotension. Adrenaline does not have a role in pure severe asthma at this point in the RCH pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma)

explanation.summary: RCH severe asthma escalation past first-hour salbutamol-ipratropium-steroid is intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes. If that fails, intravenous salbutamol infusion is the next step, then aminophylline. Intubation is high-risk and reserved for failure of medical escalation.
key_points: IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes is the first IV escalation in RCH severe asthma
Rising pCO2 in a tiring asthmatic is a warning sign but does not by itself mandate intubation
Intubation in severe asthma is associated with high rates of peri-intubation cardiac arrest due to dynamic hyperinflation
explanation.pearls: If you do intubate, use ketamine for induction (bronchodilator), low respiratory rate, long expiratory time, permissive hypercapnia, and disconnect from the circuit if you suspect breath-stacking arrest. Magnesium is given over 20 minutes (not as a bolus) to avoid hypotension.

stem: A 6-year-old girl with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, on day 12 post-induction chemotherapy, presents with a single temperature of 38.4 °C recorded by her parents 90 minutes ago. She has had no rigors, no localising symptoms, and no antibiotics in the last 7 days. She has a tunnelled central venous catheter that looks clean and non-tender. Her oncology unit has a written febrile neutropenia pathway and the on-call oncologist has been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 102/68 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 38.1 °C on arrival
data_table.Examination: Pale but well-perfused, capillary refill 2 seconds, no mucositis, central line site clean, no rash, chest clear, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: FBC neutrophils 0.3 x10^9/L (1.5-8.0), Hb 92 g/L (115-160), platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400); CRP 28 mg/L (<5); urinalysis nil; blood cultures from line and peripherally just drawn
data_table.Medications: Tunnelled CVC, on maintenance phase intravenous chemotherapy due in 7 days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Wait for repeat temperature to confirm a true fever before starting antibiotics
options.rationale: Repeating the temperature to wait for confirmation adds delay; a single temperature 38.5 or two of 38.0 within an hour meets RCH neutropenic fever criteria. Mortality rises with each hour antibiotics are delayed. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Neutropenia)

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and ciprofloxacin and discharge for outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Outpatient oral antibiotics are an option only in selected low-risk febrile neutropenia in adolescents on standardised pathways and never within the first 24 hours of an episode. Children with ALL on induction-phase chemotherapy are high-risk by default. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Neutropenia)

options.text: Withhold antibiotics pending the chest X-ray result and abdominal examination by the oncology registrar
options.rationale: Withholding antibiotics for any further imaging delays the time-critical first dose. Imaging proceeds after the first dose is in. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Neutropenia)

options.text: Commence intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg as soon as the cultures have been taken
options.rationale: RCH febrile neutropenia pathway requires empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics within 60 minutes of fever recognition, immediately after cultures (peripheral and from each lumen of the CVC). Piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg per dose is the standard AU paediatric empirical regimen for haemodynamically stable febrile neutropenia. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Neutropenia)

options.text: Add intravenous vancomycin to piperacillin-tazobactam empirically due to the central line
options.rationale: Vancomycin is added only if the line is overtly infected, the child is septic, there is mucositis with toxic shock features, or there is known MRSA colonisation. Routine vancomycin add-on does not improve survival and selects for resistance. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Neutropenia)

explanation.summary: Febrile neutropenia is fever 38.5 °C once or 38.0 °C twice in an hour, plus an absolute neutrophil count under 0.5 x10^9/L (or under 1.0 expected to fall). Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics within 60 minutes after cultures are the cornerstone of survival in paediatric oncology.
key_points: AU first-line for paediatric febrile neutropenia is piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg per dose
Vancomycin add-on only for septic shock, line infection, mucositis, or MRSA colonisation
Outpatient oral pathway only in selected low-risk adolescents past 24 hours
explanation.pearls: Time to first antibiotic is a key quality metric. The 60-minute door-to-needle target applies. Always culture both peripherally AND through each lumen of the central line - this differentiates line infection from a primary bloodstream infection.

subtopic_detail: Intussusception lay-language presentation and air enema vs surgery
stem:
An 11-month-old previously well boy is brought in by his mother. Over the past 6 hours she describes him as repeatedly "starting to cry, drawing both his legs up, then settling for 20 minutes" before another episode begins. Earlier today he passed a stool that she describes as "slimy and dark, a bit like jelly". He has vomited twice; the most recent vomit looked yellow-green. He has had no fever and no diarrhoea.

He was alert on triage and is now sleepy between episodes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158, BP 88/56 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale, capillary refill 2.5 seconds, soft abdomen with a vague long thin lump felt in the right upper quadrant, normal genitalia, no peritonism, no abdominal distension
data_table.Investigations: FBC unremarkable; UEC normal; abdominal ultrasound just performed shows a target-sign lesion in the right upper quadrant with peristalsis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Observe for 4 hours and reassess if any new symptoms develop
options.rationale: Watchful waiting in confirmed intussusception risks bowel ischaemia and perforation; the window for non-operative pneumatic reduction narrows with duration of symptoms. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Proceed to air enema reduction under fluoroscopy after fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Ultrasound-confirmed ileocolic intussusception in a stable child with no peritonitis is managed by air (pneumatic) enema reduction with 80 to 90% success. Bilious vomiting and somnolence are concerning but he is haemodynamically compensated and has no peritonism. Surgical reduction is the backup if pneumatic reduction fails or peritonitis develops. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Give barium contrast enema for both diagnosis and therapeutic reduction
options.rationale: Barium enema for reduction has largely been replaced by air enema in AU paediatric practice because air enema avoids barium peritonitis if perforation occurs. RCH and Royal Children's image-guided pathways use air. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Give a single dose of nasogastric polyethylene glycol and reassess in 6 hours
options.rationale: Osmotic laxatives have no role in intussusception and would worsen ileus and dehydration. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Proceed straight to laparotomy and manual reduction after induction
options.rationale: Primary surgery is reserved for failed pneumatic reduction, evidence of peritonitis or perforation, shock unresponsive to resuscitation, or a clear pathological lead point. None of those criteria are met. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Lay-language clues to intussusception in an infant are screaming episodes with leg-drawing-up, intervals of lethargy, and red jelly stool. Ultrasound shows a target sign. Pneumatic (air) enema is first-line if there is no peritonism or perforation, with surgery as backup.
key_points: Air enema reduces 80 to 90% of stable ileocolic intussusception
Surgical reduction is reserved for peritonitis, perforation, failed pneumatic reduction, or a pathological lead point
Bilious vomiting is concerning but does not by itself mandate primary laparotomy
explanation.pearls: Lead points (Meckel diverticulum, lymphoma, polyp) are more common above 2 years and below 3 months. Recurrence after reduction is 5 to 10% and usually within 24 hours, so observation post-reduction is mandatory.

subtopic_detail: First UTI in infant under 6 months - RCH imaging cascade
stem:
A 4-month-old boy is admitted with his first urinary tract infection. Suprapubic-aspirate culture grows Escherichia coli 100 sensitive to oral cefalexin. He responded clinically to 48 hours of IV gentamicin and benzylpenicillin and is now afebrile, feeding well, and ready to transition to oral antibiotics for 7 days total.

He was born at term with no antenatal renal abnormalities documented on the routine 20-week scan. He has had no other infections.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 78/52 mmHg, RR 34, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Active, well-hydrated, abdomen soft, no flank tenderness, normal genitalia, circumcised
data_table.Investigations: Suprapubic urine culture: E. coli >10^8 CFU/L, sensitive to cefalexin; UEC normal; inflammatory markers improving
data_table.Medications: IV gentamicin and benzylpenicillin (last dose 6 hours ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate post-discharge imaging plan?

options.text: Renal ultrasound during the current inpatient admission
options.rationale: RCH advises renal ultrasound for any infant under 6 months with a first UTI to look for obstructive uropathy or structural abnormality, even with a typical organism that responds to first-line antibiotics. Ideally done during admission. The further DMSA and MCUG investigations are NOT in the routine RCH cascade. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

options.text: No imaging - documented antenatal scan is sufficient
options.rationale: The 20-week morphology scan does not reliably exclude posterior urethral valves, vesicoureteric reflux, or duplex systems in a young infant; RCH still requires postnatal ultrasound under 6 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

options.text: DMSA scan in 4 to 6 months to assess for renal scarring
options.rationale: DMSA is a NICE construct not in the RCH routine cascade. RCH reserves nuclear imaging for recurrent or atypical UTI, not a first-typical UTI even under 6 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

options.text: Repeat urine microscopy and culture in 1 week to confirm clearance
options.rationale: Routine test-of-cure urine is not recommended in afebrile, clinically improving infants because of false positives from contaminants and because most relapses present clinically. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

options.text: Micturating cystourethrogram performed before discharge
options.rationale: MCUG carries radiation and procedural distress and is not in the RCH cascade for a first typical UTI. It is considered only for atypical or recurrent UTI or where the ultrasound is abnormal. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

explanation.summary: RCH UTI imaging cascade requires renal ultrasound for any infant under 6 months with a first UTI, ideally during the admission. DMSA and MCUG are reserved for atypical UTI (non-E. coli, sepsis, raised creatinine, poor 48-hour response, abdominal mass) or recurrent UTI.
key_points: Under 6 months first UTI: renal ultrasound (RCH); no routine DMSA or MCUG
Atypical UTI features trigger DMSA or MCUG: non-E. coli organism, sepsis, raised creatinine, abdominal mass, poor 48-hour response
RCH diverges from NICE: do NOT auto-cite KHA-CARI or NICE thresholds when AU practice is RCH
explanation.pearls: Atypical UTI is itself an indication for inpatient renal ultrasound during the admission. The 6-month threshold reflects the higher prevalence of structural abnormalities in this age group and the limits of antenatal imaging.

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA fluid plan with cerebral oedema risk
stem:
A 6-year-old girl, body weight 20 kg, presents with a 1-week history of polyuria, polydipsia and 3 kg weight loss. She vomited three times today and is now drowsy.

The paediatric registrar has confirmed new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus with DKA. She is clinically about 7% dehydrated. There has been one fluid bolus of 10 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride given over 30 minutes for poor peripheral perfusion. Her conscious state is now stable with GCS 13.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140, BP 90/60 mmHg, RR 32 (Kussmaul pattern), SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, capillary refill 3 seconds, no focal neurology, no headache
data_table.Investigations: BSL 28 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.6, VBG pH 7.10 pCO2 18 mmHg HCO3 8 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), corrected sodium 138 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next fluid and insulin plan?

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol over 30 minutes to correct the metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is not routine in paediatric DKA because it does not improve recovery, can paradoxically lower CSF pH, and is associated with cerebral oedema. Reserved for life-threatening hyperkalaemia with cardiac instability. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetes Mellitus)

options.text: Commence 0.9% sodium chloride at maintenance with 7% deficit over 48 hours and insulin after 1 hour
options.rationale: RCH paediatric DKA pathway gives maintenance plus a deficit calculated at 5 to 8% over 48 hours (not 24), starts insulin after at least 1 hour of fluids at 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour, and uses 0.9% saline initially with potassium 40 mmol/L once urine is documented. This minimises the cerebral oedema risk that is highest in younger, sicker children with new-onset diabetes. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetes Mellitus)

options.text: Commence 5% dextrose / 0.45% sodium chloride immediately with insulin 0.1 unit/kg/hour bolus
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluids and an insulin bolus both increase the cerebral oedema risk in paediatric DKA. Initial fluids should be 0.9% sodium chloride; dextrose is added later when BSL falls below 14 to 15. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetes Mellitus)

options.text: Start subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin 0.1 unit/kg and intravenous fluids at maintenance only
options.rationale: Subcutaneous insulin in DKA gives unpredictable absorption with the peripheral vasoconstriction of dehydration; the standard is IV insulin infusion. Maintenance-only fluids underestimate the volume needed to correct dehydration. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetes Mellitus)

options.text: Repeat 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus then commence insulin 0.1 unit/kg/hour immediately
options.rationale: Aggressive bolus fluids and early insulin both raise the cerebral oedema risk in paediatric DKA. RCH and ISPAD permit one 10 mL/kg bolus only if shocked, then move to maintenance plus replacement over 48 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetes Mellitus)

explanation.summary: RCH paediatric DKA management replaces deficit slowly (over 48 hours) with isotonic saline and starts insulin at least 1 hour into fluids at 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour, to reduce cerebral oedema risk. Bicarbonate is not routine. Headache, drowsiness, irritability, bradycardia, or rising BP signal evolving cerebral oedema needing 3% saline or mannitol.
key_points: Replace deficit over 48 hours, not 24, in paediatric DKA
Start insulin 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour after at least 1 hour of fluid - no bolus
Sodium bicarbonate is contraindicated for routine paediatric DKA correction
explanation.pearls: Cerebral oedema usually presents 4 to 12 hours after starting treatment. Risk factors: age under 5, new-onset diabetes, severe acidosis, high blood urea, treatment with bicarbonate, rapid fluid replacement. Treat with 3% saline 3 to 5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg IV.

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease diagnosis and IVIG decision
stem:
A 14-month-old boy of Korean heritage has had 7 days of fever, peaking at 39.6 °C, unresponsive to paracetamol and ibuprofen. He is irritable but consolable. His mother reports he had a rash for 24 hours on day 3 that has now resolved and one episode of conjunctival redness without discharge that also resolved. He has had no cervical lymphadenopathy and no mucosal changes.

The paediatric registrar has reviewed and the AHA "incomplete Kawasaki" supplementary criteria have been considered. An echocardiogram has been ordered.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 39.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Irritable, mild peri-anal desquamation, no oral mucosal changes today, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no rash visible, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: WCC 19 x10^9/L (5-15), neutrophils 14 x10^9/L (1.5-8), platelets 612 x10^9/L (150-400) on day 7, CRP 156 mg/L (<5), ESR 78 mm/hr (<20), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), ALT 96 U/L (<45), Na 132 mmol/L (135-145), urinalysis 25 leukocytes/HPF with sterile culture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg for occult bacteraemia and reassess in 24 hours
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone for occult bacteraemia in a stable child does not address the highly elevated cardiovascular risk of incomplete Kawasaki and risks delaying IVIG past the 10-day treatment window. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Await echocardiogram and treat only if coronary artery dilatation is documented
options.rationale: Awaiting echocardiogram for confirmation delays IVIG. Coronary aneurysms develop in 25% of untreated cases; the window for prevention by IVIG closes around day 10. Echocardiogram informs prognosis but the decision to treat in incomplete Kawasaki is laboratory-criteria driven. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence intravenous flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
options.rationale: SSSS presents with widespread erythema and bullae, not isolated peri-anal desquamation in a child without oral mucosal changes. The laboratory pattern (thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, raised ALT, sterile pyuria) points away from staphylococcal infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse for 3 days as primary therapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroid pulse is reserved for patients at very high risk of IVIG resistance (Kobayashi score, age <12 months, severe anaemia) and used as adjunct to IVIG rather than primary monotherapy. Primary monotherapy with steroids is not AU standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with high-dose aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg in four divided doses
options.rationale: This presentation meets the AHA / RCH criteria for incomplete Kawasaki: fever 5 or more days with fewer than 4 classic criteria, plus supportive laboratory features (4 of: CRP ≥3, ESR ≥40, platelets ≥450 after day 7, albumin ≤30, sterile pyuria, ALT raised, WCC ≥15, anaemia for age). She meets 6 of 7 laboratory criteria so treatment proceeds even before echocardiogram returns - delaying IVIG past day 10 increases coronary aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki is diagnosed when there are fewer than 4 of the 5 classic criteria but the child has prolonged fever and supportive laboratory features. RCH and AHA use the 6-of-7 laboratory criteria to confirm. IVIG 2 g/kg and aspirin must be given by day 10 to minimise coronary aneurysm risk - do not wait for echocardiogram.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki uses 6 laboratory criteria (CRP, ESR, platelets, albumin, ALT, pyuria, WCC, anaemia) to confirm when classical criteria are not met
IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 hours with high-dose aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg/day is the AU first-line regimen
Day 10 of illness is the IVIG-window cut-off for preventing coronary aneurysm
explanation.pearls: Aspirin is one of the few paediatric indications where the Reye's risk is accepted because of the larger cardiovascular benefit. Switch to low-dose aspirin (3 to 5 mg/kg/day) once afebrile for 48 hours, continue for 6 to 8 weeks until repeat echo at 6 to 8 weeks. Risk of IVIG resistance is up to 20%; second-dose IVIG or infliximab are options.

stem:
A 15-year-old previously well girl is brought in by her parents with a 10-day history of progressive personality change. They report new agitation, paranoid statements that strangers are stealing from her, and a 4 kg weight loss. Yesterday she had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds with full recovery, and this morning she developed orofacial dyskinesias and rhythmic limb posturing. There has been no fever, no recent infection, no overseas travel, and no drug use.

The family history is unremarkable. Toxicology screen on arrival is negative. She is currently being investigated as part of a paediatric neurology workup.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Fluctuant agitation alternating with mutism, intermittent orofacial dyskinesia, mild autonomic instability with episodic BP swings, no focal weakness, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: FBC and UEC within normal limits, CRP 4 mg/L (<5), MRI brain normal, EEG generalised slowing without focal epileptiform activity, CSF protein 0.42 g/L (0.15-0.45) lymphocytes 18 x10^6/L (<5) glucose 3.6 mmol/L (paired BSL 5.2), HSV PCR negative, serum and CSF anti-NMDA receptor antibodies pending
data_table.Medications: Lorazepam 2 mg IV given for dyskinesia 1 hour ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to mental health for first-episode psychosis and start olanzapine 10 mg orally daily
options.rationale: Treating this as primary psychosis misses the encephalitic features (dyskinesias, seizure, autonomic instability, CSF pleocytosis) that mandate organic workup and immunotherapy. Antipsychotics also worsen NMS-like reactions and movement disorders in anti-NMDA encephalitis. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange routine MRI brain with contrast on the next available outpatient slot and review in clinic
options.rationale: An outpatient delay misses the inpatient time-critical immunotherapy window. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis has up to 25% mortality if untreated and 80% functional recovery with early immunotherapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Encephalitis)

options.text: Commence high-dose methylprednisolone and IVIG and arrange pelvic ultrasound for ovarian teratoma
options.rationale: Subacute psychiatric prodrome plus seizures plus orofacial dyskinesias plus autonomic instability plus a CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis is the textbook anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis presentation. AU paediatric neurology starts first-line immunotherapy (steroid plus IVIG, plus or minus plasma exchange) empirically before the antibody result returns, because delay worsens outcomes. Ovarian teratoma is identified in up to half of post-pubertal girls and removal is curative. (Source: RCH CPG: Encephalitis)

options.text: Commence intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg three times daily and complete a 14-day course pending HSV PCR
options.rationale: Aciclovir is appropriate empirical cover for HSV encephalitis until the PCR returns, but the CSF HSV PCR is already negative, and the constellation of orofacial dyskinesias and prolonged psychiatric prodrome is not HSV. Continuing aciclovir to 14 days when PCR is negative does not address the autoimmune diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Encephalitis)

options.text: Commence levetiracetam 60 mg/kg/day for seizure prophylaxis without other intervention
options.rationale: Antiepileptic monotherapy treats the seizure symptom but not the underlying autoimmune encephalitis; the dyskinesias, autonomic instability, and progressive course will worsen and the prognosis depends on early immunotherapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Encephalitis)

explanation.summary: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis in adolescents and young adults presents with a subacute psychiatric prodrome, seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic instability and CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis. AU first-line immunotherapy is steroid plus IVIG plus or minus plasma exchange, started empirically before antibody confirmation. Ovarian teratoma is present in up to half of post-pubertal girls and is curative when removed.
key_points: The psychiatric prodrome can dominate the early picture and delay the diagnosis - always do an organic workup including CSF in subacute psychosis with movement disorder
First-line immunotherapy: steroid + IVIG plus or minus plasma exchange, before antibody confirmation
Look for ovarian teratoma in post-pubertal girls and testicular tumour in young men
explanation.pearls: Rituximab and cyclophosphamide are second-line if first-line therapies fail at 10 to 14 days. Antipsychotics commonly worsen the dyskinetic features and may cause NMS-like reactions; minimise their use. The CSF anti-NMDA antibody is more sensitive than serum and should be sent.

subtopic_detail: Methaemoglobinaemia in infant from topical anaesthetic
stem:
A 5-month-old boy is brought to ED 90 minutes after his mother applied a generous layer of an over-the-counter teething gel containing benzocaine to his gums every 30 minutes for the past 3 hours. She thought he was teething because of poor sleep. He has become progressively pale and dusky around the lips despite warming and looks slate-grey on inspection.

Nasal cannula oxygen at 4 L/min has not changed his appearance. He is alert.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 84/52 mmHg, RR 56, SpO2 86% on 4 L/min nasal-prong oxygen (unchanged on 8 L/min), temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Slate-grey central cyanosis, no respiratory distress beyond tachypnoea, chest clear, capillary refill 2 seconds, alert with normal tone
data_table.Investigations: Arterial blood gas pH 7.36 pCO2 36 mmHg pO2 198 mmHg on 8 L/min, lactate 1.8; co-oximetry methaemoglobin level 32% (<2%), Hb 110 g/L (95-130); chest X-ray clear
data_table.Medications: Benzocaine teething gel (frequent application in last 3 hours)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence broad-spectrum antibiotics for sepsis with cyanosis
options.rationale: He is afebrile, well-perfused, alert, with a normal CRP and lactate; the saturation gap between pulse oximetry 86% and pO2 198 on ABG is pathognomonic of dyshaemoglobinaemia, not sepsis. (Source: RCH CPG: Methaemoglobinaemia)

options.text: Administer methylene blue 1 mg/kg intravenously over 5 minutes
options.rationale: Methaemoglobinaemia above 30% with end-organ symptoms (or 20 to 30% with risk factors) requires methylene blue 1 to 2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes. Co-oximetry confirms methaemoglobin (standard pulse oximeters read falsely around 85% as both forms absorb the same wavelength). Topical benzocaine in infants is a recognised AU and US public-health warning trigger. (Source: RCH CPG: Methaemoglobinaemia)

options.text: Administer ascorbic acid 200 mg intravenously and observe
options.rationale: Ascorbic acid reduces methaemoglobin slowly over hours and is reserved for patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency where methylene blue is contraindicated, or as second-line. With 32% met-Hb the slower reductant is not first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Methaemoglobinaemia)

options.text: Increase oxygen to 15 L/min via non-rebreather and observe
options.rationale: Methaemoglobin cannot carry oxygen; raising FiO2 raises dissolved oxygen modestly but does not address the underlying defect. The persistently low pulse-oximetry reading despite high pO2 on ABG is the give-away. (Source: RCH CPG: Methaemoglobinaemia)

options.text: Arrange transfusion of one unit of packed red blood cells
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is third-line for refractory or G6PD-deficient methaemoglobinaemia where methylene blue and ascorbic acid are ineffective or contraindicated. Methylene blue is faster and avoids transfusion exposure. (Source: RCH CPG: Methaemoglobinaemia)

explanation.summary: Topical benzocaine is the classic AU paediatric trigger for acquired methaemoglobinaemia in young infants because of reduced NADH-methaemoglobin reductase activity. Clinical features are slate-grey cyanosis, refractory pulse oximeter saturation gap (Sp 85% with normal pO2 on ABG), and chocolate-brown blood. Treat with methylene blue 1 to 2 mg/kg IV.
key_points: Methylene blue 1 to 2 mg/kg IV is first-line above 30% met-Hb or 20 to 30% with symptoms
Pulse oximetry reads about 85% in significant methaemoglobinaemia regardless of true oxygen saturation - co-oximetry is required
Avoid methylene blue in G6PD deficiency - use ascorbic acid or exchange transfusion
explanation.pearls: AU consumer regulators have warned against benzocaine teething gels in infants under 2 years for exactly this reason. Other paediatric triggers include nitrites in deli meats, dapsone, prilocaine (EMLA), nitrate-contaminated water in bore-water rural settings.

stem:
A 4-month-old boy is brought to the paediatric emergency department by his parents in winter with 3 days of runny nose, cough and noisy breathing. He has been feeding only half his usual volumes for 24 hours and his nappies are drier. He was born at 38 weeks and has had no previous admissions. His parents are non-smokers and he is up to date with immunisations.

He has been on nasal prong oxygen 1.5 L/min for 2 hours since arrival. The bedside nurse asks you to review him because his work of breathing has worsened over the last 20 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 72, SpO2 89% on nasal prong 1.5 L/min, temperature 37.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert but tiring, marked subcostal and intercostal recession, head bobbing, widespread fine inspiratory crackles and expiratory wheeze, capillary refill 2 seconds, no apnoeas observed
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.30, pCO2 56 mmHg, HCO3 26, lactate 1.6; nasopharyngeal viral PCR pending; chest X-ray hyperinflation with no focal consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Commence humidified high-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis pathway escalates to HFNC at 2 L/kg/min after failure of low-flow nasal prong (defined by persisting work of breathing, SpO2 below 90% despite 1-2 L/min, or rising CO2) for at least 1-2 hours. HFNC provides PEEP and washout of upper-airway dead space; trials including PARIS support its use for moderate-severe bronchiolitis under 12 months. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Start nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back-to-back for three doses
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months and add no benefit in this age group; trials show no change in admission rate or oxygen requirement. They are not part of the RCH bronchiolitis algorithm. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Give a single intramuscular dose of dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not change outcome in bronchiolitis and are not recommended in the RCH guideline. Dexamethasone has a role in croup, not bronchiolitis. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Intubate and commence pressure-controlled ventilation
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for true respiratory failure (severe acidosis, recurrent apnoeas, exhaustion despite HFNC). A pH of 7.30 with mild hypercapnia and a tiring but alert infant is an indication to escalate to HFNC before considering invasive ventilation. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Trial nebulised hypertonic saline 3% with chest physiotherapy
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline has inconsistent evidence and is not first-line escalation in RCH guidance. Routine chest physiotherapy is contraindicated in bronchiolitis as it does not improve outcomes and can worsen distress. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: RCH bronchiolitis pathway uses low-flow nasal prong oxygen 1-2 L/min as first-line, with SpO2 target of 90%. HFNC at 2 L/kg/min is the next-step escalation when low-flow fails after a 1-2 hour trial, indicated by persisting work of breathing, falling SpO2, or rising CO2. Bronchodilators, steroids and routine physiotherapy are NOT used in bronchiolitis under 12 months. Intubation is reserved for HFNC failure or apnoeas.
key_points: RCH SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is 90% (not 92-94%)
Low-flow 1-2 L/min first; HFNC 2 L/kg/min only after low-flow fails
Bronchodilators, steroids and routine physiotherapy not recommended under 12 months
explanation.pearls: PARIS trial supports HFNC for escalation only; do not start it before a low-flow trial as it does not reduce ICU admission compared with standard oxygen as primary therapy.

stem:
A 9-year-old girl with known asthma is brought to the paediatric resuscitation bay by ambulance after 6 hours of worsening shortness of breath at home. She normally uses fluticasone 100 mcg twice daily and salbutamol PRN. Her last admission was 18 months ago with a 2-day ward stay.

On arrival paramedics had given continuous nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium and a single oral prednisolone dose. She has had three back-to-back salbutamol/ipratropium nebulisers in the resuscitation bay over the last 20 minutes with minimal change. The paediatric registrar is at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 152, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 44, SpO2 90% on 8 L/min via face mask, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Sitting forward, speaking 2-3 word sentences, subcostal recession, widespread expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry bilaterally, no silent chest, alert and frightened
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.34, pCO2 44 mmHg (rising from 38 on arrival), HCO3 23, lactate 3.2; chest X-ray hyperinflation, no pneumothorax
data_table.Medications: Salbutamol 2.5 mg/ipratropium 250 mcg back-to-back nebulisers x 3, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg given 30 minutes ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to continuous nebulised salbutamol 10 mg/hour for the next hour
options.rationale: Continuous salbutamol provides no benefit over back-to-back dosing once delivery is already maximised; this patient has already failed three back-to-back nebulisers with rising CO2 and lactate. Escalation, not repetition, is needed. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes
options.rationale: RCH severe acute asthma pathway escalates to IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes after failure of inhaled bronchodilators and systemic corticosteroid. Magnesium acts as a smooth muscle relaxant and is the first parenteral agent to add. The rising CO2 and lactate plus reduced air entry indicate severe disease requiring this step. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Commence intravenous aminophylline loading dose 5 mg/kg over 60 minutes
options.rationale: IV aminophylline is reserved for asthma not responding to magnesium AND salbutamol infusion; it is a later-line agent because of its narrow therapeutic index. Magnesium is the next escalation here. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline 10 mcg/kg into the lateral thigh
options.rationale: Intramuscular adrenaline is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, not for acute asthma without anaphylactic features. There is no urticaria, angioedema, or hypotension to suggest anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Intubate and ventilate after rapid-sequence induction with ketamine
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for actual or imminent respiratory arrest (exhaustion, silent chest, coma, or severe acidosis). This child is alert, talking in short sentences and has not yet had IV magnesium - parenteral pharmacotherapy is the next step before intubation. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: Severe asthma not responding to inhaled bronchodilators and oral steroid escalates to IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes per the RCH pathway. IV salbutamol infusion (5 mcg/kg/min) is the next addition if magnesium fails. Aminophylline is third-line. Intubation is reserved for true respiratory failure - alert, talking patients are managed pharmacologically first.
key_points: RCH severe asthma escalation order: nebulised salbutamol/ipratropium -> oral steroid -> IV magnesium -> IV salbutamol -> aminophylline
IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes
Intubation reserved for actual or imminent respiratory arrest
explanation.pearls: A rising CO2 from a previously hyperventilating asthmatic is a red flag for fatigue; the venous pCO2 normalising or rising in severe asthma signals decompensation rather than improvement.

stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the paediatric emergency department at 2 am by his parents with a 12-hour history of barking cough and 2 hours of noisy breathing. He has had a coryzal illness for 3 days. He is not immunised against any disease because his parents have not yet engaged with their GP. He has no previous admissions and no known allergies.

On the way to the ambulance bay he became increasingly distressed. The triage nurse has placed him in his mother's lap in the resuscitation cubicle and called you.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 93% in room air, temperature 38.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Loud biphasic stridor at rest, marked tracheal tug and intercostal recession, agitated and clinging to mother, barking cough, no drooling, no trismus, no neck swelling
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed - imaging or bloods would distress the child further

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose and discharge home after 1 hour observation
options.rationale: 0.15 mg/kg is the RCH dose for mild to moderate croup. This child has biphasic stridor at rest with tracheal tug and agitation - severe croup. He needs the higher dose AND nebulised adrenaline, with longer observation. Discharge after 1 hour is unsafe. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as monotherapy and admit for observation
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is an alternative when oral or IV dexamethasone is not tolerated, but it is not the first-line monotherapy in severe croup. Dexamethasone (oral or IV) with concurrent nebulised adrenaline is the standard combination. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg with concurrent nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000
options.rationale: Severe croup (stridor at rest with marked respiratory distress or agitation) is treated with dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally (or IV/IM if oral not tolerated) AND nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 (a flat dose, not per kg). Observe for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline nebuliser because of rebound. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg empirically with airway preparation in theatre
options.rationale: There is no drooling, no tripod position, no muffled voice and no marked toxicity to suggest epiglottitis. Manipulation including IV cannulation in a child with possible epiglottitis is contraindicated. Empirical antibiotics are not part of croup management. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Intubate in theatre with an anaesthetist and ENT surgeon present
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for impending or actual airway obstruction unresponsive to medical therapy. Initial management with steroid plus nebulised adrenaline resolves the majority of severe croup. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: Severe croup is defined by stridor at rest with marked retractions, decreased air entry or agitation. Treatment is oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (0.15 mg/kg is mild-moderate) PLUS nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 (flat dose). Minimum observation 3 hours after the last adrenaline dose because of rebound stridor.
key_points: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild-moderate, 0.6 mg/kg for severe
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 is a FLAT dose, not weight-based
Observe minimum 3 hours after last nebulised adrenaline
explanation.pearls: If a child needs more than 2-3 doses of nebulised adrenaline within an hour, escalate to ICU for closer monitoring or consideration of airway support; rebound is a normal phenomenon, not a treatment failure marker.

stem:
A 6-week-old girl is brought to the children's hospital ED by her mother with a 9-day history of cough. She was born at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery and has been well otherwise. Her mother declined the pertussis vaccine in pregnancy. Her older brother (age 4) has had a runny nose and cough for 3 weeks.

Her cough comes in clusters and she goes red and then briefly blue with the spells, followed by exhausted feeding. Between spells she looks well. She has had two brief pauses in breathing during spells today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 144, BP 78/46 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 96% in room air between spells (drops to 88% during spells), temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Well-perfused between spells, chest clear, no recession at rest, paroxysmal coughing fits with brief facial cyanosis observed
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 32 x10^9/L with marked lymphocytosis 22 x10^9/L (1.5-8.5), CRP 6 mg/L, chest X-ray clear, nasopharyngeal PCR pertussis pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with safety-netting advice and outpatient follow-up review in 3 days
options.rationale: Infants under 6 months with paroxysmal cough and observed apnoea or cyanosis must be admitted regardless of how well they appear between spells, because apnoea, secondary pneumonia and pulmonary hypertension can develop rapidly. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Admit for inpatient cardiorespiratory observation alone while awaiting PCR confirmation
options.rationale: Empirical treatment should not wait for PCR confirmation when clinical suspicion is high (paroxysmal cough, cyanotic spells, marked lymphocytosis, contact, unimmunised). Delaying treatment delays infectivity reduction and prolongs household risk. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Admit and start intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily for community-acquired pneumonia
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone covers neither Bordetella pertussis nor the clinical picture, which is consistent with pertussis rather than bacterial pneumonia (clear chest, no infiltrate, classic paroxysms with lymphocytosis). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit and start oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days plus contact prophylaxis
options.rationale: RCH and the Australian Immunisation Handbook recommend macrolide treatment for pertussis in infants under 6 months. Azithromycin (10 mg/kg daily for 5 days) is preferred in this age group because erythromycin in under-1-month-olds is associated with pyloric stenosis - azithromycin is the safer macrolide. Treatment reduces infectivity and household contacts (especially the older brother and pregnant women) need prophylaxis. Admission is mandatory for monitoring of apnoea and oxygen need. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit and start oral erythromycin 10 mg/kg four times daily for 7 days with monitoring
options.rationale: Erythromycin in infants under 1 month is associated with pyloric stenosis and is no longer preferred. Azithromycin is the recommended macrolide for young infants. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Pertussis in infants under 6 months is treated with azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days and requires admission for monitoring of apnoea, cyanotic spells and secondary complications. Household contacts (especially under-6-month-olds and pregnant women) need prophylaxis. Erythromycin is avoided under 1 month because of pyloric stenosis association. Treatment reduces infectivity even if started in the paroxysmal phase.
key_points: Azithromycin preferred over erythromycin in under-1-month-olds (pyloric stenosis)
