Admit all under-6-month-olds with pertussis for monitoring
Household contact prophylaxis essential
explanation.pearls: Marked lymphocytosis (>20 x10^9/L) with normal CRP in an infant with paroxysmal cough is highly suggestive of pertussis; raise the index of suspicion even before PCR returns.

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media in young child
stem:
A 19-month-old Aboriginal boy presents with his mother to the remote area clinic with 36 hours of ear pulling and fever to 39.0 °C. He was treated for an acute otitis media in the same ear 6 weeks ago with a 5-day course of amoxicillin. He has been drinking less but is still wetting nappies normally. He has had two previous courses of antibiotics for ear infections this year.

Today he is irritable but consolable. His mother says he has been pulling at the same ear and crying with feeds.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Right tympanic membrane bulging, opaque and erythematous with no perforation; left tympanic membrane normal; no mastoid tenderness or post-auricular swelling; alert and consolable
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Watchful waiting for 48 to 72 hours with paracetamol cover and clinical review
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is appropriate for non-severe acute otitis media in healthy children over 2 years; Aboriginal children, those under 2 years, those with severe symptoms or recurrent episodes warrant immediate antibiotics because of high rates of chronic suppurative otitis media. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral cefuroxime 15 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days as second-line cover
options.rationale: Cefuroxime is not the preferred first or second-line agent for acute otitis media in Australian guidelines. Amoxicillin at high dose or amoxicillin-clavulanate are preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 3 days as second-line cover
options.rationale: Azithromycin has poor activity against drug-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most common organism in acute otitis media after recent amoxicillin exposure, and is not recommended as a first or second-line agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 50 mg/kg as a single one-off dose
options.rationale: Intramuscular benzathine penicillin is used for syphilis, group A strep eradication and rheumatic fever prophylaxis. It is not a treatment for acute otitis media; it does not provide useful middle-ear concentrations of beta-lactamase-resistant cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days as second-line
options.rationale: When acute otitis media recurs within 30 days of amoxicillin OR fails high-dose amoxicillin, Australian guidelines escalate to amoxicillin-clavulanate to cover beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis. Aboriginal children with recurrent AOM are prioritised for immediate treatment because of high rates of chronic suppurative otitis media. The 5-day course is appropriate for this age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in Aboriginal children, those under 2 years, or with recurrent episodes warrants immediate antibiotic therapy because of the high risk of chronic suppurative otitis media. First-line is high-dose amoxicillin 30 mg/kg every 8 hours for 5 days; recurrence within 30 days or failure escalates to amoxicillin-clavulanate. Watchful waiting is reserved for non-severe AOM in over-2-year-olds without these risk factors.
key_points: Aboriginal children with AOM are not candidates for watchful waiting
Recurrence within 30 days of amoxicillin escalates to amoxicillin-clavulanate
5-day course for under 2 years, longer courses NOT routinely needed
explanation.pearls: Chronic suppurative otitis media prevalence in remote Aboriginal communities can exceed 10-20%; aggressive treatment of acute episodes plus regular ENT follow-up is the cornerstone of preventing conductive hearing loss and educational impact.

stem:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the paediatric outpatient clinic by her parents with an 18-month history of infrequent stools. She passes hard pebble-like stools every 4 to 6 days with abdominal pain and occasional soiling of her underwear between motions. She has tried lactulose and dietary fibre for 8 weeks without improvement. She is otherwise developmentally normal, has been growing along the 50th centile and has no red flags.

Her parents report she now actively withholds stool because passing them is painful.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen with a palpable faecal mass in the left lower quadrant; perianal inspection unremarkable; spine and lower limb neurology unremarkable; growth on the 50th centile for weight and height
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated - functional constipation is a clinical diagnosis
data_table.Medications: Lactulose 10 mL twice daily for 8 weeks (poor response)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral macrogol 3350 disimpaction for 3 days then maintenance dose for 6 months
options.rationale: Functional constipation with a palpable faecal mass on examination indicates impaction, which must be treated with a disimpaction regimen before maintenance therapy can work. Macrogol 3350 (PEG with electrolytes) at escalating disimpaction dose for 3 to 7 days is first-line in Australian and international guidance, followed by maintenance dose for at least 6 months to prevent relapse. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Increase the lactulose dose and add senna stimulant at bedtime for 8 weeks
options.rationale: Lactulose has already failed for 8 weeks. Stimulant laxatives like senna may be added later in maintenance, but disimpaction with macrogol is the priority when there is a palpable faecal mass. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Refer for a contrast enema study to exclude Hirschsprung disease this week
options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease typically presents in the first weeks of life with delayed passage of meconium or in the first year with failure to thrive. A normally growing 5-year-old with classic withholding behaviour does not require structural imaging. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Admit for a phosphate enema and digital rectal examination under anaesthetic
options.rationale: Phosphate enemas are reserved for failure of oral disimpaction and have significant electrolyte risks (hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia) in young children. Anaesthetic disimpaction is a last resort. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Refer to paediatric gastroenterology for anorectal manometry under sedation
options.rationale: Anorectal manometry is used when an organic cause is suspected (Hirschsprung disease, anorectal dysmotility). In the absence of red flags, functional constipation is a clinical diagnosis and treated empirically with macrogol first. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation with faecal impaction is treated with macrogol 3350 (PEG with electrolytes) at disimpaction dose for 3 to 7 days, followed by maintenance dose for at least 6 months. Lactulose alone is often insufficient. Behavioural toileting program and education about withholding are essential adjuncts. Red flags (failure to thrive, delayed meconium, neurological signs) require structural workup.
key_points: Disimpaction with macrogol before maintenance therapy
Maintenance for at least 6 months to prevent relapse
Lactulose is inferior to macrogol for disimpaction
explanation.pearls: Soiling between hard stools is overflow soiling, not encopresis as a primary behavioural issue; treating the constipation resolves the soiling without the need for behavioural therapy in most cases.

stem:
A term male newborn weighing 4.6 kg (above 97th centile) is admitted to the neonatal unit on day 1 with recurrent symptomatic hypoglycaemia. He was born at 39 weeks by emergency caesarean section for failure to progress to a 32-year-old G2P1 woman whose pregnancy was complicated by gestational diabetes treated with insulin from 28 weeks. The baby developed jitteriness and a low blood glucose of 1.4 mmol/L at 90 minutes after birth, treated with feeds and IV dextrose.

He has now required escalating dextrose infusions. Despite a glucose infusion rate of 14 mg/kg/min he has had two further symptomatic episodes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 162, BP 64/38 mmHg, RR 52, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Macrosomic, mild plethora, no obvious dysmorphism, no organomegaly, no umbilical defect, tone slightly reduced when hypoglycaemic, normal between episodes; cardiac and respiratory examinations within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: BSL during episode 1.6 mmol/L (>2.6); insulin 18 mIU/L (suppressed when normoglycaemic), C-peptide elevated, beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.1 mmol/L (low), free fatty acids low, ammonia 38 micromol/L (<50), cortisol 380 nmol/L, growth hormone 14 mIU/L, lactate 1.1; karyotype 46XY pending; abdominal ultrasound and brain MRI unremarkable; ear examination normal pinnae
data_table.Medications: Intravenous 10% dextrose at 12.5 mg/kg/min glucose infusion rate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase glucose infusion rate to 18 mg/kg/min through a central venous line
options.rationale: Persistent glucose infusion rates above 10 mg/kg/min in a macrosomic infant with detectable insulin during hypoglycaemia, low ketones and low free fatty acids confirms congenital hyperinsulinism. Simply pushing more dextrose treats the symptom not the cause and risks fluid overload and hyperosmolality - pharmacotherapy is now indicated. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Commence oral diazoxide 5 mg/kg per day in divided doses plus chlorothiazide
options.rationale: Congenital hyperinsulinism is the diagnosis: persistent hypoglycaemia with glucose infusion rate above 10 mg/kg/min, detectable insulin during a low BSL, suppressed ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate below 1.5 mmol/L) and suppressed free fatty acids. Diazoxide opens KATP channels on beta cells to suppress insulin secretion; chlorothiazide is added to counter sodium and fluid retention and may potentiate the effect. Diazoxide responsiveness suggests a focal or diffuse KATP channel disorder amenable to medical therapy; non-response triggers 18F-DOPA PET to localise focal lesions for partial pancreatectomy. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Start hydrocortisone 5 mg/kg per day for possibly inadequate stress cortisol
options.rationale: Cortisol of 380 nmol/L during stress is appropriate; hydrocortisone is not indicated and does not address hyperinsulinism. Stress-dose steroid would only apply if adrenal insufficiency were proven. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Refer urgently for partial pancreatectomy without medical trial of diazoxide
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for diazoxide-unresponsive focal disease confirmed by 18F-DOPA PET. A medical trial is essential before surgical referral. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Continue current management as macrosomic infants typically resolve by 72 hours
options.rationale: Infant-of-diabetic-mother hyperinsulinism usually resolves by 48 to 72 hours and does not require a glucose infusion rate above 10 mg/kg/min. Persistent requirement at this level points to congenital hyperinsulinism rather than transient. The biochemistry (low ketones, low FFA, detectable insulin) confirms this. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: Congenital hyperinsulinism is diagnosed by hypoglycaemia with detectable insulin, suppressed ketones (BOHB below 1.5 mmol/L) and low free fatty acids, plus a glucose infusion rate above 10 mg/kg/min. First-line therapy is diazoxide with chlorothiazide. Non-responders undergo 18F-DOPA PET to identify focal versus diffuse disease - focal lesions are cured by partial pancreatectomy while diffuse disease requires near-total pancreatectomy with subsequent diabetes risk.
key_points: Glucose infusion rate above 10 mg/kg/min is the threshold for diagnosing hyperinsulinism
Diazoxide opens KATP channels; chlorothiazide is added for synergy and to counter fluid retention
18F-DOPA PET differentiates focal from diffuse disease in diazoxide non-responders
explanation.pearls: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is on the differential for hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia in a macrosomic baby - look for macroglossia, ear pits/creases, omphalocele, hemihypertrophy, and order methylation studies of 11p15.5 if features are present.

stem:
A term male newborn becomes cyanotic in the postnatal ward at 6 hours of age. He was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery to a 28-year-old G1P0 woman with no antenatal concerns; her 20-week anomaly scan was reported as normal. Apgars were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. He fed once at the breast and pinked up initially.

On nursing review for cyanosis he has central blue discolouration but is not in respiratory distress. The paediatric registrar is at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 162, BP 64/40 mmHg in right arm and 62/38 mmHg in right calf, RR 48, SpO2 65% pre-ductal (right hand) and 64% post-ductal (right foot), temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Centrally cyanosed, well perfused, no respiratory distress, single S2 with no murmur, femoral pulses palpable and equal, liver not enlarged, no facial features of trisomy 21 or DiGeorge phenotype
data_table.Investigations: Hyperoxia test SpO2 rose to 69% after 10 minutes in 100% O2 face mask; chest X-ray shows narrow superior mediastinum with "egg on side" cardiac silhouette and pulmonary plethora; ECG normal neonatal axis; capillary blood gas pH 7.32, pCO2 38, lactate 2.6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase inspired oxygen to FiO2 1.0 by head box and reassess in 20 minutes
options.rationale: The hyperoxia test has already failed (SpO2 rose only marginally with FiO2 1.0). Continuing to push oxygen has minimal benefit in fixed right-to-left shunting and may even close the ductus in some duct-dependent lesions, worsening cyanosis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Intubate, ventilate and administer surfactant via the endotracheal tube immediately
options.rationale: There is no tachypnoea or respiratory distress and the chest X-ray shows a cardiac silhouette, not the ground-glass appearance of RDS. Cyanosis without distress and a failed hyperoxia test points to cyanotic congenital heart disease. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) 10 ng/kg/min and urgent echo
options.rationale: Cyanosis with a failed hyperoxia test, egg-on-side cardiac silhouette and equal pre and post-ductal saturations is highly suggestive of transposition of the great arteries (TGA) with restricted intracardiac mixing. The duct must be kept open with prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) starting at 10 nanograms/kg/min until urgent echo confirms the diagnosis and a balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind) or arterial switch can be planned. Lower starting doses (5 to 10 ng/kg/min) reduce apnoea risk compared with the older 50 ng/kg/min dose. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Administer intramuscular vitamin K plus intravenous furosemide for cardiac failure
options.rationale: Vitamin K should already have been given routinely; diuretics treat pulmonary congestion but the issue here is fixed right-to-left shunt requiring ductal patency, not pulmonary overcirculation alone. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Perform four-limb blood pressure measurement and arrange aortic CT angiogram
options.rationale: Four-limb BPs have already been recorded as equal; coarctation typically presents with weak femoral pulses and right-arm-to-leg gradient, not equal pressures with cyanosis. Echocardiography is the first-line modality, not CT. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: Cyanosis with failed hyperoxia test (PaO2 fails to rise above 100 mmHg or SpO2 below 90% in FiO2 1.0) indicates duct-dependent cyanotic congenital heart disease until proven otherwise. Start prostaglandin E1 at 10 nanograms/kg/min and arrange urgent echocardiography. TGA classically shows an egg-on-side cardiac silhouette and equal pre and post-ductal saturations because mixing depends on PFO/ASD plus PDA. Lower-dose PGE1 (10 ng/kg/min) reduces apnoea while maintaining ductal patency.
key_points: Failed hyperoxia test = cyanotic congenital heart disease until proven otherwise
TGA: equal pre and post-ductal saturations, egg-on-side cardiac silhouette
Prostaglandin E1 10 ng/kg/min - lower doses reduce apnoea risk
explanation.pearls: Equal pre and post-ductal saturations rule out simple right-to-left ductal shunting (which gives a saturation gradient); they suggest fixed intracardiac mixing as in TGA. A balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure) is often the first definitive intervention before arterial switch.

stem:
A 9-month-old boy is brought to the children's hospital emergency department by his mother. Over the past 18 hours he has had episodes of inconsolable crying lasting 10 to 15 minutes during which he draws his legs up to his tummy, then falls asleep exhausted between episodes. He had a single episode of redcurrant jelly nappy this morning and his mother says he has been pale and very tired. He had a runny nose a week ago.

He last fed 6 hours ago and has vomited twice. The paediatric surgical registrar has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 156, BP 92/56 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 37.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Sleepy but rousable, slightly pale, soft abdomen with a palpable long thin lump in the right upper quadrant during a quiet period; no peritonism, no abdominal distension; capillary refill 2 seconds; rectal inspection shows red mucoid stool on the gloved finger
data_table.Investigations: FBC haemoglobin 108 g/L (105-135), WCC 14 x10^9/L; UEC within normal limits; venous blood gas pH 7.36, lactate 2.0; abdominal ultrasound shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant consistent with ileocolic intussusception, no free fluid, no pneumatosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial of bowel rest with intravenous fluid resuscitation and reassess in 6 hours
options.rationale: Conservative observation risks bowel ischaemia and perforation. Once intussusception is confirmed on ultrasound and there is no contraindication, reduction should proceed promptly. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Proceed immediately to open laparotomy for manual reduction without enema trial
options.rationale: Surgical reduction is reserved for failed pneumatic/hydrostatic reduction, peritonitis, free intraperitoneal air or shock. None of these are present, so a non-operative approach should be attempted first. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy to look for a pathological lead point before reduction
options.rationale: A pathological lead point (Meckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma) is more common in children over 2 years or recurrent cases; in a 9-month-old with classic presentation and ultrasound diagnosis, non-operative reduction is first-line and laparoscopy is reserved for failures or atypical cases. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Resuscitate with intravenous fluids then proceed to air enema with surgical standby
options.rationale: Air enema (or hydrostatic) reduction with fluoroscopic guidance is the first-line treatment for uncomplicated ileocolic intussusception, with success rates of 80 to 95%. Surgical standby is mandatory because of the 0.5 to 1% perforation risk during reduction. IV access, fluid resuscitation and theatre availability should be arranged before the procedure. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Insert nasogastric tube and give intravenous antibiotics with observation only
options.rationale: Antibiotic administration is appropriate adjunct but does not address the obstruction. The definitive next step is reduction (air enema), not observation. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception is the commonest cause of intestinal obstruction in 3 to 36-month-olds. Classic triad is intermittent severe colicky pain, palpable mass and redcurrant jelly stool, though most patients have only one or two features. Ultrasound (target sign) is diagnostic. First-line treatment is air enema reduction under fluoroscopy with surgical standby. Surgery is reserved for failure, perforation or shock.
key_points: Air enema reduction first-line, 80-95% success
Surgical standby mandatory because of 0.5-1% perforation risk
Surgery reserved for failed reduction, peritonitis, or shock
explanation.pearls: Children under 3 months or over 5 years with intussusception have a higher rate of pathological lead point; in these atypical age groups, plan for CT or laparoscopic assessment after reduction even if reduction succeeds.

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media in Aboriginal child
stem:
A 22-month-old Aboriginal girl is brought to your remote clinic by her mother with 2 days of fever and pulling at her right ear. Her mother reports she has been waking and crying at night and is feeding less. She is fully immunised, attends day care, and has had two previous similar episodes in the last six months. There is no ear discharge.

On examination she is irritable but consolable, and there is no neck stiffness or rash. The right tympanic membrane is bulging and opaque with no perforation; the left tympanic membrane appears normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Right ear: bulging opaque tympanic membrane, no discharge. Left ear normal. Throat injected without exudate. No cervical lymphadenopathy. Chest clear.
data_table.Investigations: Not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics and review in 48 hours with safety-net advice
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is the default for non-severe acute otitis media in low-risk children, but Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children have substantially higher rates of suppurative complications and chronic perforation, so eTG recommends prompt antibiotics rather than delayed prescribing in this group. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg twice daily for five days for this patient
options.rationale: First-line oral amoxicillin at the higher 30 mg/kg twice-daily dose for five days is the eTG-recommended regimen for acute otitis media in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children because of higher rates of chronic suppurative otitis media and pneumococcal disease. The dose covers intermediately penicillin-resistant pneumococci. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily for seven days
options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure after 48 to 72 hours of amoxicillin, recurrent acute otitis media within 30 days, or concurrent purulent conjunctivitis. It is not first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer urgently to ENT for myringotomy and grommet insertion as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Grommets are considered after recurrent acute otitis media (three episodes in six months or four in a year) or chronic otitis media with effusion causing hearing loss greater than three months, not at the acute presentation. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Prescribe intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 50 mg/kg as a single dose
options.rationale: Single-dose IM benzathine benzylpenicillin is used in remote settings for streptococcal pharyngitis prevention of rheumatic fever, not as first-line acute otitis media therapy where oral amoxicillin is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children carries a much higher risk of suppurative complications and chronic perforation than in non-Indigenous children. eTG departs from the watchful-waiting default and recommends prompt high-dose oral amoxicillin. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is for treatment failure or recurrent disease. Grommets and IM benzathine are not first-line acute treatments.
key_points: eTG: Aboriginal child with AOM gets antibiotics without delay
Amoxicillin 30 mg/kg BD for 5 days first-line
Step up to amoxicillin-clavulanate if no response at 48-72 hours
Grommets for recurrent disease or persistent effusion with hearing loss
explanation.pearls: Higher 30 mg/kg twice-daily amoxicillin dose covers intermediately penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae and is the AU standard for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children.

stem:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to your GP clinic by her father for a routine check. He reports she is well, walks confidently and has a vocabulary of about 30 words. She has been drinking around 1 litre of cow's milk daily since 12 months and is a fussy eater who refuses red meat. She was breastfed exclusively until six months.

On examination she is pale around the mouth and conjunctivae but otherwise well, with normal growth percentiles. There is no organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or rash. Routine FBC is sent at the father's request.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110, BP 92/56 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival pallor, no glossitis, no koilonychia, no organomegaly. Tone and tendon reflexes normal. Heart sounds dual with no murmur. Chest clear.
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (110-140), MCV 64 fL (70-86), MCH 22 pg (24-30), platelets 460 x10^9/L (150-450), white cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (5-15), reticulocytes 0.6%; ferritin pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral elemental iron 3 mg/kg daily, reduce cow's milk to 500 mL daily, repeat FBC in 4 weeks
options.rationale: RCH recommends oral elemental iron 3-6 mg/kg/day for established iron deficiency anaemia in a toddler with classic dietary drivers, with concurrent reduction of cow's milk to under 500 mL daily because excess cow's milk both displaces iron-rich foods and causes occult enteric blood loss. Reassess at 4 weeks for haemoglobin rise of at least 10 g/L. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Refer for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and faecal occult blood testing as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Endoscopy is not indicated when the dietary history and clinical picture explain the iron deficiency. Investigation for occult blood loss is reserved for failure to respond to iron replacement after 4-6 weeks of adherence, or atypical features such as failure to thrive or overt bleeding. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Arrange haemoglobin electrophoresis and send blood film before commencing any therapy
options.rationale: Thalassaemia trait is in the microcytic differential but is usually distinguished from iron deficiency by the Mentzer index (MCV/RBC), family history, ethnicity and ferritin. A clear nutritional history with low ferritin warrants empirical iron trial first; electrophoresis is reserved for cases with normal ferritin and persistent microcytosis. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Arrange intravenous iron carboxymaltose infusion as a single dose as the proposed approach
options.rationale: IV iron in children is reserved for malabsorption, intolerance of oral iron, or inflammatory bowel disease with ongoing losses. Oral iron is first-line in nutritional iron deficiency, with response expected by 4 weeks. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

options.text: Recommend dietary modification alone and review with repeat FBC in 12 weeks as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Dietary modification alone is insufficient once iron deficiency anaemia is established because the deficit requires replacement that cannot be met by diet within a reasonable timeframe. Oral iron supplementation plus dietary change is the standard approach. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: Microcytic anaemia in a toddler with high cow's milk intake and fussy eating is overwhelmingly nutritional iron deficiency. Oral elemental iron at 3-6 mg/kg/day plus reduction of cow's milk to under 500 mL/day is first-line, with FBC review at 4 weeks. Endoscopy and electrophoresis are reserved for non-responders or atypical pictures. IV iron is reserved for malabsorption or intolerance.
key_points: Iron 3-6 mg/kg/day oral elemental iron is RCH-recommended dose
Cap cow's milk at 500 mL/day to reduce displacement and occult loss
Reassess at 4 weeks; expect Hb rise ≥10 g/L
IV iron only for malabsorption or oral failure
explanation.pearls: Excess cow's milk above 500 mL/day in toddlers causes both iron displacement and microscopic enteric blood loss; capping intake is therapeutic, not just preventive.

stem:
A 7-month-old girl has been an inpatient for 30 hours with RSV bronchiolitis. She required nasal prong oxygen 1 L/min for the first 12 hours, weaning to room air overnight. She is taking 70% of her usual feed volumes by bottle, with normal wet nappies. Her parents are reliable and live a 15-minute drive from the hospital.

On morning round she is alert and playful between feeds. There is mild subcostal recession but no head bobbing, grunting or nasal flaring. Her parents ask when she can go home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 142, BP 92/54 mmHg, RR 44, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession, scattered fine crackles bilaterally, no wheeze, hydration adequate, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Not repeated overnight

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange overnight pulse oximetry monitoring at home through community paediatric outreach
options.rationale: Home pulse oximetry is not routinely used after bronchiolitis discharge in Australia, and the criteria for discharge in this child are already met without it. The RCH pathway uses clinical and feeding criteria, not home monitoring. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Continue inpatient observation until respiratory rate is below 40 breaths/min
options.rationale: Respiratory rate is not a discharge criterion in the RCH bronchiolitis pathway; persistent tachypnoea is expected for several days post-infection and does not preclude discharge if work of breathing is mild and feeding is adequate. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days before discharge as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not alter the course of bronchiolitis in children under 12 months and are not part of the RCH bronchiolitis pathway. They have no role in discharge planning. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Discharge home now with safety-net advice and routine GP review in 1-2 days
options.rationale: RCH discharge criteria for bronchiolitis are met: SpO2 sustained at or above 92% on room air for at least 4 hours including a sleep period, taking at least 50% of feeds, mild or absent work of breathing, and reliable parents able to return. Routine GP follow-up at 1-2 days completes the safety net. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Repeat chest X-ray and capillary blood gas before deciding on discharge
options.rationale: Routine repeat imaging or blood gas is not recommended in clinically improving bronchiolitis. Imaging at any stage is reserved for unexpected deterioration or diagnostic uncertainty. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: RCH bronchiolitis discharge requires SpO2 at or above 92% on room air for at least 4 hours including a sleep period, mild or absent work of breathing, feeding at or above 50% of normal, and reliable carers with safety-net access. Respiratory rate is not a discharge criterion. Steroids, repeat imaging, and home pulse oximetry are not used. Routine GP review at 1-2 days completes the plan.
key_points: SpO2 ≥92% RA for 4 hours including sleep is the RCH oxygenation criterion
Feeding ≥50% of normal is the hydration criterion
Tachypnoea persists for days and is not a discharge criterion
No role for steroids, repeat CXR, or home oximetry
explanation.pearls: RCH bronchiolitis discharge criteria are clinical: SpO2 92% on RA across a sleep period plus feeding at half of normal plus mild work of breathing plus reliable carers.

stem:
A 14-month-old boy is admitted on day 6 of fever to 39.5 °C unresponsive to paracetamol and ibuprofen. He has been irritable and off feeds. His mother reports a non-pruritic rash that appeared on day 3 and faded, and his lips are now red and cracked. He has not had conjunctival injection or lymphadenopathy noted on previous reviews.

On examination today his lips are red and fissured with a strawberry tongue. There is firm dorsal hand and foot oedema with peeling skin at the fingertips. He has no neck node enlargement and no rash currently. He has been started on empirical IV flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone for possible staphylococcal toxic shock.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 162, BP 88/52 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Red fissured lips, strawberry tongue, BCG scar erythema, peripheral oedema and periungual desquamation, no conjunctival injection, no cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (110-140), white cell count 22 x10^9/L (5-15), platelets 740 x10^9/L (150-450), CRP 152 mg/L (<5), ESR 78 mm/h, ALT 88 U/L (<40), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), sodium 131 mmol/L (135-145), urinalysis sterile pyuria
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol, ibuprofen, IV flucloxacillin, IV ceftriaxone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue empirical antibiotics for a further 48 hours before reassessing as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Persistent fever beyond 5 days with mucocutaneous changes and a markedly inflammatory profile should redirect away from staphylococcal toxic shock toward Kawasaki disease. Delay risks coronary artery aneurysm. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Refer for percutaneous coronary angiography to evaluate for coronary involvement
options.rationale: Echocardiography is the first-line imaging for coronary surveillance in Kawasaki disease in children, with high sensitivity for proximal coronary aneurysms. Invasive angiography has no first-line role. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Commence IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse therapy as initial monotherapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are added in IVIG-resistant Kawasaki or risk-stratified primary therapy, but the standard initial treatment is IVIG plus aspirin. Steroid monotherapy is not used at presentation in AU practice. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture to exclude bacterial meningitis before further therapy
options.rationale: LP is not indicated in the absence of meningism, altered consciousness or seizure, and would delay urgent IVIG. Aseptic meningitis can occur in Kawasaki but is a supportive feature, not an indication for LP. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Arrange transthoracic echocardiogram and commence IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with high-dose aspirin
options.rationale: This child meets American Heart Association incomplete Kawasaki criteria (fever ≥5 days plus two principal features - rash and oral changes - plus supportive labs: CRP ≥30, anaemia for age, platelets ≥450, albumin ≤30, ALT elevated, sterile pyuria). Treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours plus aspirin to reduce coronary artery aneurysm risk; echocardiogram baselines coronary anatomy. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when fever lasts at least 5 days with fewer than four classical criteria but supportive laboratory abnormalities (CRP, anaemia, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, transaminitis, sterile pyuria) are present. Treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin, with baseline echocardiography. Delaying treatment past day 10 increases coronary aneurysm risk substantially. Steroids, LP, and angiography are not first-line.
key_points: Fever ≥5 days + 2 features + lab criteria = incomplete KD by AHA
IVIG 2 g/kg + aspirin within first 10 days reduces aneurysm risk
Echocardiogram is the imaging modality of choice
BCG scar erythema is a supportive AU-specific feature
explanation.pearls: Treating Kawasaki within 10 days of fever onset cuts coronary aneurysm rate from about 25% to under 5%. BCG scar erythema is a useful local feature in AU practice.

stem:
A 5-month-old boy presents to your paediatric assessment unit with 24 hours of fever to 39 °C, irritability and reduced feeds. A clean-catch urine grows pure Escherichia coli at greater than 10^8 cfu/L sensitive to all tested agents. He responds well to IV gentamicin and benzylpenicillin within 24 hours and is afebrile by hour 36. His antenatal scans were reported as normal at his birth hospital in regional NSW.

On examination today he is well-perfused, feeding fully and playful. There is no abdominal mass, no spinal anomalies, and his external genitalia are normal. Renal function and electrolytes have normalised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no palpable bladder, normal external genitalia, no spinal dimple or hair tuft
data_table.Investigations: Urine MC&S Escherichia coli >10^8 cfu/L pansusceptible; sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 28 micromol/L, CRP peak 88 mg/L now 22 mg/L, blood cultures negative
data_table.Medications: IV gentamicin, IV benzylpenicillin (now switching to oral cefalexin to complete 7 days)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: No imaging required as the UTI was typical with a good antibiotic response
options.rationale: Although a typical first UTI in a child older than 6 months does not require routine ultrasound, this child is under 6 months which independently triggers ultrasound under the RCH guideline. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: DMSA scan in 4-6 months to assess for renal scarring as the proposed approach
options.rationale: DMSA is part of the NICE pathway, not the RCH cascade. The RCH guideline does not routinely use DMSA after first typical UTI. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Micturating cystourethrogram to exclude vesicoureteric reflux
options.rationale: MCUG is not part of the RCH cascade after a single typical UTI. It is reserved for recurrent UTI with abnormal ultrasound, or atypical features such as poor response to antibiotics or a non-E coli organism. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound during this admission as the proposed approach
options.rationale: RCH recommends renal tract ultrasound during the index admission for infants under 6 months with their first febrile UTI, OR when antenatal monitoring is not confirmed reliable. This child's antenatal scans are reported as normal but the under-6-month age alone meets the imaging criterion. Ultrasound assesses anatomy and excludes hydronephrosis or obstruction. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Cystoscopy and posterior urethral valve assessment under urology
options.rationale: Cystoscopy is reserved for suspected posterior urethral valves in a male infant with antenatal hydronephrosis, poor stream, or palpable bladder. With normal antenatal scans and a typical UTI presentation this is not indicated. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: The RCH UTI imaging cascade recommends renal tract ultrasound after a first febrile UTI in infants under 6 months. DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs and not part of the RCH cascade for typical first UTI. Further imaging is added only for atypical features (poor response, non-E coli, abnormal ultrasound) or recurrent UTI. This case meets the under-6-month criterion regardless of antenatal scan history.
key_points: Under 6 months + first febrile UTI = ultrasound
DMSA and MCUG are not in the RCH cascade after typical UTI
Atypical features (non-E coli, poor response, mass, raised creatinine) escalate imaging
Recurrent UTI with abnormal US triggers MCUG
explanation.pearls: RCH imaging cascade differs from NICE: AU practice uses ultrasound as the index investigation and reserves DMSA/MCUG for atypical or recurrent disease, not first typical UTI.

stem:
A 6-year-old boy is reviewed in the paediatric clinic 3 weeks after diagnosis of IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura). At diagnosis he had palpable purpura on the buttocks and lower limbs, arthralgia of the ankles, and one episode of colicky abdominal pain that settled with paracetamol. His baseline urinalysis was clear and renal function normal.

Today his rash has faded, the arthralgia has resolved, and he is back at school. On routine follow-up urinalysis he has 2+ protein and 1+ blood. His blood pressure today is 116/76 mmHg, on the 95th centile for age and height.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 116/76 mmHg (95th centile for age/height), RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Fading purpura over lower limbs, no joint swelling, no abdominal tenderness, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis protein 2+, blood 1+; urine protein:creatinine ratio 88 mg/mmol (<25); creatinine 42 micromol/L (28-66), albumin 36 g/L (35-50), urine MC&S no growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure and continue weekly urinalysis with routine GP follow-up
options.rationale: A urine protein:creatinine ratio of 88 mg/mmol is well above the nephrotic-range threshold of 250 and significantly above the upper limit of normal of 25; this level of proteinuria with co-incident hypertension at the 95th centile triggers paediatric nephrology referral, not reassurance. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 4 weeks as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Steroids in HSP are used for severe abdominal pain or arthritis and do not prevent or reliably treat HSP nephritis; treatment decisions for HSP nephritis follow renal biopsy histology and are guided by paediatric nephrology. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Refer to paediatric nephrology for assessment within 1-2 weeks
options.rationale: RCH HSP follow-up triggers nephrology referral for any of: persistent proteinuria (uPCR over 25 mg/mmol beyond 4 weeks), hypertension, raised creatinine, or nephrotic syndrome. This child has proteinuria approaching nephrotic range with hypertension at the 95th centile and needs early renal biopsy planning. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Start oral perindopril 1 mg daily and review BP in 4 weeks
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are commonly used in HSP nephritis with persistent proteinuria but the choice and dosing should be guided by a paediatric nephrologist after histology, not initiated in GP follow-up without specialist input. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Arrange 24-hour urinary protein collection before any specialist referral
options.rationale: A spot urine protein:creatinine ratio is the recommended quantification in paediatric practice and 24-hour collection is impractical in young children. Specialist referral should not wait on additional confirmatory testing. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: HSP renal involvement appears within 6 months of presentation in up to 40% of children and is the main determinant of long-term outcome. RCH triggers paediatric nephrology referral for persistent proteinuria, hypertension, raised creatinine, or nephrotic syndrome. Steroids do not prevent HSP nephritis. Antihypertensives and ACE inhibitors are initiated by specialists after biopsy assessment.
key_points: HSP renal monitoring with serial urinalysis and BP for at least 6 months
Trigger for nephrology: persistent proteinuria, hypertension, raised creatinine
uPCR over 25 mg/mmol is significant; over 250 mg/mmol is nephrotic range
Steroids do not prevent or reliably treat HSP nephritis
explanation.pearls: HSP nephritis severity is dictated by biopsy histology, not clinical features alone; AU practice escalates early to paediatric nephrology when proteinuria with hypertension co-exist.

stem:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to your GP clinic by her mother with 3 weeks of perianal and vulval itch worse at night, with occasional white-yellow vaginal discharge. Her mother has noted small white worms on the perianal skin when applying nappy cream. Her 3-year-old brother has been scratching his bottom for the last week. The girl is otherwise well, fully immunised, and attends preschool.

On examination there is mild erythema around the perianal area and vulva, with a small amount of non-offensive discharge. Bedside microscopy of a perianal tape sample shows oval eggs flattened on one side.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 94/58 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild perianal and vulval erythema, scant non-offensive discharge, no excoriation breaks, no anal fissure, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Perianal tape: oval eggs flattened on one side. Vulval swab: mixed normal flora, no Candida, no STI organisms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Single dose oral mebendazole 100 mg now to the girl only, with a repeat dose in 2 weeks as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Treating only the index child misses the household reservoir; reinfection and ongoing symptoms are highly likely without simultaneous family treatment. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

options.text: Refer to paediatric gynaecology for assessment of vulvovaginitis and possible sexual abuse as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Threadworm is a common cause of childhood vulvovaginitis with characteristic itch and discharge. There is no clinical feature here triggering child protection referral; explicit features (recurrent unexplained STI, disclosure, anogenital injury) would prompt that pathway. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Topical clotrimazole cream twice daily to the vulva and perianal area for 7 days as the proposed approach
options.rationale: The vulval swab excludes candidiasis and the perianal tape confirms enterobiasis. Antifungal therapy does not treat threadworm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Single dose oral mebendazole 100 mg now and repeated at 2 weeks for all household members aged 6 months and over, with hygiene advice
options.rationale: AMH recommends treating the index case and all household members aged 6 months and older with mebendazole 100 mg single dose repeated at 2 weeks to interrupt the egg-laying cycle. Hygiene measures (nail trimming, daily morning shower, hot wash of bed linen and underwear) are essential adjuncts. The repeat dose targets larvae that mature after the first dose. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

options.text: Single dose oral albendazole 400 mg once with no repeat and no household treatment as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Albendazole is an alternative agent but a single dose without repeat allows larvae to mature and re-establish infection; the repeat at 2 weeks is essential. Treating the household is also required. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

explanation.summary: Threadworm (Enterobius vermicularis) is a common cause of perianal itch and secondary vulvovaginitis in girls. AU practice treats with oral mebendazole 100 mg single dose repeated at 2 weeks for the index case and all household members aged 6 months and over, plus hygiene measures. Topical antifungals do not treat threadworm. Vulvovaginitis from threadworm does not warrant protection referral without explicit suspicious features.
key_points: Tape test eggs are pathognomonic for Enterobius vermicularis
Mebendazole 100 mg single dose + repeat at 2 weeks; treat household
Hygiene: nail trimming, morning shower, hot wash linen
Vulvovaginitis is a common secondary feature in girls
explanation.pearls: The repeat dose at 2 weeks targets larvae that mature after the first dose (mebendazole has no larvicidal effect on eggs in utero); skipping it is the commonest treatment failure.

stem:
A 13-year-old girl with established type 1 diabetes is brought in by ambulance with 18 hours of vomiting and abdominal pain. She has been managing on a basal-bolus regimen with continuous glucose monitoring. Her usual home blood sugar logs have been stable until 3 days ago when she stopped eating and self-reduced her insulin.

In the resuscitation bay she is drowsy with Kussmaul respiration. Her abdomen is tender in the right iliac fossa with rebound and guarding. Bedside glucose 24 mmol/L, blood ketones 6.2 mmol/L. She is started on the RCH DKA pathway with 10 mL/kg saline bolus, fluid replacement, and an insulin infusion at 0.05 unit/kg/hour after 1 hour. Two hours into therapy her ketones are 4.8 mmol/L and her abdominal tenderness has not improved.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 102/68 mmHg, RR 36 Kussmaul, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 13, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, right iliac fossa tenderness with rebound and guarding, bowel sounds reduced
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 24 mmol/L, ketones 6.2 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.10, HCO3 6 mmol/L, base deficit -22, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L; lipase 38 U/L (<60); white cell count 22 x10^9/L (5-15); abdominal ultrasound: dilated non-compressible appendix 9 mm with surrounding fluid
data_table.Medications: DKA pathway: maintenance + deficit replacement saline with KCl, insulin infusion 0.05 unit/kg/hour

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discuss urgent surgical review and theatre once initial fluid and potassium resuscitation is established, continuing the insulin infusion intraoperatively
options.rationale: The ultrasound is diagnostic for appendicitis and the abdominal signs are not explained by DKA alone (no lipase rise, focal RIF rebound persisting after fluid resuscitation, leucocytosis above DKA baseline). RCH and ANZCA paediatric peri-operative DKA guidance support proceeding to theatre once circulation is restored and potassium is replacing, with continuous insulin infusion plus glucose-containing fluid to prevent hypoglycaemia. Source control is the priority; pH need not normalise pre-operatively. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Continue DKA pathway and reassess the abdomen once acidosis fully resolves before any surgical decision as the proposed approach
options.rationale: The ultrasound finding of a non-compressible 9 mm appendix with surrounding fluid is diagnostic of acute appendicitis; persisting tenderness with rebound and guarding despite 2 hours of resuscitation, plus a white cell count of 22 and normal lipase, points to true surgical pathology rather than ketoacidosis-related abdominal pain. Delay until DKA resolution risks perforation. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Stop the insulin infusion to allow ketones to clear before surgical review as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Stopping insulin worsens ketoacidosis and is contraindicated; insulin infusion is continued through and after surgery in known DKA. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Give intravenous tramadol and morphine and trial conservative management with intravenous antibiotics alone as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Non-operative management of paediatric appendicitis is investigational and not recommended in a child with established DKA, drowsiness, and ultrasound evidence of complicated appendicitis; surgery is the primary management. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

options.text: Arrange immediate CT abdomen with contrast to confirm appendicitis before any surgical referral as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Ultrasound has already confirmed appendicitis in this child; CT adds ionising radiation and contrast load in established DKA without changing the management decision. Paediatric appendicitis imaging is ultrasound-first in AU practice. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: DKA can cause abdominal pain that mimics surgical pathology and resolves with rehydration, but persistent focal signs with confirmatory imaging require surgical source control. The default 'rehydrate and re-examine' branch is the wrong branch when imaging is positive and signs persist. Insulin is continued through surgery and a glucose-containing fluid is added once blood sugars fall. CT is not first-line for paediatric appendicitis when ultrasound is diagnostic.
key_points: DKA can mimic acute abdomen; persistent focal signs plus positive imaging override
Restore circulation and start K+ replacement before theatre
Continue insulin infusion intra-operatively; add glucose if BSL <14 mmol/L
Ultrasound is first-line paediatric appendicitis imaging
explanation.pearls: In paediatric DKA with focal RIF signs, an ultrasound positive for appendicitis flips the textbook default - resuscitate, do not normalise pH, then proceed to theatre with insulin infusion running.

stem:
A 4-week-old infant presents to your emergency department with a 5-day history of progressive coughing fits. His mother describes bouts in which 'he goes red, then blue around the lips, then takes a deep noisy breath in and is exhausted'. He has fed poorly during these bouts. His sister had a cough 3 weeks ago and was told she had a viral chest infection. His mother did not receive the antenatal pertussis booster.

On examination he is afebrile and settled between paroxysms. There are bilateral subconjunctival haemorrhages and an audible inspiratory whoop is observed after one cough cluster in the department. The chest is clear on auscultation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 78/46 mmHg, RR 56 (paroxysmal bursts to 80), SpO2 nadir 84% during paroxysm and 96% at rest, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Subconjunctival haemorrhages bilaterally, inspiratory whoop, chest clear to auscultation, fontanelle soft, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Total white cell count 32 x10^9/L (5.0-19.5), lymphocyte 22 x10^9/L (3.0-9.5), CRP 6 mg/L (<5), chest X-ray clear, nasopharyngeal swab PCR pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family, give paracetamol for comfort, and discharge home with cough safety-net advice
options.rationale: Infants under 6 months with paroxysmal cough, whoop, and desaturations require admission for monitored apnoea risk; discharge underestimates progression and contact-tracing duty. (Source: CDNA SoNG Pertussis)

options.text: Admit for cardiorespiratory monitoring, commence azithromycin orally for 5 days, and apply droplet precautions
options.rationale: Infant pertussis with desaturation, lymphocytosis, and household exposure mandates admission for apnoea observation; azithromycin shortens infectivity and is preferred under 1 month over erythromycin (pyloric stenosis risk reduced). Droplet precautions plus public health notification are required. (Source: CDNA SoNG Pertussis; RCH CPG: Pertussis)

options.text: Discharge on oral amoxicillin and arrange general practitioner review for an audible wheeze in 48 hours
options.rationale: Amoxicillin has no activity against Bordetella pertussis; macrolides are required. There is also no wheeze documented. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium and admit to the short-stay observation unit overnight
options.rationale: Beta-agonists do not modify pertussis paroxysms; bronchodilators are reserved for documented reactive airways. Short-stay observation is also inappropriate for an infant under 6 months with apnoea risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Pertussis)

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous ceftriaxone for unrecognised early-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis
options.rationale: Sepsis screen is reasonable in unwell infants under 28 days, but afebrile lymphocytosis with whoop after exposure favours pertussis; ceftriaxone is also contraindicated under 1 month if jaundiced or receiving calcium and is not the targeted treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

explanation.summary: Pertussis in infants under 6 months has high apnoea, pneumonia, and death rates. A characteristic triad of paroxysmal cough, inspiratory whoop, and post-tussive emesis or apnoea, with marked lymphocytosis, is enough to start macrolides empirically while PCR returns. Azithromycin is preferred under 1 month given infant pyloric stenosis risk reported with erythromycin. Notification to public health and post-exposure prophylaxis for close contacts (including non-immunised household members) is required. Antenatal maternal vaccination at 20-32 weeks reduces severe infant disease.
key_points: Admit any infant under 6 months with proven or suspected pertussis for apnoea monitoring
Azithromycin preferred under 1 month (pyloric stenosis risk with erythromycin)
Notifiable disease - contact tracing and prophylaxis for vulnerable contacts
Antenatal maternal booster at 20-32 weeks is the primary prevention strategy
explanation.pearls: Azithromycin 10 mg/kg orally once daily for 5 days is the AU first-line for treatment and post-exposure prophylaxis in infants under 1 month.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

stem:
A previously well 22-month-old boy presents 90 minutes after a sudden coughing and choking episode at his grandmother's house. He had been eating a handful of peanuts on the lounge floor. His mother says 'he turned bright red, coughed for a few minutes, and now seems alright but is breathing a bit oddly'. He has no fever, no preceding cough, and no asthma history.

On examination he is alert, mildly tachypnoeic, and speaks in full short sentences. The trachea is central. There is reduced air entry over the right lower zone with a localised monophonic wheeze; the left chest is clear. A chest X-ray in inspiration looks essentially normal; expiratory and right lateral decubitus films show hyperinflation of the right lower lobe and mediastinal shift away from that side.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, no stridor, central trachea, reduced air entry right lower zone, localised monophonic right-sided wheeze, no drooling
data_table.Investigations: Inspiratory chest X-ray reported normal; expiratory and right lateral decubitus views show right lower lobe hyperinflation with mediastinal shift away from the affected side

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol and a short course of oral prednisolone, with respiratory clinic review in two weeks
options.rationale: Beta-agonists and steroids are appropriate for asthma but do not address a retained foreign body, and delay risks distal infection and granulation. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)

options.text: Five back blows and five chest thrusts in head-down position, then admit for overnight observation
options.rationale: Back blows are reserved for the conscious choking child with complete airway obstruction; this child is settled, talking, and oxygenating. The retained foreign body still needs definitive removal. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

options.text: Refer urgently for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthetic for retrieval of the foreign body
options.rationale: Witnessed choking with localised wheeze, focal reduced air entry, and expiratory hyperinflation with mediastinal shift on the right is a classic ball-valve foreign body. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthetic by an experienced ENT or paediatric airway team is the diagnostic and therapeutic intervention; flexible bronchoscopy is diagnostic only. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)

options.text: Order a computed tomography scan of the chest before deciding on further airway management
options.rationale: Most aspirated organic foreign bodies are radiolucent and CT can be falsely reassuring; the diagnosis is clinical and the next step is bronchoscopy. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)

options.text: Empirical oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and outpatient chest physiotherapy with review in three days
options.rationale: Antibiotics and physiotherapy are not the answer to a retained foreign body and do not relieve obstruction; missed foreign bodies lead to post-obstructive pneumonia and bronchiectasis. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)

explanation.summary: Inhaled foreign body in toddlers presents as a witnessed choking episode followed by an asymptomatic period before localised signs reappear. Peanuts and dry pulses are the most frequent culprits. Expiratory or decubitus films demonstrate air trapping from a ball-valve effect; a normal inspiratory film does not exclude the diagnosis. Definitive management is rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthetic, and the index of suspicion - not imaging - drives the referral.
key_points: Witnessed choke plus focal monophonic wheeze is bronchoscopy until proven otherwise
Normal inspiratory CXR does not exclude foreign body
Rigid bronchoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic - flexible is diagnostic only
Peanuts under 3 years - dietary education at every well-child check
explanation.pearls: On expiratory or lateral decubitus chest X-ray, the obstructed side stays hyperinflated and the mediastinum shifts away - the opposite of the side you might expect.

stem:
A 14-year-old boy presents to your emergency department with 2 hours of sudden severe left-sided scrotal pain that woke him at 5 am. He has vomited twice. He says 'it started straight away, not a slow build, and it hurts down to my belly button'. There is no dysuria, no urethral discharge, no recent trauma, and he denies sexual activity.

On examination he is in obvious distress. The left hemiscrotum is swollen and erythematous. The left testis is exquisitely tender, lies higher than the right, and is held horizontally. The cremasteric reflex is absent on the left and present on the right. There is no penile discharge. A bedside scrotal ultrasound is available but would take 90 minutes to arrange with formal Doppler reporting.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Left testis tender, high-riding, horizontal lie, absent cremasteric reflex; right side normal; no penile discharge; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis blood and leukocytes negative; FBC and inflammatory markers not yet returned

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed directly to surgical scrotal exploration without waiting for ultrasound imaging
options.rationale: Classic torsion features (sudden pain, absent cremasteric reflex, high-riding horizontal lie, vomiting) within the salvage window of about 6 hours mandate immediate exploration; imaging that delays surgery reduces salvage rates. Contralateral fixation is performed at the same operation. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotal pain; Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Arrange formal scrotal colour Doppler ultrasound before any decision about operative exploration
options.rationale: Doppler can miss intermittent or partial torsion and any imaging delay reduces salvage; clinical features here are diagnostic. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotal pain)

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline for presumed epididymo-orchitis
options.rationale: Epididymo-orchitis usually has a more gradual onset, dysuria, preserved cremasteric reflex, and Prehn sign relief on elevation; antibiotic empirical cover here delays surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Attempt outward manual detorsion at the bedside as definitive treatment with discharge afterwards
options.rationale: Manual detorsion can temporise pain in delayed presentations while theatre is readied but is never definitive; orchidopexy is still required. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotal pain)

options.text: Administer intramuscular morphine and observe for 6 hours with repeat examination at intervals
options.rationale: Watchful waiting risks irreversible ischaemia; the window to salvage is approximately 6 hours from onset. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotal pain)

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a time-critical diagnosis. Sudden severe scrotal pain, vomiting, an absent cremasteric reflex, and a high-riding, horizontal testis is sufficient clinical evidence to proceed to theatre without ultrasound. Salvage rates fall sharply after 6 hours of ischaemia; bilateral orchidopexy is performed at exploration because the contralateral side shares the bell-clapper anatomy. Differentials (epididymo-orchitis, torsion of testicular appendage, idiopathic scrotal oedema) typically have a more gradual onset and preserved cremasteric reflex.
key_points: Torsion is a clinical diagnosis - never delay surgery for imaging
Salvage falls after about 6 hours of ischaemia
Bilateral orchidopexy performed at exploration (bell-clapper is bilateral)
Absent cremasteric reflex is the most specific bedside sign
explanation.pearls: Sudden-onset scrotal pain in a teenage boy with an absent cremasteric reflex goes straight to theatre - ultrasound is for equivocal cases, not classic ones.

sources.label: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand

stem:
A 5-day-old, term, exclusively breastfed boy is brought to the early-discharge clinic by his mother who says 'he looks more yellow today and is bringing his feeds up'. Birth weight 3.4 kg, now 3.05 kg (10% below birth weight). He was discharged at 28 hours of age with normal newborn screening swab pending and a normal transcutaneous bilirubin at 24 hours. His mother is blood group O Rhesus positive; baby's blood group is not yet known. Latch has been variable and feeds are short.

On examination he is sleepy but rousable, with jaundice extending to mid-thigh. There is no hepatosplenomegaly and the neurological exam is normal. Total serum bilirubin is 360 micromol/L with a conjugated fraction of 8 micromol/L. The phototherapy nomogram threshold for a well term infant at this postnatal age and risk profile is 340 micromol/L; the exchange transfusion threshold is 480 micromol/L. Direct antiglobulin test, baby's blood group, FBC, and reticulocyte count have been sent and remain pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 72/44 mmHg, RR 44, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Visible jaundice to mid-thigh, sleepy but rousable, soft fontanelle, normal tone, no hepatosplenomegaly, mild dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin 360 micromol/L, conjugated bilirubin 8 micromol/L; phototherapy threshold 340 micromol/L; exchange threshold 480 micromol/L; DAT, blood group, FBC, reticulocyte count pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother, advise more frequent feeds, and review with repeat bilirubin in 24 hours
options.rationale: The total serum bilirubin already exceeds the phototherapy threshold; waiting another 24 hours risks rapid escalation toward exchange and acute bilirubin encephalopathy. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Arrange immediate exchange transfusion in a neonatal intensive care unit setting today
options.rationale: Total bilirubin is well below the exchange threshold of 480 micromol/L and there are no signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy; exchange transfusion carries significant procedural risks. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Discontinue breastfeeding for 48 hours and switch to a standard infant formula by bottle
options.rationale: Breastfeeding cessation is not first-line; phototherapy plus continued breastfeeding with lactation support is the AU standard. Cessation undermines establishment and is rarely required. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Admit for intensive phototherapy and continue breastfeeding with lactation support and feed top-ups
options.rationale: Bilirubin above the phototherapy line at this postnatal age requires admission for intensive phototherapy. Breastfeeding should continue with lactation support and expressed breast milk or formula top-ups to address suboptimal feeding contributing to dehydration and weight loss; DAT and group results guide whether haemolysis is contributing. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice; Australian College of Midwives Position Statement)
source_refs: Australian College of Midwives Position Statement

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin empirically before the direct antiglobulin test result returns
options.rationale: IVIG is indicated for confirmed isoimmune haemolytic disease with rising bilirubin near exchange threshold despite phototherapy, not empirically before serology. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice management is plotted on age- and risk-adjusted nomograms. A value above the phototherapy line at day 5 in a well infant warrants admission for intensive phototherapy and continued breastfeeding with adequate feeding support. Conjugated bilirubin over 15% of total (or over 20 micromol/L) raises concern for biliary atresia and prompts urgent paediatric assessment. Acute bilirubin encephalopathy features (hypertonia, opisthotonus, high-pitched cry, lethargy refractory to feeding) demand immediate exchange.
key_points: Plot bilirubin on age-and-risk nomogram - thresholds are time-dependent
Continue breastfeeding with support during phototherapy where possible
Conjugated > 15% of total or > 20 micromol/L: think biliary atresia, urgent referral
Send DAT, group, FBC, reticulocyte count when above phototherapy line
explanation.pearls: Severe weight loss (>10% of birth weight by day 5) plus jaundice usually reflects insufficient breast milk intake; lactation support is essential alongside phototherapy.

sources.label: Australian College of Midwives Position Statement

stem:
A 6-year-old girl is reviewed in your general paediatric outpatient clinic after a 3-day history of a non-blanching rash on her buttocks and lower legs. Two days before the rash she had bilateral ankle swelling and pain. Her mother says 'she's been gripping her tummy when it cramps, but it goes off after a minute and she's eating'. There is no haematemesis, melaena, or testicular pain. She had a sore throat 10 days ago that settled without antibiotics.

On examination she is well and afebrile, with palpable purpura on the buttocks, posterior thighs, and shins. Joints are not warm and ranges are full. The abdomen is soft with mild central tenderness, no peritonism, and audible bowel sounds. Blood pressure is normal. Urinalysis shows 1+ blood and trace protein; spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 18 mg/mmol (normal <20). Renal function, FBC, and coagulation are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura buttocks and lower limbs, joints non-swollen, abdomen soft, mild central tenderness, no peritonism, no testicular involvement
data_table.Investigations: FBC and platelet count within normal limits, coagulation profile normal, creatinine 38 micromol/L, urinalysis blood 1+ trace protein, urine protein:creatinine ratio 18 mg/mmol (<20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and renal biopsy within the next 48 hours
options.rationale: Methylprednisolone pulses and biopsy are reserved for nephritic-range proteinuria, declining renal function, or biopsy-proven crescentic disease; this child has mild urinalysis findings only. (Source: KHA-CARI; RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for the cutaneous purpura and review in one week
options.rationale: Steroids do not alter the natural history of purpura or prevent renal involvement; they are reserved for severe abdominal pain, orchitis, or established nephritis. Routine prescription overtreats. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Commence empirical oral amoxicillin for 10 days given the recent sore throat as a presumed trigger
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not modify the post-infectious vasculitis course; treat any concurrent group A streptococcal pharyngitis on its own merits, not prophylactically. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric nephrology for an immediate inpatient renal biopsy this admission
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated for nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension, declining renal function, or persistent significant proteinuria beyond 3 months, not for mild transient urinary changes. (Source: KHA-CARI)

options.text: Discharge home with analgesia, written safety-net advice, and weekly urinalysis and BP checks for 6 months
options.rationale: Mild IgA vasculitis with normal blood pressure, normal renal function, and a urine protein:creatinine ratio under 20 mg/mmol is managed conservatively. Ongoing surveillance is essential because nephritis can declare itself up to 6 months after rash onset and dictates referral. Written advice covers when to return (severe abdominal pain, testicular pain, frank haematuria, hypertension). (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura; KHA-CARI)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is the commonest childhood vasculitis. Most cases are self-limiting with palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and microscopic haematuria. Management is supportive analgesia and longitudinal urinalysis plus blood pressure surveillance for 6 months because renal involvement can present late. Steroids are reserved for severe gut pain, orchitis, or proven nephritis. Refer to nephrology for nephrotic-range proteinuria, declining function, or hypertension.
key_points: Steroids do not prevent nephritis - reserve for severe gut, orchitis, biopsy-proven disease
Surveillance for 6 months: weekly urinalysis and BP, then taper
Refer for nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension, or rising creatinine
Most arthralgia and skin disease settles within 4 weeks
explanation.pearls: Urine protein:creatinine ratio over 250 mg/mmol or nephritic syndrome features within 6 months of HSP onset warrants paediatric nephrology referral for biopsy consideration.

stem:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after a 90-second generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home. She had been febrile to 39.4 °C since waking that morning with a runny nose. The seizure stopped before paramedics arrived; she is now alert, taking fluids, and back to her usual play. Her mother says 'she had one of these six months ago when she had tonsillitis and we were told it was a febrile fit, but I'm worried it's becoming a habit'.

Family history is unremarkable; there is no family history of epilepsy. Development is age-appropriate, immunisations are up to date, and the most recent seizure description matches a typical simple febrile seizure. Neurological examination is normal. The chest is clear, tympanic membranes are pink without effusion, and the throat is mildly erythematous without exudate.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, playful, soft fontanelle closed, normal tone, brisk symmetrical reflexes, plantars downgoing, no neck stiffness, mildly erythematous oropharynx
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 5.2 mmol/L, no other tests indicated by guideline; viral upper respiratory tract infection clinically
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg given at home 90 minutes ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management for this child and her family?

options.text: Admit for inpatient electroencephalogram and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain this admission
options.rationale: Routine EEG and MRI are not indicated after simple febrile seizures even when recurrent; investigations are reserved for focal, prolonged, or atypical seizures. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

options.text: Discharge with parental seizure education, antipyretic-as-needed advice, and rectal diazepam only for prolonged events
options.rationale: Simple febrile seizures, even recurrent, do not need investigations, anti-epileptic prophylaxis, or routine antipyretic prophylaxis (which does not prevent recurrence). Education on safe positioning, timing the seizure, and rescue rectal diazepam if a seizure exceeds 5 minutes is the AU standard. Long-term epilepsy risk is only modestly increased; reassurance is appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence regular oral sodium valproate prophylaxis until age five for the recurrent febrile seizures
options.rationale: Valproate prophylaxis is not used for febrile seizures; the small benefit is outweighed by adverse effects and the natural history is benign in simple cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Prescribe alternating paracetamol and ibuprofen at the first sign of fever to prevent further events
options.rationale: Antipyretics improve comfort but do not reduce febrile seizure recurrence; routine alternating dosing risks medication error and adverse effects. (Source: RCH CPG: Fever in children)

options.text: Refer for routine outpatient paediatric neurology review and consider rectal diazepam prophylaxis daily
options.rationale: Routine neurology referral is unnecessary for simple recurrent febrile seizures; daily rectal diazepam prophylaxis is not evidence-based. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

explanation.summary: Simple febrile seizures are generalised, last under 15 minutes, do not recur within 24 hours, and occur in a child aged 6 months to 6 years with fever from a clear extracranial source. Recurrence happens in around 30%, and the long-term risk of epilepsy is only modestly above background. Investigations, anti-epileptic prophylaxis, and routine antipyretic prophylaxis do not change outcomes. Parental education on positioning, timing, and rescue medication for seizures longer than 5 minutes is the cornerstone of care.
key_points: Simple febrile seizure: 6 months to 6 years, generalised, under 15 minutes, no recurrence in 24 hours
No investigations or anti-epileptic prophylaxis - even after recurrence
Parental education and rescue plan for seizures over 5 minutes
Refer if focal features, prolonged, recurrence within 24 hours, or atypical age
