explanation.pearls: Rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg or buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg is the AU rescue dose if any seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes - this is the prescription on discharge, not daily prophylaxis.

stem:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to your general practice clinic with daily soiling for the past 3 months. His father says 'he poos into his underpants without realising, and he hasn't sat on the toilet for a proper poo for at least 6 weeks'. Hard stools have been infrequent. He started school recently and avoids the school toilets. Diet is variable, fluid intake adequate, and growth has tracked the 50th centile throughout.

There is no blood per rectum, no vomiting, no abdominal distension at infancy, and meconium passed within 24 hours of birth. On examination he is afebrile with a soft, non-tender, palpably loaded left iliac fossa and faecal mass extending across to the right. Spine, anal position, sacral and lower limb neurological examination are normal. Recent abdominal X-ray taken at the emergency department demonstrates heavy faecal loading throughout the colon without evidence of obstruction.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 100/62 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, palpable faecal mass left iliac fossa extending to right, normal perianal exam, normal anal position, normal lower limb tone and reflexes, normal sacral skin
data_table.Investigations: Abdominal X-ray heavy faecal loading throughout colon, no air-fluid levels, no obstruction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for paediatric surgical opinion regarding suspected Hirschsprung disease and contrast enema studies
options.rationale: Hirschsprung typically presents in the first months of life with delayed meconium and a tight rectum on examination; this boy passed meconium normally and has overflow encopresis after age 3 - features against Hirschsprung. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Recommend dietary fibre and fluid changes alone with general practitioner review in four weeks
options.rationale: Lifestyle measures alone do not clear established faecal impaction; disimpaction is required before maintenance and behavioural work can succeed. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Commence high-dose oral macrogol disimpaction over three days then a maintenance dose, plus toilet sit routine
options.rationale: Functional constipation with overflow soiling and palpable faecal mass requires disimpaction first. Oral macrogol with electrolytes escalated over three days then continued at maintenance is the AU first-line, paired with a sit routine after meals, a star chart, and de-shaming the soiling. Stimulant laxatives are added if macrogol alone fails. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Commence regular daily phosphate enemas as outpatient treatment for the next two weeks at home
options.rationale: Phosphate enemas risk hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia in children and are not first-line outpatient therapy; oral macrogol is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Investigate with thyroid function tests, coeliac serology, and serum calcium before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Functional constipation is a clinical diagnosis without red flags; routine endocrine and coeliac screening is reserved for growth faltering, failure to respond to standard treatment, or other clinical concern. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Childhood functional constipation with overflow encopresis is managed in two phases: disimpaction (high-dose macrogol over a few days) and maintenance (daily macrogol with toilet behaviour work). De-shaming the soiling and a structured sit routine after meals reframes the family understanding. Stimulant laxatives are added for refractory cases. Red flags (delayed meconium, ribbon stool from birth, neurological signs, faltering growth) prompt referral for Hirschsprung or other organic disease.
key_points: Disimpaction must precede maintenance laxative use
Oral macrogol with electrolytes is first-line; phosphate enemas avoided
Behavioural sit routine after meals plus de-shaming the soiling is essential
Hirschsprung red flags: delayed meconium, tight rectum, neonatal obstruction
explanation.pearls: Oral macrogol with electrolytes (e.g. Movicol) at the AU paediatric disimpaction schedule clears most impactions within three to five days before transitioning to a maintenance dose.

stem:
You are the paediatric surgical registrar called to assess a term 40-hour-old boy born to non-consanguineous parents. The midwife reports 'he hasn't passed meconium yet and his tummy looks puffier this afternoon'. He has had two non-bilious vomits but is feeding poorly. There is no family history of cystic fibrosis. Antenatal scans were unremarkable; karyotype not performed.

On examination he has visible abdominal distension and reduced bowel sounds. Anal position is normal and the anocutaneous reflex is present, but per-rectal examination yields a snug rectum and an explosive passage of meconium after gentle finger withdrawal. He has no obvious dysmorphism. Abdominal X-ray shows distended gas-filled small and large bowel loops to a transition point at the rectosigmoid level with collapsed distal rectum. Newborn screening swab is pending. He is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 64/40 mmHg, RR 50, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Abdominal distension, reduced bowel sounds, snug rectum with explosive passage of meconium after rectal examination, normal anal position, no dysmorphism
data_table.Investigations: Abdominal X-ray with multiple distended bowel loops, rectosigmoid transition zone, collapsed distal rectum; FBC, electrolytes, blood gas pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Rectal suction biopsy with histological assessment for ganglion cells and acetylcholinesterase staining
options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease is suspected from delayed meconium passage, abdominal distension, the explosive 'squirt sign' after rectal examination, and rectosigmoid transition zone on X-ray. Rectal suction biopsy demonstrating absent ganglion cells with hypertrophied nerve trunks and increased acetylcholinesterase activity is the diagnostic gold standard before staged pull-through. Contrast enema can support but is not diagnostic and can miss ultra-short segment disease. (Source: ANZAPS Hirschsprung consensus; RCH CPG: Neonatal bowel obstruction)

options.text: Water-soluble contrast enema looking for a string sign and microcolon in the descending colon
options.rationale: Contrast enema findings of microcolon are characteristic of meconium ileus from cystic fibrosis - not Hirschsprung where a transition zone with proximal dilatation is seen. The string sign is a small bowel pattern, not a Hirschsprung feature. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal bowel obstruction)

options.text: Urgent anorectal manometry to assess the rectoanal inhibitory reflex in the neonatal intensive care unit
options.rationale: Manometry detects the absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex but is technically difficult and unreliable in the neonatal period; suction biopsy is the AU standard in newborns. (Source: ANZAPS Hirschsprung consensus)

options.text: Plain abdominal ultrasound to characterise bowel wall thickness at the suspected transition zone level
options.rationale: Ultrasound does not characterise mural innervation; it cannot diagnose aganglionosis and is not part of the diagnostic algorithm. (Source: ANZAPS Hirschsprung consensus)

options.text: Sweat chloride testing on a properly weighted sample collected in the second week of life as next step
options.rationale: Sweat testing assesses cystic fibrosis-related meconium ileus, not Hirschsprung; antenatal scans, no family history, and the squirt sign with rectosigmoid transition point do not fit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionosis of the distal bowel) typically presents in the first 48 hours of life with delayed meconium, abdominal distension, and an explosive rectal squirt after digital examination. A rectosigmoid transition zone is the commonest site; long-segment and total colonic aganglionosis are rarer. Rectal suction biopsy is the diagnostic gold standard, followed by definitive pull-through surgery once enterocolitis is excluded. Enterocolitis (sepsis, severe distension, explosive diarrhoea) is the principal short-term mortality risk and demands rectal washouts, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and decompression.
key_points: Delayed meconium beyond 48 hours plus distension plus squirt sign = suspect Hirschsprung
Rectal suction biopsy is the gold-standard neonatal diagnostic test
Anorectal manometry is unreliable under 1 month; not first-line
Hirschsprung enterocolitis is the principal short-term mortality risk
explanation.pearls: Rectal suction biopsy shows absent ganglion cells in the submucosal plexus with hypertrophied unmyelinated nerve trunks; acetylcholinesterase staining or calretinin loss confirms the diagnosis.

stem:
A 9-year-old boy is brought to your emergency department after 3 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and 4 kg weight loss. His mother says 'he's been drinking from the tap at night and wet the bed twice last week, which he never does'. He has had no vomiting, no abdominal pain, and is eating normally. He has had no recent viral illness and no family history of autoimmune disease.

On examination he is alert, well-perfused, with moist mucous membranes and a capillary refill under 2 seconds. There is no Kussmaul breathing and his breath is not ketotic. Bedside finger-prick glucose is 22 mmol/L. Capillary blood ketones measure 0.6 mmol/L (under 0.6 normal). Venous blood gas shows pH 7.36 (7.35-7.45) and bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22-26). Urine dipstick shows glucose 3+, ketones trace, no nitrites or leukocytes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused, mucous membranes moist, no Kussmaul breathing, no abdominal tenderness, weight tracking 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 22 mmol/L, capillary ketones 0.6 mmol/L, venous pH 7.36, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, urine glucose 3+ ketones trace

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride bolus and commence a fixed-rate insulin infusion
options.rationale: Intravenous fluids and an insulin infusion are reserved for diabetic ketoacidosis (pH under 7.3 or bicarbonate under 15 mmol/L) or significant dehydration; this child is normoglycaemic-range for new-onset diabetes without acidosis. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Handbook)

options.text: Admit under the paediatric endocrinology team for subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin and structured education
options.rationale: New-onset paediatric type 1 diabetes without ketoacidosis is admitted for subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin initiation, structured family education, and arrangement of outpatient diabetes team follow-up. RCH and APEG protocols use a multi-day inpatient education pathway before discharge. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Handbook; RCH CPG: Diabetes mellitus)

options.text: Arrange outpatient oral glucose tolerance testing and dietary review with the general practitioner in 1 week
options.rationale: OGTT is unnecessary when a child has classical symptoms and a random glucose over 11.1 mmol/L; outpatient management without insulin risks rapid progression to ketoacidosis. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Handbook)

options.text: Commence empirical oral metformin and lifestyle measures pending islet autoantibody and C-peptide results
options.rationale: Metformin is the first agent for paediatric type 2 diabetes; this child has the type 1 phenotype (rapid weight loss, classical symptoms over weeks) and requires insulin. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Handbook)

options.text: Discharge with a glucose meter, finger-prick instructions, and a written safety-net to return if vomiting
options.rationale: Discharge without insulin or formal education is unsafe in newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes; vomiting after discharge would already represent decompensation. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetes mellitus)

explanation.summary: New-onset paediatric type 1 diabetes without acidosis is managed by admission for subcutaneous insulin initiation and structured family education over several days. Acidosis (pH under 7.3 or bicarbonate under 15 mmol/L) defines DKA and triggers a separate fluid and infusion pathway. Diagnosis rests on random glucose over 11.1 mmol/L with symptoms; OGTT is not required when symptomatic. Islet autoantibody and C-peptide testing supports type but does not delay insulin start.
key_points: DKA threshold: pH under 7.3 OR bicarbonate under 15 mmol/L
Symptomatic plus random glucose over 11.1 mmol/L confirms diabetes - no OGTT
Subcutaneous basal-bolus initiation in absence of acidosis
Family education during admission is part of the standard pathway
explanation.pearls: Diabetic ketoacidosis fluid replacement in children uses 0.9% sodium chloride at a maintenance rate calculated over 48 hours, never as repeated large boluses, to reduce cerebral oedema risk.

stem:
A 7-year-old girl with known asthma is brought to your emergency department with 6 hours of worsening shortness of breath and wheeze. Her mother says 'she usually uses her blue puffer twice a week, but today she's needed it every 20 minutes and it's not really helping'. She has had a runny nose for 3 days. She is on a daily preventer (low-dose inhaled corticosteroid).

On arrival she is talking in short phrases, sitting upright, with audible wheeze and visible accessory muscle use. There is no cyanosis and she remains alert. She is given salbutamol 12 puffs by spacer and oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg. After three back-to-back salbutamol cycles, her tachypnoea has improved partially but the work of breathing remains moderate. There is good air entry bilaterally with persistent expiratory wheeze. Mum reports she had one prior admission for asthma 2 years ago and no history of intubation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 92% on room air rising to 96% on supplemental oxygen, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Sitting upright, talking in short phrases, suprasternal and subcostal recession, widespread expiratory wheeze with good air entry, no silent chest, alert
data_table.Investigations: Bedside finger-prick glucose 5.4 mmol/L, capillary blood gas not yet performed; chest X-ray clear
data_table.Medications: Daily inhaled corticosteroid (preventer); salbutamol 12 puffs by spacer x 3 cycles and oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg given so far

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intubate immediately and ventilate for impending respiratory failure with permissive hypercapnia
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for exhaustion, silent chest, falling oxygen saturation, or altered consciousness; this child remains alert with good air entry and improving tachypnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Add nebulised ipratropium bromide 250 mcg with the next two salbutamol doses given back-to-back
options.rationale: Severe asthma not fully responsive to initial salbutamol plus oral steroid receives nebulised ipratropium bromide 250 mcg added to the first three back-to-back salbutamol doses; this is the AU paediatric step-up at this severity. Intravenous magnesium sulfate is the next escalation if she fails. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma; National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.text: Commence an intravenous aminophylline loading dose with cardiac monitoring on the resuscitation bay
options.rationale: Aminophylline is a later step in life-threatening asthma after magnesium has failed; it has a narrow therapeutic window and significant adverse effects. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Discontinue inhaled salbutamol and start a subcutaneous adrenaline 1:1000 0.01 mg/kg injection
options.rationale: Subcutaneous adrenaline is used for anaphylactic bronchospasm or as a temporising measure when inhaled therapy cannot be delivered; nebulised therapy is being delivered effectively here. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Discharge home with a written asthma action plan and review by general practitioner in 24 hours
options.rationale: Children requiring continuous bronchodilator and accessory muscle use require ongoing inpatient observation; discharge is unsafe until the salbutamol interval has stretched to at least 3 hours. (Source: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

explanation.summary: Acute paediatric asthma is graded mild, moderate, severe, or life-threatening by work of breathing, air entry, oxygen saturation, and conscious state. Severe disease starts with back-to-back salbutamol, oral prednisolone, and oxygen as needed; persistent severity adds nebulised ipratropium to the first three back-to-back doses. Failure to respond escalates to intravenous magnesium sulfate, then aminophylline. Silent chest, exhaustion, or altered conscious state mandates paediatric intensive care escalation.
key_points: Severity grades: mild, moderate, severe, life-threatening
Severe: back-to-back salbutamol plus ipratropium plus oral steroid
Failure of severe pathway: IV magnesium sulfate next
Life-threatening features: silent chest, exhaustion, altered consciousness
explanation.pearls: Nebulised ipratropium 250 mcg is added to the first three back-to-back salbutamol doses in severe asthma in children under 12, and stopped thereafter to avoid no incremental benefit.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

stem:
A 13-year-old boy is brought to your general practice clinic with 6 weeks of right knee and thigh pain and a limp that has worsened over the past week. His mother says 'he stopped running around because his leg hurts and he keeps turning his foot out when he walks'. He has had no fever, no trauma, and no recent illness. He is at the 95th centile for weight and 50th for height.

On examination he is afebrile. He prefers to lie with the right leg externally rotated. Passive flexion of the right hip causes obligate external rotation and produces pain. Internal rotation of the right hip is limited to 5 degrees. Knee examination is unremarkable. He can weight-bear but limps with an out-toed gait. Lower limb neurovascular examination is normal. Plain frog-lateral pelvic X-ray shows a posterior and medial slip of the right capital femoral epiphysis on the metaphysis; the contralateral side is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 116/68 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Obligate external rotation on passive hip flexion, restricted internal rotation right hip, knee unremarkable, neurovascular intact
data_table.Investigations: Plain pelvis X-ray with frog-lateral views: posterior and medial slip of right capital femoral epiphysis; left hip normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Strict non-weight-bearing with crutches and urgent paediatric orthopaedic referral for surgical pinning
options.rationale: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is a paediatric orthopaedic emergency. The patient is made non-weight-bearing immediately to reduce the risk of slip progression and avascular necrosis, and admitted for urgent in-situ percutaneous pinning. Bilateral prophylactic pinning is considered in selected high-risk patients but the contralateral side is usually monitored. (Source: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position)
source_refs: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position

options.text: Outpatient referral to physiotherapy for hip range of motion strengthening and a 6-week activity plan
options.rationale: Physiotherapy in active SCFE risks acute-on-chronic progression of the slip; this is a surgical emergency. (Source: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position)
source_refs: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the right hip before discussing definitive orthopaedic management options
options.rationale: Diagnosis has been made on plain X-ray with frog-lateral views; MRI is reserved for pre-slip suspicion with normal X-rays. Imaging delay risks progression. (Source: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position)
source_refs: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position

options.text: Prescribe oral ibuprofen analgesia for activity-related pain and routine review by general practitioner in 1 week
options.rationale: Analgesia masks pain that protects against further slip; routine review in a week is unacceptable for an emergency. (Source: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position)
source_refs: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position

options.text: Investigate for transient synovitis with hip ultrasound and a course of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory cover
options.rationale: Transient synovitis presents acutely in younger children with a recent viral illness and an irritable hip on examination; the X-ray diagnosis here is SCFE. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping or non-weight-bearing child)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Limping or non-weight-bearing child

explanation.summary: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is the commonest hip disorder in adolescents, particularly overweight boys aged 10-15 years. Knee or thigh pain with a limp is the most common presentation; obligate external rotation on hip flexion is the classic examination sign. Diagnosis is by plain pelvis X-ray with frog-lateral views demonstrating slip; MRI detects pre-slip with normal X-rays. Treatment is urgent in-situ percutaneous pinning with strict non-weight-bearing in the interim to prevent acute-on-chronic slip and avascular necrosis.
key_points: SCFE is a paediatric orthopaedic emergency - immediate non-weight-bearing
Obligate external rotation on passive hip flexion is the classic sign
Plain pelvis with frog-lateral views is the diagnostic test
Avascular necrosis risk rises with delay and weight-bearing
explanation.pearls: Knee or thigh pain in an adolescent with no clear knee pathology should prompt a hip examination; SCFE can present as referred knee pain without any hip complaint.

sources.label: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position
RCH CPG: Limping or non-weight-bearing child

subtopic_detail: Brief resolved unexplained event risk stratification
stem:
A 5-week-old, term, exclusively breastfed boy is brought to your emergency department after a 30-second episode during feeding in which his mother says 'he went floppy and his face turned a bit blue around the lips, then he came right after I patted his back'. He is now alert and feeding normally. He was born at 39+5 weeks gestation by uncomplicated vaginal birth, with no neonatal nursery admission.

There have been no other episodes and no recent illness. He has no fever and no cough. There is no family history of sudden unexpected death in infancy. Examination is entirely normal: tone, fontanelle, chest auscultation, abdominal examination, hip examination, oxygen saturation in room air, and capillary refill are all normal. Bedside finger-prick glucose is 4.8 mmol/L. He has fed twice in the department and remained well-perfused with stable observations. His mother asks 'do we get to go home?'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140, BP 78/48 mmHg, RR 42, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused, tone normal, fontanelle soft, chest clear, abdomen soft, hips stable, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Finger-prick glucose 4.8 mmol/L; no other tests indicated by guideline at this point

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for cardiorespiratory monitoring, send pertussis PCR, electrocardiogram, and electroencephalogram during admission
options.rationale: This is a low-risk BRUE (age over 60 days when assessed, term, no concerning features, normal examination, single brief episode); panel testing and admission is not part of the low-risk algorithm. (Source: AAP BRUE Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Discharge after shared decision-making with safety-net advice and early review by general practitioner
options.rationale: This infant is under 60 days of age, which classifies him as a higher-risk BRUE; outright discharge without observation does not meet low-risk criteria. (Source: AAP BRUE Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Observe in a short-stay unit for at least 4 hours with continuous saturation and cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Infants under 60 days are not classified as low-risk BRUE even when otherwise reassuring. A period of monitored short-stay observation, capturing repeat events and reviewing feeding, is the AU pathway, with discharge once observation is unremarkable and parental education and safety-netting are documented. (Source: RCH CPG: Brief resolved unexplained event; AAP BRUE Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief resolved unexplained event

options.text: Refer to gastroenterology for upper endoscopy for suspected gastro-oesophageal reflux disease workup
options.rationale: Routine gastroenterology workup is not indicated after an isolated BRUE without recurrent feeding-related events or growth failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Brief resolved unexplained event)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief resolved unexplained event

options.text: Order a metabolic screen, ammonia, lactate, and a head magnetic resonance imaging study urgently
options.rationale: Broad metabolic and imaging panels are reserved for higher-risk BRUEs with concerning features (recurrent events, persistent abnormal examination, family history of metabolic disease). (Source: AAP BRUE Clinical Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: A brief resolved unexplained event (BRUE) replaces the older ALTE term. Low-risk BRUE requires age over 60 days, gestation over 32 weeks with corrected age over 45 weeks, a single brief episode under 1 minute, no cardiopulmonary resuscitation by a trained provider, and a normal examination. Low-risk BRUE allows discharge after shared decision-making; higher-risk BRUE is observed and selectively investigated. Pertussis testing, ECG, and head imaging are pursued only when targeted features (cough exposure, dysrhythmia clues, focal neurological signs) are present.
key_points: Low-risk BRUE criteria include age over 60 days
Higher-risk: short-stay observation and selective testing
Pertussis PCR if cough exposure or paroxysmal episode
ECG for any suspected arrhythmia or syncope-like features
explanation.pearls: BRUE is by definition unexplained: a clear precipitant (gastro-oesophageal reflux event observed, choking on milk, breath-holding spell) means the event is not a BRUE and is managed on its own pathway.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Brief resolved unexplained event

stem:
A 14-month-old girl is admitted to your general paediatric ward with 6 days of persistent fever to 39.4 °C. Her father says 'she's been miserable, her eyes look really pink and she's chewing her lip because it's all cracked'. There has been no diarrhoea, no cough, and no contact with anyone unwell. She was previously well; immunisations are up to date.

On examination she has bilateral non-purulent bulbar conjunctival injection, dry fissured lips, and an erythematous oropharynx without exudate. There is a 1.8 cm right anterior cervical lymph node and a fading non-vesicular trunk rash. Her hands and feet are slightly swollen and tender; she has not desquamated. The remaining examination is unremarkable. Bloods show platelets 612 x10^9/L (200-450), CRP 142 mg/L (under 5), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), ALT 92 U/L (under 35), and a urine dipstick showing leukocyte 2+ with negative culture and no nitrites.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 30, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, dry fissured lips, erythematous oropharynx, 1.8 cm right anterior cervical node, fading trunk rash, oedematous tender hands and feet
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 612 x10^9/L (200-450), CRP 142 mg/L (under 5), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), ALT 92 U/L (under 35), urine leukocyte 2+ culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours plus high-dose aspirin and arrange echocardiography
options.rationale: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when fever has lasted at least 5 days with 2-3 of the 5 principal features and supportive laboratory abnormalities (CRP over 30, platelets over 450, albumin under 30, ALT raised, sterile pyuria). IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin started before day 10 reduces coronary artery aneurysm risk. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Disease Scientific Statement; RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Initiate empirical intravenous flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone for suspected bacterial cervical lymphadenitis
options.rationale: Cervical adenopathy in Kawasaki is part of the syndrome and not a bacterial node; isolated antibiotic therapy delays IVIG and does not prevent aneurysm. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Wait until the 10-day mark of fever to commence intravenous immunoglobulin in the routine treatment window
options.rationale: IVIG given as soon as the diagnosis is established (and ideally before day 10) reduces aneurysm risk; waiting until day 10 worsens cardiac outcome. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Disease Scientific Statement)

options.text: Treat with oral prednisolone alone for suspected systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis with quotidian fever
options.rationale: Systemic JIA typically has a quotidian fever with an evanescent rash and arthritis; conjunctivitis, lip changes, and acute-phase reactant pattern point toward Kawasaki disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Continue supportive care with paracetamol and recheck inflammatory markers in 48 hours before deciding
options.rationale: Each day of untreated Kawasaki disease past day 5 of fever raises coronary aneurysm risk; supportive care alone is unacceptable. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a paediatric vasculitis with five principal features: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, oral mucosal changes (red cracked lips, strawberry tongue), peripheral changes (oedema, erythema, desquamation), and unilateral cervical adenopathy (over 1.5 cm). Complete disease requires fever at least 5 days plus four of five features; incomplete requires fever plus 2-3 features supported by laboratory abnormalities. The treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin within the first 10 days to prevent coronary artery aneurysms. Baseline echocardiography is performed.
key_points: Complete: fever >=5 days plus 4 of 5 features
Incomplete: fever plus 2-3 features plus supportive labs
IVIG before day 10 reduces aneurysm risk
Baseline echocardiography to detect early coronary changes
explanation.pearls: Incomplete Kawasaki disease in infants under 12 months is the highest aneurysm risk group; treat empirically when the supportive lab pattern fits even if features are incomplete.

stem:
A 3-year-old girl is brought to your emergency department 90 minutes after falling from a sofa onto a carpeted floor. Her mother says 'she cried straight away, didn't pass out, vomited once on the way in, and now she just wants to sleep on me'. The fall height was about 80 cm. She has had no further vomiting and is consolable when alert. She has had no fever or recent illness.

On examination she is GCS 15 when stimulated, drowsy at rest but easily roused with appropriate interaction. There is a 3 cm boggy parietal haematoma on the right and no other scalp injury. Fontanelles are closed. Pupils are equal and reactive at 3 mm bilaterally. Tympanic membranes are intact, no haemotympanum, and no CSF rhinorrhoea. No focal neurological deficit on screening. The remaining systemic examination is unremarkable. She has not had any anti-emetic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: GCS 15, drowsy at rest, easily roused, right parietal 3 cm boggy haematoma, pupils 3 mm bilaterally reactive, no focal deficit, tympanic membranes intact
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.1 mmol/L, no other investigations performed yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with written head injury safety-net advice and review by general practitioner in 48 hours
options.rationale: The combination of age under 2 to 3 with a parietal non-frontal scalp haematoma and observed lethargy fails the PECARN low-risk criteria for under-2s and requires observation or imaging. (Source: PECARN Paediatric Head Injury Rule)

options.text: Observe in the emergency department for at least 4-6 hours with serial neurological examinations
options.rationale: Under PECARN intermediate-risk criteria (non-frontal scalp haematoma in under 2, lethargy, single vomit) the choice is between observation and imaging, with parental input. A period of observation with serial GCS, pupil checks, and trend of conscious state is the AU first-line approach in a stable child with no focal signs. CT is the next step if deterioration or persistent symptoms occur. (Source: RCH CPG: Head injury; PECARN Paediatric Head Injury Rule)

options.text: Order a non-contrast computed tomography head scan immediately for the high-risk features described
options.rationale: Immediate CT is reserved for high-risk PECARN features (GCS under 15 at 2 hours, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, signs of basal skull fracture, suspected non-accidental injury); observation is acceptable for intermediate-risk children. (Source: PECARN Paediatric Head Injury Rule)

options.text: Arrange skull X-ray series to look for a linear or depressed fracture before further decision-making
options.rationale: Plain skull X-ray has been superseded by clinical decision rules; it neither rules in nor out clinically important traumatic brain injury reliably. (Source: RCH CPG: Head injury)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain on the next available outpatient slot to avoid radiation exposure
options.rationale: MRI is the second-line imaging modality for paediatric head injury (typically follow-up) and is impractical acutely without anaesthesia; CT is the acute test where imaging is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Head injury)

explanation.summary: PECARN stratifies paediatric blunt head injury into high, intermediate, and low risk. High-risk features mandate CT; low-risk allows discharge. Intermediate risk allows observation versus CT with parental input. In children under 2, an isolated non-frontal scalp haematoma is intermediate. Observation with serial examination spares unnecessary radiation in an at-risk paediatric brain. Children with high-risk features (GCS under 15 at 2 hours, palpable depressed fracture, basal skull fracture signs, non-accidental injury concerns) are imaged.
key_points: PECARN high-risk: GCS under 15 at 2 hours, suspected depressed or basal skull fracture, NAI
Intermediate-risk under 2: non-frontal scalp haematoma is a positive predictor
Observation with serial examination is acceptable in intermediate risk
CT not MRI for acute decision-making
explanation.pearls: In children under 2, an isolated non-frontal scalp haematoma is an intermediate-risk PECARN feature; a frontal haematoma in an otherwise well child does not elevate risk.

subtopic_detail: Pulse oximetry screening for critical congenital heart disease
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward. A term newborn boy at 28 hours of age is screened with the routine pulse oximetry protocol. The midwife reports the readings to you. He is feeding, has had a wet nappy, and his mother says 'he looks pink to me'. His mother had unremarkable antenatal scans including a 20-week morphology scan. There is no family history of congenital heart disease.

On examination he is pink centrally and well-perfused, with normal tone. Cardiac auscultation reveals normal first and second heart sounds, no murmur, and femoral pulses are present and synchronous. Chest auscultation is clear. Capillary refill is under 2 seconds and the abdomen is soft. The four-limb blood pressure is unremarkable. Pre-ductal (right hand) SpO2 is 95% and post-ductal (right foot) SpO2 is 92% on three readings each, separated by 2 minutes; the difference is consistent across readings.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 142, BP 72/44 mmHg, RR 44, pre-ductal SpO2 95%, post-ductal SpO2 92%, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Pink centrally, well-perfused, soft fontanelle, no murmur, normal heart sounds, synchronous femoral pulses, clear chest, soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Pulse oximetry protocol over 6 minutes shows persistent pre-post differential 3% with both feet under 95%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother, repeat pulse oximetry in 24 hours, and continue routine ward observations meanwhile
options.rationale: Persistent pre-post differential under 95% on the AU pulse oximetry algorithm at this stage triggers urgent echocardiography rather than delayed re-screening. (Source: NSW Health Pulse Oximetry Screening Newborn Guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health Pulse Oximetry Screening Newborn Guideline

options.text: Refer urgently for echocardiography and discuss with the on-call paediatric cardiology service today
options.rationale: The AU pulse oximetry screening algorithm fails when either limb is under 90%, or both limbs under 95%, or a persistent pre-post differential of more than 3%; failure prompts urgent echocardiography to exclude critical congenital heart disease (duct-dependent lesions). Prostaglandin E1 is held in reserve pending the result. (Source: NSW Health Pulse Oximetry Screening Newborn Guideline; RCH CPG: Critical congenital heart disease)
source_refs: NSW Health Pulse Oximetry Screening Newborn Guideline
RCH CPG: Critical congenital heart disease

options.text: Commence empirical prostaglandin E1 infusion immediately before any further imaging investigation
options.rationale: Empirical prostaglandin is reserved for clinically unwell duct-dependent neonates; the screen has identified an asymptomatic child for whom prompt echocardiography is the appropriate step. (Source: RCH CPG: Critical congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Critical congenital heart disease

options.text: Discharge home with general practitioner follow-up and a 1-week outpatient cardiology clinic appointment
options.rationale: Discharge before imaging in a baby with a positive screen is unsafe; duct closure (which usually occurs in the first week) can precipitate decompensation of a duct-dependent lesion. (Source: NSW Health Pulse Oximetry Screening Newborn Guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health Pulse Oximetry Screening Newborn Guideline

options.text: Order arterial blood gas first and only proceed to echocardiography if metabolic acidosis is documented
options.rationale: Echocardiography is the definitive imaging step; awaiting blood gas changes delays diagnosis and may miss asymptomatic anatomic disease before deterioration. (Source: RCH CPG: Critical congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Critical congenital heart disease

explanation.summary: Australian neonatal pulse oximetry screening detects critical congenital heart disease (CCHD) at 24-48 hours of age, before duct closure typically unmasks duct-dependent lesions. The protocol measures pre-ductal (right hand) and post-ductal (foot) saturation. A fail occurs with either limb under 90%, both limbs under 95% on three readings 1 hour apart, or a persistent pre-post differential of more than 3%. Failed screen mandates urgent echocardiography; prostaglandin E1 is reserved for clinical decompensation pending the result.
key_points: Screen at 24-48 hours of age, before discharge
Fail thresholds: either limb under 90%, both under 95%, or pre-post differential over 3%
Failed screen: urgent echocardiography, not repeat screening
Prostaglandin E1 reserved for clinical decompensation
explanation.pearls: Duct closure in the first week of life unmasks duct-dependent CCHD (HLHS, critical AS, severe coarctation, IAA); the pulse oximetry screen is designed to find these before that catastrophe.

sources.label: NSW Health Pulse Oximetry Screening Newborn Guideline
RCH CPG: Critical congenital heart disease

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to assess a previously well 4-year-old boy of Mediterranean heritage who has presented with 24 hours of fatigue, pallor, and dark coloured urine. His mother says 'his wee looks like Coca-Cola and the whites of his eyes have gone yellow today'. Three days ago he ate fresh fava beans at a relative's gathering and was started on oral co-trimoxazole for an ear infection. He has no fever now and no abdominal pain.

On examination he is alert, pale, with scleral icterus. Cardiovascular examination shows a quiet flow murmur at the left sternal edge; the spleen tip is palpable but not enlarged. There is no lymphadenopathy and no petechiae. Bloods show haemoglobin 72 g/L (115-150), reticulocytes 240 x10^9/L (50-100), unconjugated bilirubin 68 micromol/L (under 17), LDH 1480 U/L (under 250), haptoglobin under 0.1 g/L (0.3-2.0), direct antiglobulin test negative. A blood film reports bite cells and Heinz bodies. He has no known prior haemolytic episodes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, pale, scleral icterus, soft systolic flow murmur, spleen tip just palpable, no lymphadenopathy, no purpura
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 72 g/L (115-150), reticulocytes 240 x10^9/L (50-100), unconjugated bilirubin 68 micromol/L (under 17), LDH 1480 U/L (under 250), haptoglobin under 0.1 g/L (0.3-2.0), DAT negative, blood film bite cells and Heinz bodies
data_table.Medications: Oral co-trimoxazole started 3 days ago for otitis media

lead_in: What is the single best initial management step?

options.text: Withdraw co-trimoxazole, treat any persistent infection with an alternative agent, and supportive transfusion if symptomatic
options.rationale: Acute G6PD-mediated haemolysis is precipitated by an oxidative trigger (fava beans, sulfonamides such as co-trimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, dapsone, methylene blue, rasburicase). Removal of the trigger is the foundation; red cell transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia, haemodynamic compromise, or rapid haemoglobin fall. Re-introduce safe antibiotics for the otitis. (Source: HSANZ; RCH CPG: Haemolytic anaemia)

options.text: Empirical intravenous methylprednisolone pulses for warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia presumption
options.rationale: Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is DAT-positive (typically with IgG, with or without complement); this child has DAT-negative haemolysis with bite cells and Heinz bodies, characteristic of G6PD deficiency, not autoimmune disease. (Source: HSANZ)

options.text: Urgent splenectomy referral for management of compensated chronic haemolysis with hyperbilirubinaemia
options.rationale: Splenectomy is considered in hereditary spherocytosis with chronic transfusion need or symptomatic anaemia; G6PD deficiency haemolysis is episodic and trigger-related, and splenectomy is rarely useful. (Source: HSANZ)

options.text: Administer rasburicase prophylactically for tumour lysis prevention before chemotherapy assessment
options.rationale: Rasburicase is one of the agents that can precipitate severe G6PD haemolysis and should be avoided; this child has a non-malignant haemolytic picture. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Commence methylene blue infusion for any associated methaemoglobinaemia before haematology review
options.rationale: Methylene blue is also contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because it relies on NADPH-dependent reduction and itself precipitates haemolysis. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: G6PD deficiency is X-linked and most common in boys from Mediterranean, African, Middle Eastern, and South-East Asian backgrounds. Acute haemolysis is triggered by oxidative stress (fava beans, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, dapsone, methylene blue, rasburicase, infection). Blood film shows bite cells, blister cells, and Heinz bodies; the direct antiglobulin test is negative. Management removes the trigger and supports with transfusion if symptomatic or haemodynamically compromised. G6PD enzyme assay during the acute haemolysis can be falsely normal because reticulocytes have higher activity; repeat 2-3 months after the episode. A familial G6PD test list and an avoid-list for future medications is essential.
key_points: Oxidative trigger list: fava beans, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, dapsone, methylene blue, rasburicase
DAT-negative with bite cells and Heinz bodies
Repeat enzyme assay 2-3 months post-event - acute assay can be falsely normal
Family screening and a written avoid-medication list
explanation.pearls: Methylene blue and rasburicase are both contraindicated in G6PD deficiency despite their utility elsewhere; check G6PD status before either drug in at-risk populations.

stem:
A 5-month-old, term, previously well boy is admitted to your general paediatric ward with 3 days of coryza, cough, and progressive work of breathing. His mother says 'he just won't take the bottle anymore and his ribs are sucking in when he breathes'. He is breastfed with some formula top-ups and is wet nappies five times per day.

On arrival 90 minutes ago he was started on nasal prong oxygen 1 L/min for SpO2 88% on room air; his saturation rose to 93% within 10 minutes. He is afebrile, alert, and well-perfused. Auscultation shows widespread fine crepitations and a few expiratory wheezes with good air entry. His subcostal recession has not improved despite the low-flow oxygen and his oral intake is now under 50% of normal volume. Capillary blood gas shows pH 7.34 (7.35-7.45), pCO2 50 mmHg (35-45), and bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22-26). His nasopharyngeal swab is positive for respiratory syncytial virus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 88/52 mmHg, RR 64, SpO2 93% on 1 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused, marked subcostal recession, fine widespread crepitations, scattered expiratory wheeze, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Capillary pH 7.34, pCO2 50 mmHg (35-45), bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22-26), NPA positive for RSV
data_table.Medications: Nasal prong oxygen 1 L/min for the past 90 minutes; no bronchodilators given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and reassess work of breathing again in another 2 hours
options.rationale: Low-flow oxygen has reached its ceiling and has not improved work of breathing or feeding; the AU bronchiolitis pathway escalates after failure rather than waiting further. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence high-flow nasal cannula therapy at 2 L/kg/min titrated to a target oxygen saturation of 90% or above
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance escalates to high-flow nasal cannula after failure of low-flow oxygen, defined as ongoing increased work of breathing, feeding compromise, or rising pCO2 despite 1-2 L/min for at least 2 hours. The saturation target is 90% or above (not 92-94%) and the flow is set at 2 L/kg/min. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; PARIS trial)

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back-to-back with nebulised 3% hypertonic saline as a respiratory adjunct
options.rationale: Salbutamol and hypertonic saline are not recommended in routine bronchiolitis under 12 months; trials have not shown a length-of-stay benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Administer a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg with airway clearance physiotherapy added concurrently
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not improve bronchiolitis outcomes in this age group; chest physiotherapy is similarly not routine. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Intubate and ventilate now for the rising carbon dioxide of 50 mmHg and the persistent increased work of breathing
options.rationale: A pCO2 of 50 mmHg with a near-normal pH does not by itself mandate intubation; high-flow nasal cannula is the next escalation before invasive ventilation in stable bronchiolitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a viral lower respiratory tract infection (RSV predominant) peaking at age 2-6 months. Australian (RCH) guidance starts oxygen at low-flow nasal prongs 1-2 L/min when SpO2 is under 90% and escalates to high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min when low-flow fails after at least 2 hours, with a target SpO2 of 90% or above. Salbutamol, corticosteroids, hypertonic saline, antibiotics, and physiotherapy are not routine. Failure of high-flow nasal cannula prompts paediatric intensive care escalation.
key_points: Low-flow oxygen first at 1-2 L/min; target SpO2 >=90%
Escalate to HFNC at 2 L/kg/min after at least 2 hours of low-flow failure
Salbutamol, steroids, hypertonic saline NOT routine
Failure of HFNC: PICU escalation
explanation.pearls: In bronchiolitis under 12 months the AU SpO2 target is 90% (not 92-94%) - lower targets reduce overtreatment without harm in well-perfused infants.

stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to your emergency department at 0200 with a barking cough and noisy breathing. His mother says 'he sounded like a seal barking and now he's making this loud noise when he breathes in, even when he's just lying still'. He has had 2 days of coryza. He has had no contact with anyone unwell at home.

On examination he is alert but anxious, sitting on his mother's lap. He has audible stridor at rest with marked suprasternal and intercostal recession. He is moving air symmetrically with no wheeze. Oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Capillary refill is under 2 seconds. He has not been febrile and he is well-hydrated. He has had no medication so far. The croup score (Westley) is calculated at 7, with stridor at rest, marked recession, and decreased air entry without cyanosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert anxious, sitting on mother's lap, stridor at rest, marked suprasternal and intercostal recession, no wheeze, symmetrical air entry
data_table.Investigations: Westley croup score 7 (severe); no blood tests indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg only and review the work of breathing in 30 minutes time
options.rationale: Mild and moderate croup are treated with dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, but severe croup with stridor at rest requires a higher dose (0.6 mg/kg) and concurrent nebulised adrenaline. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 plus oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg and observe for at least 3 hours
options.rationale: Severe croup (Westley score 6 or above, stridor at rest with marked recession) receives concurrent nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 (a flat dose, not weight-based) and dexamethasone at the higher 0.6 mg/kg oral dose. Children are observed for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline dose to detect rebound. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Intubate now for impending respiratory failure with persistent stridor and intercostal recession at rest
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for severe croup that fails nebulised adrenaline and steroids or shows exhaustion, altered consciousness, or cyanosis; first-line pharmacological treatment has not yet been trialled. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Administer nebulised budesonide 2 mg as the sole steroid agent and arrange admission for observation
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is an alternative when oral dexamethasone cannot be given, but is not first-line and does not replace adrenaline in severe disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Discharge home with a written information sheet on humidified air and a paracetamol dosing schedule
options.rationale: Severe croup with stridor at rest requires pharmacological treatment and at least 3 hours of monitored observation; discharge before adrenaline trial is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is a viral upper-airway infection typically in children aged 6 months to 6 years. The Westley score (5 components - level of consciousness, cyanosis, stridor, air entry, retraction) grades mild (under 3), moderate (3-5), severe (6-11), and impending failure (12 or above). Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally is given for mild or moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe disease. Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 (flat dose) is added in severe disease and any child is observed for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline dose.
key_points: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild/moderate; 0.6 mg/kg for severe
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 (flat dose)
Observation at least 3 hours after last adrenaline
Westley score >=6 = severe
explanation.pearls: Nebulised adrenaline is a temporising measure; without concurrent dexamethasone the stridor can rebound within 2-3 hours.

stem:
A 4-month-old boy is admitted to your paediatric ward with fever to 39.2 °C and irritability. His mother says 'he just goes red and screams when he wees and his nappies have been really smelly for two days'. He has had no cough, no diarrhoea, and no rash. He was born at term and was not screened on antenatal ultrasound for renal anomalies because his mother had no antenatal care.

On examination he is alert but unsettled, with a soft abdomen and no flank mass. Urinalysis from a clean catch sample shows leukocytes 3+ and nitrites positive; microscopy reports more than 100 white cells per high-power field. Empirical intravenous gentamicin plus benzylpenicillin was started 48 hours ago. He remains febrile to 38.6 °C and is still feeding poorly. Urine culture has now returned showing Klebsiella pneumoniae at 10^8 CFU/mL with the gentamicin being the only sensitive listed antibiotic; the sensitivity strip confirms susceptibility.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 42, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, unsettled, soft abdomen, no flank mass, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis leukocytes 3+ nitrites positive, microscopy WCC >100/HPF, urine culture Klebsiella pneumoniae 10^8 CFU/mL gentamicin-sensitive, CRP 96 mg/L (under 5), creatinine 36 micromol/L (15-37)
data_table.Medications: Intravenous gentamicin once daily plus benzylpenicillin for 48 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue current intravenous antibiotics and arrange a renal ultrasound scan during the current admission
options.rationale: This child has atypical UTI features (under 6 months of age, non-E coli pathogen, poor response within 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics, no antenatal renal ultrasound documentation). RCH guidance triggers a renal tract ultrasound during the current admission for atypical UTI. DMSA and MCUG are not part of the RCH cascade. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Continue intravenous antibiotics and arrange a dimercaptosuccinic acid scan in 6 months as routine assessment
options.rationale: DMSA is a NICE-derived investigation and is not part of the RCH AU UTI imaging cascade. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Switch to oral co-trimoxazole prophylaxis only and arrange outpatient renal ultrasound in 6 weeks time
options.rationale: Oral switch before clinical response and before imaging risks missing structural abnormality; prophylaxis alone is not first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Continue intravenous antibiotics and arrange a micturating cystourethrogram during the current admission
options.rationale: MCUG is not part of the RCH cascade and is reserved for selected paediatric urology cases; AU first-line imaging is the renal tract ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Cease intravenous antibiotics, observe off treatment, and repeat urine culture in 48 hours from a fresh sample
options.rationale: Ceasing antibiotics in a confirmed UTI with poor response risks worsening pyelonephritis and bacteraemia; escalation not cessation is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Australian (RCH) paediatric UTI guidance reserves renal tract ultrasound for atypical UTI (poor antibiotic response within 48 hours, non-E coli, sepsis, abdominal mass, raised creatinine) or recurrent UTI. Infants under 6 months also receive imaging where no antenatal ultrasound coverage has been documented. DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs and are not part of the RCH cascade. Single typical UTI in a child over 6 months with rapid response does not need routine imaging. The intravenous antibiotic course continues until clinical response and culture sensitivities guide the oral switch.
key_points: Ultrasound during admission for atypical UTI or under 6 months without antenatal imaging
Atypical features include non-E coli, poor 48-hour response, sepsis
DMSA and MCUG NOT in the RCH cascade
Single typical UTI over 6 months does not need routine imaging
explanation.pearls: Recurrent UTI (two or more upper UTIs, or one upper plus one or more lower) triggers ultrasound regardless of age; DMSA still has no place in the RCH algorithm.

stem:
A 9-year-old girl with known persistent asthma is in your paediatric resuscitation bay with severe acute asthma. Her mother says 'her chest is sucking in and she can hardly say a word'. She has had three back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium bromide 250 mcg added to each dose, and was given oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg 40 minutes ago. She has had a normal chest X-ray and there is no pneumothorax.

On examination she remains using accessory muscles with persistent subcostal recession and only marginally improved tachypnoea. Her air entry is fair throughout with persistent expiratory wheeze; the chest is not silent. She is GCS 15 but tired. Cardiac monitoring shows sinus tachycardia at 156. Her capillary blood gas shows pH 7.30 (7.35-7.45), pCO2 46 mmHg (35-45), bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22-26). She has no history of intubation. Intravenous access is established and her potassium is 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 156, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 91% on 6 L/min mask oxygen, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Sitting upright, tired, single words, accessory muscle use, persistent expiratory wheeze with fair air entry, no silent chest, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: Capillary pH 7.30, pCO2 46 mmHg (35-45), bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22-26), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), chest X-ray clear
data_table.Medications: Three back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg plus ipratropium 250 mcg; oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg 40 minutes ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg as a slow infusion over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Severe paediatric asthma that fails the initial back-to-back salbutamol plus ipratropium plus oral steroid step is escalated with intravenous magnesium sulfate at 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) infused over 20 minutes under cardiac monitoring. Aminophylline is the next step thereafter if magnesium fails. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma; National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.text: Commence intravenous aminophylline loading dose 10 mg/kg over 1 hour and then a maintenance infusion
options.rationale: Aminophylline is the next step after magnesium failure, not before; the narrow therapeutic window and adverse effect profile place it lower on the escalation ladder. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Add nebulised hypertonic saline 3% as a respiratory adjunct and continue continuous nebulised salbutamol
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not indicated in acute asthma; the AU escalation step is intravenous magnesium sulfate. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Intubate and commence mechanical ventilation with permissive hypercapnia and inhaled volatile anaesthesia
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for life-threatening features (silent chest, exhaustion, altered consciousness, cardiopulmonary arrest); the child here is still moving air with fair entry and is GCS 15. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Commence non-invasive ventilation with bi-level positive airway pressure as the next escalation modality
options.rationale: Non-invasive ventilation is not standard of care in paediatric severe asthma in Australia; the next pharmacological step is intravenous magnesium sulfate. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

explanation.summary: Severe paediatric acute asthma is treated with continuous oxygen, back-to-back salbutamol plus ipratropium for the first hour, and oral or intravenous corticosteroids. Failure of this initial therapy escalates to intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring, then aminophylline if magnesium fails. Life-threatening features (silent chest, exhaustion, altered consciousness) mandate paediatric intensive care escalation and consideration of intubation. The capillary blood gas trend is a better marker than a single value.
key_points: Salbutamol plus ipratropium plus steroid for first hour
Magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg IV (max 2 g) next
Aminophylline reserved for magnesium failure
Life-threatening features: silent chest, exhaustion, altered consciousness
explanation.pearls: Hypokalaemia from salbutamol use is common in severe asthma and is monitored on serial venous gases; potassium replacement is given when below 3.5 mmol/L during continuous bronchodilator therapy.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to your emergency department after eating a peanut-containing biscuit at a birthday party 20 minutes ago. His mother says 'his face puffed up, he came out in hives and now he's wheezing and saying he can't breathe properly'. He has had two prior reactions to peanuts treated with antihistamines without adrenaline. He has been previously well and is not on any regular medications.

On examination he has facial and periorbital angioedema, generalised urticaria, and audible wheeze with intercostal recession. He is alert but anxious. His weight is documented as 16 kg from a recent immunisation visit. Intravenous access has not yet been established. He has had no prior fluid bolus. Oxygen is being delivered by mask at 6 L/min. The ED nursing team is preparing intramuscular adrenaline at your direction. There is no inspiratory stridor at rest yet.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 80/46 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 92% on 6 L/min mask oxygen, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert anxious, facial and periorbital angioedema, generalised urticaria, audible wheeze with intercostal recession, no stridor at rest
data_table.Investigations: Documented weight 16 kg, no IV access yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first dose of adrenaline?

options.text: Adrenaline 150 microgram (EpiPen Junior equivalent) intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh now
options.rationale: ASCIA paediatric anaphylaxis dosing uses banded intramuscular adrenaline by weight, not weight-based arithmetic. EpiPen Junior 150 microgram covers children 10-20 kg; EpiPen 300 microgram covers children 20-50 kg. A 16 kg child falls into the EpiPen Junior band. The dose may be repeated every 5 minutes if needed. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Acute Management Guidelines)

options.text: Adrenaline 160 microgram (10 microgram/kg) intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh now as a calculated dose
options.rationale: Weight-based arithmetic is not the AU standard; the ASCIA banded table protects against dose errors during anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Acute Management Guidelines)

options.text: Adrenaline 300 microgram (EpiPen equivalent) intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh now
options.rationale: EpiPen 300 microgram is the band for children 20-50 kg; this child at 16 kg is in the EpiPen Junior band (150 microgram). (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Acute Management Guidelines)

options.text: Adrenaline 16 microgram (1 microgram/kg) intravenously as a single bolus dose without an infusion
options.rationale: Intravenous adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis with intravenous access and infusion pump capability; intramuscular adrenaline is the AU first-line. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Acute Management Guidelines)

options.text: Adrenaline 1.6 milligram (100 microgram/kg) nebulised via a paediatric nebuliser mask immediately
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is used for upper airway oedema with stridor as an adjunct; it is not a substitute for intramuscular adrenaline in systemic anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Acute Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is treated with prompt intramuscular adrenaline to the anterolateral thigh. ASCIA's banded paediatric dosing avoids weight-based arithmetic during emergencies. EpiPen Junior 150 microgram covers 10-20 kg children, EpiPen 300 microgram covers 20-50 kg children, and 0.5 mg ampoule doses are used in adolescents and adults at 50 kg or more. Doses may be repeated every 5 minutes. Intramuscular is preferred over intravenous unless refractory; intravenous adrenaline requires an infusion pump and dilution to avoid arrhythmia.
key_points: EpiPen Junior 150 microgram = 10-20 kg
EpiPen 300 microgram = 20-50 kg
Adolescent/adult 0.5 mg if 50 kg or more
Repeat every 5 minutes; IV requires infusion pump
explanation.pearls: Biphasic anaphylaxis occurs in roughly 1 in 20 cases at 4-12 hours after the initial reaction; ASCIA recommends observation for at least 4 hours after symptom resolution before discharge.

stem:
A 2-year-old girl is brought to your paediatric ED with 36 hours of vomiting and watery diarrhoea. Her father says 'she keeps throwing up everything she sips, and her wee is dark like apple juice'. There is no blood in the stool. Her older sibling has had similar symptoms. She has had one wet nappy in the last 8 hours.

On examination she is alert but tired, with dry mucous membranes, a sunken anterior fontanelle (still partially open), and reduced skin turgor. Capillary refill is 2.5 seconds. She has no abdominal tenderness or peritonism. Her weight today is 11 kg, down from a documented baseline of 12 kg 3 weeks ago. A trial of small frequent oral rehydration solution (10 mL every 5 minutes by syringe) was given for 60 minutes; she has vomited each time and continues to refuse fluids. Bedside finger-prick glucose is 4.6 mmol/L. A single oral ondansetron wafer 2 mg was given 30 minutes ago without effect on the vomiting.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 144, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert tired, dry mucous membranes, partially sunken fontanelle, reduced skin turgor, capillary refill 2.5 seconds, soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Bedside finger-prick glucose 4.6 mmol/L; weight 11 kg down from 12 kg (estimated 8% dehydration)
data_table.Medications: Single oral ondansetron 2 mg given 30 minutes ago without effect

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and start continuous rehydration with oral rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg/hour for 4 hours
options.rationale: RCH guidance for moderate dehydration that has failed oral rehydration uses nasogastric tube rehydration as first-line ahead of intravenous fluids, with oral rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg/hour over 4 hours. NGT is preferred over IV because of reduced complications, lower cost, and equivalent outcomes. IV is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, ileus, or NGT failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Commence intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride bolus 20 mL/kg followed by a maintenance infusion immediately
options.rationale: Intravenous fluid is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, persistent vomiting after NGT trial, ileus, or electrolyte derangement requiring controlled correction; NGT rehydration is the AU first-line for moderate dehydration that fails oral. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Continue trial of oral rehydration solution at 5 mL every 5 minutes for a further 2 hours of observation
options.rationale: She has already failed an adequate trial of oral rehydration and is continuing to vomit; persisting risks further deterioration without correcting the deficit. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Administer a repeat dose of oral ondansetron wafer 4 mg and continue the oral fluid trial only
options.rationale: Repeat ondansetron does not address the existing fluid deficit; a single dose is the recommended ceiling per encounter and dose escalation is not the AU pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Send stool sample for culture and viral testing and discharge home with oral rehydration sachets for parents
options.rationale: Discharge with established 8% dehydration is unsafe; rehydration must be completed in hospital before any consideration of discharge. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric gastroenteritis dehydration is graded mild (under 4%), moderate (4-6%), or severe (over 7%) by clinical signs. The Australian (RCH) pathway uses oral rehydration first; failed oral rehydration moves to nasogastric tube rehydration at 25 mL/kg/hour for 4 hours, not intravenous fluids. Intravenous rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration with shock, persistent ileus, NGT failure, or electrolyte derangement requiring controlled correction. Ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose (weight-banded: 2 mg if under 15 kg, 4 mg if 15-30 kg) reduces vomiting and admission rates.
key_points: Mild under 4%; moderate 4-6%; severe over 7%
NGT rehydration at 25 mL/kg/hour for 4 hours is first after oral failure
IV reserved for severe dehydration, shock, ileus, NGT failure
Single dose ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg (banded by weight)
explanation.pearls: NGT rehydration in moderate paediatric dehydration has equivalent outcomes to intravenous rehydration with fewer complications and reduced length of stay; RCH explicitly prefers it.

stem:
A 16-month-old Aboriginal boy is brought to your remote primary care clinic with 24 hours of fever to 39.0 °C and ear-pulling. His mother says 'he keeps grabbing at his right ear and crying when he lies down to sleep'. He has had no diarrhoea, no rash, and no respiratory distress. He is fully immunised. He attends a remote community kindergarten and has had three previous episodes of acute otitis media in the past 6 months.

On examination both tympanic membranes are bulging and erythematous, with loss of light reflex on the right. There is no perforation and no purulent discharge. The neck is supple, the throat is unremarkable, and the chest is clear. His hydration is satisfactory. He is otherwise alert and consoles in his mother's lap. The clinic has access to oral amoxicillin and intramuscular ceftriaxone but not a same-day audiology service. The community has high rates of chronic suppurative otitis media in older children.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Both tympanic membranes bulging and erythematous, loss of light reflex right, no perforation, no discharge, supple neck, clear chest
data_table.Investigations: None indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe high-dose oral amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day in two divided doses for 7 days and review in person at 48 hours
options.rationale: In Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, otitis media is treated with antibiotics immediately rather than watchful waiting because of the high background risk of perforation and chronic suppurative otitis media. The AU first-line is oral amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day divided BD for 7 days. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; CARPA Standard Treatment Manual)

options.text: Adopt watchful waiting with regular paracetamol and review in 48 hours if symptoms persist or worsen
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is reasonable in low-risk non-Indigenous children over 2 years with mild unilateral disease, not in Aboriginal children in remote settings where perforation rates are high. (Source: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual)

options.text: Administer a single intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg dose now as initial therapy and review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is reserved for severe disease, vomiting, or failure of first-line amoxicillin in this age group; first-line is oral amoxicillin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin with clavulanic acid 90 mg/kg/day amoxicillin component divided three times daily for 14 days
options.rationale: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is reserved for treatment failure at 48-72 hours or recurrent otitis media despite adequate first-line therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer urgently for tympanocentesis and culture of middle ear fluid before commencing any antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Tympanocentesis is reserved for treatment failure, immunocompromise, or complicated disease; empirical antibiotics are first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children carries a much higher risk of progression to perforation and chronic suppurative otitis media than in non-Indigenous children, and watchful waiting is not appropriate as initial therapy. Australian (CARPA/Therapeutic Guidelines) first-line is high-dose oral amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day divided twice daily for 7 days, with in-person review at 48 hours. Treatment failure escalates to amoxicillin with clavulanic acid and audiology follow-up. Recurrent otitis media (three episodes in 6 months or four in 12) prompts ENT referral and consideration of grommets.
key_points: No watchful waiting for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children
First-line: high-dose amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day BD for 7 days
Failure at 48-72 hours: switch to amoxicillin with clavulanic acid
Recurrent disease: ENT referral and grommet consideration
explanation.pearls: Audiology assessment after recurrent acute otitis media is essential in remote Australia because of the long-term language and learning impact of even mild conductive hearing loss in early childhood.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on call. A 22-month-old girl is on the general paediatric ward 36 hours after a first dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg for complete Kawasaki disease (8 days of fever, conjunctivitis, oral changes, peripheral oedema, polymorphous rash). The bedside nurse calls you because she has spiked a fever to 39.2 °C again 12 hours after the IVIG completed. Her CRP, which had fallen to 84 mg/L at the end of the infusion, is now 138 mg/L on a repeat measurement.

On examination she remains miserable, with persistent dry fissured lips and bilateral conjunctival injection. There is no new petechiae, no shock, and no new murmur. Her aspirin 80 mg/kg/day in four divided doses is ongoing. The baseline echocardiogram at 24 hours showed no coronary artery dilatation (Z-score plus 0.6 in the left main coronary, plus 0.4 in the right). Her family is from a Japanese background and her parents ask 'is there something stronger now?'. She has had no live vaccines in the last 4 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 154, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Miserable, persistent dry fissured lips, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, no shock, no new murmur, no new rash
data_table.Investigations: CRP 138 mg/L rising from 84 mg/L post-IVIG, albumin 27 g/L (35-50), echocardiogram coronary Z-score plus 0.6 LMCA plus 0.4 RCA at 24 hours
data_table.Medications: IVIG 2 g/kg completed 12 hours ago; aspirin 80 mg/kg/day divided four times daily ongoing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as the next step in escalation for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease
options.rationale: IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease (persistent or recurrent fever at 36 hours or more after the first IVIG infusion) is treated with a second IVIG dose 2 g/kg as the AU first-line escalation. Intravenous methylprednisolone pulses, oral prednisolone, and infliximab are reserved for second IVIG failure or high coronary aneurysm risk scores. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Disease Scientific Statement; RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Administer intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse daily for 3 days as the second-line escalation step
options.rationale: Pulsed methylprednisolone is reserved for second IVIG failure or high-risk scores at baseline; the AU first escalation is a second IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Add intravenous infliximab 5 mg/kg single dose as the second-line escalation step ahead of further IVIG
options.rationale: Infliximab is third-line in Australia after second IVIG and pulsed steroids have failed; placing it first is not the recommended order. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Continue current therapy and observe for a further 48 hours before any decision to escalate treatment
options.rationale: Persistent fever beyond 36 hours after IVIG defines IVIG resistance and requires escalation; observation increases coronary aneurysm risk. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Disease Scientific Statement)

options.text: Cease aspirin and commence anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin instead pending repeat echocardiogram
options.rationale: Aspirin is continued through IVIG resistance unless coronary aneurysms over 8 mm in diameter develop, when adjunctive anticoagulation is added; aspirin is not ceased. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Disease Scientific Statement)

explanation.summary: IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease is defined by persistent or recurrent fever 36 hours or more after the first IVIG dose has completed. About 10-20% of children meet this definition. The AU and AHA first-line escalation is a second IVIG dose 2 g/kg. If that fails, pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone or infliximab is the next step. Aspirin is continued at high anti-inflammatory dose until inflammatory markers normalise (typically 48-72 hours after fever resolution) before reducing to low-dose antiplatelet for at least 6-8 weeks. Echocardiography is repeated at 2 weeks and 6 weeks regardless of treatment course.
key_points: IVIG-resistant: fever 36+ hours after first IVIG dose
First escalation: second IVIG 2 g/kg
