Second escalation: pulsed methylprednisolone or infliximab
Echocardiography at 2 and 6 weeks regardless
explanation.pearls: Risk scores predicting IVIG resistance (Kobayashi, Egami) developed in Japanese cohorts do not perform well in non-Japanese populations; AU practice is to escalate empirically on the 36-hour fever rule rather than on a score.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called urgently to the ward. A 10-year-old girl was admitted 6 hours ago with new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus presenting in diabetic ketoacidosis (pH 7.05, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, glucose 32 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L). She has received 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride as a single bolus, then 0.9% sodium chloride at a 48-hour rehydration rate, plus a fixed-rate insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour. Her glucose is now 14 mmol/L and her pH has improved to 7.18.

The nurse says 'she's been a bit harder to rouse over the last 20 minutes and her headache is worse'. On examination her GCS has dropped from 15 to 13 (eyes open to voice, confused conversation). Her pulse is 64 (down from 122 on arrival), blood pressure is 142/88 mmHg (up from 102/60), and respiratory rate has slowed from 38 to 22. Pupils are 4 mm and equal, with sluggish reactions. The fontanelle is closed. There is no focal neurological deficit. Bedside glucose is now 12 mmol/L; ketones 4.1 mmol/L; bicarbonate 12 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 64 (was 122), BP 142/88 mmHg (was 102/60), RR 22 (was 38), SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (eyes open to voice, confused), pupils 4 mm equal sluggish, no focal deficit, fontanelle closed
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 12 mmol/L, ketones 4.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (was 6)
data_table.Medications: Fixed-rate insulin infusion 0.05 units/kg/hour and 0.9% sodium chloride at 48-hour rehydration rate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous mannitol 1 g/kg over 20 minutes and reduce intravenous fluid rate by one-third immediately
options.rationale: Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of paediatric DKA mortality; the diagnostic triad of declining GCS, bradycardia with hypertension, and slowed respiration is the Cushing reflex. Hypertonic saline 3% (2.5-5 mL/kg) or mannitol (0.5-1 g/kg over 20 minutes) is given immediately; intravenous fluids are reduced by one-third; insulin infusion is continued but the rate may be lowered. Neuro-imaging follows stabilisation, not precedes it. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines on DKA; RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines on DKA

options.text: Increase the intravenous fluid rate to compensate for ongoing osmotic diuresis and continue insulin at the present rate
options.rationale: Increasing fluids in suspected cerebral oedema can worsen the oedema; the AU pathway reduces the rate by one-third while giving osmotherapy. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines on DKA)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines on DKA

options.text: Cease the insulin infusion entirely to allow biochemical stabilisation before any further osmotic therapy
options.rationale: Insulin is continued (possibly at reduced rate) to maintain ketone clearance; ceasing insulin causes acidosis rebound and does not treat cerebral oedema. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines on DKA)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines on DKA

options.text: Order an urgent computed tomography head scan before any intervention to confirm cerebral oedema or other cause
options.rationale: Imaging follows immediate osmotic therapy; the clinical syndrome with the Cushing reflex pattern is treated empirically without waiting for imaging. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines on DKA)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines on DKA

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single dose for presumed inflammatory cerebral oedema
options.rationale: Steroids have no role in DKA cerebral oedema; the mechanism is osmotic and inflammatory steroid response is not part of the pathway. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines on DKA)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines on DKA

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of paediatric DKA mortality and morbidity. Risk factors include young age (under 5), severe acidosis at presentation (pH under 7.1), hyponatraemia, high urea, bicarbonate use, and rapid sodium or fluid administration. The diagnostic clinical triad is declining GCS, bradycardia with hypertension, and slowed respiration (Cushing reflex). Treatment is osmotherapy with hypertonic saline 3% (2.5-5 mL/kg) or mannitol (0.5-1 g/kg over 20 minutes), reduce intravenous fluid rate by one-third, head-up positioning, neuroprotection, and PICU transfer. Neuro-imaging is performed after stabilisation.
key_points: Cushing reflex: declining GCS plus bradycardia plus hypertension plus slowed respiration
Hypertonic saline 3% (2.5-5 mL/kg) OR mannitol (0.5-1 g/kg) over 20 min
Reduce IV fluid rate by one-third while giving osmotherapy
Imaging after stabilisation, never before treatment
explanation.pearls: Effective serum osmolality (2 x sodium plus glucose) under 320 mosm/kg in a child with DKA who deteriorates is highly suggestive of cerebral oedema rather than dehydration.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines on DKA

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the postnatal ward. A 36-hour-old, term, exclusively breastfed boy has had two episodes of green vomiting in the last 4 hours. The midwife says 'his vomits have gone from milk-coloured to bright green and his tummy looks a bit bloated now'. He had been feeding well until this morning and had one meconium pass at 18 hours of life.

On examination he is alert but quiet, with a mildly distended abdomen and no palpable mass. The abdomen is soft without peritonism. Bowel sounds are present. Anus is patent on inspection. The remaining examination is unremarkable. Bedside finger-prick glucose is 4.4 mmol/L. The mother had normal antenatal scans including a 20-week morphology scan; there was no polyhydramnios. He has had no syndromic features identified. A nasogastric tube placed on your direction drains 25 mL of bilious fluid. He has had no further meconium since the first pass.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 152, BP 72/44 mmHg, RR 48, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert quiet, mildly distended soft abdomen, no peritonism, patent anus, no syndromic features
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.4 mmol/L; NGT drains 25 mL bilious fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent upper gastrointestinal contrast study to assess duodenojejunal flexure position and rule out volvulus
options.rationale: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proved otherwise. The diagnostic gold standard is an urgent upper GI contrast study showing the position of the duodenojejunal flexure (DJ flexure). A normal DJ flexure crosses to the left of the spine at the L2 level; an abnormal DJ flexure on the right of the spine is diagnostic of malrotation. Definitive treatment is Ladd's procedure. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting in the neonate; RACS Position on Paediatric Surgical Emergencies)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting in the neonate
RACS Position on Paediatric Surgical Emergencies

options.text: Reassure the team and observe with intravenous maintenance fluids while continuing breastfeeding on demand
options.rationale: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is a surgical emergency; observation risks bowel necrosis from undiagnosed volvulus within hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting in the neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting in the neonate

options.text: Arrange supine and erect abdominal X-rays only and review again at 6 hours from the time of presentation
options.rationale: Plain abdominal X-rays may be normal early in malrotation; relying on them alone delays diagnosis. The AU pathway is urgent contrast study. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting in the neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting in the neonate

options.text: Arrange a barium enema as the first imaging modality to assess caecal position and possible obstruction
options.rationale: Barium enema can localise the caecum but does not show DJ flexure position; upper GI contrast study is the AU first-line for suspected malrotation. (Source: RACS Position on Paediatric Surgical Emergencies)
source_refs: RACS Position on Paediatric Surgical Emergencies

options.text: Stop oral feeding and start trial of probiotic for a presumed neonatal feeding intolerance with green vomits
options.rationale: Green vomits are bilious and not benign reflux or feeding intolerance; probiotic has no role in suspected malrotation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting in the neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting in the neonate

explanation.summary: Bilious (green) vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proved otherwise. Other differentials include duodenal atresia/stenosis, jejunal atresia, meconium ileus, Hirschsprung's disease, and necrotising enterocolitis. The diagnostic test is the urgent upper GI contrast study showing the duodenojejunal flexure position; a flexure to the right of the spine is diagnostic of malrotation. Plain X-ray showing the double bubble (with no distal gas) suggests duodenal atresia. Definitive treatment for malrotation with volvulus is Ladd's procedure: detorsion, division of Ladd's bands, broadening of the mesentery, appendicectomy, and bowel placement with small bowel right and colon left.
key_points: Bilious vomiting in neonate = malrotation with volvulus until proved otherwise
Upper GI contrast study is the diagnostic test
Normal DJ flexure to left of spine at L2 level
Definitive treatment: Ladd's procedure
explanation.pearls: Time to surgery is critical: midgut volvulus that obstructs the superior mesenteric artery can produce total intestinal necrosis within hours, leading to short-bowel syndrome or death.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting in the neonate
RACS Position on Paediatric Surgical Emergencies

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-month-old girl brought to a metropolitan emergency department by her mother and the mother's partner after a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting four minutes that resolved before arrival. She was previously well, immunisations are up to date, and she is exclusively breastfed.

On examination she is afebrile and alert with a normal cry. Anterior fontanelle is soft and flat. There is a 2 cm bluish bruise over the left cheek and a small bruise on the left pinna. Her mother explains the baby rolled off the change table this morning while she was answering the door, and the mother's partner is the primary daytime carer while father is on a fly-in fly-out roster. Coagulation profile, capillary glucose, ammonia and electrolytes are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused; left cheek bruise 2 cm, small left pinna bruise; anterior fontanelle soft; no other surface marks; tone normal
data_table.Investigations: BSL 4.6 mmol/L; sodium, urea, creatinine within normal limits; INR within normal limits; ammonia within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Non contrast CT head and skeletal survey, then notify child protection services
options.rationale: In a less than 6 month old with unexplained bruising plus a seizure, urgent neuroimaging plus skeletal survey is mandated and statutory notification is non-discretionary in every Australian jurisdiction. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse; RACP Position Statement)
source_refs: RACP Position Statement on Child Abuse

options.text: Discharge home with safety net advice and paediatric outpatient follow up in two weeks
options.rationale: A bruise in a non-cruising infant is a sentinel injury for abusive head trauma until proven otherwise; discharging without imaging or notification breaches the RCH child protection pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Outpatient EEG and developmental review through the local community paediatrician
options.rationale: Outpatient EEG addresses a recurrent seizure workup but ignores the inflicted injury pattern; priority is excluding intracranial haemorrhage and occult fractures, not characterising epilepsy. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Admit overnight for observation only, with discharge to the mother in the morning
options.rationale: Observation alone neither investigates the injury pattern nor protects the child on discharge; notification and imaging cannot be deferred to morning rounds. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Request a metabolic screen including plasma amino acids and urine organic acids
options.rationale: Metabolic screen is appropriate for unexplained encephalopathy with abnormal gas or glucose; with normal glucose, gas and ammonia plus an explanatory injury pattern this misdirects the workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Any bruise in a pre-cruising infant must trigger an abusive head trauma workup because the positive predictive value of bruising in a non-mobile child for inflicted injury is extremely high. The RCH pathway pairs urgent non contrast CT head with a skeletal survey within 24 hours, ophthalmology review for retinal haemorrhages, and same-day statutory notification. A normal coagulation profile and metabolic screen do not exclude inflicted injury and must not delay imaging. The treating clinician makes the report; consent from the carer is not required.
key_points: Bruising in non-mobile infants under 6 months is a sentinel injury with very high specificity for abuse
RCH workup: non contrast CT head plus skeletal survey within 24 hours plus ophthalmology
Mandatory reporting applies to suspicion, not certainty
Normal coagulation studies do NOT exclude inflicted injury
explanation.pearls: TEN-4-FACESp bruising rule: any bruise in a child under 4 months, or torso-ear-neck bruise under 4 years, carries >97% specificity for abuse and triggers immediate CT plus skeletal survey within 24 hours.

sources.label: RACP Position Statement on Child Abuse

stem:
A 14-month-old previously well boy is reviewed on day 7 of fever above 38.5 °C that has not abated despite oral amoxicillin started by a general practitioner on day 4. He is irritable and feeding poorly. His mother reports red eyes for the last four days and a maculopapular trunk rash that came and went on day 5.

On examination he has bilateral non purulent conjunctival injection, fissured red lips with a strawberry tongue, and erythema of the palms with periungual desquamation just starting on the right second finger. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy and no peripheral oedema. Throat swab and urine culture sent on day 4 are negative; a chest radiograph was clear. Echocardiography this morning shows coronary arteries within normal limits for body surface area.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168/min, BP 90/55 mmHg, RR 32/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.1 °C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 95 g/L (105-135); platelets 612 x10^9/L (150-400); WCC 18.2 x10^9/L (5-15); CRP 142 mg/L (<5); ALT 78 U/L (<40); albumin 28 g/L (35-50); sodium 131 mmol/L (135-145); urinalysis sterile pyuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold immunoglobulin and observe for 48 hours pending fever resolution
options.rationale: Treatment cannot be deferred because coronary aneurysm risk rises sharply if IVIG is given after day 10 of fever; the laboratory picture already meets incomplete criteria. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Repeat echocardiography in 7 days before deciding on immunoglobulin treatment
options.rationale: A normal initial echocardiogram does NOT rule out Kawasaki; coronary changes often emerge after day 10, by which time IVIG benefit on aneurysm prevention has been lost. (Source: AHA Scientific Statement)

options.text: Switch antibiotic therapy to intravenous ceftriaxone for occult bacterial infection
options.rationale: Cultures are negative and the syndrome fits Kawasaki; antibiotic escalation delays the time critical IVIG window and treats a phantom diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Administer high dose oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily as primary monotherapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy is not standard initial therapy in Australia; steroids are added to IVIG only for high risk or refractory disease, not as substitute first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 10 hours plus oral aspirin
options.rationale: He meets incomplete Kawasaki criteria with supportive laboratory findings (CRP, thrombocytosis, anaemia, hypoalbuminaemia, transaminitis, sterile pyuria); IVIG must be given within 10 days regardless of normal echocardiography. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease; AHA Statement)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki is diagnosed when prolonged fever is accompanied by two or three principal features and supportive laboratory findings, even without the full five-criterion picture. Treatment is identical to complete Kawasaki: IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion plus aspirin, ideally between day 5 and day 10. Aneurysm rates fall from approximately 25% untreated to 4% with timely IVIG. A normal initial echocardiogram does not exclude diagnosis or remove the treatment indication, because coronary changes may emerge in the convalescent phase. Cardiology follow up at 2 and 6 weeks is mandatory.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: fever ≥5 days plus 2 to 3 features plus supportive labs
Lab support: CRP, ESR, thrombocytosis, anaemia, transaminitis, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria
IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion plus aspirin within day 10
Steroids added only in high risk or IVIG resistant cases
explanation.pearls: IVIG given after day 10 of fever loses most of its aneurysm-preventive benefit; do not wait for a complete five-criterion picture if labs and clinical features already support incomplete Kawasaki.

stem:
You are the rural ED registrar at a regional hospital seeing a 22-month-old girl brought in 90 minutes after falling backwards off a kitchen chair onto a carpeted floor. The fall was witnessed by her father. There was no loss of consciousness. She vomited once at home and once in triage, then settled in her father's arms and accepted a bottle.

On arrival she is calm, smiles when distracted with bubbles, and her father states she is acting like herself. There is a 4 cm boggy haematoma over the right parietal scalp without overlying laceration. Anterior fontanelle is closed. Pupils are equal and reactive, tone is normal, and she tracks toys with both eyes. There is no palpable skull step. Glasgow coma score is 15.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 94/58 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: GCS 15, calm in father's arms, accepts bottle; 4 cm boggy right parietal scalp haematoma; no palpable skull step; pupils equal and reactive
data_table.History: Fall from kitchen chair onto carpet, witnessed, no loss of consciousness, 2 episodes of vomiting, normal behaviour now

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate non contrast CT head and admit under the paediatric team
options.rationale: Non frontal scalp haematoma alone in an otherwise normal child meets PECARN intermediate risk; the PECARN authors recommend observation versus CT based on clinician experience and parental preference, not automatic scan. (Source: PECARN head injury rule)

options.text: Discharge home immediately with written head injury advice for her father
options.rationale: Two episodes of vomiting plus a non frontal boggy haematoma fall into the PECARN intermediate-risk group; same-day discharge without an observation period is unsafe. (Source: PECARN head injury rule)

options.text: Observe in the emergency department for 4 to 6 hours with neurological observations
options.rationale: She has a single intermediate PECARN feature (non frontal scalp haematoma) without LOC, altered mental status, severe mechanism, or palpable skull fracture; PECARN supports a planned observation strategy which halves CT use without missing clinically important traumatic brain injury. (Source: PECARN head injury rule; RCH CPG: Head Injury)

options.text: Arrange a skull radiograph series to exclude a linear parietal fracture
options.rationale: Plain skull radiographs are not part of PECARN or RCH pathways; they neither rule in nor rule out clinically important traumatic brain injury and add radiation without benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury)

options.text: Transfer urgently to a tertiary paediatric centre by retrieval team
options.rationale: Retrieval is reserved for GCS deterioration, focal neurology, suspected open or depressed fracture, or positive CT findings; a well child with one intermediate feature does not meet retrieval thresholds. (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury)

explanation.summary: The PECARN under-2 rule stratifies blunt head injury by mental status, signs of skull fracture, scalp haematoma, loss of consciousness >5 seconds, severe mechanism, and parental concern about behaviour. Children with NO predictors can be discharged. Children with intermediate predictors (non frontal scalp haematoma, LOC <5 s, severe mechanism, abnormal behaviour) have a clinically important TBI rate of approximately 0.9% and can be managed by observation or selective CT based on age, clinician experience, multiple predictors and parental preference. Children with high risk features (GCS <15, altered mental status, palpable skull fracture) need CT.
key_points: PECARN under-2 high risk: GCS <15, altered mental status, palpable skull fracture
PECARN intermediate: non frontal haematoma, LOC <5 s, severe mechanism, abnormal behaviour
Observation halves CT use without missing important injury in intermediate group
Plain skull radiograph is not part of the pathway
explanation.pearls: PECARN under-2 intermediate group has a clinically important TBI rate of ~0.9%; a 4 to 6 hour observation period is supported and avoids unnecessary CT radiation in toddlers.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar caring for a 9-year-old girl admitted to the ward four hours ago with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes and diabetic ketoacidosis. She received a 10 mL/kg saline bolus on arrival, was started on 0.05 units/kg/hour intravenous insulin two hours ago, and is now on 0.45% saline plus 5% dextrose with potassium running at her calculated maintenance plus 48-hour deficit replacement rate.

Her mother calls you because the child has just complained of a new severe headache and has vomited once. On review she is drowsy, opens eyes only to voice and her speech is slurred. The bedside nurse reports the blood pressure has risen from 105/65 to 132/82 over the last 30 minutes and the heart rate has fallen from 122 to 88. Pupils are equal and reactive. Sodium has fallen from 138 to 131 since admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Neurology: Drowsy, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5), pupils equal and reactive, no focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: BSL 14 mmol/L; sodium 131 mmol/L (135-145, was 138); pH 7.18 (was 7.05); ketones 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue the current fluid regimen at the same rate and reassess her neurology and pupils in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Headache plus drowsiness plus rising BP plus falling HR in DKA represents Cushing's response from cerebral oedema; passive observation worsens outcomes and delays neuroprotection. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis; ISPAD 2022 guidelines)

options.text: Administer mannitol 0.5 g/kg or hypertonic 3% saline 2.5 mL/kg and reduce IV fluid rate by one third
options.rationale: Suspected cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA mandates immediate hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg or hypertonic 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg) plus reduction of fluid rate by one third; do not wait for CT confirmation. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis; ISPAD 2022 guidelines)

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion to 0.1 units/kg/hour and add a second saline bolus
options.rationale: Accelerating insulin and re-bolusing fluid both worsen cerebral oedema by driving an osmotic gradient into the brain; this is the opposite of what is required. (Source: ISPAD 2022 guidelines)

options.text: Stop the insulin infusion entirely and check serum osmolality before any further action
options.rationale: Stopping insulin allows ketogenesis to rebound; with a syndrome of cerebral oedema the clock is short, and osmolality testing should not delay neuroprotective therapy. (Source: ISPAD 2022 guidelines)

options.text: Arrange an urgent non contrast CT head to confirm cerebral oedema before treatment
options.rationale: Cerebral oedema in DKA is a clinical diagnosis; CT is normal in up to 40% of cases at presentation and should NEVER delay mannitol or hypertonic saline. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema complicates approximately 0.5 to 1% of paediatric DKA episodes with mortality up to 25%. The Muir criteria stratify clinical features into diagnostic (abnormal motor response, decorticate posturing, cranial nerve palsy, abnormal breathing pattern), major (altered mental status, sustained heart rate deceleration, age-inappropriate incontinence), and minor (vomiting, headache, lethargy, BP >90th centile, age <5 years). One diagnostic, two major, or one major plus two minor criteria mandate immediate treatment. The Cushing response (rising BP with falling HR) is a late and ominous sign. Hyperosmolar therapy is the time-critical intervention; CT must not delay it.
key_points: Cushing response in DKA = cerebral oedema until proven otherwise
Mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg OR hypertonic 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg immediately
Reduce IV fluid rate by one third concurrently
CT is normal in up to 40%, do NOT delay therapy for imaging
explanation.pearls: Hypertonic 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg is the preferred first-line hyperosmolar agent in paediatric DKA cerebral oedema per ISPAD 2022; mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg is an acceptable alternative.

stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his grandmother after an episode at home four hours ago where he started coughing suddenly while eating peanuts on the couch and then settled. He has been intermittently coughing since and his grandmother says his breathing sounds noisier on one side.

On arrival he is alert and talking in full sentences. There is no audible stridor. Auscultation reveals reduced air entry and end-expiratory wheeze over the right lower zone with normal breath sounds on the left. There is no fever and no recent viral illness. He has never wheezed before and has no atopy. An inspiratory chest radiograph performed in the department is reported as showing no focal consolidation, no pneumothorax, equal lung volumes and no radio-opaque foreign body.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 30/min, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Talking in full sentences; mild subcostal recession; reduced air entry plus end-expiratory wheeze over right lower zone; left chest clear; no stridor
data_table.Investigations: Inspiratory chest radiograph: no consolidation, no pneumothorax, equal lung volumes, no radio-opaque foreign body

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for urgent flexible bronchoscopy under sedation in the emergency department
options.rationale: Flexible bronchoscopy is diagnostic only and lacks the working channel for retrieval; once aspiration is suspected the procedure of choice is rigid bronchoscopy in theatre. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Inhalation)

options.text: Trial salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer and reassess auscultation in 20 minutes
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are appropriate for viral wheeze or asthma but do not address an aspirated foreign body and delay definitive retrieval; persistent unilateral wheeze after choking is the discriminator. (Source: RCH CPG: Wheeze in Children)

options.text: Refer urgently to ENT or paediatric surgery for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: History of a choking episode plus unilateral wheeze plus reduced air entry is the classic foreign body triad; a normal inspiratory chest radiograph does NOT exclude an organic foreign body, which is radiolucent in over 80% of cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Inhalation; ANZCA Position Statement)
source_refs: ANZCA Position Statement on Paediatric Airway

options.text: Discharge home with safety net advice and outpatient paediatric review next week
options.rationale: Discharge risks distal migration, post obstructive pneumonia and lobar collapse; once the syndrome is recognised, bronchoscopy is mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Inhalation)

options.text: Order a non contrast chest CT to identify the level of the aspirated foreign body
options.rationale: CT has diagnostic utility but should NOT delay rigid bronchoscopy when clinical suspicion is high and bronchoscopy is required regardless of CT findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Inhalation)

explanation.summary: Foreign body aspiration peaks between 1 and 3 years; peanuts, beads, small toys and battery cells are the classic culprits. The diagnostic triad is choking episode plus unilateral wheeze plus reduced air entry on auscultation. A normal chest radiograph does NOT exclude the diagnosis because organic objects such as peanuts are radiolucent in over 80% of cases; expiratory or lateral decubitus films may show air trapping but their absence is not reassuring. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia in theatre is both diagnostic and therapeutic and should not be delayed by further imaging. Button battery aspiration is a parallel emergency that demands immediate retrieval given the rapid mucosal injury.
key_points: Triad: choking episode + unilateral wheeze + reduced air entry
Normal CXR does NOT exclude foreign body (radiolucent in >80%)
Rigid bronchoscopy in theatre, not flexible bronchoscopy or CT
Button battery is a parallel emergency requiring immediate retrieval
explanation.pearls: Peanuts and other organic foreign bodies are radiolucent in over 80% of paediatric aspirations; a normal inspiratory chest radiograph must NOT delay rigid bronchoscopy once the choking-plus-unilateral-wheeze pattern is recognised.

sources.label: ANZCA Position Statement on Paediatric Airway

stem:
An 8-year-old known asthmatic boy presents to a metropolitan emergency department with worsening cough and shortness of breath for 12 hours after running outside this morning. He has had asthma since age 4 on twice-daily fluticasone 100 mcg and a salbutamol reliever as needed. He has used his blue puffer six times in the last two hours at home with no sustained improvement.

On arrival he speaks in short phrases, is sitting forward, and uses accessory muscles. Auscultation reveals widespread polyphonic wheeze with reduced air entry bilaterally. He receives three back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg plus ipratropium 250 mcg combinations over 30 minutes and oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg. After this he remains tachypnoeic with continued accessory muscle use and SpO2 92% on 4 L/min via nasal prongs; he is still speaking in short phrases only.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, RR 38/min, SpO2 92% on 4 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Sitting forward, accessory muscle use; widespread polyphonic wheeze, reduced air entry bilaterally; speaks in short phrases
data_table.Medications given: Three back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg plus ipratropium 250 mcg; oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes (max 2 g)
options.rationale: Acute severe asthma not responding to back-to-back salbutamol plus ipratropium plus systemic steroid is the trigger for IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes per the National Asthma Council and RCH pathway. (Source: National Asthma Council Handbook; RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

options.text: Add nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 to the next bronchodilator cycle
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for croup and anaphylaxis-related airway oedema, NOT bronchospasm; the bronchodilator escalation in asthma is IV magnesium followed by aminophylline or salbutamol infusion. (Source: National Asthma Council Handbook)

options.text: Increase the inhaled fluticasone dose to 250 mcg twice daily before discharge
options.rationale: Increasing the daily preventer is appropriate at outpatient review, but does not relieve acute severe bronchospasm in the emergency setting. (Source: National Asthma Council Handbook)

options.text: Commence broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics for presumed bacterial chest infection
options.rationale: There is no fever or focal consolidation; antibiotics are not indicated for acute asthma in the absence of infective signs and do not relieve bronchospasm. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

options.text: Switch from nasal prong oxygen to high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min
options.rationale: High flow oxygen alone does not treat bronchospasm; oxygenation supports the work of breathing but the failure point here is airflow obstruction, which requires IV magnesium. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

explanation.summary: Acute severe asthma in children is staged as mild, moderate, severe and life-threatening based on speech, work of breathing, oxygen saturation and conscious level. First line is back-to-back nebulised or spacer-delivered salbutamol plus ipratropium plus systemic steroid. Failure to respond after three cycles defines acute severe asthma and triggers IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes (max 2 g). Further failure escalates to IV salbutamol or aminophylline infusion and PICU referral. Reassessment after each intervention is the heartbeat of acute paediatric asthma care.
key_points: First line: back-to-back salbutamol plus ipratropium plus oral prednisolone
IV magnesium 50 mg/kg over 20 min (max 2 g) for failure to respond
Next escalation: IV salbutamol or aminophylline plus PICU
Antibiotics not indicated without infective signs
explanation.pearls: IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes (maximum 2 g) is the standard next step in paediatric asthma not responding to three back-to-back nebulised salbutamol plus ipratropium cycles plus systemic steroid.

stem:
A 22-month-old boy is brought to your general practice clinic by his mother for a third episode of audible wheeze in the past 6 months. Each episode followed a runny nose by 24 to 48 hours and lasted 4 to 5 days. Between episodes he is completely well and runs around without breathlessness. He has had no nocturnal wheeze. There is no family history of asthma, eczema or hay fever, and he has had no admissions.

On examination today he is afebrile, talking in normal phrases for his age, and his work of breathing is normal. Auscultation reveals scattered end expiratory wheeze with normal air entry bilaterally. His mother has been giving 4 puffs of salbutamol via a small-volume spacer at the onset of each cold which she says reduces symptoms within 30 minutes. He has had no salbutamol use today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 92/56 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Talking in normal phrases for age, no accessory muscle use; scattered end expiratory wheeze; normal air entry; afebrile
data_table.History: 3 episodes wheeze in 6 months, each cold-triggered, well between episodes; no nocturnal wheeze; no atopy; salbutamol responsive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence inhaled corticosteroid fluticasone 50 mcg twice daily as a daily preventer
options.rationale: Daily ICS is not first-line for episodic viral wheeze in a child this age without interval symptoms or atopy; reassessment at age 5 is the better strategy. (Source: National Asthma Council Handbook; RCH CPG: Wheeze)

options.text: Trial montelukast 4 mg orally each evening for 12 weeks then reassess
options.rationale: Montelukast has marginal benefit in episodic viral wheeze and now carries a TGA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric adverse events; it is not first-line in this scenario. (Source: AMH; TGA Safety Advisory Montelukast)

options.text: Continue salbutamol as needed via spacer and review again if symptoms change
options.rationale: Episodic viral wheeze in a 1 to 3 year old who is well between episodes and lacks atopy is best managed with as-needed bronchodilator via spacer; daily preventer is reserved for frequent episodic, persistent, or atopy-positive children. (Source: National Asthma Council Handbook; RCH CPG: Wheeze)

options.text: Refer for skin prick allergen testing to common inhaled and food allergens
options.rationale: Skin prick testing has low yield without interval symptoms or other atopic features and would not change today's management. (Source: ASCIA Position Statement on Allergy Testing)
source_refs: ASCIA Position Statement on Allergy Testing

options.text: Prescribe an oral prednisolone course for use at the start of each viral episode
options.rationale: Parent-initiated oral steroids at viral onset do NOT prevent attacks in preschool wheeze and have been deprescribed in current Australian guidelines. (Source: National Asthma Council Handbook)

explanation.summary: Preschool wheeze splits into episodic viral wheeze (well between, no atopy) and multi-trigger wheeze (interval symptoms, atopy, family history). Episodic viral wheeze is managed with as-needed salbutamol via spacer; daily inhaled corticosteroid is reserved for frequent or persistent episodes, multi-trigger pattern, or strong atopy where the modified Asthma Predictive Index is positive. Montelukast has limited efficacy and is now boxed-warning for neuropsychiatric effects. Most children with episodic viral wheeze stop wheezing by school age and a planned reassessment around age 5 differentiates persistent asthma.
key_points: Episodic viral wheeze in 1 to 3 year olds without atopy: salbutamol via spacer as needed
Daily ICS reserved for frequent/persistent or atopy-positive patterns
Montelukast has TGA neuropsychiatric boxed warning, low first-line value
Most episodic viral wheezers resolve by school age
explanation.pearls: The modified Asthma Predictive Index (mAPI) positive picture is frequent wheeze plus one major criterion (parent asthma, eczema, aeroallergen sensitisation) or two minor criteria (food allergy, eosinophilia ≥4%, wheeze without cold) and predicts persistent asthma.

sources.label: ASCIA Position Statement on Allergy Testing

stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a 32 week, 1.4 kg male preterm infant now 12 days old who has had bloody stools and bilious aspirates for the last 18 hours. He had been tolerating expressed breast milk via gavage at 120 mL/kg/day until two days ago. He was started on broad spectrum antibiotics and bowel rest 12 hours ago and has had an umbilical arterial catheter inserted for serial gases.

Over the last 6 hours his platelet count has fallen from 145 to 62 x10^9/L and lactate has risen from 1.8 to 5.4 mmol/L. He is now intubated and on dopamine 10 mcg/kg/min for mean arterial pressure 28 mmHg. His abdomen is tense, discoloured and quiet to auscultation. The on-call radiographer reports the upright abdominal radiograph shows extensive pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas and a small amount of free intra-abdominal gas in the right upper quadrant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178/min, MAP 28 mmHg on dopamine, RR 60/min ventilated, SpO2 92% on 60% FiO2, temperature 35.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Tense discoloured abdomen with absent bowel sounds; mottled lower limbs; CRT 5 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L (140-220); platelets 62 x10^9/L (was 145); lactate 5.4 mmol/L (was 1.8); pH 7.18; base excess -12; CRP 142 mg/L
data_table.Imaging: Upright abdominal radiograph: extensive pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, free gas in right upper quadrant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent paediatric surgical referral for laparotomy or peritoneal drain insertion
options.rationale: Free intraperitoneal gas in necrotising enterocolitis is an absolute Bell stage IIIB surgical indication; immediate paediatric surgical involvement is mandatory, with the choice between primary laparotomy and primary peritoneal drainage guided by birth weight (<1000 g often drained first) and stability. (Source: RANZCO Neonatal Surgery Guidelines; Royal Hospital for Women Neonatal Handbook)
source_refs: Royal Hospital for Women Neonatal Handbook

options.text: Continue medical management with bowel rest, antibiotics and inotropic support
options.rationale: Pneumoperitoneum is an absolute surgical indication regardless of clinical stability; ongoing medical management alone risks lethal sepsis from contained perforation. (Source: RANZCO Neonatal Surgery Guidelines; Royal Hospital for Women Neonatal Handbook)
source_refs: Royal Hospital for Women Neonatal Handbook

options.text: Add intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as adjunctive therapy for severe sepsis
options.rationale: IVIG has no proven role in necrotising enterocolitis or neonatal sepsis and does not address the surgical perforation indicated by free gas. (Source: Royal Hospital for Women Neonatal Handbook)
source_refs: Royal Hospital for Women Neonatal Handbook

options.text: Repeat the abdominal radiograph in 6 hours to confirm progression before referral
options.rationale: Free gas already establishes the surgical indication; repeating imaging delays definitive treatment and risks decompensation. (Source: RANZCO Neonatal Surgery Guidelines)

options.text: Switch enteral feeds to a hydrolysed amino acid formula via continuous nasogastric infusion
options.rationale: Any enteral feeding is contraindicated with proven NEC and free gas; this question is surgical not nutritional. (Source: Royal Hospital for Women Neonatal Handbook)
source_refs: Royal Hospital for Women Neonatal Handbook

explanation.summary: Necrotising enterocolitis is staged by the modified Bell criteria from suspected (I) through definite medical NEC (II) to advanced NEC with intestinal perforation or impending perforation (III). Free intraperitoneal gas defines Bell IIIB and is an absolute surgical indication. In extremely low birth weight infants (<1000 g) primary peritoneal drainage may be preferred as a bridge to laparotomy. Pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas without free gas are managed medically with bowel rest, broad spectrum antibiotics (typically ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole) and supportive care. Mortality in Bell IIIB approaches 50% in extremely preterm infants and survivors face short gut syndrome.
key_points: Bell IIIB = perforation = surgical, regardless of stability
Pneumatosis alone or portal venous gas alone = Bell II = medical management
Extremely low birth weight (<1000 g) may have primary peritoneal drainage
Antibiotics: ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole
explanation.pearls: Pneumoperitoneum in NEC mandates immediate surgical referral; in infants under 1000 g, primary peritoneal drainage at the bedside under local anaesthesia is an evidence-supported temporising option per the NET trial when laparotomy is not immediately feasible.

sources.label: Royal Hospital for Women Neonatal Handbook

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional emergency department reviewing a 5-week-old boy brought in by his mother with 4 days of paroxysmal cough now associated with brief blue-around-the-lips episodes during feeds. He was born at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery; mother received her routine antenatal whooping cough booster at 18 weeks rather than the recommended 20 to 32 weeks window. He has not yet received any of his own scheduled vaccinations.

On examination between paroxysms he is alert and afebrile. During an observed paroxysm he goes briefly cyanotic with SpO2 dropping to 87% before recovering. Chest auscultation between episodes is clear. There are no inspiratory crepitations and no hepatosplenomegaly. White cell count is 28 x10^9/L with a lymphocyte predominance and a nasopharyngeal Bordetella pertussis PCR is positive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158/min, BP 88/54 mmHg, RR 44/min, SpO2 94% room air between paroxysms, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert between paroxysms; cyanotic during paroxysm with SpO2 87%; chest clear on auscultation; no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: WCC 28 x10^9/L (5-15) with lymphocyte predominance; nasopharyngeal Bordetella pertussis PCR positive; CXR no focal consolidation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for inpatient observation and commence oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 5 days
options.rationale: Infants under 6 months with confirmed pertussis and observed apnoea or cyanosis require admission for cardiorespiratory monitoring; macrolide therapy reduces transmission and is recommended within 21 days of cough onset. (Source: RCH CPG: Pertussis; CDNA SoNG)
source_refs: CDNA Series of National Guidelines Pertussis

options.text: Treat only household contacts with azithromycin prophylaxis and discharge the infant home today
options.rationale: Contact prophylaxis is recommended but does not substitute for treating an unwell case; the index infant needs both admission and macrolide therapy. (Source: CDNA SoNG; Australian Immunisation Handbook)
source_refs: CDNA Series of National Guidelines Pertussis

options.text: Admit for nebulised salbutamol with chest physiotherapy and reassess oxygenation hourly
options.rationale: Salbutamol and chest physiotherapy do not modify pertussis paroxysms and may aggravate cough; macrolide and supportive care are the standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Pertussis)

options.text: Discharge home with safety net advice and arrange a paediatric clinic review within 48 hours
options.rationale: Observed cyanosis or apnoea in a confirmed pertussis case under 6 months is an admission indication because deterioration can be sudden and unpredictable. (Source: RCH CPG: Pertussis)

options.text: Admit and commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg six-hourly for presumed pneumonia
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin has no activity against Bordetella pertussis and the chest is clear; targeted macrolide therapy is preferred over broad spectrum antibiotic cover. (Source: eTG Antibiotic; CDNA SoNG)
source_refs: CDNA Series of National Guidelines Pertussis

explanation.summary: Pertussis in infants under 6 months is the high-risk group, with apnoea, cyanosis, secondary pneumonia and rarely pulmonary hypertension as life-threatening complications. The maternal whooping cough booster is recommended at 20 to 32 weeks gestation in every pregnancy to provide passive immunity until the infant's own 6-week dose. Macrolides (azithromycin first-line) limit transmission and shorten infectivity; treatment is recommended within 21 days of cough onset though clinical benefit on symptom duration diminishes after the catarrhal phase. Household and close contact prophylaxis is offered to vulnerable contacts including infants and pregnant women.
key_points: Infants under 6 months with cyanosis or apnoea require admission
Azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days is the AU paediatric standard
Maternal antenatal booster at 20 to 32 weeks is the key prevention
Lymphocytosis with WCC over 20 x10^9/L raises suspicion in classical picture
explanation.pearls: In infants under 12 months with pertussis, a peak white cell count above 50 x10^9/L predicts severe disease and pulmonary hypertension; exchange transfusion has been used in extreme cases per Royal Children's Hospital practice.

sources.label: CDNA Series of National Guidelines Pertussis

stem:
A 5-week-old first-born male is referred from a peripheral hospital with 7 days of forceful non-bilious vomiting after every feed. He has lost 280 g since his 4-week weigh-in. His mother reports he appears hungry immediately after vomiting and wants to feed again.

On examination he is sleepy, with sunken anterior fontanelle and dry mucous membranes. After a test feed visible peristalsis is observed crossing the upper abdomen left to right and a 2 cm olive-shaped mass is palpable just lateral to the right rectus border above the umbilicus. Capillary refill is 4 seconds. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.52, pCO2 52 mmHg, bicarbonate 36 mmol/L, chloride 88 mmol/L, potassium 3.0 mmol/L and an abdominal ultrasound has just confirmed pyloric muscle thickness 5 mm and pyloric channel length 19 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168/min, BP 78/48 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Sleepy, sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes; visible upper abdominal peristalsis; palpable olive; CRT 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.52, pCO2 52, HCO3 36, Cl 88, K 3.0; abdominal ultrasound pyloric muscle 5 mm, channel 19 mm

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order an upper gastrointestinal contrast study before commencing any fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Diagnosis is already confirmed on ultrasound; contrast studies add no information and delay correction of life-threatening electrolyte derangement. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Resuscitate with 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus then maintenance with 0.9% saline and added potassium
options.rationale: The infant has hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from gastric loss; pre-operative correction of chloride, potassium and bicarbonate with normal saline plus potassium is mandatory before pyloromyotomy. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis; Royal Hospital for Women Neonatal Handbook)
source_refs: Royal Hospital for Women Neonatal Handbook

options.text: Trial of small volume thickened formula via nasogastric tube before any further intervention
options.rationale: Mechanical obstruction at the pylorus will not respond to thickened feeds; enteral feeds will be re-vomited and worsen dehydration. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Commence intravenous erythromycin 3 mg/kg six-hourly as a prokinetic before any surgery
options.rationale: Erythromycin is contraindicated in this age group due to risk of pyloric stenosis itself, and prokinetics cannot relieve mechanical obstruction. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Proceed directly to laparoscopic Ramstedt pyloromyotomy in the next available theatre
options.rationale: Pyloromyotomy is the definitive treatment but is NEVER an emergency; operating on a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalotic infant risks postoperative apnoea from CSF alkalosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

explanation.summary: Pyloric stenosis classically presents at 3 to 6 weeks of age with progressive non-bilious projectile vomiting in an otherwise hungry infant. Gastric loss of hydrogen and chloride produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Ultrasound diagnostic criteria are muscle thickness over 3 mm and channel length over 14 mm. Preoperative correction of fluid deficit and electrolyte and acid-base derangement is essential because anaesthesia on an alkalotic infant predisposes to postoperative apnoea via reduced respiratory drive in CSF. Normal saline with potassium supplementation is given until chloride is over 100 mmol/L and bicarbonate is under 28 mmol/L. Definitive treatment is Ramstedt pyloromyotomy, usually laparoscopic.
key_points: Classic age 3 to 6 weeks, first-born male predominance
Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis is the metabolic signature
US criteria: muscle thickness over 3 mm, channel length over 14 mm
Correct alkalosis before theatre to prevent postoperative apnoea
explanation.pearls: Pre-operative biochemical targets before Ramstedt pyloromyotomy: chloride over 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate under 28 mmol/L, potassium over 3.5 mmol/L per RCH guidance; surgery proceeds when these are met regardless of how many hours pass.

sources.label: Royal Hospital for Women Neonatal Handbook

stem:
A 16-month-old boy is brought to the general practice by his mother because preschool staff said he looks pale and is becoming a fussy eater. He was breastfed exclusively until 11 months and is now drinking around 1500 mL of cow's milk daily from a bottle. He refuses red meat and most vegetables but accepts crackers and yoghurt. Birth was uncomplicated and his immunisations are up to date.

On examination he is pale with no jaundice and no organomegaly. There is no lymphadenopathy and his developmental milestones are appropriate for age. There is no history of melaena and faecal occult blood testing is negative. Full blood count shows haemoglobin 78 g/L (105-135), mean corpuscular volume 58 fL (75-85), platelets 412 x10^9/L, white cell count 9.4 x10^9/L. Ferritin is 6 mcg/L (20-200), transferrin saturation 5%, CRP under 5.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 92/55 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale, alert, no jaundice; no hepatosplenomegaly; no lymphadenopathy; developmental milestones appropriate
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 g/L (105-135); MCV 58 fL (75-85); ferritin 6 mcg/L (20-200); transferrin saturation 5%; CRP under 5; FOBT negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Transfuse 10 mL/kg packed red cells before any oral iron supplementation is started
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia with cardiorespiratory compromise; haemodynamically stable nutritional iron deficiency responds rapidly to oral iron. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management)

options.text: Switch to a soy-based formula and arrange follow-up full blood count in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Soy formula does not correct established deficiency and the absorption of iron from soy formula is less than from cow's milk supplements; oral iron therapy is the primary treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Commence oral elemental iron 3 mg/kg once daily and counsel to limit cow's milk to 500 mL
options.rationale: First-line for paediatric iron deficiency anaemia without active bleeding is oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg/day plus addressing dietary drivers; cow's milk over 500 mL/day inhibits iron absorption and is the primary modifiable factor here. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency; AMH)

options.text: Trial a multivitamin without iron and cease cow's milk completely for 6 weeks
options.rationale: Multivitamins without iron will not correct iron deficiency, and complete milk cessation is unnecessarily aggressive; volume restriction is the appropriate intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Refer to day stay for intravenous ferric carboxymaltose infusion as a single dose
options.rationale: IV iron is reserved for failure of oral iron, malabsorption or intolerance; oral iron is effective and cheaper as initial therapy with normal absorption. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency in Australian toddlers most often follows prolonged exclusive milk feeding past 12 months, with intake over 500 mL/day inhibiting non-haem iron absorption and displacing iron-rich solids. Diagnostic biochemistry shows microcytic anaemia with low ferritin and low transferrin saturation; ferritin under 12 mcg/L is diagnostic in children. First-line treatment is oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg/day for 3 months to replenish stores, plus dietary counselling. Haemoglobin rise of around 10 g/L over 2 to 4 weeks confirms response. Failure to respond should prompt review of adherence, malabsorption (coeliac), or ongoing loss.
key_points: Cow's milk under 500 mL/day in toddlers, prefer iron-rich solids
Oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg/day for 3 months
Ferritin under 12 mcg/L is diagnostic in children
Persistent failure to respond, screen for coeliac disease
explanation.pearls: Oral iron is best absorbed on an empty stomach with vitamin C-containing fluid; co-administration with cow's milk, calcium or tea cuts absorption by approximately 50% per RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency.

stem:
You are the general paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-year-old previously well girl referred by her general practitioner with widespread petechiae on the trunk and lower limbs noticed by her mother yesterday. She had a coryzal illness ten days ago which resolved without treatment. There has been no epistaxis, gum bleeding, melaena or haematuria, and her mother denies any minor trauma that could explain the bruising. She is up to date with vaccinations and is fully immunised against measles.

On examination she is afebrile and well perfused, running around the consulting room. There is no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly and no bone tenderness. She has scattered petechiae on the trunk and a 1 cm wet purpura on the lower lip but no other mucosal bleeding. The full blood count shows haemoglobin 122 g/L, white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L with normal differential and morphology, and platelets 11 x10^9/L; the blood film comment from the haematologist is 'normal red cell and leucocyte morphology, occasional giant platelets, no blasts'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102/min, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Active, well perfused; scattered petechiae trunk and lower limbs; 1 cm wet purpura lower lip; no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122 g/L, WCC 7.4 x10^9/L with normal differential, platelets 11 x10^9/L; film: normal red cell and leucocyte morphology, occasional giant platelets, no blasts

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for urgent bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy before any therapeutic decision
options.rationale: Bone marrow study is not required for the diagnosis of typical paediatric ITP when blood film is normal and there are no atypical features; pre-treatment marrow is only required if features suggest alternative pathology. (Source: RCH CPG: ITP)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 4 mg/kg/day for 4 days then taper over 14 days as outpatient
options.rationale: Short-course steroid is an alternative active treatment for paediatric ITP with significant bleeding but is not indicated for cutaneous-only bleeding because remission rate matches observation. (Source: RCH CPG: ITP)

options.text: Single dose intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as inpatient with observation overnight
options.rationale: IVIG is reserved for significant mucosal bleeding or before urgent procedures because it shortens time to platelet rise; it does not change long-term outcome and exposes the child to a blood product. (Source: RCH CPG: ITP)

options.text: Outpatient observation with written bleeding advice and repeat platelet count in 1 week
options.rationale: Australian guidance is to observe paediatric ITP with platelets above the bleeding threshold when there is only minor cutaneous bleeding; randomised data show no outcome benefit of immediate IVIG or steroid in the absence of significant bleeding. (Source: RCH CPG: ITP; HSANZ Position Statement)
source_refs: HSANZ Position Statement on Paediatric ITP

options.text: Single bag of platelets 10 mL/kg now and proceed to bone marrow examination today
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion is only indicated for life-threatening haemorrhage in ITP because transfused platelets are destroyed immediately by the same autoantibody. (Source: RCH CPG: ITP; NBA Patient Blood Management)

explanation.summary: Acute immune thrombocytopenia in children is the most common cause of new isolated thrombocytopenia, typically following a viral illness, with peak incidence between 2 and 6 years. The diagnosis is clinical, supported by isolated thrombocytopenia with normal white cell and red cell lines on a normal blood film. The treatment decision hinges on bleeding severity not platelet count; over 80% of paediatric cases resolve within 6 months and observation is preferred for cutaneous bleeding only. Active treatment options for significant bleeding are IVIG, short course steroid, or anti-D in Rh-positive children. Marrow examination is reserved for atypical features such as constitutional symptoms, lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, or abnormal blood film.
key_points: Watchful waiting is the AU first-line for paediatric ITP without significant bleeding
Marrow study only if blood film abnormal or atypical features
IVIG or steroid for active mucosal or life-threatening bleeding
Over 80% of paediatric ITP resolves spontaneously within 6 months
explanation.pearls: In paediatric ITP, the presence of wet purpura (mucosal bleeding) is a more useful trigger for treatment than the absolute platelet count, per RCH CPG; isolated cutaneous petechiae with platelets even under 10 x10^9/L can usually be observed safely.

sources.label: HSANZ Position Statement on Paediatric ITP

stem:
A 14-year-old girl is referred to the paediatric clinic from her general practitioner with three weeks of daily frontal headache that is worse on waking and worse on bending forward. She has also noticed transient grey-outs in both eyes lasting seconds when she stands up quickly. Her body mass index has risen from 27 to 31 kg/m2 over the last 12 months. She has been taking isotretinoin 30 mg daily for severe acne for four months and the combined oral contraceptive pill for three months for cycle control.

On examination her blood pressure is normal and she is afebrile. Visual acuity is 6/6 each eye. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral grade 2 papilloedema. Cranial nerve examination is otherwise normal. Non contrast magnetic resonance imaging shows partial empty sella, posterior globe flattening, prominent perioptic cerebrospinal fluid spaces and no mass lesion or venous sinus thrombosis. Lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position shows an opening pressure of 32 cmH2O with normal CSF cell count, glucose and protein.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally; bilateral grade 2 papilloedema on fundoscopy; cranial nerves otherwise intact
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: partial empty sella, posterior globe flattening, no mass, no venous sinus thrombosis; LP opening pressure 32 cmH2O, CSF cell count, glucose, protein within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Isotretinoin 30 mg daily for 4 months; combined oral contraceptive pill for 3 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: High dose intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse for 3 days then taper
options.rationale: Systemic steroids are no longer recommended in IIH because the rebound when ceased can be severe and they cause weight gain which worsens the disease. (Source: RCH CPG: IIH)

options.text: Refer for ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion within 2 weeks for cerebrospinal fluid diversion
options.rationale: CSF shunting is reserved for refractory IIH with progressive vision loss despite maximal medical therapy; it is not first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: IIH)

options.text: Refer urgently for optic nerve sheath fenestration to protect visual function
options.rationale: Optic nerve sheath fenestration is reserved for fulminant visual loss despite medical therapy; visual acuity is preserved here so medical therapy should be tried first. (Source: RCH CPG: IIH; RANZCO Position Statement)

options.text: Sumatriptan 50 mg orally during attacks with propranolol 40 mg twice daily prophylaxis
options.rationale: Migraine pharmacotherapy does not address raised intracranial pressure and risks delaying treatment that could prevent permanent visual loss. (Source: National Headache Network Guidelines)

options.text: Start oral acetazolamide 25 mg/kg/day in divided doses and discontinue isotretinoin
options.rationale: First-line for paediatric IIH is acetazolamide plus identification and removal of the precipitant; isotretinoin is a recognised cause of secondary intracranial hypertension and must be stopped. (Source: RCH CPG: IIH; AMH Acetazolamide)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension in adolescents typically affects post-pubertal girls with rapid weight gain. Diagnosis requires papilloedema, normal MRI brain and MR venogram, and elevated CSF opening pressure (over 25 cmH2O in non-obese, over 28 cmH2O in obese adolescents) with normal CSF composition. Common secondary precipitants include isotretinoin, tetracyclines, vitamin A excess, growth hormone therapy and oral contraceptives; identification and cessation is essential. Acetazolamide is first-line; topiramate is an alternative when migraine coexists. Untreated IIH can cause permanent visual field loss from chronic papilloedema. Weight loss is a key non-pharmacological intervention.
key_points: Diagnosis: papilloedema, normal imaging, raised CSF pressure with normal composition
Secondary causes: isotretinoin, tetracyclines, vitamin A, growth hormone, COCP
First-line: acetazolamide plus precipitant removal plus weight loss
Surgical intervention for progressive visual loss despite medical therapy
explanation.pearls: Isotretinoin is the strongest medication-associated cause of secondary intracranial hypertension in adolescent acne treatment; the Roche Australian product information advises ceasing the drug at the first sign of headache and papilloedema.

stem:
A 3-year-old girl with known homozygous sickle cell disease is brought to the emergency department by her parents, who recently migrated from West Africa, with 6 hours of progressive lethargy and a visibly distended abdomen. Her baseline haemoglobin is 80 g/L. She received penicillin V prophylaxis from diagnosis at 9 months and is fully immunised including pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccines.

On examination she is pale and drowsy but responsive to her name. Capillary refill is 4 seconds and her hands are cool to the wrists. The abdomen is distended and the spleen is palpable extending to the umbilicus. There is no focal abdominal tenderness, no jaundice, and the chest is clear on auscultation with no murmur. Haemoglobin is 38 g/L, reticulocytes 12% (baseline 8%), white cell count 16 x10^9/L, platelets 124 x10^9/L. Group and crossmatch is in progress.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 162/min, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale, drowsy; CRT 4 seconds; abdomen distended with spleen palpable to umbilicus; chest clear; no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: Hb 38 g/L (baseline 80); reticulocytes 12% (baseline 8%); WCC 16 x10^9/L; platelets 124 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Urgent simple top-up transfusion of leucodepleted phenotyped red cells to a target haemoglobin
options.rationale: Acute splenic sequestration crisis with hypovolaemia is treated with urgent simple top-up transfusion of leucodepleted phenotyped red cells aiming to restore circulating volume without over-transfusing because the sequestered red cells will re-enter circulation. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric Haematology Handbook; Royal Children's Hospital Sickle Cell Pathway)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Sickle Cell Pathway

options.text: Continue penicillin prophylaxis only and observe overnight with serial haemoglobin checks
options.rationale: Observation alone in haemodynamic decompensation risks death from hypovolaemic shock; transfusion is the time-critical intervention. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric Haematology Handbook)

options.text: Refer urgently for emergency splenectomy to remove the sequestering reservoir
options.rationale: Emergency splenectomy is not first-line in acute sequestration; the volume sequestered returns to circulation after transfusion and acute splenectomy is reserved for failed conservative management. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric Haematology Handbook)

options.text: Commence hydroxycarbamide 15 mg/kg/day and oxygen at 6 L/min via non rebreather mask
options.rationale: Hydroxycarbamide is an outpatient disease-modifying therapy and has no role in the acute crisis; oxygen alone does not address acute anaemic hypovolaemia. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric Haematology Handbook)

options.text: Urgent exchange transfusion targeting haemoglobin S fraction under 30% and oxygen via mask
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for acute chest syndrome, stroke, or multi-organ failure; it is not first-line in isolated sequestration where volume restoration is the urgent need. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric Haematology Handbook)

explanation.summary: Acute splenic sequestration crisis is a life-threatening complication of sickle cell disease in children under 6 years, in whom the spleen has not yet auto-infarcted. Massive trapping of sickled red cells in the spleen produces sudden anaemia and hypovolaemic shock. The classical findings are a rapidly enlarging tender spleen, pallor, tachycardia, hypotension, and haemoglobin drop of at least 20 g/L below baseline. Management is urgent simple transfusion with leucodepleted phenotyped red cells, with caution to avoid over-transfusion because release of sequestered red cells can produce hyperviscosity. Recurrence rate is over 50% and elective splenectomy is offered after the second episode.
key_points: Sequestration: age under 6, enlarging spleen, anaemia and shock
Urgent simple transfusion to restore volume
Avoid over-transfusion: sequestered cells release on recovery
Recurrence over 50%; elective splenectomy after 2nd event
explanation.pearls: In acute splenic sequestration the transfusion target is typically half the haemoglobin deficit because sequestered red cells will re-enter circulation as the spleen recovers; aiming for full pre-crisis haemoglobin risks hyperviscosity per HSANZ paediatric guidance.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Sickle Cell Pathway

stem:
A 12-day-old female infant is brought to the emergency department by her parents with poor feeding and three episodes of forceful vomiting today. She is the first child of non-consanguineous parents and was discharged at day 3 with a normal newborn screen pending. Birth weight was 3.4 kg and she has now lost 12% of her birth weight.

On examination she is mottled, lethargic and minimally responsive to handling. Her anterior fontanelle is sunken and capillary refill is 5 seconds. There is unexpected mild clitoromegaly and posterior labial fusion noted today by the registrar; the clitoral length is at the upper limit of normal and the urethral opening sits within the clitoral shaft. There is no abdominal mass and the chest is clear. Capillary blood gas shows pH 7.22, base excess minus 12. Bedside sodium is 122 mmol/L, potassium 7.4 mmol/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L and the on-call biochemist has rung to confirm the newborn screening 17-hydroxyprogesterone is markedly elevated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 184/min, BP 58/32 mmHg, RR 64/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Mottled, lethargic; sunken fontanelle, CRT 5 seconds; mild clitoromegaly and posterior labial fusion
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.22, base excess -12; sodium 122 mmol/L; potassium 7.4 mmol/L; glucose 2.6 mmol/L; 17-hydroxyprogesterone markedly elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous insulin 0.05 units/kg/hour with dextrose infusion and urgent karyotype analysis
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose is a temporising hyperkalaemia measure but the priority is reversing adrenal insufficiency with hydrocortisone; karyotyping is appropriate later but not now. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Insufficiency)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg stat plus 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg bolus with 10% dextrose maintenance
options.rationale: Salt-losing CAH crisis is treated with immediate IV hydrocortisone 25 mg (under 6 months) plus 0.9% saline volume resuscitation and dextrose for hypoglycaemia; this corrects mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency simultaneously. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Insufficiency; Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

options.text: Empirical intravenous cefotaxime 50 mg/kg and urgent lumbar puncture for septic workup
options.rationale: Sepsis workup may be appropriate alongside CAH treatment but does not address the dominant biochemical signature of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia in a virilised female. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Insufficiency; RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Salbutamol 0.5 mL of 5 mg/mL nebulised solution with calcium gluconate 10% 0.5 mL/kg
options.rationale: Treating the hyperkalaemia symptomatically without addressing the underlying adrenal insufficiency is incomplete; hydrocortisone reverses the mineralocorticoid deficit causing the potassium rise. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Insufficiency)

options.text: Intravenous 10% dextrose 5 mL/kg bolus then oral fludrocortisone 100 mcg via nasogastric tube
options.rationale: Oral fludrocortisone has no immediate effect and cannot be reliably absorbed in a shocked infant; intravenous hydrocortisone and saline are the time-critical interventions. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency presents in the salt-losing form between days 7 and 21 of life, after maternal cortisol has waned. Affected female infants are virilised at birth (clitoromegaly, labial fusion) but normal external genitalia in males may delay recognition. The biochemical signature is hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, hypoglycaemia and grossly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Acute management is intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg (under 6 months), 50 mg (6 months to 6 years) or 100 mg (over 6 years), with saline volume resuscitation and dextrose. Long-term management is glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone) plus mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone) plus salt supplementation.
key_points: Salt-losing CAH presents day 7 to 21 with vomiting, dehydration, shock
Biochemistry: low Na, high K, acidosis, hypoglycaemia, raised 17-OHP
IV hydrocortisone 25 mg (under 6 months) plus saline plus dextrose
Long-term: hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone plus salt
explanation.pearls: Newborn screening for 17-hydroxyprogesterone has been included in the Australian program since 2018 across all states; phone notification of a markedly elevated result must trigger immediate hydrocortisone and saline rather than awaiting confirmatory testing.

stem:
You are the on-call neonatology registrar at a tertiary centre called to a 72-hour-old term male infant on the postnatal ward. He fed well for the first 36 hours and was discharge planned. Over the last 12 hours he has become progressively lethargic, has refused 3 consecutive feeds, vomited twice and now has irregular hyperventilation. He is the second child of consanguineous parents; the first child died at 5 days of age of presumed sepsis without a confirmed cause.

On examination he is encephalopathic with poor tone and absent suck. Heart rate is regular and the chest is clear; the abdomen is soft with no organomegaly. There is no rash and the anterior fontanelle is soft. Capillary glucose is 4.2 mmol/L. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.50, pCO2 22 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L with a normal anion gap. Sodium 138, potassium 4.0, lactate 2.0. Plasma ammonia returned 30 minutes ago at 580 micromol/L (under 50). LFTs and coagulation are within normal limits. Urinary ketones are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 156/min, BP 64/38 mmHg, RR 76/min irregular, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Encephalopathic with poor tone, absent suck; soft abdomen, no organomegaly; soft fontanelle
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.50, pCO2 22, HCO3 18, normal anion gap; glucose 4.2 mmol/L; lactate 2.0; ammonia 580 micromol/L (<50); LFTs and coagulation within normal limits; urinary ketones negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Therapeutic hyperventilation with intubation and intravenous mannitol 0.5 g/kg for cerebral oedema
options.rationale: Cerebral oedema management is supportive but does not remove ammonia; only dialysis combined with protein withdrawal and dextrose suppression of catabolism reverses the metabolic insult. (Source: APEG Metabolic Emergencies)

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin and obtain blood cultures
options.rationale: Sepsis is in the differential but the biochemical picture (normal glucose, low lactate, low CO2, high ammonia, no acidosis) is not septic; antibiotics may run concurrently but the priority is ammonia removal. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Cease all protein intake, commence intravenous 10% dextrose and arrange urgent haemodialysis transfer
options.rationale: Hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with ammonia above 500 micromol/L and respiratory alkalosis in a neonate is a urea cycle disorder until proven otherwise; immediate protein withdrawal, high glucose to suppress catabolism and urgent dialysis (extracorporeal) are time critical because mortality and neurological injury rise sharply after 24 hours above 200 micromol/L. (Source: Royal Hospital for Women Neonatal Handbook; APEG Metabolic Emergencies)
source_refs: Royal Hospital for Women Neonatal Handbook

options.text: Loading dose of phenobarbital 20 mg/kg for presumed neonatal seizures with maintenance therapy
options.rationale: There is no clinical seizure description and phenobarbital treats the symptom not the cause; in urea cycle disorders, valproate is also contraindicated as it precipitates hyperammonaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Seizures; AMH)

options.text: Intravenous thiamine, pyridoxine and biotin trial alongside continued enteral feeds at half rate
options.rationale: Vitamin cofactor trials are appropriate in suspected organic acidaemias with acidosis and ketosis; continuing protein feeds will worsen ammonia and risks fatal cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG Metabolic Emergencies)

explanation.summary: Urea cycle disorders are the leading cause of neonatal hyperammonaemia outside organic acidaemias and present typically between day 2 and day 5 of life after the catabolic load of feeding. The biochemical signature is a high ammonia with a primary respiratory alkalosis (ammonia stimulates respiratory drive), normal anion gap, normal glucose, normal lactate, and absent ketonuria. Organic acidaemias by contrast usually have metabolic acidosis, ketonuria, raised anion gap and lactate. Time to dialysis is the strongest determinant of neurological outcome. Acute management is the triad of protein withdrawal, 10% dextrose to suppress catabolism, and ammonia scavenger therapy (sodium benzoate plus sodium phenylacetate) en route to extracorporeal removal. A family history of unexplained neonatal death in a sibling is a critical clue.
