key_points: Toddler + choking history + lateralised signs = aspirated foreign body until proven otherwise.
Expiratory CXR shows hyperinflation on side of obstruction; inspiratory may be normal.
Rigid bronchoscopy under GA in theatre is the AU standard for removal.
Postural physiotherapy is contraindicated; risk of converting partial to complete obstruction.
Peanuts cause chemical bronchitis; remove urgently.
explanation.pearls: A normal CXR does not exclude foreign body aspiration in a toddler with a clear choking history and lateralised signs - rigid bronchoscopy under GA both diagnoses and treats.

subtopic_detail: Testicular torsion - direct to theatre without imaging delay
stem:
A 14-year-old boy is brought to the metropolitan emergency department by his father with a 5 hour history of sudden severe left scrotal pain that woke him from sleep at 2 am. The pain is constant and rated 9 out of 10. He has had two episodes of vomiting. There is no history of trauma, no recent unprotected sexual activity, and no urinary symptoms.

On examination he is in severe distress lying still. The left hemiscrotum is swollen, exquisitely tender, with the testis riding high and lying transversely. The left cremasteric reflex is absent. The right testis is normal in position and lie with a normal cremasteric reflex. There is no urethral discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110/min, BP 130/78 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Left hemiscrotum swollen, exquisitely tender; testis high-riding and transverse; absent left cremasteric reflex; right testis normal lie and position with intact cremasteric reflex; no urethral discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis clear; no nitrites, no leucocytes, no blood; FBC and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Urgent colour Doppler ultrasound of the scrotum to assess testicular blood flow before any surgical decision is made on operative management of this presentation
options.rationale: Doppler ultrasound has high false negative rates and delays theatre; clinical diagnosis is sufficient to proceed direct to scrotal exploration in classic presentation within the 6 hour window. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

options.text: Procedural sedation in emergency department with manual detorsion attempt by rotating testis outward (book opening direction) and surgical exploration only if pain does not resolve immediately
options.rationale: Manual detorsion is a temporising measure when surgery is delayed, not a substitute for definitive exploration and bilateral orchidopexy. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

options.text: Empirical IV cefotaxime 50 mg/kg and supportive analgesia for presumed acute epididymo-orchitis with reassessment in 4 hours for response to antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Epididymo-orchitis is unlikely without urinary symptoms, no urethral discharge, no fever, in a 14 year old with sudden onset pain; missing torsion in the 6 hour window costs the testis. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

options.text: Discharge home with analgesia and urgent next-day outpatient urology clinic review for further assessment and definitive imaging in the morning at the earliest opportunity
options.rationale: Discharge in suspected testicular torsion is negligent; salvage rate drops sharply after 6 hours of ischaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

options.text: Direct transfer to the operating theatre for scrotal exploration, manual detorsion and bilateral orchidopexy under general anaesthesia by the on-call urologist without further investigations
options.rationale: Classic torsion (sudden severe pain, vomiting, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex) within 5 hours requires immediate theatre; salvage rate approximately 90% under 6 hours, then falls sharply. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency with a 6 hour window for testicular salvage. Classic features (sudden severe pain, vomiting, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex) should prompt direct theatre without Doppler delay. Bilateral orchidopexy is performed even if the contralateral testis appears normal because the anatomical predisposition (bell-clapper deformity) is bilateral. Differential includes epididymo-orchitis (gradual onset, fever, urinary symptoms, normal cremasteric, pyuria) and torsion of the appendix testis (gradual onset, blue dot sign). Imaging may be reserved for atypical presentations only.
key_points: Salvage rate ~90% under 6 hours; drops to ~50% by 12 hours and near zero by 24 hours.
Direct theatre without Doppler for classic clinical presentation.
Bilateral orchidopexy because bell-clapper is bilateral.
Absent cremasteric reflex has high sensitivity (about 99%).
Manual detorsion (rotate medial to lateral, book opening) only if theatre delay >1 hour.
explanation.pearls: Classic torsion does not need Doppler - the 6 hour clock is more sensitive than imaging. Bilateral orchidopexy is mandatory because the bell-clapper anomaly is bilateral.

sources.label: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute scrotum guidance

subtopic_detail: Convulsive status epilepticus - second dose of benzodiazepine
stem:
A 4-year-old previously well boy is brought to the metropolitan emergency department by paramedics after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that began at school 12 minutes ago. Paramedics gave a single dose of buccal midazolam 5 mg en route 6 minutes ago without effect. He continues to seize on arrival.

He has no prior history of seizures. He has been febrile with a 24 hour history of viral upper respiratory tract symptoms. There is no head trauma, no toxic exposure, and no relevant family history. No peripheral intravenous access has yet been established. The on-call paediatric registrar is at bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 162/min, BP 105/68 mmHg, RR 30/min via bag-valve-mask 100% oxygen, SpO2 96% with oxygen, temperature 39.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Continuous generalised tonic-clonic activity; pupils equal and reactive; jaw not relaxed; airway patent with manoeuvres; no purpura, no rash, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.5-6.5); ECG sinus tachycardia rate 162; no other investigations yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intramuscular midazolam 0.15 mg/kg now, while preparing IV or IO access and second-line agent if seizure continues beyond 15 minutes from onset
options.rationale: Second benzodiazepine dose is appropriate at 10 minutes if first dose ineffective and IV access not yet obtained; IM midazolam absorbs reliably; second-line agent (levetiracetam or phenytoin) follows at 15-20 minutes. (Source: APLS Australia Algorithm: Status epilepticus)

options.text: Phenytoin 20 mg/kg intravenously over 20 minutes once IV access is obtained as the second-line definitive agent for ongoing convulsive seizure activity in this child
options.rationale: Phenytoin is a valid second-line agent but should follow a second benzodiazepine dose; jumping straight to phenytoin without a second benzo is not the AU APLS pathway. (Source: APLS Australia Algorithm: Status epilepticus)

options.text: Levetiracetam 40 mg/kg intravenously as a single rapid bolus over 5 minutes immediately, without further benzodiazepine, given the seizure has continued past first benzo dose now
options.rationale: Levetiracetam is a valid alternative second-line but should follow a second benzodiazepine; ESETT trial shows levetiracetam, phenytoin, and valproate are all equivalent second-line agents but second benzo precedes them. (Source: APLS Australia Algorithm: Status epilepticus)

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation with thiopentone 5 mg/kg now and admission to paediatric intensive care for thiopentone infusion and continuous EEG monitoring with neurology input
options.rationale: Intubation and thiopentone are reserved for refractory status (>30 minutes despite first and second line); current step is second benzo. (Source: APLS Australia Algorithm: Status epilepticus)

options.text: Urgent CT head before further pharmacological intervention to exclude an acute structural cause for status epilepticus such as bleed or space-occupying lesion or hydrocephalus
options.rationale: Imaging is appropriate after the seizure is controlled and the airway secured; pursuing imaging before stopping the seizure prolongs ictal injury. (Source: APLS Australia Algorithm: Status epilepticus)

explanation.summary: Convulsive status epilepticus follows a time-based algorithm: first benzodiazepine (buccal/IM midazolam, IV lorazepam, or IV diazepam) at 5-10 minutes, second benzodiazepine if still seizing at 10-15 minutes, second-line agent (levetiracetam, phenytoin, or sodium valproate) at 15-25 minutes, and intubation with thiopentone infusion in PICU for refractory status >30 minutes. IM midazolam is a reliable second benzodiazepine when IV access is delayed. ESETT (2019) showed levetiracetam, phenytoin, and valproate are equivalent as second-line agents. Always check glucose, electrolytes, and consider underlying cause once seizure is controlled.
key_points: Time-based algorithm: 1st benzo 5 min, 2nd benzo 10-15 min, 2nd line 15-25 min.
IM midazolam reliable when IV access is delayed.
ESETT: levetiracetam, phenytoin, valproate equivalent for second-line.
Intubation with thiopentone for refractory status >30 minutes.
Check glucose first; treat hypoglycaemia (2 mL/kg 10% dextrose).
explanation.pearls: A second benzodiazepine dose precedes the second-line agent in the APLS Australia algorithm - jumping straight to phenytoin or levetiracetam at 12 minutes is non-standard.

stem:
A 2-year-old girl presents to the metropolitan emergency department with septic shock and a 12 hour history of fever, lethargy and reduced wet nappies. She has cool mottled peripheries with delayed capillary refill, is drowsy and minimally responsive. Two attempts at peripheral venous cannulation by the paediatric emergency registrar over the past 75 seconds have failed; both attempts targeted antecubital fossae.

The paediatric retrieval team has been called and is 30 minutes away. The team is preparing for further peripheral attempts. Empirical antibiotics are drawn up and ready. The mother is at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 188/min, BP 65/40 mmHg, RR 50/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 39.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 12; cool mottled peripheries; capillary refill >5 seconds; respiratory rate elevated with shallow effort; no rash or purpura
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.5 mmol/L (3.5-6.5); rapid bedside lactate 5.5 mmol/L (<2.0); blood cultures yet to be obtained because peripheral access failed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for vascular access?

options.text: Continue peripheral intravenous cannulation attempts for up to 5 more minutes by the most experienced operator available before considering alternative access strategies
options.rationale: APLS Australia and RCH paediatric sepsis pathway mandate IO insertion after 2 failed peripheral attempts or 90 seconds in shocked children; further peripheral attempts delay resuscitation. (Source: APLS Australia: Vascular access)

options.text: Insert intraosseous needle into proximal tibia 1-2 cm below tibial tuberosity on medial flat surface, commence resuscitation including fluid bolus 20 mL/kg and IV antibiotics now
options.rationale: AU APLS and RCH sepsis pathway mandate IO insertion after 2 failed peripheral attempts or 90 seconds; proximal tibia is the standard paediatric site; IO can deliver all fluids, drugs and bloods can be drawn. (Source: APLS Australia: Vascular access)

options.text: Wait for paediatric anaesthetist or retrieval team to insert ultrasound-guided central venous catheter once they arrive on site within the next 30 minutes for definitive resuscitation access
options.rationale: Waiting 30 minutes for retrieval risks death from untreated septic shock; IO can be inserted in <60 seconds by any APLS-trained clinician. (Source: APLS Australia: Vascular access)

options.text: Perform venous cut-down to the long saphenous vein at the ankle by paediatric surgical registrar in the next 10 minutes to achieve large-bore access for ongoing resuscitation
options.rationale: Venous cut-down is slower, requires surgical skill, and has largely been replaced by IO insertion in paediatric resuscitation; it is not first-line in 2026. (Source: APLS Australia: Vascular access)

options.text: Administer subcutaneous fluids via the hyaluronidase-assisted hypodermoclysis technique into both thighs while continuing peripheral attempts for next ten minutes with senior clinician
options.rationale: Subcutaneous fluids have no role in shock resuscitation; absorption is too slow. (Source: APLS Australia: Vascular access)

explanation.summary: Intraosseous access is the recommended next step after 2 failed peripheral attempts or 90 seconds in a critically ill child requiring resuscitation. Proximal tibia (1-2 cm below tibial tuberosity on medial flat surface) is the standard paediatric site, with proximal humerus and distal femur as alternatives. IO can deliver all fluids and drugs (including adrenaline, bicarbonate, blood products), and blood can be drawn for cultures and gases. EZ-IO power driver is the AU standard device. IO should be replaced by definitive IV/central access within 24 hours due to risk of osteomyelitis if used longer.
key_points: IO insertion after 2 failed peripheral attempts or 90 seconds in resuscitation.
Proximal tibia: 1-2 cm below tibial tuberosity, medial flat surface.
All fluids and drugs can be given via IO; blood samples can be drawn.
Replace with definitive access within 24 hours.
Avoid in fractured bone or recent IO attempt in same bone.
explanation.pearls: EZ-IO power-driven proximal tibia takes under 60 seconds and accepts every resuscitation drug - waiting for the retrieval team or doing a cut-down in 2026 is an anti-pattern.

subtopic_detail: Toxic shock syndrome - clindamycin and source control
stem:
A 14-year-old girl presents to the paediatric emergency department on day 4 of menstruation with fever to 40 °C, diffuse erythematous rash that looks like sunburn, watery diarrhoea and one episode of vomiting over the past 24 hours. She is confused and unable to give a coherent history. She is using high-absorbency tampons.

On examination she is in shock with cool peripheries and capillary refill 4 seconds. The rash is a diffuse blanching erythroderma over the trunk and limbs without target lesions. There is non-purulent conjunctival injection and a strawberry tongue. A tampon is in situ on examination. No surgical wound, no skin abscess. Vaccinations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140/min, BP 75/40 mmHg, RR 30/min, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 40.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Confused, GCS 13; diffuse blanching erythroderma; conjunctival injection; strawberry tongue; tampon in situ; cool peripheries CRT 4 seconds; no abscess or wound
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18 x10⁹/L (4-11), platelets 130 x10⁹/L (150-400), Na 130 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 180 micromol/L (45-90), CK 880 U/L (<200), ALT 95 U/L (<40), INR 1.4 (0.9-1.2), lactate 4.5 mmol/L (<2.0); blood cultures sent

lead_in: After IV access, 20 mL/kg sodium chloride bolus, and PICU activation, what is the most appropriate antimicrobial and source control strategy?

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 15 mg/kg six-hourly monotherapy with tampon removal at presentation and supportive intensive care management of fluid resuscitation and inotropes
options.rationale: Vancomycin alone does not suppress toxin production; clindamycin is added specifically to inhibit ribosomal toxin synthesis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg daily and metronidazole 12.5 mg/kg eight-hourly without tampon removal, escalation only if antibiotic response is poor over the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone + metronidazole covers intra-abdominal sepsis, not staphylococcal TSS; source control by tampon removal is the first priority in menstrual TSS. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg six-hourly plus clindamycin 15 mg/kg eight-hourly, immediate tampon removal as source control, and consider IVIG 1-2 g/kg if shock is refractory
options.rationale: Menstrual TSS is staphylococcal toxin-mediated; flucloxacillin treats organism, clindamycin suppresses toxin synthesis at the ribosome, tampon removal is source control, IVIG neutralises circulating toxin in severe cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg six-hourly as broad-spectrum monotherapy with delayed tampon removal once shock has been adequately stabilised over the first 4 hours of care
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam is broad-spectrum but inferior anti-staphylococcal activity to flucloxacillin and does not suppress toxin; delayed source control increases ongoing toxin release. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome

options.text: Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus intravenous gentamicin 7 mg/kg daily for empirical sepsis cover pending blood culture and microbiology susceptibility results overnight
options.rationale: Oral therapy in shocked patient is inappropriate; gentamicin lacks anti-staphylococcal toxin suppression activity; doxycycline is not adequate monotherapy in fulminant TSS. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome

explanation.summary: Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome is a toxin-mediated illness presenting with fever, hypotension, diffuse erythroderma, multi-organ dysfunction and (later) desquamation. Menstrual TSS is associated with prolonged tampon use; non-menstrual TSS with surgical/burn wounds or skin abscesses. Management has three pillars: (1) organism eradication with flucloxacillin (or vancomycin if MRSA suspected), (2) toxin suppression with clindamycin (binds ribosome inhibiting exotoxin synthesis), and (3) source control (tampon removal, wound debridement). IVIG 1-2 g/kg is considered for refractory shock to neutralise circulating superantigen. Streptococcal TSS is the differential and is treated similarly (penicillin + clindamycin).
key_points: Three pillars: anti-staphylococcal antibiotic + clindamycin (toxin suppression) + source control.
Clindamycin binds ribosome to inhibit exotoxin synthesis - critical adjunct.
Tampon removal is immediate source control in menstrual TSS.
IVIG 1-2 g/kg for refractory shock to neutralise superantigen.
Differential streptococcal TSS treated with penicillin + clindamycin.
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin within the first hour suppresses ongoing toxin production at the ribosome - flucloxacillin alone kills the organism but does not switch off the exotoxin already being made.

subtopic_detail: Exertional heatstroke - cold water immersion target
stem:
A 16-year-old male competitive runner collapses 9 km into a 10 km charity run on a 38 °C ambient temperature day. Paramedics arrive within 8 minutes and find him confused, ataxic, with hot dry red skin and a tympanic core temperature of 41.2 °C. There is no history of seizure, drug use, or psychiatric medication. He has no significant medical history.

On arrival to the paediatric emergency department he is confused (GCS 13), unable to stand, with profound hyperthermia. He is hypotensive and tachycardic. He has not had any oral fluids since the start of the race 90 minutes ago and last urinated 4 hours ago before the start.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140/min, BP 95/55 mmHg, RR 32/min, SpO2 99% room air, tympanic temperature 41.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Confused GCS 13; hot dry red skin; no rash, no neck stiffness; ataxic gait; muscles tender to palpation; no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Na 148 mmol/L (135-145), K 5.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 200 micromol/L (45-90), CK 8000 U/L (<200), lactate 6.2 mmol/L (<2.0), pH 7.30, HCO3 16 mmol/L (22-26); urinalysis 3+ blood, no red cells on microscopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate cooling strategy?

options.text: Tepid sponging and oral cold fluids in resus bay with active cooling fan only, antipyretic paracetamol 1 g orally, monitor over the next hour for response to passive cooling measures
options.rationale: Tepid sponging is too slow for exertional heatstroke with core >40 °C; paracetamol does not lower temperature in non-pyrogen-mediated hyperthermia. (Source: Sports Medicine Australia: Heat illness)

options.text: Paracetamol 1 g orally and evaporative cooling with continuous fanning of misted skin alone in resus bay aiming to cool gradually over the next 60 minutes with reassessment
options.rationale: Evaporative cooling is acceptable when CWI is unavailable but is slower (cooling rate 0.05 vs 0.2 °C/min) and inferior to CWI for exertional heatstroke; paracetamol is ineffective. (Source: Sports Medicine Australia: Heat illness)

options.text: Endovascular cooling catheter insertion via right femoral vein in resus bay with target temperature 36 °C over the next 60 minutes under continuous arterial line monitoring of core
options.rationale: Endovascular cooling has slower cooling rate than CWI, requires expertise and equipment usually unavailable in ED, and is reserved for ICU when other methods fail. (Source: Sports Medicine Australia: Heat illness)

options.text: Immediate cold water immersion target core temperature of 39 °C achieved within 30 minutes, with continuous rectal probe core temperature monitoring throughout the cooling intervention period
options.rationale: Cold water immersion (2-15 °C) targeting cool-to-39 °C within 30 minutes is the most rapid cooling method (rate 0.2 °C/min) and has the lowest mortality in exertional heatstroke; stopping at 39 °C avoids overshoot to hypothermia. (Source: Sports Medicine Australia: Heat illness)

options.text: Whole body application of ice packs to neck axillae and groin without water immersion, with continuous rectal probe monitoring of core temperature to a target of 36 °C over 60 minutes
options.rationale: Ice packs at major vessels are slower than CWI (cooling rate 0.03 °C/min) and inferior for exertional heatstroke; targeting 36 °C risks overshoot to hypothermia. (Source: Sports Medicine Australia: Heat illness)

explanation.summary: Exertional heatstroke in young athletes is defined by core temperature >40 °C with central nervous system dysfunction in the context of exertion. Cold water immersion (CWI) at 2-15 °C is the fastest cooling method (rate 0.15-0.2 °C/min) and is associated with the lowest mortality when applied within 30 minutes of collapse. The target is to cool TO 39 °C within 30 minutes - not lower - to avoid overshoot hypothermia. Evaporative cooling is an acceptable alternative when CWI is not feasible. Complications include rhabdomyolysis (CK >5000), AKI, DIC, hepatic injury, and arrhythmias - resuscitation with IV crystalloid and electrolyte correction proceeds concurrently. Paracetamol and dantrolene do NOT have a role.
key_points: Cold water immersion is first-line for exertional heatstroke; cooling rate ~0.2 °C/min.
Target cool to 39 °C within 30 minutes; avoid overshoot to hypothermia.
Evaporative cooling is acceptable when CWI unavailable but slower.
Paracetamol has no role in exertional hyperthermia (no pyrogen).
Monitor for rhabdomyolysis (CK >5000), AKI, DIC, hepatic injury.
explanation.pearls: Cold water immersion cools at 0.2 °C per minute - target 39 °C then stop, because overshoot hypothermia kills as readily as the original hyperthermia.

subtopic_detail: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula recognition at first feed
stem:
A newborn boy at 12 hours of life, born at 39 weeks via uncomplicated normal vaginal birth to a primigravida mother, develops frothy white secretions from the mouth and brief desaturation to 85% during his first attempted breastfeed in the postnatal ward. He coughed, spluttered, and recovered to baseline saturations on room air within 90 seconds without intervention. He has been spitting up small amounts of clear fluid between feeds since birth.

Antenatal anomaly scan at 20 weeks was reported as polyhydramnios with amniotic fluid index 26 cm; no other anomaly was visualised. Family history is non-contributory. On examination he is alert and pink on room air. The abdomen is scaphoid. There is no facial or limb anomaly. Cardiac examination is normal with no murmur.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, BP 70/40 mmHg, RR 50/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, pink on air; frothy oral secretions reaccumulating; scaphoid abdomen; no facial dysmorphism; symmetric chest movements; no cardiac murmur; anus patent
data_table.Investigations: Routine antenatal serology negative; no postnatal investigations yet performed; no vertebral or limb anomaly on cursory examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial of paced bottle feeds with thickened formula and reassessment of feeding tolerance over the next 24 hours in the postnatal ward with lactation consultant support and review
options.rationale: Thickened formula in tracheo-oesophageal fistula risks ongoing aspiration; the clinical picture (frothy oral secretions, choking with feed, scaphoid abdomen with polyhydramnios) demands urgent workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula)

options.text: Discharge with home apnoea monitor and lactation support with paediatric outpatient review within 7 days for ongoing reassessment of feeding and breathing in the home environment
options.rationale: Suspected TOF cannot be discharged; failure to recognise leads to repeated aspiration, pneumonia, and abdominal distension from gas via fistula. (Source: RCH CPG: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula)

options.text: Echocardiogram only as the priority investigation today, as cardiac anomalies are common in this cohort, before any consideration of further alimentary tract investigations or surgical referral
options.rationale: Echo is part of VACTERL workup but does not diagnose TOF; passage of orogastric tube with chest and abdomen X-ray is the immediate confirmation. (Source: RCH CPG: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula)

options.text: Barium swallow study under fluoroscopy this morning to dynamically assess swallowing mechanics and detect any tracheal communication before paediatric surgical referral is finalised today
options.rationale: Contrast swallow is CONTRAINDICATED in suspected TOF due to aspiration into lungs causing chemical pneumonitis; OGT + plain film is the safe diagnostic approach. (Source: RCH CPG: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula)

options.text: Pass a 10 French orogastric tube to estimate distance to coiling or resistance, then obtain a plain chest and abdominal X-ray to assess tube position and gas pattern, and refer to paediatric surgery
options.rationale: OGT passage with coiling at 10-12 cm plus gas-filled stomach on plain X-ray confirms oesophageal atresia with distal TOF (most common type); contrast study is contraindicated due to aspiration risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula)

explanation.summary: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula presents in the neonate with the classic triad of frothy oral secretions, choking/coughing/cyanosis with first feeds, and inability to pass an orogastric tube. Antenatal polyhydramnios (from inability to swallow amniotic fluid) is suggestive. The most common type (85%) is oesophageal atresia with distal TOF (Gross type C) - identified by OGT coiling in upper pouch at 10-12 cm with gas-filled stomach on plain abdominal film (gas reaches stomach via the distal fistula). Pure oesophageal atresia (no fistula) shows OGT coiling AND a gasless abdomen. Contrast studies are contraindicated due to aspiration into the lungs causing chemical pneumonitis. Look for VACTERL associations (Vertebral, Anorectal, Cardiac, TE, Renal, Limb). Definitive management is paediatric surgical repair.
key_points: Triad: frothy oral secretions, choking with first feeds, OGT cannot pass.
Antenatal polyhydramnios is suggestive.
OGT coiling at 10-12 cm + gas in stomach on CXR = Gross type C (85%).
Contrast swallow CONTRAINDICATED (aspiration risk).
Screen for VACTERL associations: vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, renal, limb.
explanation.pearls: OGT plus a plain chest-and-abdomen X-ray confirms TOF in under 10 minutes - never order a barium swallow in a neonate with frothy oral secretions, the contrast will spill into the lungs.

stem:
A 5-month-old boy is admitted to a regional paediatric ward with 3 days of coryza followed by 24 hours of laboured breathing and reduced feeding. He is taking about 50% of usual milk volumes and has wet nappies 4 hourly. He was born at 38 weeks gestation with no perinatal complications and has no chronic conditions.

On arrival he is alert with moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, widespread fine inspiratory crackles, and scattered wheeze. Nasopharyngeal aspirate returns positive for respiratory syncytial virus. He has been on room air for the first 4 hours, with SpO2 fluctuating between 88% and 91%. Low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min has been running for the past 2 hours and SpO2 is now persistently 89%-90% with ongoing moderate work of breathing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168/min, BP 88/52 mmHg, RR 62/min, SpO2 90% on 1 L/min nasal prong, temperature 37.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, no head bobbing, no apnoeas; bilateral crackles and wheeze; capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.34, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); nasopharyngeal aspirate RSV positive; chest x-ray hyperinflation only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Commence high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with heated humidified oxygen titrated to maintain SpO2 at 90% or above
options.rationale: RCH defines low-flow failure as ongoing moderate work of breathing or SpO2 below 90% after 2 hours on maximal low-flow; HFNC at 2 L/kg/min is the next step in escalation in the ward. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Increase low-flow nasal prong oxygen from 1 L/min to 4 L/min through the standard nasal prongs and continue monitoring in the ward
options.rationale: Standard nasal prongs deliver up to 2 L/min in infants under 12 months per RCH; flows above this are uncomfortable, dry the airway, and are not part of the bronchiolitis escalation pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Continue low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and reassess work of breathing and saturations again in another 2 hours
options.rationale: After 2 hours on low-flow with persistent saturations below the 90% target and ongoing moderate work of breathing, continuing the same therapy meets the RCH definition of low-flow failure and risks delayed escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Administer a 5 mg salbutamol nebuliser and reassess respiratory effort and oxygen requirement 20 minutes after the dose has finished
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended for bronchiolitis under 12 months and do not change outcomes or oxygen requirement; the wheeze reflects small-airway plugging, not bronchospasm. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Switch directly to bilevel positive airway pressure via tight-fitting face mask in the high dependency area for ongoing respiratory support
options.rationale: BiPAP bypasses the HFNC step in the RCH escalation ladder; HFNC failure (rising pCO2, rising RR despite 2 L/kg/min, exhaustion) is the trigger to escalate to non-invasive ventilation in PICU. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: RCH bronchiolitis pathway escalates respiratory support in steps: room air, then low-flow nasal prong oxygen (1-2 L/min for infants), then high-flow nasal cannula (2 L/kg/min heated humidified) on the ward, then non-invasive ventilation in PICU. The SpO2 target is 90% or above on minimal support. Bronchodilators, nebulised hypertonic saline, systemic corticosteroids, and routine chest physiotherapy are not recommended for bronchiolitis. Apnoeas, exhaustion, or rising pCO2 are PICU-level triggers.
key_points: SpO2 target is 90% (not 92-94%) in bronchiolitis under RCH
Low-flow oxygen via nasal prongs is capped at 2 L/min in infants
HFNC 2 L/kg/min is the standard ward-level escalation step
Bronchodilators have no role in bronchiolitis under 12 months
Apnoeas, rising pCO2, or HFNC failure trigger PICU transfer
explanation.pearls: Low-flow nasal prong oxygen flow rate in infants is 2 L/min maximum; if persistent SpO2 under 90% or moderate work of breathing after 2 hours, escalate to HFNC at 2 L/kg/min.

stem:
A 13-month-old girl is brought to a paediatric emergency department 15 minutes after a single bite of a peanut butter sandwich at home. The parents report rapid onset of facial swelling, widespread red blotchy rash on the trunk, persistent harsh barking cough, and one episode of vomiting on the way to hospital. She has known egg and dairy allergy but no previous reaction to peanut.

In the resuscitation cubicle she is alert but distressed with audible inspiratory stridor and bilateral wheeze. A cot weight is unavailable but a recent weighing card states 11 kg. Intravenous access has not yet been established. The nurse has the paediatric anaphylaxis tray open and is asking which adrenaline dose to draw up.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 172/min, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 48/min, SpO2 93% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Lip and periorbital oedema, urticarial rash trunk and limbs; inspiratory stridor with bilateral wheeze; capillary refill 3 seconds; not yet cannulated
data_table.Investigations: Bedside investigations deferred pending resuscitation; weight on weighing card 11 kg (no current cot weight)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate single best initial adrenaline dose and route?

options.text: Adrenaline 110 micrograms (0.11 mg of 1:1000) intramuscular into the anterolateral mid-thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if no response
options.rationale: Calculating 10 mcg/kg arithmetic from a non-current weight is the historical method that ASCIA replaced; the per-kg formula is no longer the preferred prescribing approach in the emergency setting. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Adrenaline 50 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1:10 000) slow intravenous bolus over 5 minutes after rapid IV cannulation has been established
options.rationale: IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after at least 2 IM doses and only with cardiac monitoring; first-line is always IM into the anterolateral thigh. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Adrenaline 300 micrograms (0.30 mg of 1:1000) intramuscular into the anterolateral mid-thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if no response
options.rationale: 300 mcg (EpiPen) is the ASCIA banded dose for children 20 kg or more (approximately 6 years and older), not for an 11 kg toddler; overdose risks tachyarrhythmia in small children. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Adrenaline 150 micrograms (0.15 mg of 1:1000) intramuscular into the anterolateral mid-thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if no response
options.rationale: The ASCIA banded table assigns 150 mcg IM adrenaline to children 1 to under 6 years (approximately 10-20 kg), independent of exact weight; matches an EpiPen Jr. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Adrenaline 5 mg nebulised (5 mL of 1:1000) via face mask immediately to treat the upper airway oedema and the audible stridor
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline can supplement upper airway oedema management AFTER IM adrenaline; it does not address systemic anaphylaxis and is never the first single best initial intervention. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: ASCIA recommends a banded weight-and-age table for IM adrenaline in paediatric anaphylaxis to remove calculation error in resuscitation: under 1 year (under 10 kg) 100 mcg, 1 to under 6 years (10-20 kg) 150 mcg, 6 to under 12 years (20-50 kg) 300 mcg, 12 years or older (over 50 kg) 500 mcg. The IM site is the anterolateral mid-thigh. Repeat every 5 minutes if no response. IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory cases after 2 IM doses with cardiac monitoring.
key_points: ASCIA paediatric IM adrenaline uses banded doses, not per-kg arithmetic
10-20 kg child receives 150 mcg IM (EpiPen Jr equivalent)
Anterolateral mid-thigh is the only IM site
Repeat at 5 minute intervals if persistent symptoms
IV adrenaline only after 2 failed IM doses with cardiac monitoring
explanation.pearls: 150 mcg IM adrenaline is the ASCIA dose for any child 10-20 kg; the banded table is the AU standard precisely because resuscitation is not the moment for mg/kg arithmetic.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

stem:
A 22-month-old boy is brought to a metropolitan emergency department with 36 hours of profuse non-bloody diarrhoea and 24 hours of vomiting up to 6 times daily. His older brother had similar symptoms last week. Parents report he is taking small sips of water but vomiting most of them.

He is alert but irritable on assessment. He weighs 12 kg today; the family Red Book records 12.7 kg three weeks ago. Eyes appear sunken, mouth is dry, capillary refill is 2 to 3 seconds, peripheries are warm. He has had no wet nappy for 6 hours. A first dose of oral ondansetron 2 mg was given on triage 30 minutes ago and he has just vomited again. He has no abdominal distension, no peritonism, no bilious vomit, and no blood in the stool.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 142/min, BP 92/60 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, soft non-tender abdomen, no organomegaly; capillary refill 2-3 seconds; weight loss 5.5%
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.34, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 2.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); urea and electrolytes within normal limits; venous glucose 4.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Encourage small frequent oral sips of clear fluids at home and review with the general practitioner in the next 24 to 48 hours for clinical reassessment
options.rationale: Discharge home is inappropriate when oral intake has just failed in the department with a documented 5.5% weight loss and ongoing vomiting after ondansetron. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Insert an intravenous cannula and administer a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus over the next 30 minutes followed by maintenance intravenous fluids
options.rationale: IV rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, NGT failure, or significant electrolyte derangement; NGT is preferred for moderate dehydration with normal electrolytes and no shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and commence oral rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg over the first hour followed by ongoing maintenance plus deficit
options.rationale: RCH first-line for moderate dehydration after failed oral intake is NGT rehydration with ORS; faster, safer, and equally effective as IV in moderate dehydration without shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Repeat ondansetron 4 mg orally and reassess oral fluid tolerance again in 30 minutes before considering any further intervention or escalation
options.rationale: Ondansetron is a single dose only in paediatric gastroenteritis and the dose for 8-15 kg is 2 mg; repeated dosing is not recommended and delays definitive rehydration. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Send urgent stool sample for microscopy culture sensitivity and rotavirus PCR before commencing any active rehydration to confirm the underlying cause
options.rationale: Stool studies are not routine in uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis and do not change acute management; rehydration is the priority and is not stool-result dependent. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: Australian paediatric practice prefers NGT rehydration over IV for moderate dehydration without shock because it is faster to start, less invasive, has fewer complications, and matches outcomes of IV therapy. A single dose of oral ondansetron (2 mg for 8-15 kg, 4 mg for 15-30 kg) is recommended for vomiting; repeat doses are not. IV is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, NGT failure, decreased conscious state, or significant electrolyte/acid-base derangement. Routine stool studies and antibiotics are not indicated in uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis.
key_points: NGT rehydration is first-line for moderate dehydration without shock
Ondansetron is single-dose only: 2 mg (8-15 kg) or 4 mg (15-30 kg)
IV reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or NGT failure
Routine stool studies do not change acute management
Antibiotics are not indicated for uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis
explanation.pearls: NGT ORS at 25 mL/kg over the first hour is the RCH protocol for moderate dehydration after failed oral intake; IV access is needed only if NGT fails or shock develops.

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease in an infant
stem:
A 7-month-old girl is reviewed on day 7 of a febrile illness in a regional paediatric ward. Persistent daily fevers to 39.5 °C have not responded to paracetamol or ibuprofen; oral amoxicillin started by the GP on day 3 has made no difference. She has been miserable, off feeds, and her mother reports erythema of the hands which has now begun to peel around the fingertips.

On examination she has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, a faint perineal rash, and a single 1.5 cm cervical lymph node. Lips are red but not fissured. There is no oropharyngeal exudate. Three of the five classical Kawasaki criteria are present. Inflammatory markers are markedly elevated and a transaminitis is noted; urine has sterile pyuria. A focused echocardiogram has been arranged and is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158/min, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival injection bilateral non-exudative, single 1.5 cm cervical node, perineal rash, peeling fingertips; no joint swelling; mild hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: CRP 145 mg/L (<5), ESR 78 mm/h, WCC 18.4 x10^9/L with neutrophilia, platelets 612 x10^9/L, ALT 96 U/L (<35); urine microscopy 80 x10^6/L leucocytes with negative culture; albumin 28 g/L (35-50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Wait for completion of the echocardiogram and only commence treatment if coronary artery z-score is greater than 2.5 on the formal report
options.rationale: Treatment of suspected Kawasaki disease is not contingent on a coronary abnormality; delaying IVIG beyond day 10 of illness markedly increases the risk of coronary aneurysm. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Continue supportive care alone and reassess clinically in 48 hours given that classical criteria for Kawasaki disease are not yet fully met
options.rationale: Infants under 12 months are at highest risk of coronary aneurysms and most often present with incomplete criteria; AHA and RCH explicitly recommend treating incomplete Kawasaki on supportive laboratory features. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours together with high-dose aspirin pending the formal echocardiogram report
options.rationale: Incomplete Kawasaki in an infant with 3 of 5 criteria plus elevated CRP, transaminitis, sterile pyuria, hypoalbuminaemia and thrombocytosis meets RCH IVIG criteria; treat within 10 days of fever onset. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Switch oral amoxicillin to intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily for empirical cover of an unidentified bacterial focus before any other intervention
options.rationale: Persistent fever for 7 days with documented sterile pyuria, no localising focus, and Kawasaki features makes broadened antibiotics inappropriate as a primary intervention; the diagnosis is Kawasaki until proven otherwise. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence a 3-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg/day as primary therapy and review the response after the third pulse
options.rationale: Pulse steroids are reserved for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease or selected high-risk cases (Kobayashi score, infants under 12 months may be considered for adjunctive steroid); they are NOT primary monotherapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is the rule in infants and a leading cause of acquired coronary artery disease in children. AHA/RCH supplementary laboratory criteria (CRP over 30 mg/L plus 3 of: anaemia for age, platelets over 450 after day 7, albumin under 30 g/L, ALT elevation, WCC over 15, sterile pyuria) support empirical IVIG when fewer than 4 of 5 classical features are present. IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin should be given within 10 days of fever onset. Steroids are adjunctive in IVIG-resistant disease or high-risk infants; echocardiography is performed to baseline coronary status but does not gate initial treatment.
key_points: Treat incomplete Kawasaki on supportive lab criteria, do not wait for echo
IVIG within 10 days of fever onset reduces aneurysm risk to about 5%
Infants under 12 months have the highest aneurysm risk
Sterile pyuria, transaminitis, hypoalbuminaemia, thrombocytosis are supportive
Pulse steroids are adjunctive (Kobayashi-high or IVIG-resistant), not primary
explanation.pearls: IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin within day 10 of fever onset cuts coronary aneurysm risk from around 25% to under 5%; infants under 12 months should be treated on lower thresholds because incomplete presentation is the norm.

sources.label: AHA 2017 Scientific Statement Diagnosis Treatment and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

stem:
A 5-year-old boy with newly diagnosed B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presents to a metropolitan paediatric emergency department on day 10 of induction chemotherapy. The mother brings him in because of a single fever to 38.6 °C tympanic and a brief shaking chill. He has a tunnelled central venous line in place that looks clean and is non-tender.

He appears tired but alert, with capillary refill of 2 seconds and warm peripheries. There is no oral mucositis, no abdominal tenderness, no perianal tenderness, and no focal infective findings on examination. The leukaemia treatment team has been notified. Blood cultures have been drawn from both line lumens and a peripheral site. Empirical antibiotic choice is being prepared in the resuscitation cubicle.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 102/60 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Central line site clean and non-tender, no oral mucositis, soft abdomen, no perianal tenderness, no skin lesions
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophil count 0.3 x10^9/L, platelets 42 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 92 g/L; CRP 65 mg/L; venous lactate 1.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); chest x-ray clear; urine microscopy bland; blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical intravenous antibiotic regimen for this child?

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg per dose every 6 hours as monotherapy after blood cultures have been drawn from line and peripheral sites
options.rationale: ChildKidsCAN and eviQ paediatric febrile neutropenia guidance recommends piperacillin-tazobactam monotherapy as empirical first-line in haemodynamically stable children without focal severe infection or known resistant organism. (Source: ChildKidsCAN Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia Guideline; eviQ)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily plus oral amoxicillin twice daily for empirical streptococcal and gram-negative cover until cultures are reported
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone has no antipseudomonal activity and oral amoxicillin is inappropriate in a febrile neutropenic patient; AU paediatric guidance requires antipseudomonal IV cover empirically. (Source: ChildKidsCAN Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 15 mg/kg every 6 hours and intravenous gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg once daily without any beta-lactam pending final blood culture results
options.rationale: Empirical vancomycin is reserved for shock, line infection, severe mucositis, MRSA-colonised patients, or gram-positive growth; routine empirical vancomycin is not indicated and aminoglycoside monotherapy is never appropriate. (Source: ChildKidsCAN Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous meropenem 20 mg/kg every 8 hours immediately as empirical broad-spectrum cover and add filgrastim 5 mcg/kg subcutaneously on the day of admission
options.rationale: Meropenem is reserved for prior ESBL colonisation, recent broad-spectrum exposure, or critical illness; first-line stable febrile neutropenia is piperacillin-tazobactam. Routine G-CSF is not recommended empirically. (Source: ChildKidsCAN Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia Guideline)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily combined with oral ciprofloxacin discharge home with daily outpatient haematology phone review
options.rationale: Australian paediatric practice admits ALL children with febrile neutropenia for IV antibiotics; outpatient oral regimens for low-risk febrile neutropenia exist in adult/adolescent care but not as default in induction-phase paediatric ALL. (Source: ChildKidsCAN Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia Guideline)

explanation.summary: Paediatric febrile neutropenia (single tympanic temperature 38.5 °C or above OR two readings 38.0 °C an hour apart with neutrophils under 0.5 x10^9/L) is a medical emergency requiring blood cultures and IV antipseudomonal beta-lactam within 60 minutes. Piperacillin-tazobactam is the AU first-line empirical choice; add vancomycin only for shock, line tunnel infection, severe mucositis, MRSA colonisation, or gram-positive growth. Meropenem is reserved for ESBL, recent broad-spectrum failure, or critical illness. Routine G-CSF is not indicated. ALL induction patients are admitted regardless of risk score.
key_points: Empirical piperacillin-tazobactam monotherapy is AU first-line for stable paediatric febrile neutropenia
Antibiotic should be in within 60 minutes of arrival
Vancomycin add-on for shock, line, severe mucositis, MRSA, or gram-positive growth
Meropenem reserved for ESBL or critical illness
Induction-phase paediatric ALL patients always admitted for IV therapy
explanation.pearls: Piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg per dose 6-hourly within 60 minutes of arrival is the AU paediatric febrile neutropenia first-line; door-to-antibiotic time is the auditable quality metric.

subtopic_detail: Hypercyanotic spell in tetralogy of Fallot
stem:
A 10-month-old girl with known unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after a brief episode at home of inconsolable crying, deepening lip colour, and limpness. She has previously had two milder spells which resolved as her mother brought her knees to her chest. The cardiology team is aware and a primary repair is planned for next month.

In the resuscitation bay she is irritable but rousable. SpO2 has been 72% to 78% on room air for the last 10 minutes despite knee-to-chest positioning by the parent and 8 L/min facemask oxygen. She has a barely audible right upper sternal edge systolic murmur. Peripheries are cool and dusky. Capillary refill is 4 seconds centrally. Intravenous access has been established. Cardiology has been called and is en route.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 184/min, BP 78/44 mmHg, RR 56/min, SpO2 76% on 8 L/min mask, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Central cyanosis, knees drawn up to chest, soft systolic ejection murmur (previously grade 3, now grade 1), cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.18, lactate 5.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), bicarbonate 14 mmol/L; haemoglobin 168 g/L; venous glucose 5.2 mmol/L; bedside echo deferred to inpatient team

lead_in: After positioning, oxygen, and intravenous fluid bolus, what is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion at 0.05 micrograms/kg/min to keep the ductus arteriosus open and improve oxygenated pulmonary blood flow at this age
options.rationale: The ductus closes within days of birth and is not reopenable at 10 months of age; PGE1 has no role in hypercyanotic spells in an older infant with established tetralogy. (Source: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg push as inotropic support given the cool peripheries and the prolonged centralised capillary refill time of 4 seconds
options.rationale: Catecholamines increase infundibular contraction and worsen right ventricular outflow obstruction; adrenaline is contraindicated in unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot hypercyanotic spells. (Source: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell

options.text: Intravenous morphine 0.1 mg/kg by slow injection to reduce hyperpnoea and break the spiral of right ventricular outflow tract spasm and cyanosis
options.rationale: After knee-to-chest, oxygen, and IV fluids, morphine 0.05-0.1 mg/kg IV reduces hyperpnoea and infundibular spasm and is the recommended next step in unbroken hypercyanotic spells. (Source: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell

options.text: Intravenous furosemide 1 mg/kg to offload the right ventricle and reduce pulmonary congestion before the cardiology team arrives at the bedside
options.rationale: Hypercyanotic spells reflect right-to-left shunt with reduced pulmonary blood flow, not pulmonary congestion; diuretics drop systemic vascular resistance and preload and worsen the spell. (Source: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg as an immediate buffer for the metabolic acidosis demonstrated on the bedside venous blood gas analysis
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is reserved for refractory acidosis after positioning, oxygen, fluid, morphine and phenylephrine have failed; it is not the next step ahead of morphine which addresses the mechanism. (Source: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell

explanation.summary: Hypercyanotic spells in tetralogy of Fallot arise from acute right ventricular outflow tract infundibular spasm with worsened right-to-left shunt across the VSD. The sequenced approach is knee-to-chest positioning (raises systemic vascular resistance), supplemental oxygen, and IV fluid bolus to increase preload. Morphine 0.05-0.1 mg/kg IV reduces hyperpnoea and infundibular spasm. Phenylephrine boluses (1-5 mcg/kg) raise systemic vascular resistance for refractory cases. Adrenaline is contraindicated because it worsens infundibular contraction; PGE1 has no role beyond the neonatal period.
key_points: Sequence: positioning, oxygen, IV fluids, morphine, then phenylephrine
Morphine 0.05-0.1 mg/kg IV reduces hyperpnoea and infundibular spasm
Adrenaline is contraindicated; phenylephrine raises SVR without infundibular spasm
PGE1 has no role after the ductus has closed in older infants
Refractory spells require intubation, paralysis, and urgent cardiology
explanation.pearls: In a hypercyanotic spell, the audible murmur quietens because right-to-left shunt has bypassed the RVOT; a previously loud murmur going silent is a marker of severity, not improvement.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell

stem:
A 4-week-old boy is reviewed at a paediatric outpatient clinic for severe constipation since birth. The mother reports he did not pass any stool until day 3 of life when a paediatric resident performed a digital examination at the maternity ward, which produced a forceful explosion of meconium. Since then he opens his bowels only every 4 to 5 days with marked straining, and only after a glycerine suppository.

He is bottle fed with standard formula and is on the 25th centile for weight (down from the 50th at birth). The abdomen is mildly distended without visible bowel loops. There is no inguinal hernia and the perianal area looks normal. A focused examination shows a tight anus with an explosive release of gas and watery stool after the examining finger is removed. Plain abdominal x-ray shows dilated bowel loops with absent rectal gas.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140/min, BP 78/48 mmHg, RR 38/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild abdominal distension, soft non-tender abdomen, tight anus with explosive release of gas and stool on rectal examination; weight 25th centile, length 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Plain abdominal x-ray dilated proximal bowel with reduced rectal gas; haemoglobin 132 g/L, electrolytes within normal limits; thyroid stimulating hormone 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); coeliac serology not yet sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the underlying diagnosis?

options.text: Trial of macrogol osmotic laxative for 4 weeks at maintenance dose and review the response in clinic before considering invasive testing or referral
options.rationale: Empirical laxative trial is appropriate for functional constipation but not for an infant with delayed meconium passage and explosive release on PR; functional constipation rarely begins in the first month of life. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Suction rectal biopsy at the appropriate level above the dentate line obtained at a paediatric surgical centre for histopathology
options.rationale: Delayed meconium passage beyond 48 hours plus chronic obstructive constipation with explosive release on digital examination is Hirschsprung disease until proven otherwise; suction rectal biopsy is the gold-standard diagnostic test. (Source: RACGP red book Paediatrics; RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Sweat chloride test conducted on at least two occasions to exclude cystic fibrosis as the underlying cause for the meconium plug and constipation
options.rationale: Meconium ileus from cystic fibrosis usually presents in the first 48 hours with bilious vomiting and failure to pass meconium, not chronic explosive release on PR; this patient already has newborn screen and clinical features pointing to Hirschsprung. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Anorectal manometry to demonstrate the absence of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex via balloon distension under conscious sedation by paediatric gastroenterology
options.rationale: Anorectal manometry is technically difficult in young infants and is a screening test in older children; AU practice goes directly to suction rectal biopsy for histology in infants with classical features. (Source: RACGP Paediatric Constipation Guidelines)

options.text: Barium enema with full bowel preparation to look for the transition zone on imaging and confirm the diagnosis before progressing to definitive surgical management
options.rationale: Contrast enema can suggest a transition zone but is not diagnostic and has poor sensitivity in neonates; histological confirmation by suction rectal biopsy is required before surgery is offered. (Source: RACGP Paediatric Constipation Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Hirschsprung disease should be suspected in any neonate who has not passed meconium within 48 hours, or in an infant with chronic obstructive constipation, abdominal distension, and explosive release of stool after digital examination. Suction rectal biopsy showing absent ganglion cells and hypertrophied nerve trunks is the diagnostic gold standard. Contrast enema and anorectal manometry are supportive but not diagnostic. Definitive treatment is a pull-through procedure (Soave, Swenson, or Duhamel). Untreated Hirschsprung is complicated by enterocolitis, perforation, and death.
key_points: Failure to pass meconium beyond 48 hours is a red flag for Hirschsprung disease
Explosive release of stool after PR is the classical clinical sign
Suction rectal biopsy is the gold-standard diagnostic test
Contrast enema can suggest but not confirm the diagnosis
Hirschsprung enterocolitis is the leading cause of mortality before surgery
explanation.pearls: Failure to pass meconium beyond 48 hours of life plus explosive release of stool after PR examination triggers suction rectal biopsy referral; the biopsy must be at least 2 cm above the dentate line to avoid the normal hypoganglionic zone.

subtopic_detail: Hyperammonaemia presentation in late-onset urea cycle disorder
stem:
A 2-year-old boy is transferred from a regional emergency department after 12 hours of vomiting and progressive drowsiness. His family had a high-protein BBQ dinner the night before symptoms began. He was previously well except for two unexplained encephalopathic episodes at 9 and 14 months that were attributed to viral gastroenteritis. An older male sibling died unexpectedly at 18 months overseas; cause of death is not documented.

On arrival he opens eyes only to painful stimuli and has hyperventilation without obvious respiratory distress. There is no fever, neck stiffness, or focal neurology. Initial investigations done at the referring hospital show normal sodium, glucose, lactate, ketones, ammonia not measured. A repeat venous blood gas in your department shows respiratory alkalosis. Plasma ammonia returns markedly elevated; lactate is normal; the rest of the metabolic screen is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.2 °C
data_table.Examination: GCS E2 V2 M4 (8/15), pupils equal and reactive, no focal deficit, no rash, no organomegaly, no signs of trauma
data_table.Investigations: Plasma ammonia 480 micromol/L (<50), arterial blood gas pH 7.52 pCO2 28 mmHg HCO3 22 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), glucose 5.4 mmol/L, urine ketones negative, sodium 138 mmol/L, anion gap normal; CT brain no acute findings

lead_in: Beyond intubation and intensive care transfer, what is the single most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous dextrose 10% at 1.5 times maintenance rate plus intralipid 20% infusion and stop all enteral protein intake while awaiting metabolic team review
options.rationale: Dextrose and lipid stop protein catabolism but do not remove ammonia from the circulation; ammonia at 480 micromol/L is acutely neurotoxic and requires extracorporeal removal alongside the metabolic measures. (Source: BIMDG Hyperammonaemia Protocol; RCH CPG: Metabolic Disorders)

options.text: Give intravenous mannitol 0.5 g/kg over 20 minutes to manage incipient cerebral oedema and continue conservative metabolic management with regular ammonia rechecks
options.rationale: Hyperammonaemia-induced cerebral oedema is treated by removing ammonia, not by osmotic therapy; mannitol does not address the underlying cause and delays definitive treatment. (Source: BIMDG Hyperammonaemia Protocol)

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium benzoate 250 mg/kg load followed by sodium phenylbutyrate 250 mg/kg over 90 minutes and reassess ammonia level in 2 hours
options.rationale: Scavengers are essential adjuncts but reduce ammonia too slowly when levels exceed 400 micromol/L; they are used alongside dialysis, not as a standalone strategy at this severity. (Source: BIMDG Hyperammonaemia Protocol)

options.text: Initiate urgent extracorporeal continuous renal replacement therapy via central access at a tertiary centre to remove ammonia mechanically and rapidly
options.rationale: Plasma ammonia above 400 micromol/L with encephalopathy is the threshold for dialysis (haemodialysis preferred, CRRT acceptable); pharmacological scavengers alone cannot drop levels fast enough to avoid permanent neurological injury. (Source: BIMDG Hyperammonaemia Protocol)

options.text: Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg and aciclovir 20 mg/kg pending the lumbar puncture and CSF analysis to exclude a viral or bacterial cause of encephalopathy
options.rationale: Bacterial or viral encephalitis are reasonable differentials but the documented ammonia at 480 micromol/L and respiratory alkalosis pattern point to a urea cycle disorder; antibiotics alone do not treat the metabolic emergency. (Source: BIMDG Hyperammonaemia Protocol)

explanation.summary: Late-presenting urea cycle disorders (ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is the most common) often manifest after a protein load or catabolic stress. The classical triad is encephalopathy, respiratory alkalosis (ammonia stimulates the central respiratory drive), and absence of acidosis or hypoglycaemia. Plasma ammonia must be measured on a free-flowing sample placed on ice and run immediately. Above 400 micromol/L in a child with encephalopathy, extracorporeal removal (haemodialysis preferred, CRRT acceptable) is required alongside protein restriction, high-calorie dextrose, and intravenous ammonia scavengers (sodium benzoate and phenylbutyrate). Untreated hyperammonaemic encephalopathy carries a high risk of permanent neurological injury.
key_points: Respiratory alkalosis with encephalopathy in a child warrants an ammonia level
Plasma ammonia above 400 micromol/L plus encephalopathy is the threshold for dialysis
Scavengers reduce ammonia slowly; dialysis is the rapid intervention
Protein restriction and high-calorie dextrose stop endogenous protein catabolism
Family history of unexplained sibling death warrants high suspicion
explanation.pearls: Plasma ammonia must be measured on a free-flowing venous sample placed immediately on ice; falsely elevated levels are common with tourniquet use, haemolysis, or delayed laboratory transit.

stem:
An 18-month-old boy presents to the emergency department at 02:00 with a barking cough that began two days ago following coryza. Overnight he woke with noisy breathing audible from his cot. He has had no fevers above 38.0 degrees Celsius and is taking sips of water.

On arrival you hear inspiratory stridor at rest while he sits calmly on his mother's lap, with mild intercostal recession. He speaks in short sentences and is not drooling. Vital signs are within normal limits for age. There is no urticaria, no preceding choking episode, and immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits for age
data_table.Examination: inspiratory stridor at rest, mild intercostal recession, calm and well perfused, no drooling, oropharynx unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: clinical diagnosis, no imaging or bloods performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate corticosteroid management?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose now
options.rationale: Stridor at rest with mild recession but no agitation places this child in the moderate Westley band. RCH directs a single oral dose of 0.15 mg/kg for both mild and moderate croup; onset is within 30 minutes and a second dose is rarely needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single dose now
options.rationale: The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved by RCH for severe croup (stridor at rest with marked recession, agitation, exhaustion, or hypoxia). Using it here would expose the child to four times the steroid load without added benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is indicated for severe croup or impending obstruction, not moderate disease. Its benefit is short lived (30 to 90 minutes) and mandates 3-hour observation for rebound stridor. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Inhaled salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer with face mask now
options.rationale: Beta-2 agonists target lower-airway smooth muscle and have no role in subglottic oedema. Reaching for salbutamol misclassifies stridor as wheeze. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup; Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol and humidified air advice
options.rationale: Even mild croup warrants a single dose of dexamethasone in current RCH guidance because it shortens illness and prevents return visits. Humidification has no evidence base. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup severity in Australia is stratified using the Westley framework: mild (no stridor at rest), moderate (stridor at rest with mild to moderate recession but calm), and severe (marked recession, agitation, or exhaustion). RCH gives a single oral dose of dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for both mild and moderate croup. The higher 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe disease. Nebulised adrenaline is layered on top for severe croup and obligates a 3-hour observation window for rebound.
key_points: Stridor at rest plus calm child plus mild recession equals moderate croup
Mild and moderate croup share the same dexamethasone dose (0.15 mg/kg PO)
0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe disease and adds no benefit at lower severities
Nebulised adrenaline requires 3 hours of observation for rebound
explanation.pearls: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg acts within 30 minutes; a second dose is rarely indicated. Reserve 0.6 mg/kg for severe disease and mandate 3-hour observation after any nebulised adrenaline.

subtopic_detail: First febrile UTI imaging cascade in toddlers (RCH)
stem:
A 14-month-old girl presents with two days of fever to 39.2 degrees Celsius and reduced feeding. There is no rash, no respiratory symptoms, and no clear focus on examination. A clean-catch midstream urine sample collected with a maternal-assist technique grows greater than 10^8 colony-forming-units per litre of pure Escherichia coli, sensitive to trimethoprim and cefalexin.

She defervesces within 36 hours of starting oral trimethoprim and is feeding normally by review at 48 hours. Her antenatal scans were normal, she is fully immunised, and her growth tracks the 50th centile. There is no history of constipation, no abdominal mass, and no family history of vesicoureteric reflux.

data_table.Vital signs: afebrile at review, otherwise within normal limits
data_table.Examination: well perfused, no abdominal mass, normal external genitalia, no spinal anomaly
data_table.Investigations: MSU pure growth >10^8 CFU/L E. coli (sensitive to trimethoprim and cefalexin), renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging recommendation?

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound during the acute illness, before discharge
options.rationale: RCH reserves acute-phase ultrasound for atypical UTI features such as poor response to 48 hours of antibiotics, non-E. coli organism, sepsis, abdominal mass, or rising creatinine. None of these apply. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: No routine imaging; arrange clinical review and treat any recurrence promptly
options.rationale: This is a typical first UTI in a child over 6 months with normal antenatal imaging and prompt response. RCH does not recommend routine renal ultrasound, DMSA, or MCUG after a single typical UTI in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: DMSA scan at 4 to 6 months to assess for renal cortical scarring
options.rationale: DMSA scanning sits in NICE pathways but is not part of the RCH cascade for a single typical UTI. Routine scarring screens add radiation without changing management here. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Micturating cystourethrogram to exclude vesicoureteric reflux
options.rationale: MCUG is reserved for recurrent UTI, abnormal ultrasound findings, or atypical infection within the RCH cascade. It is not indicated after a single typical infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Outpatient renal ultrasound within 6 weeks of completing antibiotics
options.rationale: Routine delayed ultrasound after a single typical UTI is a NICE construct that RCH does not adopt for children with normal antenatal imaging. It generates incidental findings with no management change. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: The RCH urinary tract infection guideline diverges from NICE on imaging after a first UTI. For a child over 6 months with a typical first UTI (E. coli, prompt response, no atypical features), no routine imaging is recommended provided antenatal scans were normal. Ultrasound during illness is reserved for atypical features. DMSA and MCUG are not part of the RCH cascade and are deployed only after recurrent UTI or abnormal ultrasound.
key_points: Typical first UTI in a child over 6 months requires no routine imaging at RCH
Atypical features that trigger acute ultrasound: non-E. coli, no response by 48 h, sepsis, abdominal mass, rising creatinine
DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs not in the RCH cascade for a single typical UTI
Antenatal renal imaging history changes the threshold for any further imaging
explanation.pearls: RCH does not perform routine post-UTI ultrasound after the first typical infection over 6 months; reserve imaging for atypical features or recurrence within 6 months.

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis low-flow oxygen first-line per RCH
stem:
A 4-month-old infant is admitted with three days of coryza followed by worsening wheeze and feeding difficulty. He has taken approximately 40 percent of his usual milk volume over the preceding 24 hours.

On arrival to the ward he has pulse 160, blood pressure 86 by 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 56, SpO2 88 percent in room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius. He has moderate subcostal recession and audible widespread wheeze with bilateral inspiratory crackles. He is alert and consolable in his mother's arms. There has been no apnoea reported by parents or nursing staff, immunisations are up to date, and there is no relevant past medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 160, BP 86/50, RR 56, SpO2 88% room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: moderate subcostal recession, widespread wheeze with bilateral crackles, alert, well perfused
data_table.Investigations: clinical diagnosis of bronchiolitis, no chest X-ray performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial respiratory support?

options.text: Heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min from the outset
options.rationale: PREDICT and RCH reserve HFNC for failure of low-flow oxygen after a defined trial (usually 1 to 2 hours). Initial escalation to HFNC has not been shown to reduce ICU transfer compared with starting low-flow. (Source: PREDICT Australasian Bronchiolitis Guideline; RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer plus oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg
options.rationale: Bronchiolitis in under-12-month-olds does not respond to beta-2 agonists or systemic corticosteroids; both are explicitly discouraged by the PREDICT guideline. (Source: PREDICT Australasian Bronchiolitis Guideline)

options.text: Low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min titrated to SpO2 at least 90 percent
options.rationale: RCH and PREDICT both start with low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min targeting SpO2 of at least 90 percent. HFNC is reserved for failure of this approach after 1 to 2 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; PREDICT Australasian Bronchiolitis Guideline)

options.text: Nebulised hypertonic saline 3 percent with oxygen via face mask
options.rationale: Nebulised hypertonic saline does not reduce admission length or ICU transfer in Australian trials and is not part of standard RCH or PREDICT first-line therapy. (Source: PREDICT Australasian Bronchiolitis Guideline)

options.text: Continuous positive airway pressure via face mask in a monitored bed
options.rationale: Mask CPAP is escalation therapy after low-flow and HFNC failure. Skipping to it bypasses the stepped pathway and is not appropriate first-line in an alert, consolable infant. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Australian bronchiolitis care (PREDICT 2024 + RCH) is supportive: fluids and oxygen, with a deliberately stepped approach to respiratory support. Low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min targeting SpO2 of at least 90 percent is first line; HFNC is reserved for failure of low-flow after 1 to 2 hours. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, nebulised saline, and antibiotics have no role unless an alternative diagnosis emerges.
key_points: Bronchiolitis SpO2 target is at least 90 percent (not 92 to 94)
Start low-flow nasal prong oxygen before HFNC
Salbutamol, steroids, and hypertonic saline are not first-line
HFNC is rescue therapy when low-flow fails after a 1 to 2 hour trial
explanation.pearls: Start low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min targeting SpO2 90 percent; escalate to HFNC only after 1 to 2 hours of inadequate response.

subtopic_detail: Henoch-Schonlein purpura with renal warning features
stem:
A 7-year-old girl presents to the paediatric emergency department with a one-week history of palpable purpura over the buttocks and shins, intermittent crampy abdominal pain, and bilateral ankle swelling. Her parents report her urine has been a darker colour than usual for the past 48 hours. She had a viral upper respiratory infection 10 days earlier and is otherwise well.

On examination she is alert with pulse 96, blood pressure 132 by 88 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. There is no rash above the waist and joints are not actively inflamed. Urinalysis shows protein 3+ and blood 3+. Serum creatinine is 92 micromol/L (35-65), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), and renal tract ultrasound is structurally normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 132/88, RR 18, SpO2 100% room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: palpable purpura buttocks and shins, bilateral ankle oedema, abdomen soft, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: urinalysis protein 3+ blood 3+; creatinine 92 micromol/L (35-65); albumin 28 g/L (35-50); renal ultrasound structurally normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?
