options.text: Symptomatic care with simple analgesia and primary-care review in one week
options.rationale: Although most HSP is self-limiting, this child shows three features that mandate escalation: hypertension above the 95th centile, nephrotic-range proteinuria, and an elevated creatinine. Routine community follow-up alone would miss progression to crescentic glomerulonephritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for two weeks with outpatient paediatric review
options.rationale: Steroids may reduce abdominal pain in HSP but they do not prevent or treat established nephritis. Starting steroids before specialist assessment risks anchoring on the wrong therapy while serious renal disease evolves. (Source: KHA-CARI Guidelines; RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Commence amoxicillin pending blood cultures and admit for observation
options.rationale: There is no infective source and the platelet count is normal, making sepsis or meningococcaemia unlikely. Empirical antibiotics here would not address the renal trajectory and add no benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Admit for blood-pressure management and urgent paediatric nephrology referral for biopsy
options.rationale: Hypertension, heavy proteinuria, and rising creatinine in HSP define warning features that prompt admission, blood-pressure control, and urgent nephrology referral for likely renal biopsy and immunosuppression planning. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura; KHA-CARI Guidelines)

options.text: Send antinuclear antibody and ANCA panel and review when results return
options.rationale: Serology rarely reframes a textbook HSP presentation and there is no diagnostic uncertainty here that would justify deferring management for results. Time-to-biopsy is the live decision. (Source: KHA-CARI Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) in children is usually self-limiting but renal involvement occurs in around 30 percent and drives long-term morbidity. Warning features that change management include hypertension above the 95th centile, nephrotic-range proteinuria (more than 2+ on dipstick or PCR >250 mg/mmol), and elevated creatinine. The presence of any of these triggers admission, blood-pressure control, and urgent paediatric nephrology referral with biopsy to grade nephritis and guide immunosuppression. Steroids treat abdominal and joint symptoms but do not prevent or treat nephritis.
key_points: HSP nephritis warning triad: hypertension, nephrotic-range proteinuria, raised creatinine
Most HSP is self-limiting; warning features change management entirely
Steroids do not prevent or treat nephritis - biopsy guides immunosuppression
Hypertension above the 95th centile for age and height needs immediate attention
explanation.pearls: HSP with proteinuria above 2+, hypertension above the 95th centile, or rising creatinine warrants paediatric nephrology referral within 24 hours for biopsy planning.

subtopic_detail: Pre-transfer benzylpenicillin in suspected meningococcal sepsis
stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to a rural emergency department by his parents after waking unwell with fever, irritability, and a rash that began 90 minutes before arrival. The parents describe him as 'floppy' and unwilling to be put down.

On examination he is mottled, with pulse 180, blood pressure 72 by 40 mmHg, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill at the sternum is 5 seconds. There are non-blanching purple spots over the lower limbs and trunk, expanding under observation. He does not have neck stiffness and is rousable but drowsy. Intravenous access has failed twice. The nearest paediatric retrieval team estimates 75 minutes to arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 180, BP 72/40, RR 44, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: mottled, CRT 5 sec, non-blanching purpuric rash expanding under observation, drowsy but rousable
data_table.Investigations: no peripheral IV access after two attempts; venous lactate from initial draw 6.2 mmol/L (<2.0)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next action while preparing intraosseous access?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until blood cultures can be obtained via the IO line
options.rationale: Delaying antibiotics for cultures in suspected meningococcal disease worsens mortality. Cultures are taken at the same time as IO access but never gate the first antibiotic dose. (Source: CDNA Invasive Meningococcal Disease Guideline)

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg before any antibiotic dose
options.rationale: Adjunctive dexamethasone in paediatric meningitis is given with or just before the first antibiotic dose, not as a standalone first move, and the antibiotic remains the time-critical intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give intramuscular benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg into the lateral thigh now
options.rationale: When IV access is delayed in suspected meningococcal sepsis, the CDNA guideline and Therapeutic Guidelines explicitly endorse intramuscular benzylpenicillin immediately while access is being secured. Pre-transfer antibiotics reduce mortality. (Source: CDNA Invasive Meningococcal Disease Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Defer all antibiotics until paediatric retrieval team arrival in 75 minutes
options.rationale: Each hour of antibiotic delay in invasive meningococcal disease increases mortality. CDNA mandates antibiotic administration at the point of suspicion, never withheld for retrieval. (Source: CDNA Invasive Meningococcal Disease Guideline)

options.text: Attempt a third peripheral cannula for fluid resuscitation before any antibiotic
options.rationale: Repeated peripheral attempts after two failures waste time. The RCH paediatric sepsis pathway calls for intraosseous access after failed IV and intramuscular antibiotics if even IO is delayed. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

explanation.summary: Pre-transfer antibiotics for suspected meningococcal disease save lives. CDNA and Therapeutic Guidelines both endorse intramuscular benzylpenicillin (50 to 60 mg/kg to a maximum of 1.2 g) into the lateral thigh when IV access is delayed. Cultures and adjunctive corticosteroids do not gate the first dose. Intraosseous access remains the fastest reliable route for fluids and ongoing antibiotic infusions when IV attempts fail, but should not delay an IM dose if IO insertion itself is taking time.
key_points: IM benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg is endorsed when IV/IO access is delayed
Cultures and dexamethasone never gate the first antibiotic dose
RCH paediatric sepsis pathway: IV/IO access then cultures then antibiotic within the hour
Each hour of antibiotic delay measurably increases meningococcal mortality
explanation.pearls: When IV access is delayed in suspected meningococcal sepsis, give IM benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg (max 1.2 g) into the lateral thigh while IO insertion proceeds in parallel.

subtopic_detail: Fluid resuscitation in paediatric DKA with shock
stem:
A 9-year-old girl with no past medical history is brought in by ambulance with two weeks of polyuria and polydipsia followed by 24 hours of vomiting and abdominal pain. The paramedics report she has become progressively more drowsy in the past hour.

In the resuscitation bay she has pulse 144, blood pressure 86 by 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 with Kussmaul pattern, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill at the sternum is 4 seconds and peripheries are cool. GCS is 13 (E3 V4 M6). Bedside blood glucose is 32 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), beta-hydroxybutyrate is 5.8 mmol/L (<0.6), venous pH 7.05 and bicarbonate 6 mmol/L (22-32). She weighs 28 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 144, BP 86/48, RR 38 with Kussmaul breathing, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: drowsy GCS 13, cool peripheries, CRT 4 sec at sternum, dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: BSL 32 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.8 mmol/L (<0.6), pH 7.05, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L (22-32), Na 132, K 5.1, weight 28 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid bolus?

options.text: Insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/h commenced immediately with no fluid bolus
options.rationale: Insulin in DKA must follow at least one fluid bolus, and is typically delayed 1 to 2 hours after fluid restoration begins. Starting insulin before fluid resuscitation precipitates cardiovascular collapse and worsens cerebral oedema risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

options.text: 20 mL/kg of 0.9 percent sodium chloride over 5 to 10 minutes, then reassess
options.rationale: Standard septic-shock bolus volumes in DKA are linked to cerebral oedema and worsened neurological outcomes. RCH and ISPAD explicitly halve the bolus in this context. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis; ISPAD 2022)

options.text: 20 mL/kg of compound sodium lactate over 5 to 10 minutes, then reassess
options.rationale: Hartmann's solution is acceptable as maintenance fluid in DKA but the bolus rate is the live problem here. A 20 mL/kg rapid bolus carries the same cerebral-oedema risk regardless of crystalloid choice. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022)

options.text: 10 mL/kg of 0.9 percent sodium chloride over 30 minutes, then reassess
options.rationale: RCH and ISPAD specify cautious 10 mL/kg boluses over 30 to 60 minutes in DKA with circulatory compromise, to limit the cerebral-oedema risk that rapid fluid shifts trigger. Reassess after each bolus rather than running standard sepsis volumes. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis; ISPAD 2022)

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 60 minutes to correct severe acidosis
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is contraindicated in routine paediatric DKA because it worsens cerebral oedema, paradoxical CNS acidosis, and hypokalaemia. It is not part of any current RCH or ISPAD pathway. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA with circulatory compromise sits in a deliberately separate fluid-resuscitation pathway. RCH and ISPAD specify 10 mL/kg boluses of 0.9 percent saline over 30 to 60 minutes, with reassessment after each bolus, instead of the 20 mL/kg over 5 to 10 minutes used in septic shock. The reason is cerebral oedema, the leading cause of paediatric DKA mortality, which is precipitated by rapid osmotic shifts. Insulin is delayed at least 1 hour after fluid commencement and bicarbonate is contraindicated.
key_points: DKA shock bolus: 10 mL/kg over 30 to 60 minutes (NOT 20 mL/kg over 5 to 10 min)
Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of paediatric DKA mortality
Insulin starts at least 1 hour after fluid resuscitation begins
Bicarbonate is contraindicated in routine paediatric DKA
explanation.pearls: In paediatric DKA with shock, give 10 mL/kg of saline over 30 to 60 minutes (not the standard 20 mL/kg over 5 to 10 minutes used in septic shock) to limit cerebral-oedema risk.

subtopic_detail: Classical galactosaemia in the septic neonate
stem:
A 9-day-old infant born at term to consanguineous parents is admitted with 24 hours of poor feeding, lethargy, and progressive jaundice. Antenatal screening was unremarkable and the newborn screening sample was sent on day 3 but results are not yet back.

On examination he is jaundiced, hypotonic, with pulse 180, respiratory rate 60, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees Celsius. The liver is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. Red-reflex examination at the cot reveals reduced reflex bilaterally with a grey haze.

Investigations: conjugated bilirubin 80 micromol/L (<5), ALT 220 U/L (<40), INR 2.1 (0.8-1.2), bedside glucose 1.8 mmol/L (3.0-6.0), blood culture preliminary growth of Gram-negative rods (later confirmed Escherichia coli), urine reducing substances strongly positive.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 180, RR 60, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 38.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: jaundiced, hypotonic, hepatomegaly 4 cm, bilateral reduced red reflex with grey haze
data_table.Investigations: conjugated bilirubin 80 micromol/L (<5), ALT 220 U/L (<40), INR 2.1 (0.8-1.2), glucose 1.8 mmol/L (3.0-6.0), blood culture Gram-negative rods (E. coli), urine reducing substances positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate combination of actions?

options.text: IV cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin, continue expressed breast milk feeds
options.rationale: Although the antibiotic regimen is correct for neonatal sepsis, continuing lactose-containing feeds will perpetuate galactose-1-phosphate accumulation, deepen the encephalopathy, and worsen the liver injury. The feeds must change at the same time. (Source: RCH CPG: Inherited metabolic disorders)

options.text: IV cefotaxime plus amoxicillin and switch to hydrolysed-protein cow's milk formula
options.rationale: Hydrolysed cow's milk formula still contains lactose and does not solve the galactose problem. Amoxicillin alone does not cover all relevant Gram-negative sepsis pathogens; benzylpenicillin plus cefotaxime is the standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; RCH CPG: Inherited metabolic disorders)

options.text: Continue routine feeds and await newborn screening results before changing formula
options.rationale: Newborn screening reports may take days to weeks; in classical galactosaemia, ongoing galactose exposure causes irreversible cataracts, liver failure, and brain injury during that window. Empirical feed change is mandatory once the diagnosis is suspected. (Source: RCH CPG: Inherited metabolic disorders)

options.text: Phototherapy and IV cefotaxime, defer feed change pending GALT enzyme result
options.rationale: Phototherapy addresses unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, not the conjugated picture seen here, and does not address galactose exposure. Awaiting GALT enzyme assay before changing feeds delays the only modifiable cause of ongoing injury. (Source: RCH CPG: Inherited metabolic disorders)

options.text: Stop feeds, IV dextrose-saline plus cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin, switch to soy formula
options.rationale: Suspected classical galactosaemia (E. coli sepsis, conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, hypoglycaemia, cataracts, positive urinary reducing substances) demands immediate removal of lactose and galactose while sepsis is treated and metabolic confirmation is sought. (Source: RCH CPG: Inherited metabolic disorders; Australasian Society for Inborn Errors of Metabolism)
source_refs: Australasian Society for Inborn Errors of Metabolism

explanation.summary: Classical galactosaemia (GALT deficiency) presents in the first two weeks of life with E. coli sepsis (a near-pathognomonic association), conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, hepatomegaly, coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia, and bilateral cataracts. Urinary reducing substances are positive while the glucose oxidase strip is negative. Treatment is dual: aggressive treatment of sepsis with standard neonatal cover (IV cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin) AND immediate removal of dietary galactose by switching to a soy-based formula while definitive GALT enzyme assay is processed. Delay in either limb causes irreversible injury.
key_points: Galactosaemia neonate presents with E. coli sepsis, jaundice, hepatomegaly, hypoglycaemia, cataracts
Urine reducing substances positive while glucose oxidase strip negative is the bedside clue
Treat sepsis AND remove dietary galactose simultaneously - both are time-critical
Soy-based formula is the Australian standard substitute
explanation.pearls: Suspect classical galactosaemia in any neonate with E. coli sepsis plus jaundice plus hypoglycaemia plus positive urinary reducing substances; switch immediately to soy-based formula while awaiting GALT enzyme assay.

sources.label: Australasian Society for Inborn Errors of Metabolism

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after eating a peanut butter sandwich at a birthday party. His parents say his lips swelled, he developed a widespread itchy rash, and he started coughing and saying his throat felt funny on the drive in. He has a known peanut allergy and carries an EpiPen Jr at preschool, but it was not used at the party.

On arrival he is tachypnoeic with audible wheeze and is anxious but answering questions. There is no stridor and no drooling. His weight on the resus chart is 18 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 86/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 /min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: diffuse urticaria over trunk and face, periorbital and lip swelling, bilateral expiratory wheeze, chest moving symmetrically, no stridor
data_table.Investigations: clinical diagnosis, no bloods drawn yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate adrenaline dose and route?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 150 micrograms (0.15 mL of 1 in 1000) into the anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: An 18 kg child falls within the ASCIA 10 to 20 kg band, which prescribes 150 micrograms IM (EpiPen Jr equivalent) into the mid anterolateral thigh. The banded table is the AU standard and avoids the dosing errors that occur with weight-based calculation in a stressed resus. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 300 micrograms (0.3 mL of 1 in 1000) into the anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: 300 micrograms is the ASCIA dose for the 20 kg and above band. At 18 kg this is twice the indicated dose and risks tachyarrhythmia and hypertension. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline 18 micrograms (1.8 mL of 1 in 100 000) as a slow bolus
options.rationale: IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after two IM doses have failed and must be given as a diluted infusion with cardiac monitoring. First-line is always IM into the anterolateral thigh. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: Subcutaneous adrenaline 180 micrograms (0.18 mL of 1 in 1000) at 10 micrograms per kg
options.rationale: Subcutaneous absorption is slower and less reliable than IM in shock. ASCIA explicitly recommends IM (not subcut) in the anterolateral thigh. Weight-based 10 microgram per kg arithmetic is also not the ASCIA standard. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 via face mask with high-flow oxygen
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema in croup, not systemic anaphylaxis. It does not address hypotension, shock, or peripheral vasodilation and delays definitive IM dosing. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines; RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

explanation.summary: ASCIA anaphylaxis dosing uses a banded age and weight table rather than per kg arithmetic to reduce dosing errors during resuscitation. The 10 to 20 kg band receives 150 micrograms IM (the EpiPen Jr dose); the 20 kg and above band receives 300 micrograms IM (the standard EpiPen dose). All children with airway, breathing, or circulatory features get IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh as the first action, before fluids or steroids. Repeat at 5 minutes if no improvement; consider IV infusion after two failed IM doses.
key_points: ASCIA uses a banded IM dose table: 10 to 20 kg gets 150 micrograms, 20 kg and above gets 300 micrograms
Anterolateral thigh IM is faster and more reliable than subcutaneous or deltoid injection
IV adrenaline is third-line and only after two failed IM doses, as a diluted infusion with monitoring
Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway obstruction, not systemic anaphylaxis
explanation.pearls: ASCIA IM adrenaline by band: 10 to 20 kg gets 150 micrograms (EpiPen Jr); 20 kg and above gets 300 micrograms (EpiPen). Repeat IM at 5 minutes if no improvement before escalating to an IV infusion.

sources.label: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

stem:
A 3-year-old girl is brought to a regional emergency department with three days of fever and one day of lethargy and reduced oral intake. Her parents say she has been wetting fewer nappies and is harder to rouse this afternoon.

She responds to voice but is mottled to the knees. Capillary refill is 4 seconds centrally. Her weight is 14 kg. Peripheral access is being attempted; the paediatric registrar is at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 78/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: mottled peripheries, prolonged central capillary refill, dry mucous membranes, no rash, soft abdomen, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: venous gas lactate 4.2 mmol/L; FBC, UEC, blood cultures pending

lead_in: After IV access is obtained, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Take blood cultures then give IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg, then a 20 mL/kg saline bolus
options.rationale: The RCH paediatric sepsis pathway sequences IV/IO access first, then blood cultures, then the first antibiotic dose within the hour, then a 20 mL/kg saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes (repeat to 60 mL/kg). Cultures are taken before antibiotics only if it does not delay them. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg saline bolus, then blood cultures, then IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg
options.rationale: Although fluids and antibiotics both belong in the first hour, RCH places the first antibiotic dose immediately after cultures and before the fluid bolus where access permits. Delaying antibiotics for a bolus worsens mortality in septic shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.text: Start a peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.05 micrograms per kg per minute now
options.rationale: Inotropes are reserved for fluid-refractory shock (no improvement after 40 to 60 mL/kg). Starting adrenaline before any fluid is given inverts the RCH and ANZICS paediatric sepsis pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.text: Give IV hydrocortisone 2 mg/kg as the priority before antibiotics or fluids
options.rationale: Stress-dose steroids are considered only in catecholamine-refractory shock or known adrenal insufficiency. Empiric steroids are not first-line and delay the source-directed antibiotic. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.text: Give a 10 mL/kg saline bolus over 10 minutes and reassess before any antibiotic
options.rationale: A 10 mL/kg bolus is the RCH starting volume for DKA and for neonates with suspected cardiac disease, not for paediatric septic shock. Antibiotics must not wait for the bolus to complete. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

explanation.summary: The RCH paediatric sepsis pathway runs as a sequenced first-hour bundle: recognise sepsis, secure IV/IO access, draw blood cultures, give the first IV antibiotic within the hour, and start 20 mL/kg saline boluses over 5 to 10 minutes up to 60 mL/kg. Inotropes follow fluid-refractory shock. The order matters because each step has an independent mortality signal and antibiotics should not be held for cultures if access is difficult.
key_points: Order: IV access, cultures, antibiotics, then 20 mL/kg saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes
Up to 60 mL/kg of crystalloid before declaring fluid-refractory shock and starting inotropes
10 mL/kg is the DKA and neonatal-cardiac starting bolus, not the septic shock bolus
Antibiotics within the first hour of recognition; do not delay for cultures if access is hard
explanation.pearls: RCH paediatric sepsis: 20 mL/kg saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes (up to 60 mL/kg total), first IV antibiotic within the hour, inotropes only after fluid-refractory shock. Do not delay antibiotics for cultures if access is difficult.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

stem:
A 2-year-old girl has had two days of profuse non-bloody diarrhoea and intermittent vomiting after her older brother had a similar illness. She has had small sips of water from a bottle but has refused her usual oral rehydration sachets, vomiting them back within minutes. Her parents brought her to the emergency department this afternoon because her nappies have been dry for 8 hours.

She is alert and miserable but consolable. Mucous membranes are dry. Skin turgor is reduced but capillary refill remains 2 seconds. She is estimated at 7% dehydrated. Weight is 12 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 142 /min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, capillary refill 2 seconds, sunken eyes, no peritonism, no rash
data_table.Investigations: stool PCR pending; UEC not yet drawn

lead_in: After a single dose of oral ondansetron 2 mg, she vomits her next ORS attempt. What is the most appropriate next rehydration strategy?

options.text: Continued oral ORS in 5 mL aliquots every 5 minutes for a further 4 hours
options.rationale: Two failed oral trials with ondansetron cover indicate that oral rehydration is not succeeding. Persisting risks ongoing losses outpacing intake; RCH directs a route change at this point. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride at 100 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance fluids
options.rationale: IV is reserved by RCH for severe dehydration, shock, persistent vomiting despite NGT, or electrolyte derangement that needs correction. Jumping to IV bypasses the safer first-line route. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Nasogastric rehydration with oral rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours
options.rationale: RCH lists NGT rehydration as first-line for mild to moderate dehydration that fails oral trials. Rapid NGT rehydration (typically 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours) avoids IV cannulation, preserves gut integrity, and has lower complication rates than IV in head-to-head studies. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Single 20 mL/kg saline bolus and admission for repeat dose oral ondansetron only
options.rationale: A bolus alone does not address ongoing rehydration needs over 4 hours and ondansetron is a single-dose adjunct in RCH, not a repeated antiemetic. The plan misses the actual rehydration step. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Subcutaneous hyaluronidase-assisted rehydration with normal saline over 6 hours
options.rationale: Hypodermoclysis is occasionally used in palliative and aged care settings; it is not a paediatric gastroenteritis option in the RCH cascade. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: The RCH gastroenteritis pathway places NGT rehydration above IV for mild to moderate dehydration that fails oral trials. NGT delivers ORS at 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours, with electrolyte and weight checks, and is associated with lower rates of phlebitis and shorter inpatient stays than IV. IV is for severe dehydration, shock, or NGT failure. A single dose of oral ondansetron (banded by weight) is the only RCH-supported antiemetic.
key_points: NGT rehydration is RCH first-line for mild to moderate dehydration after failed oral trials
Typical NGT rate: 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours of ORS
IV is for severe dehydration, shock, or NGT failure
Ondansetron is single-dose by weight band: 2 mg for under 15 kg, 4 mg for 15 to 30 kg
explanation.pearls: RCH gastroenteritis: NGT rehydration first-line for failed oral, ORS at 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours. Single dose ondansetron 2 mg for under 15 kg, 4 mg for 15 to 30 kg. IV only for severe dehydration, shock, or NGT failure.

stem:
A 5-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department in the late evening with a rectal temperature of 38.4 degrees Celsius measured at home and confirmed on arrival. He was born at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery, breastfed, and previously well. He has had reduced feeds today and one episode of vomiting; the bottle volumes have dropped from 90 mL to 50 mL over three feeds.

He is alert in the cot but his cry is high-pitched when handled. The anterior fontanelle is soft and flat. There is no rash. The urine dipstick from a clean catch is negative for leukocytes and nitrites. A chest film is clear. He has received his 6-week immunisations 36 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 76/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 56 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: high-pitched cry, soft fontanelle, no neck stiffness possible to assess in a 5-week-old, peripheries warm, no purpura
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 14.8 x10^9/L, CRP 22 mg/L (less than 5), urine dipstick negative, chest film clear, blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Procalcitonin level and discharge if below 0.5 micrograms per litre
options.rationale: Procalcitonin can refine risk in 1 to 3 month infants alongside other parameters but cannot exclude meningitis in an unwell appearing 5-week-old. RCH does not endorse single-marker rule out at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Reassure that post-immunisation fever within 48 hours requires no further workup
options.rationale: Post-immunisation fever can occur but RCH explicitly does NOT use the timing as an exclusion criterion for sepsis workup in an infant under 3 months. Clinical features here (high-pitched cry, reduced feeds, raised CRP) demand the full workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Catheter urine specimen for culture and discharge home with safety netting
options.rationale: A catheter urine specimen is part of the full septic screen but is not sufficient alone. RCH requires blood cultures and an LP added on top in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Lumbar puncture for CSF cell count, protein, glucose, gram stain, culture, and HSV PCR
options.rationale: RCH directs a full septic workup including lumbar puncture for any febrile infant under 4 weeks, and strongly recommends it under 3 months when the infant is unwell, has a high-pitched cry, or has a CRP raised above local thresholds. Recent immunisation does not exclude bacterial sepsis at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle to exclude intracranial infection
options.rationale: Cranial ultrasound is used for haemorrhage and hydrocephalus screening, not for diagnosing CNS infection. CSF analysis remains the diagnostic test. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

explanation.summary: Febrile infants under 3 months are at substantially higher risk of invasive bacterial infection and meningitis than older children. RCH mandates a full septic workup (blood culture, urine catheter specimen, FBC, CRP, and lumbar puncture) for any febrile infant under 4 weeks and for unwell-appearing infants between 1 and 3 months. Empiric IV cefotaxime (or per local pathway) is started after specimens are taken. Recent immunisation is NOT a reason to defer the workup at this age.
key_points: Under 4 weeks: full septic workup including LP regardless of appearance
1 to 3 months: full workup if unwell appearing or raised inflammatory markers
Post-immunisation fever does not exclude sepsis in this age group
Empiric cefotaxime after specimens; ampicillin added if under 4 weeks for Listeria cover
explanation.pearls: Under 3 months febrile: full septic workup including LP if unwell or raised CRP. Empiric IV cefotaxime; add ampicillin if under 4 weeks. Post-immunisation timing does not exempt from workup.

stem:
A 9-month-old boy is brought in by his mother with episodes where he suddenly starts screaming, draws his legs up toward his tummy, and looks pale; between episodes he is settled and breastfeeds normally. The episodes started 14 hours ago and are now every 20 minutes. He passed a smear of dark mucousy stool with a streak of blood in his nappy two hours ago.

On examination during a quiet phase, his abdomen is soft. There is a vague fullness in the right upper quadrant. He is alert and well perfused with normal capillary refill. There is no peritonism and no abdominal distension.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 142 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: intermittent inconsolable distress with leg drawing, vague RUQ fullness between episodes, soft abdomen, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: ultrasound abdomen: target lesion in the right upper quadrant with a 3 cm diameter; no free fluid; no pneumoperitoneum on supine abdominal film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial of conservative management with bowel rest and observation for 24 hours
options.rationale: Untreated intussusception progresses to bowel ischaemia, perforation, and shock. Conservative observation is not a valid strategy once the diagnosis is confirmed on ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Immediate laparotomy for manual reduction by the paediatric surgical team
options.rationale: Surgery is the next step only after failed enema reduction, peritonism, perforation, or a pathological lead point on imaging. Going directly to laparotomy in a stable child with a successfully imaged target lesion exposes the child to an unnecessary operation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: IV access and pneumatic reduction under fluoroscopy by paediatric radiology
options.rationale: Stable ileocolic intussusception without peritonism or perforation is treated by air (pneumatic) enema reduction. RCH and the Royal Australasian College of Surgeons paediatric guidance prefer pneumatic over hydrostatic in most centres given higher reduction rates and lower contamination risk. Surgery is reserved for failed enema, peritonism, or perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Repeat ultrasound in 6 hours to confirm the lesion before any intervention
options.rationale: The target lesion on ultrasound is already diagnostic. Delay introduces ischaemia risk and is not RCH practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Barium contrast enema for combined diagnosis and hydrostatic reduction
options.rationale: Barium has been replaced by air or water-soluble contrast because of peritoneal contamination risk if perforation occurs. The diagnosis is already established; the question is reduction modality. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception classically presents in 3 to 36 month olds with paroxysmal inconsolable crying with leg drawing, pallor, and later redcurrant-jelly stool. Ultrasound shows a target or doughnut lesion and is diagnostic. Treatment of stable cases is pneumatic (air) enema reduction by an experienced paediatric radiologist with surgical backup. Indications for surgery are failed enema reduction, peritonism, perforation, or a pathological lead point.
key_points: Ultrasound target lesion is diagnostic in 3 to 36 month olds with intermittent distress
Pneumatic (air) enema is preferred over hydrostatic; barium is obsolete
Surgery for failed enema, peritonism, perforation, or pathological lead point
IV access and fluid status should be optimised before enema reduction
explanation.pearls: Stable ileocolic intussusception: pneumatic enema reduction under fluoroscopy by a paediatric radiologist. Surgery only for failed enema, peritonism, perforation, or pathological lead point.

stem:
A 4-year-old previously well girl is brought to her general practitioner with widespread bruising and a petechial rash on her shins and palate that her mother first noticed three days ago after a viral illness two weeks before. She has had no nosebleeds, no menorrhagia obviously not applicable, no haematuria, and is eating and playing normally. Her parents are anxious about cancer.

On examination she is well perfused. There is no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, and no joint swelling. Bruising is scattered without a distribution suggesting trauma. Mucosal bleeding is limited to a few petechiae on the soft palate.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits for age
data_table.Examination: scattered cutaneous bruising, palatal petechiae, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no bony tenderness
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 122 g/L (110 to 140); WCC 7.6 x10^9/L with normal differential; platelets 14 x10^9/L (150 to 400); film: isolated thrombocytopenia, no blasts, normal red cells

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine before any management decision
options.rationale: Routine marrow examination is not required in classic acute ITP with a clean film and isolated thrombocytopenia. It is reserved for atypical features, treatment failure, or before steroids in some centres. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric ITP Guidelines)

options.text: IV immunoglobulin 0.8 g/kg as a single dose with paracetamol pre-medication
options.rationale: IVIG is reserved by HSANZ for active mucosal or visceral bleeding or for raising the count quickly before a procedure. Skin and minor palatal petechiae alone do not justify it. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric ITP Guidelines)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg per day for 14 days followed by a taper
options.rationale: Corticosteroids work in ITP but masking a missed leukaemia would delay diagnosis if the film were not first carefully reviewed. With a clean film, steroids may still be used for mucosal bleeding; cutaneous-only disease does not need them. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric ITP Guidelines)

options.text: Watchful waiting with safety advice, no medication, and clinic review in one week
options.rationale: First-episode acute ITP in a well child with cutaneous bleeding only is managed with observation under the HSANZ and Australian and New Zealand Childhood Haematology Oncology Group consensus. Most resolve within weeks. Treatment is reserved for active mucosal or major bleeding, not for the platelet count alone. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric ITP Guidelines)

options.text: Platelet transfusion 10 mL/kg to raise the count above 50 x10^9/L
options.rationale: Platelet transfusions are ineffective in ITP because the antibody clears infused platelets and are reserved for life-threatening bleeding only. They are not a count-raising intervention here. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric ITP Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute ITP in a well child after a viral prodrome with isolated thrombocytopenia, a clean film, no lymphadenopathy, and no organomegaly is managed by observation alone irrespective of the count if bleeding is cutaneous or minor mucosal. Most resolve within 6 weeks. IVIG, anti-D, or steroids are reserved for active mucosal, gastrointestinal, intracranial, or other significant bleeding, or to raise the count rapidly before a procedure. Platelet transfusions are ineffective due to antibody-mediated clearance and reserved for life-threatening bleeding.
key_points: Watchful waiting is HSANZ first-line in well children with cutaneous bleeding only
Treatment is driven by bleeding severity, not by the absolute platelet count
IVIG, anti-D, or corticosteroids for active mucosal or major bleeding
Routine marrow examination is not required in classic acute ITP with a clean film
explanation.pearls: Paediatric ITP: cutaneous-only bleeding is observed; IVIG 0.8 g/kg or prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for active mucosal bleeding. Platelet transfusions are reserved for life-threatening bleeding only.

stem:
A 5-week-old infant born at 37 weeks presents to the emergency department with 3 days of coryza, worsening work of breathing, and feeding at about a third of normal volume. The parents report fewer wet nappies in the last 12 hours and a quiet, less interactive baby.

On arrival he is alert but irritable with audible wheeze and moderate subcostal and intercostal recessions. There is no apnoea witnessed in the cubicle. Bedside viral PCR is positive for RSV. Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation only.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 78/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 70 /min, SpO2 88% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert but irritable, subcostal and intercostal recessions, audible wheeze with widespread fine crackles, capillary refill 2 seconds, anterior fontanelle slightly sunken
data_table.Investigations: RSV PCR positive, chest x-ray hyperinflated lungs with no focal consolidation, venous blood gas pH 7.34 pCO2 48 mmHg HCO3 24 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial respiratory support?

options.text: Commence low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and titrate to maintain SpO2 at or above 90 percent
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance directs low-flow nasal prong oxygen (typically 1 to 2 L/min) as the first respiratory support with an SpO2 target of 90 percent or above. High-flow is reserved for failure of low-flow after a defined trial. Starting low-flow first prevents premature escalation and the associated nursing acuity. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 92 to 94 percent
options.rationale: High-flow nasal cannula is reserved for infants who fail low-flow oxygen after 1 to 2 hours of trial or who are showing severe respiratory distress. The SpO2 target in RCH guidance is 90 percent and above, not 92 to 94 percent, so starting at HFNC with a tighter target overshoots the cascade. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Administer nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with ipratropium bromide 250 micrograms and reassess in 20 minutes
options.rationale: Inhaled bronchodilators are not recommended in bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months because the wheeze is from airway oedema and debris, not bronchospasm. Trials show no clinically meaningful improvement and risk of tachycardia masking deterioration. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Give nebulised 3 percent hypertonic saline 4 mL and reassess respiratory effort in 1 hour
options.rationale: Nebulised hypertonic saline is not recommended in RCH guidance for routine bronchiolitis management; the limited evidence does not support meaningful reduction in admission length, and it can trigger bronchospasm. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Give oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg once daily for 3 days and observe in short-stay unit
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are not indicated in bronchiolitis. Cochrane and RCH guidance both find no benefit on admission rate or length of stay, and there is concern about prolonged viral shedding. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Initial oxygen support in moderate bronchiolitis is low-flow nasal prong oxygen titrated to SpO2 90 percent or above, with high-flow reserved for failure of low-flow after a trial period. Bronchodilators, hypertonic saline, and corticosteroids do not change outcomes in typical bronchiolitis under 12 months. The candidate must resist defaulting to the most resource-intensive option early.
key_points: RCH SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is at or above 90 percent, not 92 to 94 percent.
Low-flow oxygen first, HFNC after 1 to 2 hours of failed low-flow.
No role for salbutamol or ipratropium under 12 months in bronchiolitis.
Steroids and hypertonic saline are not recommended.
explanation.pearls: Low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min titrated to SpO2 at or above 90 percent is first-line in bronchiolitis under RCH CPG; reassess at 1 to 2 hours before escalating to HFNC.

sources.label: Cochrane review of bronchodilators in bronchiolitis

stem:
A 2-year-old girl presents to the emergency department at 23:00 with 36 hours of coryza, fever, and a brassy nocturnal cough. Her parents say she has had stridor only when she gets upset and woke her up tonight.

In triage she is settled on her father's lap. There is occasional inspiratory stridor at rest with mild suprasternal retractions, no drooling, and no tripod posture. She tracks faces and is engaged with the toys offered. Air entry is good bilaterally with no wheeze. She has had one previous mild croup episode aged 18 months that settled with no specific treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: well perfused, mild suprasternal recession, occasional stridor at rest, good air entry both sides, no drooling, normal voice with brassy cough, normal mental state
data_table.Investigations: clinical diagnosis, no imaging or bloods indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose with discharge planning after a period of observation
options.rationale: RCH CPG categorises this as moderate croup (stridor at rest with mild recessions, no other severity features). The recommended dose is dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally for mild or moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup. Onset is within 1 to 2 hours, and most moderate cases can be discharged after observation. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single dose with discharge planning after a period of observation
options.rationale: 0.6 mg/kg is the dose for severe croup with marked recessions, tracheal tug, agitation or cyanosis. Using it for moderate croup over-treats and adds no incremental clinical benefit; RCH recommends the 0.15 mg/kg dose for mild and moderate disease. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with mandatory 4-hour observation in short-stay unit
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is for severe croup or moderate croup not responding to dexamethasone after 30 minutes of observation. Giving it first-line in a child who is stable with mild recessions exposes her to rebound and obliges unnecessary admission. RCH minimum post-adrenaline observation is 3 hours, not 4. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose with discharge planning after a period of observation
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide has equivalent efficacy to oral dexamethasone in some trials but is more expensive and harder to deliver to an upset toddler. RCH recommends oral dexamethasone as preferred first-line. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Salbutamol 600 micrograms via spacer with 4 puffs every 20 minutes for 1 hour and reassess
options.rationale: Salbutamol treats lower airway bronchospasm, not the subglottic oedema of croup. Stridor that does not change with salbutamol is the textbook finding. Using it here delays effective steroid therapy. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

explanation.summary: Moderate croup in the RCH classification (stridor at rest, mild to moderate recessions, no agitation or cyanosis) is treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg. The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup. Nebulised adrenaline is added if severe or if moderate disease does not respond after 30 minutes of observation following steroid.
key_points: RCH dexamethasone dose is 0.15 mg/kg for mild and moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg only for severe.
Post-nebulised-adrenaline observation is at least 3 hours.
Nebulised adrenaline dose is 5 mL of 1 in 1000 (a flat dose, not weight-based).
Salbutamol has no role in croup.
explanation.pearls: Use dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally for mild and moderate croup per RCH CPG; reserve 0.6 mg/kg for severe disease where adrenaline is also given.

subtopic_detail: Severe asthma exacerbation refractory to inhaled therapy
stem:
An 8-year-old girl with a background of moderate persistent asthma on daily fluticasone presents to the emergency department with progressive shortness of breath despite three salbutamol pMDI doses at home over the last hour. Her mother says she has needed her reliever six times today.

After triage she has been given continuous nebulised salbutamol 0.5 percent for 1 hour, nebulised ipratropium 250 micrograms three doses, and oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg. After 60 minutes she remains tachypnoeic, can only speak in short phrases, and SpO2 has improved from 86 to 91 percent on 6 L/min oxygen by mask. She is alert and cooperative. There are no features of impending respiratory arrest.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 /min, SpO2 91% on 6 L/min via face mask, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: tripoding, marked subcostal and intercostal recessions, prolonged expiratory phase with bilateral wheeze, no silent chest, able to speak in 3-word phrases
data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.32 pCO2 46 mmHg HCO3 23 mmol/L (24-32), peak flow not assessable, chest x-ray hyperinflation with no pneumothorax

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous aminophylline 5 mg/kg loading dose over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Aminophylline is reserved for asthma not responding to magnesium and salbutamol infusion. It has a narrow therapeutic window and significant cardiac and CNS toxicity, so it sits later in the cascade. (Source: RCH CPG Asthma acute)

options.text: Intravenous salbutamol 5 micrograms/kg bolus over 5 minutes followed by infusion at 1 microgram/kg/min
options.rationale: IV salbutamol is an option after IV magnesium has been trialled or when magnesium is unavailable or contraindicated. It carries higher risks of hypokalaemia and arrhythmia, so the cascade recommends magnesium first. (Source: RCH CPG Asthma acute)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) infusion over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: After failure of maximal inhaled therapy and systemic corticosteroid in severe acute asthma, IV magnesium sulfate is the next-line bronchodilator in the AU paediatric pathway. Dose is 50 mg/kg up to 2 g over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring. Evidence supports reduction in admission and need for ventilation. (Source: RCH CPG Asthma acute)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg of 1 in 1000 into the anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: IM adrenaline is reserved for severe asthma with impending respiratory arrest or where IV access is not yet established. The child has IV access already and is not in arrest. (Source: RCH CPG Asthma acute)

options.text: Intubate and commence pressure-controlled ventilation with permissive hypercapnia
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for impending respiratory arrest (silent chest, exhaustion, falling GCS, marked acidosis). The child is alert, cooperative, and improving on inhaled therapy. Premature intubation in severe asthma worsens outcomes. (Source: RCH CPG Asthma acute)

explanation.summary: Severe acute asthma not responding to continuous bronchodilator, ipratropium, and systemic steroid escalates to IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg up to 2 g over 20 minutes. IV salbutamol and aminophylline are subsequent rungs of the ladder. Intubation is reserved for impending arrest features which are absent here.
key_points: IV magnesium dose in paediatric severe asthma: 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes.
Order: continuous salbutamol + ipratropium + oral steroid -> IV magnesium -> IV salbutamol -> IV aminophylline.
Silent chest, exhaustion, falling GCS = impending arrest, intubate.
IM adrenaline only if no IV access or impending arrest.
explanation.pearls: When inhaled therapy plus oral prednisolone fails in paediatric severe asthma, the next step is IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg up to 2 g over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring; IV salbutamol and aminophylline follow.

subtopic_detail: RCH UTI imaging cascade after first typical UTI
stem:
An 18-month-old previously well girl is reviewed in the paediatric outpatient clinic two weeks after her first ever urinary tract infection. The infection was treated with 7 days of trimethoprim. She had fever to 38.6 degrees Celsius for 48 hours, responded clinically by hour 36 of antibiotics, and was systemically well at discharge from the short-stay unit.

MSU at presentation grew Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim. Her antenatal renal ultrasound at 20 weeks was normal. She has had a healthy growth trajectory and is fully toilet trained. Examination today is normal.

data_table.Examination: growing along the 50th centile for weight and height, abdomen soft and non-tender, no flank tenderness, no palpable bladder, external genitalia normal
data_table.Investigations: MSU at presentation grew E coli with sensitivities to trimethoprim and cefalexin, no current symptoms or repeat MSU performed, prior antenatal anomaly scan reported normal kidneys bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange a micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) within 4 to 6 weeks to screen for vesicoureteric reflux of any grade
options.rationale: MCUG is invasive, involves bladder catheterisation and significant radiation, and is not recommended after a single typical UTI in RCH guidance. It is also outside the RCH cascade as DMSA is. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

options.text: Arrange a renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks to screen for structural anomalies and post-infective changes
options.rationale: Routine renal ultrasound after a single typical UTI is not in the RCH cascade for children over 6 months who had a clinical response and a normal antenatal scan. Imaging here would only be indicated if features of atypical UTI (poor response to 48 hours of antibiotics, non-E coli organism, sepsis, abdominal mass, or raised creatinine) were present. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

options.text: Arrange a dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) scan in 4 to 6 months to look for cortical defects and renal scarring
options.rationale: DMSA and MCUG are not in the RCH UTI imaging cascade for paediatric AU practice. They are derived from NICE pathways; following RCH consistently is preferred over mixing AU and UK protocols. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

options.text: Reassure the family that no further investigation is required and provide written advice on prompt re-presentation if recurrent symptoms develop
options.rationale: RCH guidance does not recommend renal ultrasound after a single typical UTI in a child over 6 months who responded promptly to antibiotics and had antenatal monitoring. Imaging is reserved for atypical UTI, recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

options.text: Commence prophylactic trimethoprim 2 mg/kg nocte for 6 months until paediatric nephrology review at that time
options.rationale: Antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended after a first typical UTI in a child over 6 months. The PRIVENT trial and RCH guidance found no meaningful benefit, with antimicrobial resistance risk; reserve for selected children with recurrent UTI and reflux. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

explanation.summary: In a child older than 6 months with a single typical E coli UTI that responded to oral antibiotics and a documented normal antenatal renal ultrasound, RCH guidance does not require renal tract imaging or prophylactic antibiotics. Imaging is reserved for atypical features, recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring. Atypical features include poor response to 48 hours of antibiotics, non-E coli organisms, sepsis, abdominal mass, or raised creatinine. DMSA and MCUG sit outside the RCH cascade and are not pursued in this scenario.
key_points: RCH does not recommend routine renal ultrasound after a single typical UTI over 6 months of age.
Atypical UTI = poor response to 48 h antibiotics, non-E coli, sepsis, abdominal mass, or raised creatinine.
DMSA and MCUG are not in the RCH cascade.
Antibiotic prophylaxis after a single UTI is not indicated.
explanation.pearls: After a first typical paediatric UTI in a child over 6 months with antenatal monitoring documented, no renal tract imaging and no antibiotic prophylaxis are required under RCH CPG.

subtopic_detail: Suspected airway foreign body diagnostic pathway
stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his grandmother. While he was eating cashew nuts at lunch he had a sudden episode of coughing and choking. He recovered within a few minutes but has had a persistent dry cough and intermittent wheeze ever since, for about 4 hours.

He is currently calm, breathing comfortably, and feeding sips of water without distress. Inspection shows no stridor or drooling. Auscultation reveals decreased air entry on the right with localised wheeze on that side. The grandmother says he was choking on a whole nut, not a piece, and that no one performed back blows or any manoeuvres.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 122 /min, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert and playful, no stridor or drooling, reduced air entry on right with monophonic wheeze on right, no recessions, no fever
data_table.Investigations: inspiratory and expiratory chest x-ray shows air trapping on the right with mediastinal shift to the left on expiration, no opacity visible

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial inhaled salbutamol via spacer for 1 hour and review with a repeat chest x-ray before deciding on referral
options.rationale: Treating localised wheeze with bronchodilators when foreign body is the leading diagnosis delays definitive care and risks the object moving into a more compromising location. Salbutamol does not displace an inhaled foreign body. (Source: RCH CPG Foreign body airway)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the chest with low-dose protocol prior to making a definitive surgical referral
options.rationale: CT can be confirmatory in equivocal cases but adds delay and radiation when the history and inspiratory or expiratory films are already diagnostic. The next intervention is therapeutic (rigid bronchoscopy), not further imaging. (Source: RCH CPG Foreign body airway)

options.text: Urgent referral to ENT or paediatric surgery for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia in theatre
options.rationale: The combination of witnessed choking, persistent unilateral signs, and x-ray demonstrating ball-valve obstruction is diagnostic of an airway foreign body until proven otherwise. Definitive diagnosis and removal both occur at rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia. Cashews are radiolucent so plain films cannot exclude the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG Foreign body airway)

options.text: Perform five back blows followed by five chest thrusts to attempt to dislodge the suspected foreign body
options.rationale: Back blows and chest thrusts are first-aid for an actively choking child with a partially or completely obstructed airway. The child is now stable with localised signs, so blind manoeuvres can move the object centrally and create complete obstruction. (Source: ANZCOR Paediatric BLS guideline)

options.text: Admit for ward observation overnight with a repeat chest x-ray in 12 hours before deciding on intervention
options.rationale: Observation without removal delays definitive diagnosis and increases the risk of distal migration, complete obstruction, or pneumonitis from oils in the nut. Rigid bronchoscopy is the standard of care once foreign body is the leading diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG Foreign body airway)

explanation.summary: Witnessed choking with persistent unilateral respiratory signs and air trapping on expiratory chest x-ray is a clinical diagnosis of inhaled foreign body. Cashews are radiolucent, so plain films cannot rule it out. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
key_points: Inspiratory and expiratory films show air trapping on the affected side in ball-valve obstruction.
Cashews and peanuts are radiolucent; absence of opacity does not exclude airway foreign body.
Back blows and chest thrusts are first-aid for active choking, not stable children with localised signs.
Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is the standard of care.
explanation.pearls: Persistent unilateral wheeze and chest x-ray air trapping after witnessed choking go straight to rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia; do not delay for CT or trial bronchodilators.

stem:
A 9-month-old boy presents with 12 hours of episodic distress described by his parents as starting suddenly, drawing his knees up, and screaming, then settling for 15 minutes before the next episode. The last episode included a single dark red jelly-like stool. Between episodes he is pale and quiet.

In the emergency department abdominal examination during a quiet phase reveals a long thin lump in the right upper part of his tummy. Bedside ultrasound shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant. Paediatric surgery and interventional radiology are on site. Two attempts at pneumatic reduction are now complete; the second attempt confirmed only partial reduction of the intussuscipiens with persisting ileocolic invagination.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 156 /min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: settled between episodes, mildly pale, soft abdomen with palpable elongated mass in right upper quadrant, no peritonism, well-perfused peripheries
data_table.Investigations: ultrasound target sign in right upper quadrant, full blood count haemoglobin 112 g/L (110-140) white cells 11.4 x10^9/L (4-12), venous lactate 1.6 mmol/L (under 2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and re-image at 12 hours before deciding on theatre
options.rationale: Antibiotics are appropriate as adjunct cover once a decision for surgery is made, but they are not a substitute for operative reduction. Waiting 12 hours for re-imaging risks bowel ischaemia and perforation. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

options.text: Attempt a third pneumatic reduction under deeper sedation after a 1-hour rest
options.rationale: RCH guidance limits enema attempts to two or three depending on local protocol, but continued attempts in the face of partial reduction increase perforation risk and delay definitive care. With failure documented and partial reduction only, theatre is now the standard. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

options.text: Transition to hydrostatic saline reduction under ultrasound guidance as a salvage attempt
options.rationale: Switching modality (hydrostatic versus pneumatic) is not generally salvage after a documented partial reduction failure; centres pick one approach per local resources. Persisting with imaging-guided reduction now adds delay. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

options.text: Admit for observation with serial abdominal examination and repeat ultrasound in 6 hours
options.rationale: Conservative observation after a failed reduction is not appropriate because the bowel remains at risk of ischaemia and perforation. The intervention has not resolved the invagination. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

options.text: Proceed to theatre for laparotomy with manual reduction and bowel viability assessment
options.rationale: After two failed attempts at pneumatic or hydrostatic reduction in a haemodynamically stable child without perforation, the next step is operative reduction. The surgeon will perform manual reduction and resect non-viable bowel if necessary. Continuing to attempt reduction beyond two failed cycles increases the risk of perforation. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Failed image-guided reduction of intussusception (typically after two attempts or in the face of partial reduction) is an indication for operative reduction. The surgical team performs manual reduction in theatre and resects non-viable bowel. Delaying further or trying additional non-operative attempts raises perforation risk.
key_points: Two failed enema attempts (or persistent partial reduction) is a surgical indication.
Perforation risk rises with repeated enema attempts.
Operative approach is laparotomy or laparoscopy with manual reduction.
Cover with antibiotics is adjunct, not a temporising substitute.
explanation.pearls: After two failed pneumatic reduction attempts or persistent partial reduction in intussusception, take the child to theatre for laparotomy and manual reduction; further enema attempts increase perforation risk.

stem:
A 6-week-old breastfed boy is admitted with a one-week history of progressive forceful vomiting that shoots out after feeds, with no green or yellow colour reported by his mother. He is feeding eagerly but losing weight. The general practitioner found a palpable upper abdominal lump during a feed yesterday. Bedside ultrasound performed in the emergency department this morning showed pyloric muscle thickness 4.5 mm and pyloric channel length 19 mm.

He is mildly dehydrated with reduced skin turgor and a sunken anterior fontanelle. Paediatric surgery has reviewed the patient and listed him for pyloromyotomy. The surgical team is asking whether they can proceed this afternoon or whether you would like to delay until tomorrow.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 162 /min, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: mildly dehydrated, sunken fontanelle, palpable olive-shaped mass in the upper abdomen, abdomen otherwise soft, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), chloride 88 mmol/L (95-110), bicarbonate 34 mmol/L (22-32), urea 9.2 mmol/L (2.0-7.0), pH 7.52 base excess +9 mmol/L, ultrasound confirms pyloric stenosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management before pyloromyotomy?

options.text: Commence oral electrolyte rehydration solution while maintaining nil-by-mouth status overnight for next-day theatre
options.rationale: Oral intake in a child with gastric outlet obstruction is ineffective for resuscitation because the fluid will not pass the pylorus. Intravenous resuscitation is required. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Proceed directly to theatre this afternoon and correct any residual electrolyte disturbances during anaesthesia
options.rationale: Operating on an alkalotic infant predisposes to post-anaesthetic apnoea. The dehydration is not an obstructed abdomen with bowel ischaemia; there is time to resuscitate. RCH guidance is clear that biochemical correction precedes operation. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube on free drainage and operate within 4 hours regardless of current biochemistry result
options.rationale: NGT decompression is reasonable adjunct but does not address the metabolic alkalosis. Time-pressured operation in an alkalotic infant raises post-op apnoea risk. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Correct the hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with intravenous fluid resuscitation before theatre
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis is a medical resuscitation that becomes a surgical case, not the reverse. The hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic, metabolic alkalosis must be corrected before general anaesthesia because alkalosis predisposes to post-operative apnoea through central respiratory depression. The accepted biochemical thresholds for theatre are bicarbonate below 30 and chloride above 100 mmol/L. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Commence ranitidine 1 mg/kg intravenously for gastric acid suppression and proceed to theatre this evening
options.rationale: Acid suppression does not address the urgent biochemical derangement that drives the post-anaesthetic apnoea risk. It is also not part of the standard pre-operative pathway. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric stenosis)

explanation.summary: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric hydrochloric acid in the vomitus. The alkalosis is a contraindication to general anaesthesia because of post-operative apnoea risk, so the infant is resuscitated to biochemical safety before pyloromyotomy. Targets are bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L and chloride above 100 mmol/L. Resuscitation fluid is 0.9 percent saline with potassium replacement once urine output is established.
key_points: Pre-operative biochemistry targets: bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L and chloride above 100 mmol/L.
Initial fluid is 0.9 percent saline with potassium replacement once urine output established.
Alkalosis predisposes to central respiratory depression after anaesthesia.
Pyloric stenosis is not a surgical emergency.
explanation.pearls: Correct the hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis of pyloric stenosis with 0.9 percent saline and potassium replacement before pyloromyotomy; aim for bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L and chloride above 100 mmol/L.

stem:
A 4-year-old girl is brought to the general practice clinic with 8 months of stool withholding, infrequent painful bowel motions every 5 to 7 days, and recent daily soiling of small amounts of liquid stool into her underwear. Her mother says her tummy is always full and hard. She is otherwise well, eats a varied diet, and is on the 50th centile for height and weight.

Examination shows an alert child with a non-tender, distended abdomen and a palpable faecal mass in the left iliac fossa. Anal inspection is normal with no fissure and no sacral pit. There are no red flags for organic disease (no failure to thrive, no delayed first stool in the newborn period, no green vomiting, no neurological signs). Her current management is occasional lactulose with limited adherence.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: soft non-tender abdomen with palpable left iliac fossa faecal mass, normal anal inspection, no sacral dimple or tuft of hair, normal lower limb tone and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: clinical diagnosis, no imaging or bloods required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue lactulose at the current dose and emphasise dietary fibre and fluid intake at follow-up in 4 weeks time
options.rationale: Dietary advice and a low-dose osmotic alone are inadequate where there is established faecal impaction. The withheld stool reservoir must be cleared before maintenance becomes effective. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

options.text: Disimpaction with macrogol 3350 with electrolytes at an escalating regimen over 3 to 7 days then daily maintenance
options.rationale: Functional constipation with faecal impaction requires disimpaction before maintenance. RCH recommends macrogol 3350 with electrolytes (Movicol Junior or equivalent) at an escalating dose over 3 to 7 days, then a daily maintenance dose for at least 6 months. Maintenance therapy alone without disimpaction repeatedly fails. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

options.text: Administer a daily phosphate enema for 3 days in clinic to clear the impaction before commencing maintenance therapy
options.rationale: Phosphate enemas are associated with electrolyte derangement and trauma in children and are not first-line for disimpaction in the AU paediatric pathway. Oral macrogol disimpaction is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

options.text: Commence senna 2.5 mL nocte as a stimulant laxative for 4 weeks and review symptoms at the end of that course
options.rationale: Stimulant laxatives alone are not first-line for disimpaction. They are useful as adjuncts to osmotics in selected maintenance regimens but do not clear faecal mass effectively. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

options.text: Refer for urgent paediatric gastroenterology review and arrange an abdominal x-ray to confirm faecal impaction
options.rationale: Faecal impaction is a clinical diagnosis confirmed by abdominal examination and history. Abdominal x-ray is not routinely required and adds radiation without changing management. The presentation lacks red flags for organic disease that would justify subspecialist referral. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation with palpable faecal mass requires oral disimpaction with macrogol 3350 with electrolytes at an escalating dose for 3 to 7 days, followed by daily maintenance for at least 6 months. Failure to disimpact before maintenance is the most common reason for treatment failure. Dietary advice and a low-dose osmotic alone are inadequate when impaction is already established. Red flags for organic disease prompt further investigation but are absent in this child.
key_points: Disimpaction: macrogol 3350 with electrolytes, escalating regimen over 3 to 7 days.
Maintenance: macrogol 3350 daily for at least 6 months, weaned gradually.
Red flags for organic disease: failure to thrive, delayed meconium, bilious vomiting, abnormal neurology, sacral dimple or hair tuft.
Abdominal x-ray is not required when the abdomen is examinable.
explanation.pearls: Use macrogol 3350 with electrolytes for both disimpaction (escalating dose over 3 to 7 days) and maintenance (daily dose for 6 months); enemas and dietary advice alone fail because the withheld stool reservoir is not cleared.

stem:
A 7-year-old boy presents to the paediatric outpatient clinic for review 1 week after discharge with a diagnosis of Henoch-Schonlein purpura. He had palpable purpura over the buttocks and extensor surfaces of the lower legs, bilateral ankle pain that has resolved, and 3 days of cramping tummy pain that came in waves that settled with simple analgesia. He never had macroscopic haematuria.

At admission his urinalysis showed trace blood and no proteinuria, his blood pressure was at the 50th centile, and his renal function was normal. Today he is well. His mother asks how often you need to check his urine and blood pressure from here.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 100/64 mmHg (50th centile for age and height), respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: fading non-blanching purpura on buttocks and lower legs, no joint swelling, no abdominal tenderness, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: urinalysis trace blood no protein, urine albumin creatinine ratio less than 2 mg/mmol, creatinine 38 micromol/L (paediatric range), blood pressure on growth chart at 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate renal follow-up plan?

options.text: Renal ultrasound at 3 months and at 6 months as the primary screening tool for evolving nephritis or scarring
options.rationale: Renal imaging is reserved for established nephritis or in atypical clinical course. The primary screen is dipstick urinalysis with quantitative urine ACR or PCR if positive, plus blood pressure. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Repeat urinalysis only if macroscopic haematuria, peripheral oedema or hypertension develop in the next 6 months
options.rationale: HSP nephritis can be silent in its early stages with microscopic haematuria or low-grade proteinuria as the only signs. Waiting for symptomatic disease misses the treatment window. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Weekly urinalysis and blood pressure measurement for 2 months then monthly until 6 months from initial onset
options.rationale: RCH guidance recommends close renal surveillance after HSP because nephritis can develop late (up to 6 months after onset). Urinalysis and blood pressure weekly for the first 1 to 2 months, then monthly to 6 months, picks up evolving nephritis at the point where treatment intensification is meaningful. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Daily urinalysis for 6 weeks at home using parent-performed dipstick testing with weekly clinic blood pressure
options.rationale: Daily urinalysis is impractical and not supported by evidence. Weekly testing in the first months catches evolving disease without burdening the family. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Refer for percutaneous renal biopsy now to define histological prognosis before any further surveillance plan
options.rationale: Renal biopsy is reserved for nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension, or progressive renal dysfunction. A child with HSP and no renal findings does not need a biopsy. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura nephritis develops up to 6 months after initial presentation and can be silent in its early stages. RCH recommends weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for the first 1 to 2 months, then monthly to 6 months, with escalation if proteinuria, hypertension or worsening renal function emerges. Biopsy is reserved for significant proteinuria, hypertension, or rising creatinine.
key_points: Renal surveillance after HSP runs for 6 months from onset.
Weekly urinalysis and BP for first 1 to 2 months, then monthly to 6 months.
Quantify proteinuria with ACR or PCR if dipstick positive.
Biopsy indications: nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension, declining renal function.
explanation.pearls: Schedule weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for 1 to 2 months then monthly to 6 months in HSP; nephritis can be silent and biopsy is reserved for nephrotic-range proteinuria or progressive disease.

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki recognition and IVIG timing
stem:
An 11-month-old boy is admitted with 9 days of fever to 39 to 40 degrees Celsius. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, perineal desquamation, and a single right cervical lymph node 1.8 cm in diameter. He has no rash, no oral mucosal changes, and no extremity changes. He has been investigated for sepsis with negative urine, blood, and respiratory virus cultures.

C-reactive protein is 142 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/hour, platelets 612 x 10^9/L, albumin 28 g/L, ALT 78 U/L, and urine has sterile pyuria. The paediatric cardiology echocardiogram performed today shows a left anterior descending coronary artery z-score of 2.6 with perivascular brightness.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 158 /min, blood pressure 94/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, perineal desquamation, single tender right cervical lymph node 1.8 cm, no rash, no oral changes, no extremity oedema
data_table.Investigations: CRP 142 mg/L (under 5), ESR 78 mm/hour (under 15), platelets 612 x 10^9/L (150-450), albumin 28 g/L (35-45), ALT 78 U/L (under 40), urine sterile pyuria, echocardiogram LAD z-score 2.6 with perivascular brightness
