lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue observation with daily inflammatory markers and repeat echocardiogram in 1 week
options.rationale: Observation is not appropriate when the criteria for incomplete Kawasaki are met and coronary changes are present. Delay risks progression to coronary aneurysm. (Source: AHA Kawasaki disease scientific statement)

options.text: Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours with high-dose aspirin therapy
options.rationale: This is incomplete Kawasaki disease - fever 5 or more days with 2 or 3 classical features, supportive laboratory findings, and now coronary artery z-score 2.5 or above on echocardiogram. IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin should be commenced once the diagnosis is established, even after day 10 if there is ongoing inflammation or coronary involvement. (Source: AHA Kawasaki disease scientific statement; RCH CPG Kawasaki)

options.text: Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for 3 days as primary therapy without IVIG
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are an adjunct to or rescue therapy after IVIG, not a substitute for first-line treatment in non-high-risk patients. They are also used as primary adjunct in high-risk patients (Kobayashi score positive) but in addition to, not instead of, IVIG. (Source: AHA Kawasaki disease scientific statement)

options.text: Start infliximab 5 mg/kg as primary therapy in view of the high CRP and coronary z-score
options.rationale: Infliximab is reserved for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki after a first or second dose of IVIG has failed. It is not first-line therapy. (Source: AHA Kawasaki disease scientific statement)

options.text: Commence broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and re-image at 48 hours before deciding on therapy
options.rationale: Broad antibiotics have been trialled empirically with no response and cultures are negative. Withholding IVIG to chase an occult bacterial source is not justified when criteria for incomplete Kawasaki are met. (Source: AHA Kawasaki disease scientific statement)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when there is fever for 5 or more days with 2 or 3 classical features plus supportive laboratory findings (raised CRP and ESR, anaemia, thrombocytosis, raised ALT, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria) or a coronary artery z-score of 2.5 or above. First-line treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin. Treatment should not be delayed beyond day 10 if there is ongoing inflammation or evolving coronary involvement. Corticosteroids and infliximab are adjuncts or rescue therapy rather than substitutes for IVIG.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: fever 5 or more days + 2 to 3 classical features + supportive labs OR coronary z-score 2.5 or above.
IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin is first-line, even after day 10 if active inflammation persists.
Steroids are adjunct in high-risk patients (Kobayashi score positive) but not a substitute for IVIG.
Infliximab is for IVIG-resistant disease.
explanation.pearls: Incomplete Kawasaki with coronary z-score 2.5 or above mandates IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin even past day 10; steroids and biologics are adjuncts or rescue, not substitutes.

stem:
A 3-year-old girl is referred from her general practitioner with a 4-day history of bruising and a petechial rash. She had a viral upper respiratory illness 2 weeks ago. She is otherwise well, eating and drinking normally, and active at preschool. Examination shows scattered petechiae over the trunk and limbs and a few small bruises on her shins; there are no wet purpura, no mucosal bleeding, and no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy.

Full blood count shows isolated thrombocytopenia at 18 x 10^9/L with normal haemoglobin and white cell count. Blood film confirms isolated thrombocytopenia with normal red cells and white cells; there are no blasts. She has no family history of bleeding disorders and is up to date with immunisations. The haematology registrar has reviewed and confirmed the working diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 102 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: well child, scattered petechiae over trunk and limbs, small bruises on shins, no wet purpura, no mucosal bleeding, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 122 g/L (110-140), white cells 7.8 x10^9/L (4-12), platelets 18 x10^9/L (150-450), blood film isolated thrombocytopenia with normal red and white cells and no blasts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Give a platelet transfusion targeting a platelet count above 50 x10^9/L to provide short-term haemostatic cover
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion in ITP is reserved for life-threatening bleeding because transfused platelets are also rapidly destroyed by the autoantibody. It does not address the underlying immune mechanism. (Source: ASH ITP guidelines)

options.text: Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 0.8 g/kg as a single dose to raise the platelet count rapidly within hours
options.rationale: IVIG raises platelets faster but does not improve clinical outcomes in cutaneous-only ITP. It is reserved for active mucosal or organ bleeding and for procedures requiring haemostasis. (Source: ASH ITP guidelines)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 4 mg/kg/day for 4 days followed by a stepwise taper over the next 1 to 2 weeks
options.rationale: Corticosteroids raise platelet count but have steroid side effects and do not change long-term outcomes in cutaneous-only disease. Reserve for active bleeding or imminent procedures. (Source: ASH ITP guidelines)

options.text: Observation with written advice on bleeding precautions and arrange weekly platelet count for the next 4 weeks
options.rationale: Newly diagnosed paediatric ITP with cutaneous bleeding only (no wet purpura, no mucosal or major bleeding) is managed with observation regardless of platelet count. Bleeding outcomes correlate with bleeding phenotype, not the platelet number. Most cases resolve within 6 months. (Source: ASH ITP guidelines; RCH CPG ITP)

options.text: Refer for urgent bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy to exclude an underlying haematological malignancy
options.rationale: Bone marrow biopsy is not required when the clinical picture and blood film are typical of ITP. Reserve for atypical features such as lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, abnormal red or white cell line, or failure to respond to treatment. (Source: ASH ITP guidelines)

explanation.summary: Newly diagnosed paediatric ITP with cutaneous bleeding alone is managed with observation, bleeding precautions, and serial platelet counts irrespective of the absolute platelet number. Active treatment (IVIG, steroids, anti-D) is reserved for mucosal or organ bleeding or for procedures. Bone marrow biopsy is not routine when the clinical and laboratory picture is typical.
key_points: Treatment decisions in ITP are guided by bleeding phenotype, not platelet count.
Cutaneous-only bleeding is managed with observation even if platelets are below 20 x10^9/L.
IVIG, steroids, and anti-D are reserved for mucosal or organ bleeding.
Most paediatric ITP resolves within 6 months.
explanation.pearls: Manage cutaneous-only newly diagnosed paediatric ITP with watch and wait plus bleeding precautions; treat only for wet purpura, mucosal bleeding, or procedure preparation per ASH paediatric ITP guidance.

subtopic_detail: New T1DM without DKA - initiation approach
stem:
A 9-year-old boy is referred by his general practitioner with 4 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and 3 kg weight loss. A clinic capillary blood glucose was 22 mmol/L. He is alert, ambulating, and tolerating oral fluids. The general practitioner sent him to the emergency department after capillary ketones returned 0.6 mmol/L.

In the emergency department his repeat capillary blood glucose is 19 mmol/L, capillary ketones are 0.5 mmol/L, and venous blood gas shows pH 7.36 and bicarbonate 23 mmol/L. He is haemodynamically stable, mucous membranes are moist, and abdominal examination is normal. The on-call paediatric endocrinology consultant has reviewed and confirmed this is new-onset Type 1 diabetes mellitus without diabetic ketoacidosis.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert, moist mucous membranes, abdomen soft and non-tender, normal mental state, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: capillary blood glucose 19 mmol/L (under 7 fasting), capillary ketones 0.5 mmol/L (under 0.6), venous pH 7.36 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 23 mmol/L (22-32), sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial insulin regimen?

options.text: Discharge for outpatient initiation of insulin by the community diabetes team in the next 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Newly diagnosed paediatric T1DM is admitted for inpatient initiation, diabetes education, parental skill development (injection technique, carbohydrate counting, hypoglycaemia management), and arrangement of community follow-up. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous fluid bolus 10 mL/kg of 0.9 percent saline followed by an insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour
options.rationale: An IV insulin infusion is the DKA pathway. This child does not meet DKA criteria (pH 7.36, bicarbonate 23, ketones 0.5). Treating him as DKA is overtreatment that risks hypoglycaemia and electrolyte disturbance. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines)

options.text: Twice-daily premixed insulin 30/70 with breakfast and dinner as a simpler starter regimen for the family
options.rationale: Twice-daily premixed insulin is less physiological and produces inferior glycaemic outcomes compared with basal-bolus in newly diagnosed paediatric T1DM. AU and ISPAD guidance favour basal-bolus or pump therapy from diagnosis. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines)

options.text: Oral metformin 500 mg twice daily as initial therapy and arrange outpatient endocrinology review in 1 week
options.rationale: Metformin is not first-line for Type 1 diabetes; insulin is mandatory because of absolute insulin deficiency. The diagnosis is clinically Type 1 based on age, weight loss, and ketosis. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines)

options.text: Subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin (long-acting once daily plus rapid-acting with meals) with diabetes education
options.rationale: Newly diagnosed Type 1 diabetes without DKA is treated with subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin (long-acting basal plus rapid-acting with meals) and diabetes education from the multidisciplinary team. IV insulin is reserved for DKA. The child is alert, eating, and not acidotic. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines)

explanation.summary: New-onset Type 1 diabetes without DKA is treated with subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin (long-acting once daily plus rapid-acting with meals), inpatient admission for multidisciplinary diabetes education, and structured outpatient follow-up. IV insulin and large fluid resuscitation belong to the DKA pathway. Treating this non-acidotic, clinically stable child as DKA overtreats and adds risk of hypoglycaemia. Basal-bolus is preferred over twice-daily premixed insulin from diagnosis under ISPAD guidance.
key_points: DKA requires venous pH below 7.30 or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L plus ketosis.
Without DKA: subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin, oral hydration, education.
Basal-bolus is preferred over twice-daily premix from diagnosis.
Metformin has no role in established Type 1 diabetes.
explanation.pearls: New paediatric Type 1 diabetes without DKA gets subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin and inpatient education; IV insulin is the DKA pathway and is unnecessary here.

stem:
A 12-day-old phenotypically female infant is brought to the emergency department by her parents with 2 days of poor feeding and vomiting and a noticeable change in alertness this morning. She was born at term, weight 3.4 kg, and discharged on day 2. The newborn screen result is not yet back.

In the resus bay she is lethargic with mottled peripheries and prolonged capillary refill. Her parents describe ambiguous-appearing external genitalia (described in their words as a small lump with what looks like a urinary opening underneath). Bedside glucose is 2.4 mmol/L and capillary blood gas shows pH 7.22, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L, sodium 122 mmol/L, potassium 6.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 188 /min, blood pressure 58/32 mmHg, respiratory rate 50 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: lethargic, mottled, capillary refill 4 seconds, sunken fontanelle, virilised external genitalia with phallic enlargement and partial fusion of labial folds, no palpable gonads, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 6.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 2.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), bicarbonate 14 mmol/L (22-32), pH 7.22 (7.35-7.45), 17-hydroxyprogesterone sent urgently

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg bolus then 0.9 percent saline with 10 percent dextrose 10 mL/kg and admit to PICU
options.rationale: This is a salt-losing adrenal crisis in classic salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency). Hydrocortisone (stress dose 25 mg IV for infants under 1 year per AU paediatric endocrine guidance) is given immediately, followed by isotonic saline with dextrose to address hypovolaemia and hypoglycaemia. Fludrocortisone is added once oral intake is established. (Source: APEG congenital adrenal hyperplasia guidelines; RCH CPG Adrenal crisis)

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 0.1 mg/kg bolus and arrange transfer to paediatric intensive care once stabilised
options.rationale: Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and would not address the salt-wasting component of this crisis. Hydrocortisone, which has both glucocorticoid and weak mineralocorticoid activity, is the standard. Dexamethasone is also avoided in suspected CAH because it suppresses the 17-OHP result. (Source: APEG congenital adrenal hyperplasia guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate 0.5 mL/kg of 10 percent over 10 minutes for the hyperkalaemia then reassess plan
options.rationale: Calcium gluconate is reserved for hyperkalaemic ECG changes; potassium 6.8 mmol/L without ECG features in CAH crisis is treated upstream by hydrocortisone and saline correction. Treating only the potassium misses the underlying steroid deficit and risks deterioration. (Source: APEG congenital adrenal hyperplasia guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous fludrocortisone 0.1 mg single dose and 0.9 percent saline 20 mL/kg bolus then reassess perfusion
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not available as an intravenous preparation in Australia. Mineralocorticoid replacement is given orally once the infant is feeding; the acute crisis is managed with IV hydrocortisone, which has weak mineralocorticoid activity at stress doses. (Source: APEG congenital adrenal hyperplasia guidelines)

options.text: Send urgent karyotype, serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone and urinary steroid profile before any therapeutic decision
options.rationale: Investigations are sent in parallel with treatment, not before it. Withholding stress hydrocortisone in a haemodynamically compromised infant with biochemistry typical of adrenal crisis is unsafe; treat first, confirm later. (Source: APEG congenital adrenal hyperplasia guidelines)

explanation.summary: A salt-losing adrenal crisis in undiagnosed classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) presents with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and shock around 1 to 2 weeks of age. Treatment is immediate IV hydrocortisone (stress dose) and isotonic dextrose-saline resuscitation. Diagnostic samples are sent in parallel, not as a prerequisite to treatment.
key_points: Hydrocortisone stress dose under 1 year: 25 mg IV bolus then 25 mg every 6 hours.
Dexamethasone is avoided as it suppresses 17-OHP and lacks mineralocorticoid effect.
Fludrocortisone is oral only; intravenous mineralocorticoid replacement is not available.
Send 17-OHP, electrolytes, glucose, karyotype in parallel with treatment, not before.
explanation.pearls: Treat suspected paediatric salt-losing CAH crisis with IV hydrocortisone (25 mg for infants under 1 year) plus 0.9 percent saline with 10 percent dextrose bolus; never delay for confirmatory bloods, and avoid dexamethasone because it suppresses 17-OHP.

stem:
An 11-year-old girl with new-onset Type 1 diabetes is on the paediatric ward 6 hours into treatment for severe diabetic ketoacidosis. She has received 0.9 percent saline 10 mL/kg over 60 minutes, followed by maintenance plus deficit fluids over 48 hours, and an insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour. Initial venous pH was 7.05.

The nurse calls you because the patient has developed a headache that started 30 minutes ago, has become irritable, and her heart rate has fallen from 124 to 78 /min while her blood pressure has risen from 102/64 to 138/86 mmHg. She is rousable but slow to respond. The team has just checked a venous blood gas which shows pH 7.18 and glucose 14 mmol/L. The on-call consultant is en route.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), pupils equal and reactive, no focal neurology, well perfused, weight 42 kg
data_table.Investigations: venous pH 7.18 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 14 mmol/L (22-32), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 14 mmol/L (3.5-7.0 fasting), ketones 3.2 mmol/L (under 0.6)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Add 5 percent dextrose to the maintenance fluid because the glucose has fallen to 14 mmol/L
options.rationale: Adding dextrose to the IV fluid when glucose drops below 14 to 17 mmol/L is part of standard DKA management to allow the insulin infusion to continue clearing ketones. However, it is not the immediate response to cerebral oedema, which is the threat to life now. (Source: ISPAD DKA Guidelines)

options.text: Increase intravenous fluid rate by 50 percent to address presumed worsening dehydration
options.rationale: Increasing fluids in established DKA-associated cerebral oedema worsens cerebral interstitial fluid accumulation and raises intracranial pressure. The pathway is to reduce fluids and give hyperosmolar therapy. (Source: ISPAD DKA Guidelines)

options.text: Stop the insulin infusion and arrange urgent computed tomography of the head before further therapy
options.rationale: CT can be useful but is not the first step; cerebral oedema is a clinical diagnosis in this context and treatment with hyperosmolar therapy must not wait for imaging. Stopping the insulin infusion is unnecessary and will worsen acidosis. (Source: ISPAD DKA Guidelines)

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg to reduce cerebral oedema and continue current fluids
options.rationale: Dexamethasone has no role in DKA-associated cerebral oedema, which is a non-vasogenic mechanism. The standard hyperosmolar therapy is 3 percent hypertonic saline or mannitol. (Source: ISPAD DKA Guidelines)

options.text: Reduce intravenous fluid rate by one-third and give intravenous 3 percent hypertonic saline 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes
options.rationale: The triad of headache, falling heart rate, and rising blood pressure during DKA treatment is cerebral oedema (Cushing response). Immediate management per ISPAD and BSPED guidance is to reduce IV fluid rate by one-third and give hyperosmolar therapy: 3 percent hypertonic saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes, or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg. Urgent CT after stabilisation is appropriate but treatment is not delayed for imaging. (Source: ISPAD DKA Guidelines; RCH CPG DKA)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema is the most serious complication of paediatric DKA, presenting with headache, altered consciousness, and the Cushing response (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular respiration). Treatment is immediate: reduce IV fluid rate by one-third and give 3 percent hypertonic saline (2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes) or mannitol (0.5 to 1 g/kg). Treatment must not wait for imaging.
key_points: Triad of bradycardia, hypertension, and altered consciousness in DKA = cerebral oedema.
First step: reduce fluid rate by one-third and give hyperosmolar therapy.
Hypertonic saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg of 3 percent solution OR mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg.
Imaging follows stabilisation, not before.
explanation.pearls: DKA cerebral oedema is signalled by headache plus Cushing response and is treated immediately with one-third reduction in IV fluids plus 3 percent hypertonic saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes per ISPAD; do not delay for CT.

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with 6 hours of fever, vomiting, and a rapidly spreading rash. His parents say he was well at school yesterday. On the way in he became unusually drowsy.

In the resus bay he is mottled with cold peripheries, capillary refill 5 seconds, and a non-blanching purpuric rash over his trunk and legs which is visibly spreading. He is rousable but irritable. The team has obtained intraosseous access. Bedside glucose is 4.2 mmol/L. The on-call anaesthetist has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 178 /min, blood pressure 78/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: mottled, cold peripheries, capillary refill 5 seconds, non-blanching purpuric rash over trunk and limbs, drowsy but rousable, GCS 12, neck supple, no photophobia documented
data_table.Investigations: intraosseous access established, blood cultures and full blood count drawn, lactate 4.8 mmol/L (under 2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Defer antibiotic administration and perform a lumbar puncture immediately for CSF cell count and microscopy
options.rationale: Performing LP in shock, raised ICP, coagulopathy, or with a spreading purpuric rash is unsafe. Antibiotics within the first hour are the priority; CSF can still yield useful diagnostic information when sampled later, and PCR retains sensitivity for some time. (Source: RCH CPG Meningitis paediatric)

options.text: Administer intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg through the intraosseous line with 20 mL/kg saline bolus and defer LP
options.rationale: RCH paediatric sepsis pathway places antibiotics within the first hour after blood cultures, regardless of LP status. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in haemodynamic instability, raised intracranial pressure, coagulopathy, or progressive purpuric rash. Antibiotics are not delayed pending LP. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis paediatric; RCH CPG Meningitis paediatric)

options.text: Administer benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg intramuscularly through the deltoid prior to attempting intravenous access
options.rationale: IM benzylpenicillin is the field option when IV or IO access cannot be obtained. The team here has IO access available, which permits immediate IV-equivalent administration of broad-spectrum ceftriaxone. (Source: RCH CPG Meningitis paediatric)

options.text: Administer intravenous adrenaline 1 microgram/kg bolus to raise the blood pressure before any antibiotic dose
options.rationale: Inotropes are reserved for fluid-refractory shock after 40 to 60 mL/kg of fluid resuscitation; first-line is volume and antibiotics. Starting a bolus of adrenaline before adequate fluid loading is not in the sepsis pathway. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis paediatric)

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg before the first dose of empirical antibiotic for meningitis
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is not routinely given for suspected meningococcal sepsis; it has a role in confirmed pneumococcal or Haemophilus meningitis if started with or just before the first dose of antibiotic. Use here delays antibiotic administration. (Source: RCH CPG Meningitis paediatric)

explanation.summary: Suspected meningococcal sepsis with shock and a spreading purpuric rash mandates immediate antibiotics within the first hour after blood cultures and IV or IO access, plus a 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in haemodynamic instability, raised intracranial pressure, coagulopathy, or progressive purpuric rash. LP is deferred until the child is haemodynamically stable. IM benzylpenicillin is reserved for the field when IV or IO access is not available.
key_points: Antibiotics within the first hour of recognition, after cultures.
LP contraindications: shock, raised ICP, coagulopathy, progressive purpuric rash.
Fluid resuscitation: 20 mL/kg crystalloid, repeat to 60 mL/kg before inotropes.
IM benzylpenicillin only when IV or IO access is not available.
explanation.pearls: Give IV or IO ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg in the first hour of suspected meningococcal sepsis and defer LP until the child is haemodynamically stable; never delay antibiotics for CSF sampling.

stem:
A 19-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents who measured an axillary temperature of 38.2 degrees Celsius this evening. He has been feeding less in the last 12 hours and seems quieter than usual. He was born at term by uncomplicated vaginal delivery; mother had no maternal GBS swab documented in the discharge summary, and there was prolonged rupture of membranes at 19 hours.

In triage he is alert but quiet, with normal capillary refill, anterior fontanelle flat, and no rash. Fully exposed examination is unremarkable. The most senior available decision-maker is the paediatric registrar on call.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 156 /min, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 48 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert but quiet, flat anterior fontanelle, no rash, no respiratory distress, abdomen soft, no focal source on full exposed examination
data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.36 lactate 1.4 mmol/L, capillary blood glucose 4.8 mmol/L, urinalysis pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a full septic workup including lumbar puncture and commence intravenous ceftriaxone empirically
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is avoided in the neonatal period (first 28 days) because it displaces bilirubin from albumin and can cause kernicterus. Cefotaxime is preferred. Amoxicillin is required to cover Listeria. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Perform a full septic workup including lumbar puncture and commence intravenous amoxicillin plus cefotaxime empirically
options.rationale: Any febrile infant under 28 days requires a full septic workup including blood culture, urine culture, and CSF examination, followed by empirical IV antibiotic cover for the neonatal pathogen spectrum. AU guidance pairs amoxicillin (for Listeria and group B Streptococcus) with cefotaxime (Gram-negative cover). Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates due to bilirubin displacement risk. (Source: RCH CPG Febrile infant; Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Perform a full septic workup excluding lumbar puncture and observe on the ward for 24 hours before deciding on antibiotics
options.rationale: Withholding LP and antibiotics in any febrile infant under 28 days is unsafe. The neonatal immune system cannot reliably localise infection, and bacterial meningitis has a high mortality without prompt treatment. (Source: RCH CPG Febrile infant)

options.text: Take blood and urine cultures only and commence oral cefalexin once the urine result is back
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are inadequate for empirical neonatal sepsis cover and the spectrum of cefalexin does not cover Listeria. CSF must be examined. (Source: RCH CPG Febrile infant)

options.text: Apply paracetamol and observe for 4 hours; if temperature settles, discharge with safety-net advice
options.rationale: Antipyretic response is not a reliable rule-out for serious bacterial infection in any age group, and especially not in infants under 28 days. The septic workup proceeds regardless of fever response. (Source: RCH CPG Febrile infant)

explanation.summary: Any febrile infant under 28 days has a full septic workup (blood culture, urine culture, lumbar puncture) and empirical IV antibiotics covering the neonatal spectrum. AU guidance pairs amoxicillin (for Listeria and group B Streptococcus) with cefotaxime (for Gram-negative cover). Ceftriaxone is avoided in the first 28 days of life because it displaces bilirubin from albumin and can cause kernicterus. Antipyretic response is not a reliable rule-out for serious bacterial infection.
key_points: Full septic workup is mandatory for any febrile infant under 28 days.
Empirical antibiotics: IV amoxicillin plus IV cefotaxime.
Ceftriaxone is contraindicated under 28 days (bilirubin displacement, kernicterus risk).
Antipyretic response does not rule out serious bacterial infection.
explanation.pearls: Febrile infant under 28 days gets full septic workup including LP plus empirical IV amoxicillin and cefotaxime; ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates because of kernicterus risk from bilirubin displacement.

stem:
A 6-year-old boy with a known peanut allergy was given intramuscular adrenaline 300 micrograms by his mother 30 minutes ago after he developed widespread urticaria and stridor at a friend's house following biscuit ingestion. In the ambulance he received a second IM adrenaline 300 micrograms because his stridor recurred 12 minutes after the first dose.

On arrival in the emergency department he is alert, asymptomatic, with no rash, no stridor, no wheeze, and normal vital signs. His parents ask whether he can be discharged now that he looks well. He has had three previous mild anaphylactic episodes and has an ASCIA action plan; he weighs 22 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 102 /min, blood pressure 104/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert and active, skin clear with no urticaria, oropharynx clear, chest auscultation clear, no abdominal tenderness, normal mental state
data_table.Investigations: clinical diagnosis, no further investigations indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge now with a clear written action plan and a replacement adrenaline autoinjector to take home
options.rationale: Same-day discharge before completing 4 hours of post-adrenaline observation does not allow for detection of a biphasic reaction. The risk is highest in patients who needed more than one dose, which applies here. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: Observe in the emergency department for at least 4 hours from the last adrenaline dose before discharge planning
options.rationale: ASCIA recommends a minimum 4 hours of observation after the last adrenaline dose for any anaphylaxis. He received two doses (the second 18 minutes ago), so the clock restarts from the second dose. Biphasic reactions occur in around 5 percent of cases, typically within 6 to 8 hours. Children who received 2 or more adrenaline doses are at higher risk and may warrant longer observation. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: Admit to the paediatric ward for 24 hours of observation regardless of the symptom-free interval
options.rationale: Routine 24-hour admission is not required for anaphylaxis. A minimum 4-hour observation after the last adrenaline dose, with longer for high-risk features (two or more doses, severe asthma, severe initial reaction, remote location), is the AU standard. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: Discharge with a 3-day course of oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg to prevent a biphasic reaction
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions and are not recommended as monotherapy for prevention. The mainstay is observation and a clear emergency action plan. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: Discharge with oral antihistamine cetirizine 5 mg twice daily for 5 days and review by general practitioner
options.rationale: Antihistamines treat skin symptoms only and have no role in preventing or treating airway or cardiovascular components of anaphylaxis. Their use as monotherapy for discharge planning understates the risk. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

explanation.summary: ASCIA recommends a minimum of 4 hours of observation after the last adrenaline dose for any anaphylaxis, with longer observation when there are risk factors for biphasic reaction. Risk factors include needing two or more adrenaline doses, severe asthma, and severe initial reaction. Biphasic reactions occur in around 5 percent of cases, typically within 6 to 8 hours of the initial reaction. Corticosteroids and antihistamines do not prevent biphasic reactions; observation and a clear action plan with adrenaline autoinjector prescription do.
key_points: Minimum 4 hours observation from the last adrenaline dose.
Risk factors for biphasic reaction: 2 or more adrenaline doses, severe asthma, severe initial reaction.
Biphasic reactions occur in around 5 percent, typically within 6 to 8 hours.
Steroids and antihistamines do not prevent biphasic anaphylaxis.
explanation.pearls: After paediatric anaphylaxis requiring two adrenaline doses, observe for at least 4 hours from the last dose per ASCIA; biphasic reactions occur in around 5 percent and steroids do not prevent them.

sources.label: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

stem:
A 7-day-old term boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents who say he stopped feeding well 12 hours ago and is now floppy and cold. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery with no antenatal concerns; the discharge ward midwife discharged him on day 2 with no echocardiogram performed.

In the resus bay he is grey, lethargic, and tachypnoeic. Pre-ductal SpO2 on the right hand is 96 percent and post-ductal SpO2 on the foot is 84 percent. Femoral pulses are not palpable while brachial pulses are present. Four-limb blood pressures show right upper limb 92/58 mmHg and right lower limb 56/34 mmHg.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 184 /min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg right arm and 56/34 mmHg right leg, respiratory rate 64 /min, SpO2 96% right hand and 84% right foot, temperature 36.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: grey lethargic infant, capillary refill 4 seconds, absent femoral pulses bilaterally, brachial pulses present, tachypnoea with mild recessions, harsh systolic murmur left infraclavicular area
data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.18 lactate 5.4 mmol/L, sodium 137 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 6.8 mmol/L, creatinine 64 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous furosemide 1 mg/kg for the tachypnoea attributed to congestive heart failure secondary
options.rationale: Diuresis without re-establishing ductal flow worsens the obstructive picture. PGE1 first, then supportive care including selective diuresis once the duct is patent and pulmonary congestion is documented. (Source: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus and reassess perfusion before initiating any other targeted intervention
options.rationale: A standard 20 mL/kg fluid bolus in undifferentiated neonatal shock can precipitate decompensation if the underlying lesion is left-sided obstruction with a closing duct. Smaller volumes (10 mL/kg) given cautiously plus immediate PGE1 are the AU paediatric cardiology pathway. (Source: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease

options.text: Intubate and commence inotropes with a peripheral adrenaline infusion before organising interhospital transfer
options.rationale: Inotropes without restoring ductal flow do not address the obstruction at the aortic isthmus. PGE1 is the upstream intervention; inotropes are an adjunct after ductal flow is re-established. (Source: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease

options.text: Administer intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg empirically for presumed late-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis cover
options.rationale: While sepsis is a reasonable differential, the four-limb blood pressure gradient and pre versus post-ductal saturation difference strongly point to a duct-dependent cardiac lesion. Antibiotics are appropriate as adjunct cover after PGE1 is started. Ceftriaxone is also relatively contraindicated under 28 days. (Source: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease

options.text: Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion 5 nanograms/kg/min and prepare for retrieval to a cardiac centre
options.rationale: Pre- versus post-ductal SpO2 differential and the four-limb blood pressure gradient indicate duct-dependent coarctation of the aorta. The patent ductus arteriosus is supplying flow to the lower body; once it closes the infant deteriorates rapidly. PGE1 reopens or maintains ductal patency at 5 to 50 ng/kg/min while retrieval is organised to a paediatric cardiac centre. (Source: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease

explanation.summary: Differential SpO2 (pre-ductal higher than post-ductal) and a four-limb BP gradient (upper limb higher than lower limb) in a collapsing neonate at 5 to 10 days of life indicate duct-dependent coarctation. PGE1 infusion 5 to 50 ng/kg/min is the immediate intervention to reopen or maintain ductal patency. Antibiotics for possible sepsis can be given in parallel but are not the upstream therapy.
key_points: Pre versus post-ductal SpO2 difference indicates a duct-dependent right-to-left or systemic-supply lesion.
PGE1 dose: 5 ng/kg/min, titrated up to 50 ng/kg/min if no response.
Apnoea is a common side effect; have intubation equipment ready.
20 mL/kg bolus is too much for closing-duct shock; use 10 mL/kg if needed.
explanation.pearls: Collapsing 1-week-old with absent femorals, pre versus post-ductal SpO2 gradient, and four-limb BP gradient = duct-dependent coarctation; commence PGE1 5 ng/kg/min and arrange retrieval to a paediatric cardiac centre.

sources.label: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease

stem:
A 7-year-old boy was rescued from a house fire 2 hours ago. He has full-thickness circumferential burns to the right forearm and partial-thickness burns to the trunk, totalling 18 percent body surface area. He was intubated at scene for inhalational injury and is now in the resuscitation bay. He has received the calculated first 8 hours of resuscitation fluid per the AU paediatric burn formula.

You are reassessing the right upper limb. Distal capillary refill is 5 seconds, the radial pulse is just palpable on Doppler, and the hand is cool. The forearm compartments feel firm. The patient is sedated and intubated, ventilated with no airway pressure alarms.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 122 /min, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min ventilated, SpO2 98% on FiO2 0.4, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: right forearm circumferential full-thickness burn with leathery eschar, distal capillary refill 5 seconds, Doppler-only radial pulse, hand cool, forearm compartments firm, partial-thickness trunk burns
data_table.Investigations: intubated and sedated, urine output 0.8 mL/kg/hour, lactate 2.4 mmol/L (under 2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange transfer to a paediatric burns centre for theatre-based fasciotomy under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Escharotomy is performed at the bedside through the eschar, which is insensate; it does not require general anaesthesia. Fasciotomy is a different procedure indicated for true compartment syndrome and is performed after escharotomy fails to restore perfusion. Transfer should not delay escharotomy. (Source: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns)
source_refs: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns

options.text: Elevate the limb above heart level and reassess in 1 hour before deciding on intervention
options.rationale: Limb elevation does not relieve external constriction from the eschar. Once perfusion is compromised, escharotomy is needed urgently; an additional hour of ischaemia risks permanent injury. (Source: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns)
source_refs: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns

options.text: Increase the fluid resuscitation rate by 25 percent to improve distal perfusion via central pressure
options.rationale: Increasing fluids does not address mechanical external constriction by full-thickness eschar; it risks over-resuscitation, which is associated with abdominal compartment syndrome and worsened outcomes in burns. (Source: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns)
source_refs: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns

options.text: Perform urgent escharotomy of the right upper limb at the bedside to restore distal perfusion
options.rationale: Circumferential full-thickness burn with reduced distal perfusion, prolonged capillary refill, Doppler-only pulses, and firm compartments is an indication for urgent escharotomy. The procedure is performed at the bedside through devitalised eschar to relieve external constriction; it does not require theatre time. Delaying for transfer or further investigation risks limb loss. (Source: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns)
source_refs: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns

options.text: Apply silver sulfadiazine dressing and arrange repeat assessment in 4 hours
options.rationale: Topical dressings address microbial colonisation, not external mechanical constriction. Delaying intervention for 4 hours in an ischaemic limb risks irreversible injury. (Source: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns)
source_refs: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns

explanation.summary: Circumferential full-thickness burns can cause external constriction once oedema accumulates, compromising distal perfusion. Indicators include prolonged capillary refill, Doppler-only pulses, firm compartments, and cool extremity. Bedside escharotomy through the insensate eschar restores perfusion and is urgent.
key_points: Escharotomy is bedside, through full-thickness eschar (insensate), no general anaesthesia required.
Indications: circumferential burn plus distal perfusion compromise.
Fasciotomy is separate, for compartment syndrome after escharotomy fails.
Over-resuscitation worsens outcomes; do not chase pulses with fluid alone.
explanation.pearls: Circumferential full-thickness burn with cool distal limb, Doppler-only pulses, and firm compartments needs bedside escharotomy now per ANZBA; elevation, more fluid, and dressings do not relieve eschar constriction.

sources.label: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns

stem:
A 7-month-old non-mobile infant is brought to the emergency department by her father with a swollen, painful right thigh that he noticed after picking her up from her cot this morning. He says she may have rolled awkwardly. The infant cries with movement of the right leg. X-ray of the right femur shows a spiral fracture of the mid-shaft.

The infant is fully immunised, growing along the 25th centile, and on review of the parent-held record she has been seen for two previous emergency department attendances in the last 4 months: one for a frenulum tear and one for a bruise on her cheek. The father attends alone and is reluctant to provide a clear narrative about the cot event. Mother is not contactable.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 126 /min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: tender right mid-thigh with swelling, otherwise well-grown infant, no other obvious external injury on full exposed examination, no torn frenulum currently visible
data_table.Investigations: right femur x-ray spiral mid-shaft fracture, full blood count haemoglobin 110 g/L (105-135) platelets 282 x10^9/L (150-450), coagulation profile within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admit and arrange skeletal survey, ophthalmology review, hospital child protection team and statutory notification
options.rationale: A femoral fracture in a non-mobile infant has a high specificity for inflicted injury. The work-up includes admission for safety, full skeletal survey within 24 hours, ophthalmology for retinal haemorrhage screening, neuroimaging if indicated by age and clinical features, coagulation studies, and mandatory notification to the statutory child protection authority. The hospital child protection team coordinates this. (Source: RCH CPG Child abuse - physical; Australian Mandatory Reporting Frameworks)

options.text: Apply a long-leg cast under procedural sedation in the emergency department and discharge with GP follow-up in 1 week
options.rationale: Discharging without safeguarding workup or notification ignores a strong red flag (femoral fracture in non-mobile infant). The fracture also alone is not the indication for early discharge; the safety risk is. (Source: RCH CPG Child abuse - physical)

options.text: Send a urinary catecholamine sample to exclude phaeochromocytoma as a cause of fragile vessels and apparent bruising
options.rationale: Phaeochromocytoma does not cause fragile bones and is not part of the differential for an isolated femoral spiral fracture. Investigation should be guided by the differential of organic causes of bone fragility, not by unrelated rare diseases. (Source: RCH CPG Child abuse - physical)

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for elective fracture clinic follow-up and arrange outpatient social work review within 2 weeks
options.rationale: Outpatient follow-up does not protect the child or initiate the safeguarding pathway. Suspected non-accidental injury requires inpatient assessment to coordinate skeletal survey and child protection involvement. (Source: RCH CPG Child abuse - physical)

options.text: Request a haematology consultation to exclude osteogenesis imperfecta as a unifying diagnosis before notification
options.rationale: Organic bone disease (osteogenesis imperfecta, copper deficiency) is part of the differential and is considered during the workup, but notification of suspected abuse does not wait for these results when the index of suspicion is high. Notification and protection run in parallel with differential investigation. (Source: RCH CPG Child abuse - physical)

explanation.summary: A femoral fracture in a non-mobile infant carries a high probability of inflicted injury. The combined workup includes admission for safety, full skeletal survey, retinal examination, neuroimaging if indicated, and coagulation studies, with mandatory notification to the statutory child protection authority. The hospital child protection team coordinates the multidisciplinary response.
key_points: Femoral fracture in non-mobile infant is a major red flag for inflicted injury.
Standard work-up: skeletal survey, ophthalmology, neuroimaging if indicated, coagulation.
Mandatory notification is a legal obligation in all Australian jurisdictions.
Investigation of organic bone disease runs in parallel with safeguarding, not before it.
explanation.pearls: Spiral femoral fracture in a non-mobile infant triggers skeletal survey within 24 hours, retinal exam, coagulation work-up, and statutory notification per RCH CPG; do not delay protection for organic differential workup.

stem:
A 5-day-old breastfed term boy is brought to the paediatric assessment unit by his parents because they noticed yellow skin spreading down to his thighs since yesterday. He was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, weight 3.6 kg at birth and 3.4 kg today (less than 10 percent weight loss). Mother's blood group is O Rh-positive, infant's blood group is A Rh-positive, and the direct antiglobulin test (DAT) is positive.

The infant is alert, feeding 6 to 7 times in 24 hours, with adequate wet and dirty nappies. There is no hepatosplenomegaly and no petechiae. Serum bilirubin at 120 hours of age is 340 micromol/L (unconjugated component 332 micromol/L, conjugated 8 micromol/L). The treatment chart for this gestation and age placed the phototherapy line at 310 micromol/L and the exchange transfusion line at 430 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138 /min, blood pressure 70/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 42 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert and feeding, jaundice extending to thighs (zone 4), no hepatosplenomegaly, no petechiae, normal tone and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: total serum bilirubin 340 micromol/L at 120 hours (phototherapy threshold 310, exchange transfusion threshold 430), unconjugated 332 micromol/L, conjugated 8 micromol/L, DAT positive (ABO incompatibility), full blood count haemoglobin 158 g/L (140-220 newborn) reticulocytes 4.8 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease breastfeeding for 48 hours and substitute infant formula to reduce serum bilirubin levels more rapidly
options.rationale: Breastfeeding cessation is no longer recommended for breast milk jaundice. AU and international guidance continues breastfeeding with supplementation if intake is inadequate. Cessation undermines establishment of lactation. (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.text: Arrange urgent double-volume exchange transfusion because the direct antiglobulin test is positive for ABO incompatibility
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for bilirubin at or above the exchange threshold despite intensive phototherapy, or in the presence of acute bilirubin encephalopathy. The current bilirubin of 340 micromol/L is well below the exchange threshold of 430. (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy and repeat serum bilirubin in 6 hours; continue breastfeeding with supplementation
options.rationale: Total serum bilirubin above the gestational and age-specific phototherapy line, with positive DAT indicating haemolysis, is an indication for intensive phototherapy. AU practice continues breastfeeding (with supplementation if intake is inadequate) and rechecks bilirubin within 6 hours to monitor response. Exchange transfusion is reserved for bilirubin near or above the exchange line despite intensive phototherapy or in the presence of encephalopathy. (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.text: Discharge with home phototherapy biliblanket and review by community paediatrician in the next 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Home phototherapy is reserved for selected lower-risk presentations and is not first choice when bilirubin is above the inpatient phototherapy threshold and there is evidence of haemolysis. Inpatient intensive phototherapy with monitoring is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.text: Reassure the family that the jaundice is physiological and rebook for repeat serum bilirubin in 48 hours time
options.rationale: The bilirubin is above the phototherapy threshold and there is biochemical haemolysis (positive DAT, reticulocytosis). This is not physiological jaundice and observation alone is not appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

explanation.summary: Neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia is managed against gestational age and post-natal age-specific thresholds for phototherapy and exchange transfusion. Above the phototherapy line, intensive phototherapy is commenced with bilirubin rechecked in 6 hours. Exchange transfusion is reserved for levels near or above the exchange threshold despite phototherapy or encephalopathy. Breastfeeding continues throughout.
key_points: Use gestational age + post-natal age treatment threshold charts (e.g. AAP nomogram or RCH paeds jaundice chart).
Intensive phototherapy is first-line above the phototherapy line.
Exchange transfusion is for bilirubin near or above the exchange line, or for encephalopathy.
Continue breastfeeding; supplement if intake is inadequate.
explanation.pearls: Total bilirubin above the gestational and age-specific phototherapy line with positive DAT-driven haemolysis needs intensive phototherapy and a 6-hour bilirubin recheck per RCH CPG; do not cease breastfeeding.

sources.label: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

subtopic_detail: Type 1 diabetes sick day rules - intercurrent illness
stem:
A 13-year-old girl with established Type 1 diabetes (basal-bolus regimen, insulin glargine 18 units nocte and insulin aspart with meals) is brought to the paediatric short-stay unit by her father. She has had vomiting and fever from gastroenteritis for 24 hours. Her father has been omitting her basal insulin because she has not been eating, and he asks whether to continue this approach.

She is alert, mildly dehydrated, tolerating sips, with no abdominal tenderness. Her capillary blood glucose is 16.2 mmol/L and capillary ketones are 1.8 mmol/L. Venous gas shows pH 7.35 and bicarbonate 21 mmol/L. She has not been able to eat solid food but is keeping down water and electrolyte drinks.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 102 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert, mildly dehydrated, capillary refill 2 seconds, mucous membranes slightly dry, abdomen soft and non-tender, no Kussmaul respiration
data_table.Investigations: capillary blood glucose 16.2 mmol/L, capillary ketones 1.8 mmol/L (under 0.6), venous pH 7.35 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 21 mmol/L (22-32), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her insulin regimen?

options.text: Discharge home with antiemetic ondansetron and advice to omit her insulin until she is eating normal meals again
options.rationale: Discharge with insulin omission is unsafe. Sick day rules require continuation of basal insulin, with correction doses for raised ketones, and clear advice to re-present if vomiting worsens or ketones rise. (Source: ISPAD Sick Day Management Guidelines)

options.text: Withhold both basal and bolus insulin while she is not eating and restart once she is tolerating solid food again
options.rationale: Omitting basal insulin is the most common precipitant of DKA in established Type 1 diabetes during intercurrent illness. The insulin requirement is often higher, not lower, during illness because of counter-regulatory hormones. (Source: ISPAD Sick Day Management Guidelines)

options.text: Reduce her basal insulin glargine to half dose because of the reduced oral intake and review again in 12 hours
options.rationale: Reducing basal insulin in the presence of raised ketones and intercurrent illness worsens insulinopenia and risks DKA. The opposite approach (continue basal, add correction doses) is correct. (Source: ISPAD Sick Day Management Guidelines)

options.text: Switch her to an intravenous insulin infusion regardless of acid-base status to ensure reliable insulin delivery
options.rationale: IV insulin infusion is reserved for established DKA (pH below 7.30 or bicarbonate below 18). This patient has ketosis without DKA and can be managed with subcutaneous insulin per sick day rules. (Source: ISPAD Sick Day Management Guidelines)

options.text: Continue usual basal insulin glargine, give rapid-acting aspart correction doses for ketones, substitute carbohydrate fluids
options.rationale: Sick day rules in Type 1 diabetes are explicit: never omit basal insulin even when not eating, give correction doses of rapid-acting insulin (typically 10 to 20 percent of total daily dose) for raised ketones, and substitute meals with sugar-containing fluids if solid food is not tolerated. Omitting basal precipitates DKA. (Source: ISPAD Sick Day Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Sick day rules in Type 1 diabetes mandate continuation of basal insulin throughout intercurrent illness. Rapid-acting insulin correction doses are added for raised ketones (typically 10 to 20 percent of total daily dose). Meals are substituted with sugar-containing fluids when solid food is not tolerated. Omitting basal insulin is the most common precipitant of DKA in established disease and the most important sick day error to correct in parents.
key_points: Never omit basal insulin during illness.
Correction doses with rapid-acting insulin: 10 to 20 percent of total daily dose when ketones above 1.5 mmol/L.
Substitute meals with sugar-containing fluids if not tolerating solids.
Re-present for vomiting, rising ketones, abdominal pain, or drowsiness.
explanation.pearls: T1DM sick day rules: continue basal insulin, give 10 to 20 percent total daily dose as rapid-acting correction for ketones, substitute carbohydrate-containing fluids for solid meals; omitting basal is the most common DKA precipitant.

stem:
A 13-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with 3 hours of severe right-sided scrotal pain that began at school. The pain came on suddenly while he was sitting in class. He has vomited once. He has no urinary symptoms, no fever, and no preceding illness. There is no history of trauma.

On examination the right testis is high-riding and lies in a horizontal axis. There is marked tenderness on palpation. The cremasteric reflex is absent on the right. The left testis is normal. The urinary tract is otherwise normal. The on-call paediatric surgical registrar is contactable and in the hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 124/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: right testis high-riding with horizontal lie, marked tenderness, absent cremasteric reflex on right, left testis normal, no scrotal erythema
data_table.Investigations: urinalysis no leucocytes no nitrites, full blood count haemoglobin 138 g/L white cells 9.4 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent scrotal ultrasound with colour Doppler before deciding on surgical exploration
options.rationale: Doppler ultrasound has good sensitivity but is operator-dependent and false-negative results occur. When the clinical picture is classic for torsion, surgical exploration is not delayed for imaging. Ultrasound is reserved for equivocal cases. (Source: AUA paediatric urology guidance)

options.text: Urgent referral to paediatric surgery for scrotal exploration and orchidopexy
options.rationale: Sudden-onset severe testicular pain with high-riding horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex is testicular torsion until proven otherwise. Surgical exploration must occur within 6 hours of symptom onset to maximise testicular salvage. Imaging that delays surgery is unsafe; clinical diagnosis triggers theatre directly. (Source: AUA paediatric urology guidance; RCH CPG Acute scrotum)

options.text: Commence oral cefalexin 500 mg twice daily for empirical epididymo-orchitis and review in 24 hours
options.rationale: Epididymo-orchitis typically has a more gradual onset, urinary symptoms, and a normal cremasteric reflex. Antibiotic trial in a presentation classic for torsion wastes the salvage window. (Source: AUA paediatric urology guidance)

options.text: Attempt manual detorsion at the bedside and admit for surgical orchidopexy in the morning
options.rationale: Manual detorsion can be considered when there is a substantial delay before theatre, but it is not a substitute for surgical exploration; success rate is variable and confirmation of resolution still requires operative fixation of both testes within the same admission. (Source: AUA paediatric urology guidance)

options.text: Administer simple analgesia and discharge with general practitioner review in 1 to 2 days
options.rationale: Discharge from the emergency department for a high-suspicion torsion presentation is unsafe and leads to testicular loss. (Source: RCH CPG Acute scrotum)

explanation.summary: Sudden-onset severe testicular pain with high-riding horizontal lie and absent cremasteric reflex is testicular torsion. Surgical exploration within 6 hours of symptom onset maximises salvage; imaging or antibiotic trial is not appropriate when the clinical picture is typical. Both testes are fixed at surgery because of the bell-clapper anatomy.
key_points: Classic torsion: sudden pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex.
Salvage window is best within 6 hours of symptom onset.
Doppler ultrasound is reserved for equivocal presentations.
Both testes are fixed at surgery due to bell-clapper anomaly.
explanation.pearls: Testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis; take to theatre for scrotal exploration and bilateral orchidopexy within 6 hours of symptom onset rather than delaying for Doppler ultrasound.

stem:
A 14-month-old boy is brought to the paediatric emergency department on day 6 of a fever that has reached 39.4 degrees twice daily and has not responded to regular paracetamol. The parents report a blotchy red rash that came up on his trunk on day 3 and his hands now look puffy. He has been miserable, off feeds, and clingy.

On examination he is well perfused but irritable. There is bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection sparing the limbus, a strawberry-coloured tongue with cracked lips, a polymorphous trunk rash, and a single 1.8 cm right cervical lymph node. The throat is mildly erythematous without exudate or palatal petechiae. Capillary return is brisk. There is no recent overseas travel.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 158, blood pressure 92/54, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 102 g/L (105-135), platelets 612 x10^9/L (150-450), white cells 18.4 x10^9/L (5-15), CRP 142 mg/L (<5), ESR 78 mm/hr, albumin 28 g/L (35-50), ALT 92 U/L (<40), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), urinalysis sterile pyuria, throat swab pending, rapid strep antigen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours with oral aspirin 30 mg/kg per day in four divided doses
options.rationale: Five clinical criteria are met (fever five or more days, bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oropharyngeal changes, polymorphous rash, hand swelling, cervical node greater than 1.5 cm) supported by classical adjunctive laboratory findings (CRP > 30, platelets > 450, albumin < 30, sterile pyuria, transaminitis, normocytic anaemia). IVIG within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from around 25 percent to under 5 percent. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg twice daily for ten days under a working diagnosis of streptococcal scarlet fever
options.rationale: Bacterial scarlet fever is excluded by the absent exudative pharyngitis, negative rapid strep antigen, and the constellation of mucocutaneous features. Oral cefalexin delays IVIG and exposes the child to ongoing coronary artery inflammation. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Arrange outpatient transthoracic echocardiography in two weeks and continue regular paracetamol with parental safety netting
options.rationale: Outpatient deferral allows coronary artery inflammation to evolve unchecked. Echocardiography is part of the diagnostic workup but does not replace prompt IVIG when clinical criteria are met. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for three days as monotherapy without concurrent immunoglobulin
options.rationale: High dose corticosteroids are reserved for IVIG resistance or for primary therapy intensification in high risk cases (Kobayashi-style scoring is not validated outside Japanese populations). Steroid monotherapy without IVIG is not standard primary therapy in Australia. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Send blood cultures and start intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg every six hours for presumed staphylococcal toxin illness
options.rationale: Staphylococcal scalded skin or toxic shock would show bullae or hypotension and the rash pattern here is the polymorphous exanthem of Kawasaki. Flucloxacillin treats neither Kawasaki nor the small chance of group A streptococcal disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis of young children whose most feared complication is coronary artery aneurysm. The classical criteria are fever five or more days plus four of: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, oropharyngeal changes, extremity changes, and cervical node greater than 1.5 cm. Incomplete Kawasaki (two or three features plus supportive labs) is treated identically. IVIG 2 g/kg plus high dose aspirin within ten days of fever onset is the Australian standard.
key_points: Fever five or more days plus four classical features (or two or three plus supportive labs) triggers IVIG
Aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg per day in four divided doses until fever resolves, then 3 to 5 mg/kg per day for six to eight weeks
Coronary aneurysm risk falls from around 25 percent to under 5 percent with timely IVIG
Baseline and six to eight week echocardiography is mandatory
Sterile pyuria, transaminitis, low albumin, and high platelets support the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: If IVIG is given within 10 days of fever onset the absolute risk of coronary artery aneurysm at six to eight week echo drops from roughly 25 percent (untreated) to under 5 percent.

stem:
A 3-year-old previously well girl is brought to a regional emergency department with three days of fever to 39.6 degrees, a wet cough, and the parents say she is breathing fast and has stopped drinking from her cup. She has had no vomiting and her last wet nappy was four hours ago.

On examination she is alert but tachypnoeic with mild subcostal recession. Auscultation reveals reduced breath sounds and bronchial breathing at the right base with crackles audible into the mid zone. The left chest is clear. Capillary return is two seconds and mucous membranes are moist. There is no stridor or wheeze, and no rash. She is immunised on schedule including 13-valent pneumococcal and Haemophilus vaccines.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 142, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 48, SpO2 92 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: chest radiograph confirms right lower lobe consolidation without effusion, point of care blood gas within normal limits, capillary glucose 4.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit, commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg every six hours, and supplemental oxygen titrated to SpO2 92 percent
options.rationale: Australian first line inpatient therapy for typical bacterial CAP in a vaccinated child is intravenous benzylpenicillin; switch to oral amoxicillin once afebrile for 24 to 48 hours. The SpO2 of 92 percent with feeding compromise and tachypnoea satisfies admission criteria. (Source: RCH CPG: Community Acquired Pneumonia)

options.text: Discharge home on oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily for five days with general practice review at 48 hours
options.rationale: Hypoxia (SpO2 less than 93 percent), tachypnoea above 50 in this age band, and reduced oral intake mandate inpatient management under RCH criteria. Oral therapy is appropriate only when these admission triggers are absent. (Source: RCH CPG: Community Acquired Pneumonia)

options.text: Admit and commence intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily as monotherapy for empirical broad spectrum cover
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is reserved for severe disease, suspected resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae, complications such as empyema, or failure of penicillin therapy. Routine empirical use drives resistance and is not first line in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit and commence intravenous azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily as monotherapy targeting atypical bacterial pathogens
options.rationale: Mycoplasma is uncommon under five years and lobar consolidation favours typical bacterial pathogens. Macrolide monotherapy misses Streptococcus pneumoniae and is not first line in this age band. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit on intravenous fluids alone and withhold antibiotics pending respiratory viral PCR and procalcitonin results
options.rationale: Withholding antibiotics in a hypoxic febrile child with lobar consolidation risks progression and empyema. Viral PCR and procalcitonin are adjuncts and do not justify treatment delay. (Source: RCH CPG: Community Acquired Pneumonia)

explanation.summary: Paediatric community acquired pneumonia is most often pneumococcal in vaccinated under-five Australians. Admission triggers under RCH guidance include SpO2 less than 92 percent, significant respiratory distress, dehydration or inability to feed, and toxic appearance. Inpatient first line therapy is intravenous benzylpenicillin, switching to oral amoxicillin once afebrile for 24 to 48 hours. Reserve ceftriaxone for complicated disease or treatment failure.
key_points: Admission criteria: SpO2 < 92 percent, severe distress, dehydration, toxic appearance, age under 3 months, or social concerns
Inpatient first line: IV benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg every six hours
Step down to oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily once afebrile for 24 to 48 hours
Total course 5 to 7 days for uncomplicated lobar pneumonia
Add macrolide if atypical features (school age, dry cough, headache, interstitial pattern)
explanation.pearls: Reduced breath sounds with stony dullness despite IV benzylpenicillin for 48 hours prompts urgent chest ultrasound to detect early parapneumonic effusion before clinical decompensation.

stem:
A 9-month-old infant is brought to a tertiary emergency department with a 14 hour history of episodic distress. The parents describe him going pale and pulling his legs up, screaming for 90 seconds, then becoming floppy and quiet between episodes. He has now had two soft jelly-like dark red stools in his nappy and refused his last two feeds.

On examination he is pale but rouseable. The abdomen is soft with a faintly palpable long thin lump in the right upper quadrant. Bowel sounds are present. There are no peritonitic signs and no abdominal distension. Capillary return is two seconds. He has had no recent gastroenteritis or upper respiratory infection. There is no Henoch-Schonlein purpura rash.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 144, blood pressure 88/52, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.36 base excess negative 2, lactate 1.8 mmol/L, point of care abdominal ultrasound shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant with no free fluid and preserved bowel wall echogenicity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge after a normal abdominal radiograph with paracetamol and family safety netting about red flag symptoms
options.rationale: Abdominal radiography is insensitive for intussusception and discharge is unsafe with the diagnosis already confirmed on ultrasound. Untreated ileocolic intussusception progresses to bowel ischaemia within 24 to 48 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Arrange immediate laparotomy with paediatric surgery without prior attempt at radiological reduction by air enema
options.rationale: Primary laparotomy is reserved for peritonism, perforation on imaging, shock that does not respond to resuscitation, or failed radiological reduction. None of these are present here. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Resuscitate with 20 mL/kg saline, place a nasogastric tube on drainage, and arrange image guided air enema reduction
options.rationale: Air enema reduction under fluoroscopic guidance is the first line treatment for ileocolic intussusception in a haemodynamically stable child without peritonism or perforation. Success rates exceed 80 percent and surgery is reserved for failure or complications. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Admit for 24 hours nil by mouth with maintenance intravenous fluids and reassessment by surgical team in the morning
options.rationale: Observation alone allows ongoing bowel ischaemia. Definitive reduction must occur as soon as resuscitation allows. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Commence intravenous metronidazole and gentamicin and proceed to immediate diagnostic laparoscopy regardless of imaging
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics and primary laparoscopy bypass radiological reduction which is non-invasive and highly effective. Antibiotics are added only when perforation or established sepsis is suspected. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Intussusception is the commonest abdominal emergency between three months and three years. The classic triad of colicky pain, palpable mass, and redcurrant stools occurs in fewer than 20 percent, so a high index of suspicion is needed. Ultrasound is the diagnostic test of choice (target or doughnut sign). Air enema reduction succeeds in 80 to 90 percent of stable children, with surgery reserved for failure, perforation, peritonism, or pathological lead points.
key_points: Peak incidence 3 months to 3 years; ileocolic most common
Ultrasound target sign is the diagnostic test
Air enema first line if stable, no peritonism, no perforation
Nasogastric decompression and 20 mL/kg fluid bolus before reduction
Recurrence after enema reduction is around 10 percent and may need repeat enema or surgery
explanation.pearls: After successful air enema reduction at the RCH, recurrence within 72 hours is around 10 percent, so admit for at least 24 hours of observation rather than same-day discharge.

stem:
A 7-week-old infant is brought to a metropolitan emergency department because the mother noticed bruising on his right cheek and a swollen left thigh. The family attended a community drop-in immunisation clinic earlier the same day and the nurse there raised concerns. There is no reported trauma. The mother is 19, the partner she lives with is not the biological father, and the social history records financial stress and recent eviction.

On examination the infant is alert and feeding well. There is a 2 cm purple bruise on the right zygoma and a 4 cm fusiform swelling over the mid left thigh with reluctance to weight-bear when held vertically. Fundi are clear. There is no rash, no birthmarks, and the fontanelle is soft. The remainder of the systemic examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Investigations: skeletal survey not yet performed, full blood count and coagulation studies within normal limits, capillary glucose 4.6 mmol/L, urinalysis sterile, paediatric early warning score zero

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with general practitioner review in 48 hours and a safety net to return if any new bruising appears
options.rationale: Bruising in a pre-mobile infant is a sentinel injury for non-accidental injury and discharge is unsafe. Cumulative risk of further inflicted injury or death within months of a missed sentinel bruise is well described. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Reassure that bruising is common at this age, request iron studies, and arrange community paediatrician review
options.rationale: Bruising in a non-cruising infant is not normal and iron studies have no diagnostic role. Outpatient deferral allows continued exposure to a potentially unsafe environment. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Request coagulation screen and platelet function tests before deciding whether to notify the child protection authority
options.rationale: Coagulation studies are part of the workup but do not delay mandatory reporting. Statutory notification is triggered by reasonable suspicion, not by exclusion of bleeding disorders. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Admit, notify statutory child protection, request skeletal survey, retinal examination, head imaging, and social work
options.rationale: Bruising in a pre-mobile infant ('those who don't cruise rarely bruise') mandates reporting to the state child protection service and a complete non-accidental injury workup including skeletal survey, retinal examination, head imaging, and consideration of a coagulation screen. Australian medical practitioners are mandated reporters in every state and territory. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Discuss the bruising openly with the mother and notify child protection only if she fails to give a plausible account
options.rationale: Statutory notification is mandatory once reasonable suspicion arises and does not require parental admission or denial. Delaying notification undermines the protective intent of the legislation. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: Australian doctors are mandated reporters of suspected child abuse under state and territory legislation. Bruising in a pre-mobile infant is a sentinel injury and demands a structured non-accidental injury workup: skeletal survey (repeat in two weeks), retinal examination by ophthalmology, head imaging, coagulation screen, and social work involvement. Reasonable suspicion, not proof, is the threshold for notification.
key_points: Pre-mobile infants ('those who don't cruise rarely bruise') with bruising warrant a full NAI workup
Notify state child protection on reasonable suspicion - not after exclusion of bleeding diatheses
Skeletal survey is standard; repeat in two weeks improves sensitivity for healing fractures
Document carefully, photograph injuries with consent, escalate to senior paediatrics and social work
Coagulation studies and platelet function tests run in parallel, not before reporting
explanation.pearls: In Australian state law (including Children and Young People Act variants), the threshold for mandatory notification is reasonable suspicion of significant harm - higher than 'possible' but lower than 'probable on the balance of probabilities'.

sources.label: RACGP: Abuse and violence working with our patients in general practice

stem:
