A previously well 22-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after his parents found him pale and unresponsive in his cot at 6 am. He vomited twice the previous evening and went to bed without his usual milk. Paramedics measured a capillary glucose of 1.6 mmol/L and gave 2 mL/kg of 10 percent dextrose with rapid recovery of consciousness. He has had no previous similar episodes and is on the 25th centile for weight.

On examination he is now alert and playful. There is no hepatomegaly, no Cushingoid features, no hyperpigmentation, and no midline defects. Tone, reflexes, and cranial nerves are normal. The parents say he refused dinner because of the gastroenteritis but the older sister recovered without low sugars. Vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Investigations: critical sample drawn at glucose 1.6 mmol/L: ketones (3-hydroxybutyrate) 4.2 mmol/L, free fatty acids 2.6 mmol/L, insulin <2 mU/L, C-peptide <0.1 nmol/L, cortisol 612 nmol/L, growth hormone 18 mcg/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, ammonia 38 micromol/L (10-50), urine organic acids and acylcarnitine profile pending

lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Medium chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency presenting at this age
options.rationale: MCAD presents with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia because fatty acid oxidation is blocked. The high 3-hydroxybutyrate effectively excludes a fatty acid oxidation defect at presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Congenital hyperinsulinism due to a sulfonylurea receptor (KATP channel) mutation
options.rationale: Hyperinsulinism produces hypoketotic and non-lipolytic hypoglycaemia with detectable insulin and C-peptide at the time of low glucose. The high ketones, free fatty acids, and suppressed insulin here exclude this. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycaemia of childhood with appropriate counter-regulation
options.rationale: Fasting hypoglycaemia with appropriate ketosis and lipolysis, suppressed insulin and C-peptide, and a robust cortisol and growth hormone response is the textbook profile of idiopathic ketotic hypoglycaemia, peak age 18 months to 5 years. The provocation (vomiting and reduced overnight intake in a thin toddler) fits. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Glycogen storage disease type 1 (von Gierke) with subclinical hepatomegaly
options.rationale: GSD1 features hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis with hypoglycaemia, and elevated triglycerides and uric acid. Absent hepatomegaly and a normal lactate at the time of hypoglycaemia argue against this diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Adrenal insufficiency with subclinical cortisol deficiency exacerbated by vomiting
options.rationale: Adrenal insufficiency produces hypoglycaemia with an inappropriately low cortisol (under 500 nmol/L) at the time of the event. The cortisol of 612 nmol/L documents a normal stress response. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: The 'critical sample' drawn at the moment of hypoglycaemia is the most informative investigation in a paediatric hypoglycaemia workup because it preserves the metabolic snapshot. Appropriate ketosis with suppressed insulin and intact counter-regulation defines idiopathic ketotic hypoglycaemia, a diagnosis of exclusion peaking between 18 months and 5 years and self-limiting by school age. The cornerstone of management is avoidance of prolonged fasting and early carbohydrate during intercurrent illness.
key_points: Critical sample: glucose, ketones, free fatty acids, insulin, C-peptide, cortisol, GH, lactate, ammonia, urine organic acids, acylcarnitines
Hyperinsulinism: hypoketotic, hypo-lipolytic, detectable insulin/C-peptide
Fatty acid oxidation defect: hypoketotic with high free fatty acids
GSD1: hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperlipidaemia
Adrenal insufficiency: cortisol < 500 nmol/L at the time of hypoglycaemia
explanation.pearls: Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycaemia is a diagnosis of exclusion - if hypoglycaemia first occurs after age 5, MCAD or another fatty acid oxidation disorder must be actively excluded by acylcarnitine profile and urine organic acids before applying the label.

sources.label: APEG: Paediatric Endocrine Society of Australia (APEG) Hypoglycaemia

stem:
A 9-year-old girl presents to a tertiary paediatric emergency department with two weeks of fatigue, polyuria, and nocturnal wetting, and one day of vomiting. The mother says she has lost weight despite eating more, and today she looked drowsy. There is no recent overseas travel and no family history of diabetes.

On examination she is drowsy but rouseable, breathing deeply, with dry mucous membranes and capillary return three seconds. There is no abdominal tenderness, no rash, and no signs of cerebral oedema. Pulse rate 132, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 36, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees. Her actual body weight on arrival is 28 kg. A point of care capillary blood gas confirms a severe metabolic acidosis with hyperglycaemia and high ketones.

data_table.Investigations: venous pH 7.06, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, base excess negative 22, glucose 28 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.8 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145) corrected sodium 138, potassium 4.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 9.2 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, urinalysis 4+ glucose 4+ ketones

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid plan in the first hour?

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg saline bolus over 15 minutes then commence intravenous insulin infusion immediately at 0.1 units/kg/hour
options.rationale: Rapid 20 mL/kg boluses are reserved for shock; this child has compensated tachycardia and capillary refill three seconds (consistent with around 7 to 10 percent dehydration but not shocked). Bolusing 20 mL/kg over 15 minutes risks cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guidelines)

options.text: Replace the calculated fluid deficit over six hours alongside maintenance fluids to correct dehydration rapidly
options.rationale: The total deficit plus maintenance is replaced evenly over 48 hours in paediatric DKA. Six hour replacement accelerates osmotic shifts and increases the risk of cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guidelines)

options.text: Commence intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately without preceding fluid bolus resuscitation
options.rationale: Insulin before adequate fluid resuscitation causes a rapid intracellular potassium shift, intravascular volume depletion, and increases cerebral oedema risk. Australian protocols require fluid first and insulin no earlier than one hour after fluid commencement. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guidelines)

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 60 minutes to correct severe acidaemia before any other intervention
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA except in life-threatening hyperkalaemia or cardiac arrest unresponsive to standard resuscitation. It worsens cerebral oedema and paradoxical CSF acidosis. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guidelines)

options.text: Give a 10 mL/kg saline bolus over 30 to 60 minutes, withhold insulin for the first hour, and reassess perfusion at one hour
options.rationale: APEG/ISPAD-aligned RCH protocols give a single 10 mL/kg saline bolus over 30 to 60 minutes for moderate to severe DKA without shock, withhold insulin for the first hour to allow rehydration, then commence insulin at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour. This minimises rapid osmotic shifts and cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA is defined by pH less than 7.3 or bicarbonate less than 15, hyperglycaemia, and ketonaemia. The greatest threat is cerebral oedema, which carries roughly 25 percent mortality and 35 percent neurological morbidity. Modern Australian protocols (APEG, RCH) align with ISPAD: cautious rehydration with one 10 mL/kg saline bolus (only repeat for shock), insulin no earlier than one hour after fluid commencement at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour, deficit replacement over 48 hours, hourly neuro observations, and bicarbonate only for arrest or severe hyperkalaemia.
key_points: Diagnose DKA: pH < 7.3 or bicarbonate < 15, glucose > 11, ketones > 3 mmol/L
Single 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus for moderate-severe DKA without shock
Insulin 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour from one hour after fluid started
Replace deficit plus maintenance evenly over 48 hours
Cerebral oedema warning signs: headache, falling Glasgow Coma Score, hypertension, bradycardia - give 2.7 percent saline or mannitol immediately
explanation.pearls: Cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA peaks 4 to 12 hours after starting fluids - hourly neurological observations and a low threshold for hypertonic saline 2.7 percent at 2.5 to 5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg are mandatory.

stem:
A 24-day-old term infant is brought to the emergency department with a temperature recorded at home of 38.4 degrees and one day of poor feeding. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, exclusively breastfed, and gained weight at the maternal child health nurse review three days ago. There has been no rash, no vomiting, and the mother had no fevers or rash in pregnancy. The maternal Group B Streptococcus swab at 36 weeks was negative.

On examination he is alert but reduced in spontaneous movement. The anterior fontanelle is soft. There is no rash, no bulging fontanelle, no clinical jaundice, and capillary return is two seconds. The chest is clear, the abdomen is soft without organomegaly, and the umbilical stump is dry. Vital signs are within normal limits except temperature 38.2 degrees.

data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.36 lactate 2.0 mmol/L, capillary glucose 3.6 mmol/L, urinalysis nitrites negative leucocytes negative, paired blood cultures and urine sent, chest radiograph clear, viral respiratory panel pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Observe in short stay, repeat temperature in two hours, and discharge with general practice review if cultures negative
options.rationale: Infants under three months with fever cannot be discharged based on a single short observation. Bacterial meningitis and bacteraemia are missed by relying on clinical appearance alone in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant)

options.text: Admit, perform lumbar puncture, take blood and urine cultures, and start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin covers Group B Streptococcus and Listeria but provides inadequate cover for Gram negative meningitis in a four week old. RCH and Therapeutic Guidelines specify cefotaxime (with amoxicillin/ampicillin for Listeria cover if under one month) as the empirical choice. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant)

options.text: Admit, take blood and urine cultures, start intravenous flucloxacillin and gentamicin, and defer the lumbar puncture
options.rationale: Deferring lumbar puncture in a febrile infant under three months risks missing meningitis (cell counts and protein normalise within hours of antibiotic exposure). Flucloxacillin/gentamicin misses pneumococcal and listerial cover. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant)

options.text: Admit, perform lumbar puncture, take blood and urine cultures, and start intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin
options.rationale: Infants under four weeks with fever require a full septic workup including lumbar puncture and empirical intravenous cefotaxime plus amoxicillin or benzylpenicillin to cover Listeria monocytogenes (which is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins). After 4 weeks, cefotaxime monotherapy is generally adequate. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant)

options.text: Send respiratory virus polymerase chain reaction panel and discharge if positive for any seasonal respiratory virus
options.rationale: A positive viral PCR does not exclude concurrent serious bacterial infection in this age group; up to 7 percent of febrile infants under three months with a positive viral PCR also have a serious bacterial infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant)

explanation.summary: Any infant under three months with a documented fever of 38.0 degrees or above requires a full septic workup (full blood count, blood culture, urine culture, lumbar puncture, chest radiograph if respiratory features) and empirical intravenous antibiotics in Australia. The pathogen profile is age dependent: Group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, and Listeria dominate under one month; pneumococcus and meningococcus rise after one month. Cefotaxime plus amoxicillin (Listeria cover) is the empirical regimen for under-four-weeks; cefotaxime alone after that.
key_points: Fever 38.0 or above under three months mandates full septic workup including LP
Under 4 weeks: cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 6 to 8 hours plus amoxicillin or benzylpenicillin for Listeria
4 weeks to 3 months: cefotaxime alone usually adequate; reassess for Listeria risk
Positive viral PCR does NOT exclude concurrent serious bacterial infection
Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid alone is inadequate; cephalosporins do not cover Listeria
explanation.pearls: Listeria monocytogenes is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins - cover Listeria with amoxicillin or benzylpenicillin in any febrile infant under four weeks, even when cefotaxime is already running.

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is referred from a regional emergency department on day 12 of a quotidian fever spiking to 40 degrees once daily, with a salmon-coloured rash that comes and goes with the temperature. He has had two doses of IVIG and high-dose aspirin at his local hospital under a presumptive diagnosis of incomplete Kawasaki disease, but his fevers have not resolved.

On arrival to the tertiary centre he is irritable, pale, with hepatosplenomegaly and a non-tender right knee effusion. A baseline echocardiogram from day 7 was reported as normal coronary arteries. There is no conjunctival injection, no oral changes, no peripheral oedema, and no cervical lymphadenopathy now. The salmon rash appears during a temperature spike during the assessment and fades as the fever settles two hours later.

data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 88 g/L (110-145), platelets 142 x10^9/L falling from 612 a week ago, white cells 24.6 x10^9/L (5-15) neutrophils 19.8, ferritin 18400 mcg/L (15-150), triglycerides 4.8 mmol/L (<2.3), fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (1.5-4), AST 412 U/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), CRP 96 mg/L, ESR 12 mm/hr disproportionately low for CRP, D-dimer 8.6 mg/L

lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Immunoglobulin resistant complete Kawasaki disease needing second dose immunoglobulin and infliximab
options.rationale: Persistent quotidian fever with evanescent rash and falling ESR despite rising ferritin is not the Kawasaki pattern, and the absence of mucocutaneous features now (with normal coronaries on day 7) argues against KD. IVIG resistance in true KD would still show coronary inflammation or partial mucocutaneous response. (Source: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA)
source_refs: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA

options.text: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis complicated by macrophage activation syndrome
options.rationale: Quotidian fever with evanescent salmon rash, hepatosplenomegaly, an inflammatory knee effusion, IVIG resistance, and the laboratory signature of MAS (extreme hyperferritinaemia, falling platelets and ESR, rising triglycerides, falling fibrinogen, transaminitis, hyponatraemia) define sJIA-MAS. The 'paradoxical fall' in ESR with persistently high ferritin is highly suggestive. (Source: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA)
source_refs: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA

options.text: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia with diffuse bone marrow infiltration and cytokine release
options.rationale: ALL typically produces pancytopenia with circulating blasts, marrow failure, and bone pain rather than the inflammatory cytokine storm shown here. The neutrophilia of 19.8, very high ferritin, and triglyceride rise fit MAS, not leukaemia. (Source: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA)
source_refs: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA

options.text: Visceral leishmaniasis complicated by secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
options.rationale: Visceral leishmaniasis is rare in non-endemic Australian children and the absence of travel history makes it improbable. Secondary HLH from infection would still need Leishmania exposure that is not described. (Source: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA)
source_refs: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA

options.text: Periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, and adenitis syndrome decompensation
options.rationale: PFAPA presents with recurrent stereotyped fever episodes (every 3 to 6 weeks lasting 3 to 5 days) with pharyngitis, aphthous ulcers, and adenitis - a fundamentally different temporal pattern with normal laboratories between episodes. (Source: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA)
source_refs: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA

explanation.summary: Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS, secondary HLH) complicates around 10 percent of systemic JIA. The diagnostic signature is extreme hyperferritinaemia (often greater than 10000 mcg/L), a paradoxical fall in ESR despite high CRP, falling platelets and white cells, rising triglycerides, falling fibrinogen, transaminitis, and hyponatraemia. Untreated mortality approaches 20 percent. First line treatment is pulse methylprednisolone with anakinra (IL-1 blocker) as steroid-sparing; ciclosporin is added for refractory disease. Recognition requires actively considering MAS in any sJIA child with worsening fever, falling counts, or rising ferritin.
key_points: Quotidian (once daily) fever with evanescent salmon rash is sJIA
MAS signature: ferritin > 10000, falling ESR with rising CRP, low fibrinogen, high triglycerides, transaminitis, hyponatraemia
First line MAS: IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg/day pulses with anakinra 2 to 4 mg/kg/day
Differentiated from KD by quotidian fever, evanescent rash, lack of coronary involvement, IVIG resistance
PRINTO 2016 MAS classification criteria operationalise the laboratory pattern
explanation.pearls: Ferritin above 10000 mcg/L in a child with persistent inflammation has a positive likelihood ratio above 50 for MAS - escalate to pulse methylprednisolone and anakinra without waiting for bone marrow haemophagocytosis.

sources.label: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA
RCH CPG: Fever of Unknown Origin

stem:
A 22-month-old boy is brought to a regional emergency department at 2 a.m. by his parents who describe a barking cough and a hoarse cry starting earlier the previous evening and worsening overnight.

On examination he has audible inspiratory stridor at rest with mild intercostal recession but no tracheal tug and no nasal flaring. Air entry is symmetrical with no wheeze. He looks tired but engages with his parents and drinks half a cup of water in front of you. There is no drooling, no toxic appearance, and no history of a choking episode. Vaccinations including Haemophilus influenzae type b are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 140, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 36, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer a single oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg dose and observe in the department with clinical reassessment after thirty minutes
options.rationale: Stridor at rest with only mild recession in a child who is alert, drinking, and not exhausted classifies as moderate croup, for which RCH recommends a single 0.15 mg/kg dose of oral dexamethasone with observation; the 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Administer a single oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg dose and arrange immediate paediatric intensive care review by phone
options.rationale: The 0.6 mg/kg dose and intensive care notification are reserved for severe croup with marked recession, tracheal tug, exhaustion, or cyanosis. This child does not meet those criteria. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 and admit for a minimum four hour observation period after the dose
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is for severe croup; mild and moderate disease do not require it. RCH specifies a minimum three hour observation period (not four) after the last nebulised adrenaline dose. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Discharge home on oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for three days with general practice review the next morning
options.rationale: Prednisolone has higher relapse and re-presentation rates than single dose dexamethasone for croup and is not preferred in the RCH protocol. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Arrange urgent retrieval to a tertiary centre for elective intubation and direct laryngoscopy in theatre
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for impending respiratory failure with exhaustion or cyanosis despite nebulised adrenaline. This child is alert, drinking, and saturating well. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup severity in Australian paediatric practice is graded by stridor pattern, work of breathing, and conscious state. Mild and moderate croup get a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg. Severe croup gets dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline and intensive monitoring. After nebulised adrenaline, observe for at least three hours to detect rebound stridor before discharge.
key_points: Mild and moderate croup: oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose
Severe croup: oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000
Minimum three hour observation after last nebulised adrenaline
Prednisolone is inferior to dexamethasone (higher relapse)
Drooling or stridor with toxic appearance suggests epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis instead
explanation.pearls: Stridor at rest with mild recession but a smiling drinking child is moderate croup and the correct dexamethasone dose is 0.15 mg/kg, not 0.6 mg/kg.

stem:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to a metropolitan emergency department with 24 hours of watery diarrhoea up to ten times and three episodes of non-bilious vomiting. Her parents have offered sips of oral rehydration solution at home but she has refused most of it and only had one wet nappy in the last six hours.

On examination she is mildly drowsy but rouseable. Mucous membranes are tacky, eyes are slightly sunken, and capillary return is between two and three seconds peripherally. There is no abdominal distension, no peritonism, and no rash. She weighs 11 kg. There is no recent overseas travel, no antibiotic exposure, and no household member with similar symptoms beyond expected viral gastroenteritis circulating at her childcare.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 138, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees
data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas within normal limits, capillary glucose 4.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Insert two large bore intravenous cannulae and commence a 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9 percent saline over fifteen minutes followed by maintenance
options.rationale: Rapid intravenous bolus rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration with shock features (prolonged capillary return greater than three seconds, hypotension, depressed conscious state). This child has mild to moderate dehydration. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Discharge home on small frequent oral rehydration solution sips with safety netting advice and review by general practitioner within 24 hours
options.rationale: Home oral rehydration has already failed because of vomiting and refusal. Discharging without an in-department intervention risks ongoing decline and a repeat presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Administer a single 2 mg dose of oral ondansetron wafer and insert a nasogastric tube for rapid enteral rehydration over four hours
options.rationale: Single dose ondansetron (2 mg for 8 to 15 kg per RCH) reduces vomiting and admission rates. Nasogastric rehydration is first line for mild to moderate dehydration with failed oral therapy and is non-inferior to intravenous fluids while avoiding cannulation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Commence oral loperamide 0.1 mg/kg three times daily and continue oral rehydration solution as tolerated at home
options.rationale: Anti-motility agents are contraindicated in paediatric gastroenteritis because of the risk of toxic megacolon and masking of bacterial colitis. They have no role in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Send stool for multiplex polymerase chain reaction and commence empirical oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for five days
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are not indicated in suspected viral gastroenteritis without bloody stool, sepsis, or specific risk factors. Stool PCR does not change immediate rehydration management. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric gastroenteritis rehydration in Australia follows a stepped pathway based on dehydration severity. Mild to moderate dehydration that fails oral rehydration solution at home is treated in hospital with nasogastric rehydration as first line. A single dose of ondansetron facilitates oral or nasogastric tolerance. Intravenous fluids are reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or nasogastric failure.
key_points: Mild-moderate dehydration that fails oral: nasogastric rehydration is first line
Single dose oral ondansetron: 2 mg for 8 to 15 kg, 4 mg for 15 to 30 kg
Intravenous fluids only for severe dehydration, shock, or nasogastric failure
Anti-motility agents (loperamide) are contraindicated
Empirical antibiotics not indicated for routine viral gastroenteritis
explanation.pearls: Failed home oral rehydration solution plus moderate dehydration is the textbook indication for a single 2 mg ondansetron wafer plus nasogastric rehydration over four hours, not intravenous cannulation.

subtopic_detail: Anaphylaxis adrenaline dose by weight band
stem:
A 4-year-old girl is brought urgently to a metropolitan emergency department after eating a cashew biscuit at a birthday party. Within ten minutes her parents noticed lip swelling and a hoarse cry, and ambulance was called when she became wheezy and floppy in their arms en route.

On examination she is pale and lethargic with widespread urticaria and lip and tongue swelling. There is audible expiratory wheeze, mild intercostal recession, and a hoarse voice. Capillary return is three seconds and pulses are weak. She has no known prior reactions and no asthma diagnosis. Weight is documented as 16 kg from a clinic visit last week. There is no other ingestion and no recent infection. Intramuscular adrenaline has not yet been administered.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 168, blood pressure 78/40, respiratory rate 40, SpO2 91 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate adrenaline dose?

options.text: Administer intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms per kilogram of 1:10000 solution into the deltoid muscle and repeat after five minutes
options.rationale: Anaphylaxis adrenaline is 1:1000, not 1:10000, and the ASCIA banded dosing table is preferred over per-kilogram arithmetic to reduce dosing error in the resuscitation environment. (Source: ASCIA Acute Anaphylaxis Clinical Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms of 1:1000 solution into the anterolateral thigh and repeat after ten minutes if needed
options.rationale: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1:1000) is the adult and over 50 kg dose. A 16 kg child receives 150 micrograms by the ASCIA banded table. (Source: ASCIA Acute Anaphylaxis Clinical Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intravenous adrenaline 1 microgram per kilogram of 1:10000 solution over one minute and titrate an infusion as required
options.rationale: Intravenous adrenaline is reserved for cardiac arrest or refractory anaphylaxis on a senior clinician decision. Intramuscular adrenaline is first line and faster to deliver. (Source: ASCIA Acute Anaphylaxis Clinical Guidelines)

options.text: Administer subcutaneous adrenaline 300 micrograms of 1:1000 solution into the deltoid muscle and review response after five minutes
options.rationale: Subcutaneous adrenaline absorption is unreliable in anaphylaxis with peripheral shutdown; intramuscular into the anterolateral thigh is the recommended route. (Source: ASCIA Acute Anaphylaxis Clinical Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intramuscular adrenaline 150 micrograms of 1:1000 solution into the anterolateral thigh and repeat after five minutes if needed
options.rationale: The ASCIA banded paediatric dose for 10 to 20 kg is 150 micrograms (0.15 mL of 1:1000) intramuscular into the anterolateral thigh, repeatable every five minutes for ongoing reaction. (Source: ASCIA Acute Anaphylaxis Clinical Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian paediatric anaphylaxis adrenaline dosing follows the ASCIA banded table by weight rather than per-kilogram arithmetic, which reduces calculation errors during resuscitation. The 10 to 20 kg band receives 150 micrograms of 1:1000 solution intramuscular into the anterolateral thigh, repeatable every five minutes. EpiPen Junior delivers this dose; EpiPen delivers 300 micrograms for 20 kg and above.
key_points: Use ASCIA banded adrenaline table, not mg/kg arithmetic
10-20 kg: 150 micrograms (EpiPen Jr); 20+ kg: 300 micrograms (EpiPen)
Adrenaline 1:1000, intramuscular, anterolateral thigh
Repeat every five minutes for ongoing reaction
Intravenous adrenaline reserved for arrest or refractory cases
explanation.pearls: For a 16 kg child in anaphylaxis the ASCIA banded dose is 150 micrograms of 1:1000 intramuscular, equivalent to an EpiPen Junior, not 0.16 mL of 1:1000 calculated by 10 micrograms per kg.

stem:
A 9-month-old boy is referred from a regional emergency department on day 7 of fever for second opinion. The fever has stayed between 38.6 and 39.4 degrees despite a five day course of oral cefalexin started in primary care. The parents report he is miserable, off feeds, and has a rash on his trunk and limbs that comes and goes.

On examination he is irritable but consolable. There is patchy non-blanching erythema on the trunk, mildly red cracked lips, and bilateral conjunctival injection sparing the limbus. Hands and feet are not swollen. There is a 1.2 cm right cervical lymph node. Throat is clean. There is no joint swelling, no organomegaly, and no peripheral peeling. He has no overseas travel and no known sick contacts.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 162, blood pressure 88/52, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 39.1 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 96 g/L (105-135), platelets 642 x10^9/L (150-450), white cells 21.8 x10^9/L (5-15), CRP 168 mg/L (<5), ESR 84 mm/hr, albumin 26 g/L (35-50), ALT 102 U/L (<40), sodium 131 mmol/L (135-145), urinalysis pyuria with sterile culture, blood culture sterile at 48 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg every six hours pending repeat blood cultures and review at 48 hours
options.rationale: Sterile blood cultures at 48 hours plus the constellation of fever, conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash, and supportive laboratory findings argue against occult bacterial sepsis. Flucloxacillin would delay definitive treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over ten hours with oral aspirin 30 mg/kg per day in four divided doses
options.rationale: Two or three classical features (here three: conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash) plus supportive laboratory findings (CRP greater than 30, platelets greater than 450, anaemia, albumin less than 30, transaminitis, sterile pyuria) meets the American Heart Association incomplete Kawasaki criteria, particularly important under one year where coronary risk is highest. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Arrange same day outpatient echocardiography to look for coronary artery dilatation before deciding on intravenous immunoglobulin
options.rationale: Treatment for incomplete Kawasaki should not be delayed pending an echo result. Baseline echo is part of workup but treatment proceeds immediately when criteria are met. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for three days as primary monotherapy ahead of immunoglobulin
options.rationale: Pulse methylprednisolone alone is not standard primary therapy for Kawasaki in Australia. Steroids are adjunctive in high risk cases or used for immunoglobulin resistance. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Continue supportive care with regular paracetamol and discharge home with paediatric clinic review in one week
options.rationale: Discharging without immunoglobulin in an infant under one year with incomplete Kawasaki criteria allows coronary artery inflammation to evolve unchecked; risk of aneurysm is highest in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is fever for five or more days with two or three classical features plus supportive laboratory findings. The diagnosis is particularly important under one year where coronary aneurysm risk is highest and classical features are most often incomplete. Australian practice mirrors the American Heart Association criteria with intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg plus high dose aspirin within ten days of fever onset.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: fever 5 or more days plus 2-3 features plus supportive labs
Supportive labs: CRP > 30, platelets > 450, anaemia, albumin < 30, ALT raised, sterile pyuria
Highest aneurysm risk: infants under 1 year and over 8 years
Treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin 30-50 mg/kg per day during acute phase
Do not delay IVIG pending echocardiogram
explanation.pearls: A febrile infant under one year with at least two classical features and CRP above 30 plus albumin below 30 meets American Heart Association incomplete Kawasaki criteria and receives intravenous immunoglobulin immediately.

sources.label: American Heart Association Kawasaki Disease Scientific Statement 2017

stem:
A 21-day-old term boy is brought to a metropolitan emergency department after his mother noticed he felt warm and was harder to wake for feeds during the night. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with maternal group B streptococcal swab negative at 36 weeks and no rupture of membranes risk factors.

On examination he is mottled and sleepy but rouseable with vigorous handling. He is poorly perfused with capillary return of four seconds. Fontanelle is soft. There is no rash, no respiratory distress, and no focal source of infection. His mother has no history of genital herpes and no febrile illness in the third trimester. The mother is not on any antibiotics and breastfeeds exclusively.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 184, blood pressure 64/38, respiratory rate 56, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: venous gas pH 7.28 base excess negative 6, lactate 3.8 mmol/L, capillary glucose 3.2 mmol/L, urinalysis pending, point of care viral swab pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Take blood cultures, urine sample, and cerebrospinal fluid, then start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin with a 20 mL/kg saline bolus
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin is the antimicrobial pair used during the first week of life. Beyond 7 to 28 days the empirical Australian regimen typically substitutes a third generation cephalosporin to cover community pathogens. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take urine and blood cultures only, defer lumbar puncture, and start oral amoxicillin pending culture results in twenty four hours
options.rationale: Any unwell infant under 28 days requires full septic workup including lumbar puncture and parenteral empirical therapy. Oral amoxicillin is inadequate cover and deferring lumbar puncture is not appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Observe in the short stay unit with regular paracetamol and four hourly reviews to assess whether the temperature settles
options.rationale: Watchful waiting in a febrile, poorly perfused 21-day-old with elevated lactate is unsafe. Bacterial sepsis and herpes simplex virus encephalitis can both progress rapidly without antimicrobials. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Take blood culture, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid then start intravenous cefotaxime, benzylpenicillin, and aciclovir with a 20 mL/kg saline bolus
options.rationale: An unwell febrile infant aged 7 to 28 days needs a full septic workup including lumbar puncture and immediate empirical cover for late onset group B streptococcal disease (benzylpenicillin), gram negative organisms and Listeria (cefotaxime), and herpes simplex encephalitis (aciclovir). Fluid resuscitation precedes inotropes. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Take blood cultures and urine then start intravenous ceftriaxone as monotherapy with a 10 mL/kg dextrose bolus to correct hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is avoided in the first month because it displaces bilirubin and can precipitate kernicterus. Cefotaxime is preferred. Monotherapy misses Listeria and herpes simplex virus, and dextrose alone does not address shock. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Any unwell febrile infant under 28 days receives a full septic workup (blood culture, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid for bacterial and herpes simplex virus studies) and immediate empirical broad spectrum antimicrobials. From 7 to 28 days the Australian regimen is intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin to cover gram negatives, Listeria, and late onset group B streptococcus, plus aciclovir if there is any suggestion of meningitis or encephalitis.
key_points: Full septic workup including lumbar puncture in any unwell infant under 28 days
First week of life: benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin empirically
7 to 28 days: cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin empirically
Add aciclovir if seizures, encephalopathy, or HSV exposure risk
Ceftriaxone avoided in the first month (bilirubin displacement risk)
explanation.pearls: Substitute cefotaxime for ceftriaxone in the first month of life because ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin and precipitates kernicterus in the neonate.

stem:
A 5-week-old first-born boy is brought to a regional paediatric outpatient clinic with a four day history of forceful vomiting after every feed. The mother says the milk comes out in an arch and he is hungry again straight afterwards. His weight today is 4.0 kg compared with 4.3 kg at his two week check.

On examination he is alert but mildly dehydrated with sunken fontanelle and dry lips. Abdomen is soft with no palpable mass after careful palpation post-feed. Bowel sounds are present. There is no jaundice and no abdominal distension. There has been no bile-stained vomit, no haematemesis, and no diarrhoea. The mother is not on any medications and there is no family history of pyloric stenosis. He passes pale yellow urine in front of you.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 152, blood pressure 84/50, respiratory rate 38, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: venous gas pH 7.50 bicarbonate 32 mmol/L (22-28), sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), chloride 94 mmol/L (95-110), capillary glucose 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent abdominal ultrasound to measure pylorus dimensions and admit for intravenous rehydration with correction of electrolytes
options.rationale: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis in a first-born male with projectile non-bilious vomiting at the typical age is classical for pyloric stenosis. Ultrasound is the diagnostic test (pyloric muscle thickness 3 mm or more, channel length 15 mm or more). The mass is often not palpable. Surgery only follows full correction of electrolytes. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Trial of thickened oral feeds for 48 hours and review in clinic if vomiting persists or weight gain remains poor
options.rationale: Hypochloraemic alkalosis with weight loss is not consistent with simple gastro-oesophageal reflux. Delay risks worsening dehydration and electrolyte derangement before urgent surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Send urgent upper gastrointestinal contrast study to look for malrotation with volvulus and book the operating theatre
options.rationale: Malrotation with volvulus typically presents with bilious vomiting and is a surgical emergency with an upper gastrointestinal contrast study. This infant has non-bilious projectile vomiting and a metabolic picture pointing to pyloric stenosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting)

options.text: Commence oral omeprazole 1 mg/kg daily for suspected reflux oesophagitis and provide reassurance to the mother
options.rationale: Proton pump inhibitor treatment does not address mechanical gastric outlet obstruction and would delay diagnosis. Acid suppression is not the answer to projectile vomiting with weight loss. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Refer for surgical pyloromyotomy directly without imaging and start a slow intravenous infusion of 0.9 percent saline overnight
options.rationale: Ultrasound confirmation of pyloric stenosis is required before surgery, and pyloromyotomy is contraindicated until the metabolic alkalosis and hypokalaemia are corrected to avoid post-operative apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

explanation.summary: Pyloric stenosis is the most common surgical cause of vomiting in the first two months of life and classically presents in a first-born male with non-bilious projectile vomiting, weight loss, and hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Diagnosis is confirmed on ultrasound (pyloric muscle thickness 3 mm or more, channel length 15 mm or more). Pyloromyotomy is delayed until biochemistry is corrected to avoid post-operative apnoea from a respiratory compensation for ongoing alkalosis.
key_points: Classical presentation: first-born male, 3-8 weeks, non-bilious projectile vomiting
Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
Ultrasound: pyloric muscle thickness 3 mm or more, channel length 15 mm or more
Correct electrolytes BEFORE pyloromyotomy
Bilious vomiting at any age is malrotation until proven otherwise
explanation.pearls: Pyloromyotomy is deferred until bicarbonate is below 30 mmol/L and chloride is above 100 mmol/L because residual alkalosis drives post-operative apnoea through compensatory hypoventilation.

subtopic_detail: Severe DKA initial fluid and insulin timing
stem:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to a regional emergency department by his mother after three days of polydipsia, polyuria, and weight loss followed by twelve hours of vomiting and progressive lethargy. He has no prior diagnosis of diabetes. He has no headache and no focal neurology.

On examination he is mildly drowsy but rouseable with eyes-open-to-voice and engages in short sentences. Mucous membranes are dry, capillary return is three seconds, and respirations are deep and slow. Pulse rate 144, blood pressure 98/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees, weight 22 kg. Capillary glucose is 28 mmol/L. The retrieval team will arrive in 60 minutes for transfer to the tertiary paediatric centre.

data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.06, bicarbonate 7 mmol/L (22-28), base excess negative 22, sodium 134 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 9.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.8), creatinine 88 micromol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.2 mmol/L, GCS 14 (E3 V5 M6)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate fluid and insulin plan over the first hour?

options.text: Administer 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline as a rapid bolus over fifteen minutes and start intravenous insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately after the bolus
options.rationale: Rapid 20 mL/kg bolus plus immediate insulin in severe paediatric DKA increases cerebral oedema risk through abrupt osmotic shift; the Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group and ISPAD recommend slower initial fluid replacement and delayed insulin in severe DKA. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Administer 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline over thirty minutes, defer insulin until one hour after fluids commence, and arrange immediate paediatric retrieval
options.rationale: Severe DKA (pH less than 7.1, GCS depressed) in a child carries the highest cerebral oedema risk. APEG and ISPAD recommend cautious 10 mL/kg bolus over 30 to 60 minutes plus delayed insulin (start at 1 to 2 hours after fluids) at 0.05 units/kg/hour to reduce osmotic shift, and urgent paediatric retrieval. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Administer maintenance 0.9 percent saline at 0.5 mL/kg/hour and commence intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg to correct severe acidosis
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate in paediatric DKA is associated with worse outcomes including a higher rate of cerebral oedema and is not recommended outside refractory acidosis with cardiovascular compromise unresponsive to fluids. Maintenance-only fluids are inadequate. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Administer 20 mL/kg Hartmann's solution as a rapid bolus and commence intravenous insulin 0.05 units/kg/hour with added potassium 40 mmol/L
options.rationale: Hartmann's and rapid 20 mL/kg are not the recommended initial replacement in severe paediatric DKA; 0.9 percent saline at a slower rate is standard. Insulin commenced concurrently with bolus carries cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Administer subcutaneous insulin 0.3 units/kg as a stat dose and offer oral rehydration with 10 mL/kg over the next sixty minutes
options.rationale: Subcutaneous insulin is unreliable in shock states and oral rehydration is inappropriate in a vomiting child with reduced GCS at risk of aspiration. Intravenous insulin is mandatory once fluids are running. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe paediatric DKA (pH < 7.1, depressed conscious state) carries the highest cerebral oedema risk. APEG and ISPAD recommend a cautious initial 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus over 30 to 60 minutes and deliberate insulin delay (start at 1 to 2 hours after fluids commence) at 0.05 units/kg/hour, with paediatric retrieval and tertiary transfer. Faster fluid resuscitation and earlier insulin are associated with worse neurological outcomes.
key_points: Severe DKA in children: cautious 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline over 30-60 min
Delay insulin start by 1-2 hours after fluid commences
Insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour, not 0.1 units/kg/hour
Avoid sodium bicarbonate (worsens cerebral oedema outcomes)
Cerebral oedema warning signs: headache, bradycardia with hypertension, falling GCS
explanation.pearls: In a child with DKA and pH below 7.1 the insulin infusion runs at 0.05 units/kg/hour and only starts 1 to 2 hours after the cautious 10 mL/kg fluid bolus has commenced to minimise osmotic shifts that precede cerebral oedema.

stem:
A 9-year-old girl (28 kg) presents to a regional ED with a severe asthma exacerbation that has not responded to back-to-back salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers over the past 30 minutes, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg 25 minutes ago, and a stat dose of intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg given 10 minutes ago. The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG suggests proceeding to IV salbutamol or aminophylline next; the Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory algorithm lists IV salbutamol as preferred. Both guidelines explicitly note that aminophylline retains an indication when IV salbutamol is unavailable or not tolerated.

She has known atopic asthma on inhaled budesonide 200 mcg BD with a salbutamol reliever, last admitted 8 months ago for an exacerbation without ICU. She has had no recent steroid course. She does not have congenital long QT syndrome and her ECG today shows sinus tachycardia at 158 bpm with normal QTc (392 ms).

The regional hospital does not stock IV salbutamol; the pharmacy can have it from a tertiary centre in 90 minutes. IV aminophylline is stocked. The retrieval service has been activated and the transfer team will arrive in approximately 75 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158 bpm, BP 105/68 mmHg, RR 42 with marked accessory muscle use, SpO2 88% on 8 L/min via Hudson mask, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Silent chest in upper zones bilaterally; able to speak in single words; alert; no cyanosis
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.27, pCO2 52 mmHg, lactate 4.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.0); ECG sinus tachycardia, QTc 392 ms; electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management while awaiting the retrieval team?

options.text: Commence intravenous aminophylline loading dose 10 mg/kg over 60 minutes (capped at 500 mg) followed by maintenance infusion 1 mg/kg/hour, with continuous cardiac monitoring and serum theophylline level at 2 hours
options.rationale: This child meets imminent respiratory failure criteria (silent chest, rising pCO2, lactic acidosis, exhaustion). IV salbutamol is the preferred AU second-line intravenous agent per the Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG and Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory, but the regional pharmacy does not stock it and the retrieval window is 75 minutes. Aminophylline is a valid AU-listed alternative when IV salbutamol is unavailable; both guidelines retain it for this scenario. Loading at 10 mg/kg (280 mg here) over 60 minutes, capped at 500 mg, with continuous cardiac monitoring is the AMH dose and route. Serum theophylline at 2 hours guides the maintenance infusion. (Sources: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Asthma acute; Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory; Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence intravenous salbutamol loading dose 15 mcg/kg over 10 minutes followed by infusion 1 to 5 mcg/kg/min, with continuous cardiac monitoring and electrolytes every 2 hours
options.rationale: Intravenous salbutamol is the AU preferred second-line agent when stocked and is generally first-line over aminophylline. However the regional pharmacy does not stock IV salbutamol and the retrieval window is 75 minutes; aminophylline is the appropriate available alternative. Would be the correct first choice in a tertiary centre with IV salbutamol immediately available. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Repeat the intravenous magnesium sulfate bolus at 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes with continuous BP monitoring and a held dose if systolic falls below 90 mmHg
options.rationale: A single 50 mg/kg dose of intravenous magnesium sulfate is given and not routinely repeated; further magnesium does not address the persisting bronchospasm and risks hypotension. The next step is a second-line bronchodilator (IV salbutamol or aminophylline). Would be correct only if the patient improved on the first dose and the team wished to bridge a short delay; the AU guidelines do not endorse a routine repeat. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Proceed to rapid sequence induction and intubation with ketamine 1 to 2 mg/kg and rocuronium 1 mg/kg, planning low tidal volume mandatory ventilation pending retrieval team arrival
options.rationale: Intubation in paediatric severe asthma is high-risk (worsened air-trapping, peri-intubation arrest) and is reserved for true respiratory or cardiorespiratory failure after exhausting non-invasive escalations. The child is still alert and is a candidate for further pharmacological escalation; aminophylline before intubation is the AU pathway. Would be correct only with imminent or actual cardiorespiratory arrest. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Asthma acute; ANZCOR Paediatric guidelines)

options.text: Commence non-invasive bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) 12 over 5 cmH2O with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 of 94 to 98 percent, while awaiting retrieval
options.rationale: Non-invasive ventilation has a limited and contested role in paediatric acute severe asthma; it does not address the underlying bronchospasm and may delay definitive bronchodilator escalation. Pharmacological escalation (IV aminophylline here) is the AU next step. Would be considered only at a tertiary centre with respiratory team involvement after IV bronchodilator escalation has been exhausted. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Asthma acute)

explanation.summary: This is severe acute asthma with imminent respiratory failure (silent chest, hypercapnia, lactic acidosis) refractory to first-line nebulised bronchodilators plus systemic steroid plus a single dose of intravenous magnesium sulfate. The AU pathway escalates to intravenous bronchodilator therapy next: IV salbutamol is preferred where available, with aminophylline as the AU-listed alternative when salbutamol is unavailable. The discriminator is the regional context: IV salbutamol is not stocked and the retrieval window is 75 minutes, so aminophylline is the right answer despite being second-line at a tertiary centre. The candidate must hold the textbook hierarchy (IV salbutamol first) in tension with the practical AU consideration (stock + retrieval timing) and choose the available agent. In context, escalation pathways must always account for setting and stock; the AU guidelines explicitly preserve aminophylline for this reason.
key_points: AU severe asthma escalation order (RCH Melbourne CPG): nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium, systemic steroid, IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg, then IV salbutamol OR aminophylline.
IV salbutamol is the AU preferred IV second-line; aminophylline is the AU-listed alternative when IV salbutamol is unavailable.
Aminophylline loading 10 mg/kg over 60 minutes (max 500 mg), maintenance 1 mg/kg/hour, serum theophylline at 2 hours per AMH.
Intubation in paediatric severe asthma is high-risk and is reserved for true cardiorespiratory failure, not as a substitute for IV bronchodilator escalation.
explanation.pearls: Regional ED with retrieval pending often forces aminophylline over IV salbutamol despite the textbook hierarchy; cite the stock + retrieval window explicitly in the team handover.
